title: Roomwright
pitch: Moving in shouldn't take a tape measure and a weekend, nor $1000. Roomwright lets you and an AI agent design a room together in 3D, with 38 WebMCP tools that refuse bad moves and learn from each one.
about_excerpt: Moving in shouldn't take a tape measure and a weekend, nor $1000. Roomwright lets you and an AI agent design a room together in 3D, with 38 WebMCP tools that refuse bad moves and learn from each one. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Architecture Half Half Full Budget Landing Page GeneratedSchema Why WebMCP, and what's new: A room planner is a 3D canvas. There are no buttons for an agent to click, so typed tools are the only way it can act on the room at all. And because every call comes back with a real answer, the agent can fix its own mistakes instead of guessing again. That changes what collaboration looks like. You are not handing the room over and waiting for it to come back. The agent places furniture while you drag your own, both of you are refused by the same engine in the same inches, and the log says who did what. Inspiration Everyone has done this: You measure the wall, buy the dresser, carry it up the stairs, and find out the drawers hit the bed. Rules exist that decide whether a room works stay invisible until you have already spent the money. A dresser needs 30 inches of clear floor. A door sweeps a 32-inch arc. A desk needs 36 inches behind it for a chair. You have to do meticulous work to find the numbers manually and ai agents can't autonomously interact with simulation apps without prior configuration and set up. The tools meant to help do not close that gap. CAD planners enforce the geometry but have no idea what you want. AI design tools render rooms that cannot be built, because a model drawing a picture was never solving a constraint problem. One is rigorous and useless, while the other is beautiful and false. But that change with WebMCP... with Roomwright. The agent proposes. The engine disposes. What it does Roomwright is a browser-based 3D room planner. You drag furniture with a mouse. An agent places furniture by calling the page's WebMCP tools. Both go through the same geometry engine, so both get the same measured refusals and the same suggestions. Write a one-sentence brief — "nursery plus home office, I'm 6'2", under $1,200" — and OpenAI turns it into clearances and a budget the engine enforces. Real dimensions and prices from real product pages, multi-storey buildings with doors, windows, radiators, closets and staircases, saved builds, undo/redo, a PDF plan, a shopping list, live multiplayer. Sensitive agent requests, like moving a wall, wait for your approval. The moment that matters: the agent places a desk whose chair clearance runs through the radiator. The engine returns: { "ok": false, "violations": [{ "type": "clearance", "subject": "desk", "against": "radiator", "overlap_in": 11, "axis": "z", "message": "The 36 inch chair clearance behind the desk overlaps the radiator by 11 inches." }], "suggestion": { "x_in": 142, "z_in": 30, "rotation_deg": 90 } } The agent moves the desk 12 inches. Nobody re-prompted. That refusal is then written into place_item 's own description, so the next agent in the room already knows. Why this use case fits WebMCP We'd rather be precise than overclaim. Reading dimensions out of a page is solvable without WebMCP. Writing is not. move_item({id, x, z}) is one call against a stable contract, and the structured return is what makes self-correction possible — a synthesized click on a canvas gets no return value. A tool surface is also a permission surface: mutation tools don't exist until a room is loaded, so the app decides what an agent may do and when. We measured it Same agent (Claude driving Chrome), same task on the live deployment, run twice: add a crib, desk and dresser to the hard room, crib on a wall away from the window, zero conflicts. Once through the page's WebMCP tools, once through the UI alone. Method, raw logs and caveats in BENCHMARK.md . WebMCP tools UI only (screenshots, clicks, drags) Agent actions 10 tool calls 34 browser actions Wall clock 4.9 s 299 s, then stopped — task incomplete Placed with zero conflicts 3 of 3 2 of 3, one conflict left Rejections, and recovered 2, both on the next call 5, none recovered The gap isn't click speed. A rejected place_item returns the violation, the overlap in inches, and a position that would validate, so the retry is one call. A rejected drag returns a red line of prose and a new guess at a screen coordinate on a perspective floor. Four drags in the UI run were refused and the crib never moved. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Shared live state, not turn-taking. The agent works in the room while you watch. Grab a piece mid-run and move it — nothing resets, and its next placement accounts for the change. Negotiation in both directions. You state intent in English, the agent turns it into numbers, the engine says what's impossible, and the agent reports back which constraint had to give. Multiple people and agents in one room. Every change is attributed ("You moved the dresser", "Claude placed the chair"). Big changes arrive as a propose_layout ghost anyone can accept or dismiss. Never a silent overwrite. A tool surface that learns. Every refusal becomes a lesson stored with the room, returned in get_room , in later refusals, and inside the mutation tools' own re-registered descriptions. No training — memory plus feedback, shared by everyone in the room. One sentence replaces a tape measure and a weekend. The agent handles the search space, the engine guarantees the answer is physically real, and you end with a room that fits and a list you could actually buy. How we implemented WebMCP document.modelContext.registerTool is called directly in apps/web/src/tools/register.ts , behind a shim handling Chrome 150 semantics ( registerTool returns a Promise; removal via AbortSignal ): document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "search_catalog", description: "Search the furniture catalog. Returns items with real dimensions in inches, price, and required clearances. Filter by max_width_in / max_depth_in to only get items that could physically fit a given space.", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ } }); A mount-scoped React hook registers and unregisters tools as state changes: 12 tools on the landing page, 38 in a room , undo only when there's something to undo, camera tools only while the 3D view is live. The brief form uses the declarative API ( toolname , tooldescription , toolautosubmit , respondWith ), so the form is the set_brief tool. Group Tools Read get_room , get_placements , search_catalog , measure , check_clearances , get_budget , describe_view , recall_lessons , list_rooms , list_composed_tools Write place_item , place_items , move_item , rotate_item , remove_item , swap_item , undo Space create_room , extend_room , reshape_room , add_fixture , remove_fixture , add_floor , set_active_floor , connect_floors_with_stairs , open_room , delete_room Self-extension create_catalog_item , compose_tool , remove_composed_tool Collaboration propose_layout , comment , snapshot , export_plan , set_camera , record_lesson , forget_lesson Declarative set_brief compose_tool is the one to look at: an agent captures a routine as a new tool that registers with WebMCP live and persists . The engine. packages/engine is pure TypeScript — no React, no Three, no fetch. Geometry, walls, floors, validation, ops, and a command pattern with inverses for undo. It's the only place rules live; pointer handlers and tool handlers are both thin callers. State is integer inches; meters exist only at the render boundary. pointer drag ─┐ ├─→ packages/engine (ops.ts) ─→ Result{ok | rejected} WebMCP tool ─┘ │ ├─ ok → Zustand → R3F re-render → WebSocket fan-out → persist └─ rejected → structured violations back to the caller; state unchanged Stack. Next.js 15, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind on Vercel. FastAPI + Motor + MongoDB Atlas on Render, with Atlas Vector Search over catalog and lesson embeddings and a WebSocket per room. OpenAI Responses API with a strict JSON schema for brief-to-constraints, the Agents SDK for an in-app copilot running the same tools (so the app works in browsers without WebMCP), text-embedding-3-small for search and lesson recall. Key stays server-side. Challenges we ran into The namespace moved mid-trial. The rules show document.modelContext ; some docs show navigator.modelContext . We verified against Chrome 150: registerTool returns a Promise, there's no unregisterTool , removal is via AbortSignal . Everything goes through one shim. Chrome aborts an in-flight executeTool when its tool is unregistered. Re-registering a tool to add a new lesson had to be deferred until nothing is executing — getting the menu to learn without killing the call that taught it took a few tries. Physics wanted to be the truth. Rapier makes drops settle and drags push against walls, but a simulation that varies run to run would eventually differ during judging from rehearsal. Physics is presentation only; snapped integer inches are the truth. Agents invent things. The copilot m
video_transcript_excerpt: When you move into a new place and design is on you, what fits the home, what clears the door, where are the desks goes, usually finding a proper online model that is free is hard to find. An interior designer is more expensive. So, we built Room Right, where you and an AI agent in a fully provisioned platform can build a home together in parallel in one live 3D scene. There's no dumb guessing. Instead, the AI agent gets 38 dynamic Web 3D tools that receive bad moves in metric inches and learn from every single call and error that it goes. In this floor one of mouths building, I can clearly add and modify the furnishings that exist here. Like I can add a wardrobe and a blue bookcase and do whatever I want to. But now, I'll set up my external agent to furnish my room with a single prompt and a single enter. There. Now the agent is starting. While the agent is running, let's talk about what actually happens in the back end. Room Right utilizes dynamic Web 3D tools that mount and unmount based on the app state, ensuring agents can never perform actions that the room doesn't allow. Because both the user and the agent share the same geometry engine, they receive identical metric-based feedback on every placement. And since all changes operate over a shared Web Socket, the system stays perfectly synchronized allowing humans and users and external agents to work together in parallel in the same 3D. There you go. The floor of our office building was fully built and furnished by the external Cloud and Chrome agent by utilizing our customized Web 3D that stays on this website. And the best part is that all of this happened just under a minute, where an agent without the Web 3D's tools would take more than 3 minutes. On top of that, there were zero conflicts, we were under the budget, and looking at this activity, you can see all the uh the tools attached to Web 3D that our external agent utilized. For example, get room to create this new floor, it used a get budget to make sure we're on track and verify that. It used place items to place all these desks, chairs, and more furnishings. And on top of that, it used all other tools available to it to effectively do what we what what was asked of the agent itself. Now, there's so much more that we can do with this platform itself. We can export PDFs of the schema of the building that we built. We can actually talk with the co-pilot to get our layout done, but there's no point cuz it's repetitive. We can look at previous builds and utilize them. Let's go back to the nurse plus office for example. Just like this. Again, we can add things, we can modify things, we can move them around places. And finally, the beauty of our application is that everything is logged in our activity log. And this is done within the Web MCP tooling where everything all the actions taken by the human and the agent are logged in the activities and conflicts are recorded, everything's recorded, everything is transparent, and everything is really really fast. And that's it for Room Right. Thanks for listening.

title: AgentCart: WebMCP E-Commerce
pitch: An agent-native e-commerce app where AI acts as a personal shopper, using WebMCP to dynamically filter the UI and update your shopping cart in real-time.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native e-commerce app where AI acts as a personal shopper, using WebMCP to dynamically filter the UI and update your shopping cart in real-time.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Traditional e-commerce filtering is rigid, relying on endless checkboxes, sliders, and dropdown menus. We wanted to build an experience where you can just tell the store what you want, and the store adapts to you. 

 Why our use case is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 AgentCart is a perfect fit for WebMCP because it replaces complex UI navigation with natural language. By exposing search_products and add_to_cart as client-side tools, the AI agent acts as an integrated personal shopper. It instantly manipulates the live DOM based on complex user requests (e.g., "Find me a gift for a coffee lover under $50 and add it to my cart") instead of just printing out a text response. 

 How it creates a better user experience 

 Instead of an agent generating a static text list of products, the agent actively collaborates on the page. As the user chats with the AI, the actual product grid visually filters in real-time, and the cart badge updates instantly. It bridges the gap between conversational AI and traditional visual browsing, keeping the user grounded in a familiar visual UI. 

 What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before 

 Previously, integrating AI deeply into a custom frontend required complex server-side APIs, database syncs, and dedicated browser extensions to manipulate the DOM. Now, humans and agents can collaborate entirely locally in the browser. The user drives the high-level intent ("I need an ergonomic setup"), and the agent executes the precise client-side JavaScript required to build that cart, side-by-side with the human. 

 How we implemented WebMCP 

 We implemented WebMCP using a purely client-side approach in a lightweight, zero-dependency environment. Inside our index.html , we check for document.modelContext and use registerTool to expose two functions: 

 
 search_products : Accepts a schema for keywords and max price, filters the local JavaScript catalog, and immediately triggers a DOM re-render of the product grid. 
 add_to_cart : Accepts a product_id , pushes it to a local state array, and updates the cart UI badge dynamically.

title: IdentityMap Witness
pitch: Catch identity-mapping mistakes before they go live. A WebMCP agent proves every broken rule with the fewest test users, then rechecks every edit while a human keeps control.
about_excerpt: Catch identity-mapping mistakes before they go live. A WebMCP agent proves every broken rule with the fewest test users, then rechecks every edit while a human keeps control. Like Comment Story Updates A human reviews three pending safety rules before confirming them. The minimal witness: three synthetic users, four violation rows, every broken rule exposed. A relevant page edit immediately marks the previous evidence STALE. Fresh checks produce a revision-bound GREEN review packet. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Identity-mapping rules often exist only as an unsaved draft in an administrator's browser. The failures that matter tend to appear at the edges: a case-sensitive check puts a contractor in the employees group, a missing manager becomes an empty string, or stale directory data overrides HR. At that point, the page is the only place that knows the current draft, its revision, its fields, and its rules. WebMCP lets the page expose that information through five structured, least-privilege tools. The agent can work with the page's actual semantics instead of guessing from labels or DOM layout, even though the draft has not reached a server. How it creates a better user experience The administrator continues editing the draft in the normal page. The agent reads that exact draft and its revision, then stages three safety rules. Those rules stay pending until the administrator reviews their cards and clicks Confirm all . Once confirmed, the agent finds the smallest set of synthetic users that exposes every violation. For each result, the page shows which source value won, which value lost, and why. The agent can preview a redacted fix, but the administrator makes the edit. An edit immediately marks any dependent evidence STALE . The agent must test the new revision before it can prepare a GREEN review packet. There is no Save or Apply tool; applying the mapping remains a normal page control outside WebMCP. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before The administrator and agent can reason about a draft that exists only in the browser, using evidence that expires when its basis changes. Expressions, source priority, and confirmed rules can each invalidate an earlier result. Every evidence record therefore carries its revision and dependencies. When it becomes stale, the page strikes through the old rows and blocks the old packet. The agent handles the exhaustive search for edge cases across the synthetic population. The administrator confirms the rules and makes the actual edit. That division prevents proof from an older draft from being presented as proof of the current one. How we implemented WebMCP The top-level document registers five tools with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) in app.js . They read the session and draft, stage rules, find a minimal counterexample set, preview a patch, and prepare the review packet. Strict schemas reject malformed input and extra fields. Failed calls leave the committed draft unchanged. Responses have size limits and redact CANARY_ fixture strings. We initially tried to wait for human approval inside one long-running tool call. In our ChatGPT in-app-browser testing, pending calls ended after roughly 22 seconds. The implemented flow therefore stages the rule cards and returns. After the administrator responds, the agent reads the new state on its next turn. The suite has 310 passing tests. On Chrome 152, we also run fresh-session registration checks and a 12-round trace that combines real DOM edits with WebMCP calls. Inspiration Identity teams merge records from Active Directory, an HR system, and an identity provider such as Okta before the resulting profiles determine access. The merge rules may still be an unsaved browser draft while the administrator works on them. Small mistakes can have large effects. A case-sensitive condition may classify a contractor as an employee. A missing manager may turn into an empty string instead of null . Stale directory data may take precedence over HR. These problems are easy to overlook without the right edge cases. An AI agent can help search for those cases, but unrestricted UI control introduces a different set of risks. The agent may guess what a field means, use evidence from an older draft, or act before a person has reviewed the result. What it does Two boundaries are important up front. Unsaved-draft preview already exists as a first-party product pattern. A different page-local agent with access to the same state and rules could also run this engine. IdentityMap Witness contributes a page-authored safety contract and an evidence lifecycle that causes old proof to expire. IdentityMap Witness reviews an identity-mapping draft before it is saved. A witness is the smallest set of synthetic users required to expose every safety rule that the current draft violates. The workflow is: The agent reads the exact unsaved draft and its revision. It stages three safety rules. They remain pending until a person reviews the cards and clicks Confirm all . The agent finds the fewest synthetic users that demonstrate every violation. The result explains which source value won, which lost, and why. The agent previews a redacted fix, and the person performs the actual edit in the page. The edit marks dependent evidence STALE . The new revision must be tested before the agent can prepare a GREEN review packet. The agent never receives a Save or Apply tool. Apply mapping (manual page control) remains outside the WebMCP surface and is not used in the demo. Why WebMCP The page is the source of truth for the live draft. It owns the fields and rules, tracks the revision, and decides which operations are allowed. WebMCP exposes that knowledge through five structured, least-privilege tools instead of making the agent infer it from labels or DOM structure. The tools return redacted evidence tied to a particular revision and reject calls made against old state. This allows the administrator and agent to work with data that has not reached a server while confirmation and editing remain visibly under human control. A general browser agent could inspect the interface. The difference here is that the page itself defines the contract, which makes the workflow reviewable and prevents stale conclusions from being silently reused. How we built it The application uses vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, and Node 21+. Five document.modelContext tools read the session, stage rules, find a minimal counterexample set, preview a patch, and prepare the review packet. The browser, test suite, and evaluation all use the same deterministic engine. Tool inputs use strict schemas, so extra or malformed fields are rejected. A failed call does not change the committed draft. Responses are size-limited and redact CANARY_ fixture strings. Before-and-after diffs are minimized for firstName , lastName , email , displayName , and managerId . This is a synthetic tripwire, not a general-purpose PII detector. Evidence records include the revision and dependencies used to determine whether they remain valid. There are 310 passing tests. Chrome 152 runs three fresh-session registration checks and a 12-round trace with real DOM edits and WebMCP calls. A hand-audited oracle verifies that the first search returns {P2, P3, P4} . This is one of two audited minimal sets of size three, and its four violation rows cover all four seeded defect classes. Challenges we ran into The central problem was that a correct result could become unsafe after the draft changed. An edit to an expression, source priority, or confirmed rule may invalidate earlier reasoning. Evidence is therefore tied to those exact dependencies; relevant edits strike through the old rows and prevent the old packet from being used. Human approval could not remain pending inside one tool call. In our own ChatGPT in-app-browser test on 2026-08-29, pending calls ended after roughly 22 seconds. That observation is not part of the repository's automated evidence. The current tool stages the cards and returns, the administrator confirms them, and the agent reads the updated state on its next turn. We also turned stale buttons, malformed inputs, hostile text, and empty source values into executable failure cases. What's next The demo currently uses eight synthetic personas, tab-local state, and an exhaustive search sized for this fixture. It is not connected to a real identity provider or a save operation. Unsaved-draft preview is not new on its own, and another page-local agent could run the same engine. The contribution here is the page-authored safety contract and the lifecycle that expires old proof. The Browser-Use and Full-CDP comparison arms have been designed but not run, so we make no comparative claim. Next, we would connect a real provider behind the same redaction boundary, test larger datasets with consent, persist review history, and add signed audit rece

This page merges them into one profile, and this draft is broken. Broken quietly, a contractor is about to land in the employees group because of a capital letter. Someone with no manager got an empty string instead of null. I want an AI agent to catch that before I save without handing it the keys. So, the page doesn't let it guess at the DOM. It registers five Web MCP tools on document.modelcontext. Read, stage, find, preview, prepare. With strict schemas and descriptions, the agent reads. No save tool, no apply tool, they don't exist. In ChatGPT's browser, prompt one asks the agent to stage three rules in plain English. Contractors never in the employees group, no manager means null, HR owns department, then stop. Side panel, two tool calls, read then stage. The rules come back as pending cards: text, version, fingerprint. But the revision badge didn't move. Staging is a tool, confirming isn't. No tool can turn these on. A click on the page does. Mine. We learned why the hard way. In our testing, a Web MCP call that waits for a person dies in about 22 seconds. So, approval lives in page state. Prompt two, the agent rereads then calls find. Each call carries the revision it expects. A stale one is refused. Three test people: P2, P3, P4. The smallest set that trips every rule. Click a row for receipts. Which value won and why? It names the exact fix. I type it, the manager field. Version 19. Every proof that touched that field just died on screen. Dead evidence can't build a packet. The agent refines at the new revision. Two people now. Same rhythm twice more. Fix the contractor check. One, Flip the order so HR beats the directory. Zero. Green lights only on fresh evidence for every rule. And apply a plain page button not in the tool list. Under the hood, the tools keep WebMCP's budgets. Descriptions under 500 characters. Outputs under 1500. Read only hint only on red. Untrusted content hint on all five. Registration on an abort signal. 292 tests. A 12-round trace. A right oracle on every call. Two honest notes. Draft preview isn't a new idea and another agent living in this page could run the same engine. What we add is the contract. That's what WebMCP is for. The page knows the stakes, so the page authors the tools. Any site with an unsaved draft can do this. Identity map witness. The fewest synthetic people proving every broken rule. And proof that dies when you edit what it depended on.

title: Understudy
pitch: Demonstrate a routine once. The agent turns your demonstration into a named, parameterised WebMCP tool and registers it into the live page. The user grows the tool surface, not the developer.
about_excerpt: Demonstrate a routine once. The agent turns your demonstration into a named, parameterised WebMCP tool and registers it into the live page. The user grows the tool surface, not the developer. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration My wife is a dentist. A part of her week has nothing to do with teeth. She works with the SEO people on the clinic's articles, going down a long list and tagging each one by what is trending, or sorting them into the right category. The tagging is easy. Knowing which topics are trending this month is not, and that knowledge is not in the tool she is clicking in. It is in a browser tab next to it. So she works in two windows. Search in one, tag in the other, back and forth, one row at a time. The switching costs more than the actual work does. Next month there is a new list and she does it all again. She cannot automate it. Not because the routine is complicated, she knows it better than anyone, but because automating anything means writing code, and that is not her job. So it stays manual forever. She asked me once why the computer could not just do it. I did not have a good answer. So there are three things here and none of them sit in the same place. A model already knows what is trending. The page already knows how to tag. And the routine itself is not written down anywhere, it is just in her head. I wanted to find out if the page could pick it up by watching her do it one time. What it does Understudy is a triage workspace for 1000 Hacker News stories. It has six WebMCP tools when it loads. It can have more by the time you are done with it, because you make them. You press Teach and do a routine by hand. Filter for "amazon", 14 items match, tag them "big-tech", set them to high priority, done. The page records that as four commands in its own vocabulary, not as clicks or screen positions. Then you tell the agent to turn it into a skill. It reads the recording and proposes a tool called triage_title_matches with three parameters: title_phrase, tag, and priority. You look at the schema and correct it. I wanted only the phrase to change between runs, so I unbound tag and priority with two clicks and approved it. Now the page calls registerTool and that tool exists, in a live session, about ninety seconds after it did not. The last step is the one worth watching. I asked for "every other big tech company". I never said which ones. The agent named Google, Apple, Meta and Microsoft on its own and ran my tool once per company. I taught it on 14 items. It handled 115 more, using knowledge the page has no way to hold. How I built it Plain ES modules. No build step, no framework, no dependencies. You can serve it with python3 -m http.server. Everything in the interface goes through one command bus. A click and an agent call both end up dispatching the same command, so there is exactly one code path to record and one to replay. There are two layers of WebMCP: A fixed set of six tools registered when the page loads: start_recording, stop_recording, get_recording, save_skill, list_skills, run_skill. Read only ones are marked with annotations.readOnlyHint. One real tool per approved skill, registered at runtime with document.modelContext.registerTool. Each one is held by an AbortController, so revoking a skill actually unregisters its tool rather than leaving a dead entry behind. The most important rule in the whole project is that the agent never writes the steps. save_skill takes a recording id and a list of bindings, saying which field of which step becomes which parameter. The page builds the JSON Schema from that. The steps are what I did, unchanged. A learned skill therefore cannot do anything I did not demonstrate. That is the safety story and the reliability story at the same time, and it comes from the structure rather than from a check. Challenges I ran into The biggest one took a day to understand. A tool registered in the middle of a turn is callable, but the first call fails. ChatGPT's browser works from a list of tools it captured when the turn started, and the new tool is not in it. The agent explained it better than I could: "The first immediate call failed because the existing tool snapshot was stale; after refreshing the registry within the same turn, the call succeeded." That recovery cost about fourteen seconds. I lost most of a day to it because I was certain the bug was mine. I rewrote the schema. Then the tool name. Then I added waits after registerTool, which did nothing, because waiting was never the problem. The tool was registered fine. The agent was just holding an older list. So learned skills go through run_skill, which is registered at page load and is always in the snapshot. A skill you just taught is callable right away. Two smaller ones. The toolchange event fires in Chrome 149 and later but does not exist in ChatGPT's browser, where modelContext is not an EventTarget, so nothing that depends on it can be relied on. And prompt, confirm and alert do nothing at all in the in-app browser. They fail silently, with no error, which is a miserable thing to debug. Every question the app needs to ask is asked inline in the page instead. I wrote a small probe page, spike.html, to answer these properly instead of guessing. It is in the repo. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The moment where the agent names four companies I never mentioned and runs a tool I taught it two minutes earlier. Neither side could do that alone. The page knows how to filter and tag but has no idea what a big tech company is. The agent knows the category but has no reliable way to drive an interface. I am also glad the human stays in charge of the schema. The agent proposes parameters, and you change them before the tool exists. It suggested three. I wanted one. What I learned Recording clicks does not work. Recording intent does. Because every command in the app acts on the current matching set rather than on specific item ids, a recording generalises for free. SET_FILTER {contains:"amazon"} has an obvious parameter in it. SELECT_ITEMS {ids:[3,7,12]} never will. That one decision is what makes learning from a single demonstration possible at all, and it also happens to be a better way to build bulk triage. I also learned to test against both clients early. Two of the three problems above would have been invisible in Chrome alone. What's next for Understudy Skills are stored per browser today. Being able to share one, or bring your own set to a page, is the obvious next thing. Recordings only capture set based commands, which is deliberate, but nested parameters and a way to chain one skill into another would cover more real routines. And there are three things I marked as open rather than claimed: whether AbortController revocation reaches the agent, whether readOnlyHint changes anything observable, and where the tool count ceiling is. Those need a longer test than a hackathon week allows. title: Sushi Daw
pitch: A code-native browser DAW where producers, live coders, and AI agents compose together through one synchronized Strudel workspace.
about_excerpt: A code-native browser DAW where producers, live coders, and AI agents compose together through one synchronized Strudel workspace. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Sushi: A DAW Built in Code, Controlled Through WebMCP Inspiration Sushi began with a compatibility problem disguised as a music problem. My collaborator Avery and I both love making music, and we share a lot of the same taste, but we approach the process from almost opposite directions. Avery is comfortable in traditional DAWs. He uses Logic Pro, has experience with FL Studio and BandLab, and understands music through tracks, effects, timelines, and familiar production controls. I have used those tools, but they have never been the way I naturally want to make music. I am much more interested in Strudel and TidalCycles: writing patterns as code, changing them live, and treating a composition as something programmable. That left us without a good place to meet. When Avery sent me a Logic project, I could not simply open it on Linux. Even if we were using DAWs on the same platform, proprietary project formats and different software would still make collaboration awkward. In the other direction, I could send him a Strudel composition as a few lines of text, but unless he learned the syntax, there was not much he could do with it. We wanted a workspace where neither of us had to abandon the way we preferred to work. Avery should be able to interact with music through a visual interface. I should be able to work directly in Strudel. An agent should be able to participate without pretending to be a person clicking through a DAW. That shared workspace became Sushi. What it does Sushi is a browser-based, code-native DAW powered by Strudel and its TidalCycles-inspired pattern language. Underneath the interface, the composition is still code. That makes a Sushi project lightweight, inspectable, programmable, and easy to share. On top of that code, Sushi provides a more familiar music-production interface for arranging tracks, selecting sounds, adjusting effects, and shaping a composition without requiring the user to understand Strudel syntax. The important part is that these are not two separate modes. When someone changes a supported property in the interface, the Strudel source changes with it. When someone edits the source, Sushi reflects that change back into the interface. A traditional producer, a live coder, and an agent can therefore manipulate the same underlying composition instead of passing increasingly lossy translations between different tools. WebMCP adds the third side of that collaboration. An agent can inspect the composition and its current playback state directly in the page, modify or write music, validate the result, and observe the updated source and interface without requiring the user to copy code back and forth between a chat window and the editor. When an edit fails Strudel validation, the agent receives diagnostics from the running environment and can correct its work. This feedback loop makes a major difference. The agent is not writing music blindly and returning a plausible-looking block of code. It is working inside the actual instrument. Because the composition itself is programmable, the musical program becomes a high-leverage control surface for both humans and agents. The DAW is built in code, and WebMCP gives the agent access to that code in its real context. How we built it Sushi started as a relatively simple Astro application written in TypeScript. Astro was a pragmatic choice because it is the framework I already enjoy using, but it also gives the project room to grow without splitting everything into separate repositories or deployments. The application, documentation, and other supporting pages can coexist in the same project while the interactive workspace remains focused and lightweight. Inside that scaffold, we integrated Strudel as the musical runtime and built Sushi’s interface around its source representation. We deliberately avoided treating the interface as a separate DAW model that merely exports Strudel later. Instead, every feature has to respect the same contract: Anything that happens in the interface must be represented in the code, and anything represented in the supported code must remain visible and editable through the interface. That constraint shaped nearly every architectural decision in the project. A track cannot exist only as hidden application state. An effect cannot be added through a UI-only shortcut that the source does not understand. The interface must work with the musical program rather than bypassing it. We then connected the workspace to WebMCP so an agent could participate through that same underlying model. Rather than automating coordinates or simulating mouse clicks, the agent can work with the composition structurally and receive feedback from the running application. Sushi registers a typed WebMCP surface against the browser’s native model context. Agents can inspect a structured snapshot of the project, read or patch the canonical Strudel source, validate candidate source against the running Strudel engine, control playback, edit tracks and timeline state, and load or inspect composition templates. Mutating operations carry a base revision and transaction ID, so stale or duplicated actions are rejected instead of silently overwriting human changes. Successful source edits pass through the same validation and source-to-interface synchronization path as human edits, returning structured state, diffs, and diagnostics to the agent. The result is a shared artifact with three possible collaborators: one person working visually, another working in code, and an agent working through WebMCP. Challenges we ran into Performance became a challenge almost immediately. Strudel is already a mature and highly interactive environment, so Sushi could not merely produce the same output eventually. Editing and playback had to feel responsive enough to function as an instrument. As we introduced interface state and synchronization, we repeatedly found places where our application was doing substantially more work than Strudel itself. We had to become much more careful about when the composition was evaluated, what caused components to update, and how changes moved through the application. Music software makes performance problems unusually obvious: latency and interruption are not just technical metrics. They directly affect whether the creative process feels usable. The larger challenge was maintaining synchronization between code and interface. Almost every feature sounds straightforward until it has to work in both directions. Adding an effect button is easy if it only changes hidden state. It becomes much harder when that action must create valid Strudel, preserve the rest of the user’s source, remain editable as text, and still be understood by the interface after the code changes again. It was tempting at several points to introduce shortcuts: parallel state, special internal representations, or UI features that only resembled Strudel behavior. Those approaches might have made an individual feature easier to ship, but they would have broken the central promise of the project. WebMCP introduced another form of synchronization problem: an agent may act on a project while a human is still editing it. We addressed that by requiring mutating operations to carry a base revision and transaction ID. Stale or duplicated actions return a structured conflict instead of silently overwriting newer work. Over time, we established more reliable patterns for preserving these contracts. Once those patterns became part of the architecture, development became noticeably smoother. I could describe a feature to my coding agent and expect it to extend the existing model rather than inventing another path around Strudel. Accomplishments that we’re proud of The accomplishment we care about most is that Sushi stopped being merely a hackathon idea and became something we actually wanted to use. A large part of building it was the impatient feeling that we needed to finish the next feature so we could stop developing for a moment and start making music with it. Avery and I have already been able to play with the workspace from our different perspectives, which is the original problem Sushi was meant to solve. We are also proud that the visual editor and code editor are not competing sources of truth. They are two views into the same instrument. That gives Sushi the accessibility of a DAW without giving up the expressive power and portability of Strudel. The WebMCP integration demonstrates something we find especially exciting: an agent interface does not always need to be a giant catalog of tiny actions mirroring every control in an application. By exposing a coherent, programmable representation, a bounded set of high-level operations can give an agent meaningful control over an entire creative system. The agent is not clicking blindly th

title: PaperPup
pitch: A research library your AI can't wander out of — by design.
about_excerpt: A research library your AI can't wander out of — by design. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration PaperPup started as a personal itch, not a hackathon idea. It was needed to manage a real research library. There were real-world stakes in turning a recognized pattern of investigatory practices into a structured and AI-instrumented process. The frustration that actually drove the design: ask a general AI chatbot to help with research, and it happily answers from the whole internet, or from memory, or both — not from the specific papers you actually collected and have deemed useful. Drafts as well that needed controlled tests run against them against the literature that supported the research. Anyone who has followed a chatbot down a research rabbit hole and landed somewhere completely off-target knows the feeling. PaperPup was built to make that structurally impossible, not just less likely. WebMCP entered the picture partway through, and it fit almost too well. PaperPup already had a strict internal discipline — Library, Stack, and Room, each granting a narrower set of capabilities than the last with clear demarcation between them in the form of hand-off briefs. WebMCP was a way to expose any of that to an external agent with the demarcation points mapped to WebMCP site tools by context, and it was a natural fit. The hackathon became the deadline attached to work already in motion, not the reason the work started. What it does PaperPup is a personal, single-tenant research library. It is not a shared or social platform, and is organized around three deliberately narrowing contexts: Library — search, add, and organize the papers you've actually collected. Stack — pull a working set of papers together and investigate them with an AI, grounded only in that set. Room — promote a mature stack into a frozen, bounded investigation. The corpus locks at that point — nothing added, nothing removed, except through one specific human-approved channel. WebMCP added a twist to that because now the human had an AI agent on their side that, unlike the agents that PaperPup sandboxes and uses to pit literature against literature, this new agent was the user. Inside a Room is a bit more locked down for all because an investigating agent has constraints that make it genuinely useful. It can read the papers, follow a citation to a source that should be there but isn't yet, and propose adding it. What it can't do is add that source itself, or search outside the frozen set to find something else instead. There's no tool call that does either of those things registered in that context — not a rule the agent is trusting to follow, a door that structurally doesn't exist. WebMCP is what lets any AI agent someone already uses — ChatGPT, or any other WebMCP-capable client — work inside this system directly, live, in the same browser tab and session, rather than through a bespoke chat widget bolted onto the page. That enabled bring your own agent; PaperPup supplies the grounding. How we built it PaperPup is a Next.js app backed by PostgreSQL, with an adapter layer pulling papers from Zenodo, OpenAlex/Unpaywall, arXiv, bioRxiv, and CORE, plus citation resolution against PubMed and Crossref. The WebMCP layer lives entirely under one subfolder, src/webmcp/ : a declarative manifest.js listing every tool's name, schema, and which contexts register it; register.js , which walks that manifest and calls the real document.modelContext.registerTool() API, managing one AbortController per tool so the whole set can be cleanly unregistered and re-registered on every navigation; envelope.js , which maps the current context — library, stack, room, or nothing selected yet — to the tools that should be live; and one thin handler per tool. Every handler reaches application logic only over HTTPS, never a direct import of server-only code — a boundary now enforced by an automated test that walks the whole import graph and fails on any reach into the backend and database layer. Tools scoped to one specific stack or room don't take that stack or room id as a parameter - it is read directly from the page's own state since a tool visible only inside one specific room already proves which room that is. Asking the calling model to name it back would just be redundant. The user's agent translates both ways for the user to have flexibility in identifying resources in prompts and reading the responses after their agent has formatted the PaperPup response to present it however that agent knows their user likes to communicate. We tested against a real host end to end — ChatGPT's WebMCP-enabled models — and, for fast local iteration before and alongside that, against @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill , a real implementation of the same browser API with a dev-only testing shim for invoking tools directly with no AI client connected at all. Claude (architecture and design) and Claude Code (implementation and live verification) were genuine build partners throughout — a fitting way to build a project about grounding external-to-system AI agents in trustworthy work. Challenges we ran into A permission model that could actually be violated in code, even after we thought we'd designed it out. Early on, a Room-context tool for reading a paper's metadata took a global paper id. That meant there was nothing stopping an agent from simply naming a paper outside the room's frozen set and getting it back anyway. The interface didn't expose search, so it looked safe. The fix was structural, not a permission check: that tool now takes a position within the room's own paper list, not a global id. There's no way to even construct a request for something outside scope, because the parameter itself can't express it. This ended up being the single most important architectural decision in the whole submission — a stronger guarantee than any runtime check could offer. A crash that taught us to build a permanent test, not just fix the bug. One early handler reached for a server-only database module directly instead of going through an HTTP route, and it pulled pg straight into the browser bundle — crashing the app outright the moment that code path loaded. We fixed the immediate bug, then built an automated test that walks the entire import graph under the WebMCP layer and fails on any reach into server-only code, so the same mistake can't happen again silently. Getting genuine live verification, not just something that looked right in code. ChatGPT's WebMCP support turned out to depend on which underlying model was selected. One variant has it disabled entirely, which looks identical to a bug in your own tool descriptions if you don't know to check. The in-app browser also has no visible developer console by default, so confirming what was actually happening required either asking the model to report it back, or falling back to a real polyfill running locally for a tighter dev loop. Turns out, this was quite useful to see and gave us insights in how to structure the descriptions in our WebMCP site tool descriptions that allow the user's agent to learn the capabilities impressively well. Realizing a two-dimensional problem was actually a one-dimensional one. A room's frozen corpus can span multiple stacks, which made stack-plus-position addressing feel necessary at first. Checking it against an existing invariant — that a room's assigned stacks are frozen and can't change after assignment — showed a flat position across the room's whole corpus was just as safe and considerably simpler. The extra complexity wasn't buying anything. Accomplishments that we're proud of That the room-envelope guarantee is real, not asserted. An agent working inside a frozen investigation cannot search or read past its bounds. This can be confirmed by trying, not just by design intent, and it is immensely useful when running control tests whereby a standing agent must defend a corpus using only what is in that room. The only out is that the room's agent can propose a source, such as a citation reference that it wants the full text for, and the user must then intervene to approve whether that visibility will be allowed. Configurable of course, but that is a sizable document in itself to describe the capabilities envisioned and being built. That we built the discipline to actually verify claims rather than trust that code looked right: a manifest-invariants test that caught its own first-draft bug immediately; a boundary test proven with a deliberate red-then-green check rather than accepted on a single clean pass; a live investigation's output cross-checked word-by-word against the source papers to confirm it wasn't quietly blending in outside knowledge. That the two-way collaboration model — an agent can discover and propose, a human retains final authority, and neither side can silently override the other — came out of the architecture cleanly, rather than needing to be bolted on as an afterthought. title: Gulawo Tendering Workspace with a Built-in WebMCP Agent
pitch: An AI agent lives inside Gulawo: it finds open tenders, scores fit, checks your document vault, flags disqualifying deviations, and drafts proposals you approve before anything is saved.
about_excerpt: An AI agent lives inside Gulawo: it finds open tenders, scores fit, checks your document vault, flags disqualifying deviations, and drafts proposals you approve before anything is saved. Like Comment Story Updates demo demo demo Inspiration East African SME contractors don't lose government tenders on price. They lose on a missing PPDA certificate. A deadline buried in a procurement portal. A compliance gap nobody caught until it was too late. That admin, the finding, the tracking, the checking, the paperwork, is exactly what beat the teams that could actually do the work. Gulawo exists to close that gap. What it does A contractor signs in, uploads a real certificate, hands a tender to the agent, and the agent works the whole pipeline inside the app. It searches open tenders, pulls the full brief, scores fit against the company's actual profile, checks the document vault against the compliance checklist, and scans the bid security against the stated guarantee so the fatal gap is caught before anyone submits. The agent proposes. The human approves. Nothing touches the bid until someone clicks Approve. How we built it Next.js and React for the workspace, and a WebMCP layer that declares six tools in the manifest and registers the same six on the page with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool dispatches to a typed function that runs real SQL against the live database, so the workflow is identical whether a human drives the cockpit in the browser or an agent calls the tools from ChatGPT's embedded browser with WebMCP enabled. It degrades gracefully if the API isn't there and is guarded by a session cookie. Challenges we ran into Making it watchable. The unbounded agent route we tried first was slow and unreliable, so we made the recorded path deterministic and database-backed, and bounded every step so one slow call could never blow the three-minute limit. A recording quirk taught us what the eye actually follows. A new tool's result is prepended above older ones, and an early cut scrolled the bottom card into view while the narration described the new one. Fixing the recorder to center the card it was talking about, and to actually reveal the proposal and the kanban, took more patience than the app itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of Credibility over confidence. Every WebMCP tool is deterministic. It returns structured JSON computed from real SQL against real tenders, the real compliance rule set, and the real uploaded documents. If the tool says a UGX 12 million bid security is short of the required two percent, that's arithmetic against an actual tender record, not a comforting guess. And human approval isn't a checkbox. Lookup tools run freely, but nothing persists until a person approves. What we learned For a contractor, credibility beats confidence. An agent that sounds sure about compliance is worthless if it's wrong and costs them a bid. That's why Gulawo doesn't guess. And we saw firsthand what people and agents can now do together that was hard before. Before, an assistant could only read whatever the page rendered. Now a small contractor gets a defensible answer in seconds. Is this tender worth it? Are we legally ready to bid? Is there a compliant draft held for sign-off? Instead of hours of paperwork or a disqualification. What's next for Gulawo Turn the six tools into a persistent compliance watchman. Let the agent monitor open tenders against the vault continuously, alert the contractor the moment a new tender matches, and keep draft proposals current as tenders change. Grow the readable tender pool beyond Uganda into Kenya, Tanzania, and Rwanda, and let the vault check itself against each market's rule set. And push deeper on the collaborative loop that WebMCP makes possible. The agent works the pipeline in the same session, with the human holding the final say, all the way to submission. title: Longevity — Human-Agent Life Function Workspace
pitch: A privacy-first WebMCP app where your agent turns known family and life context into a visible Life Function, asks only for missing facts, and compares conditional life-extension scenarios.
about_excerpt:
A privacy-first WebMCP app where your agent turns known family and life context into a visible Life Function, asks only for missing facts, and compares conditional life-extension scenarios.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most personal-modeling products begin with a long blank form. But a person’s AI agent may already know useful fragments of family history and life context. The missed opportunity is not merely autofill: it is a shared working surface where the person sees the model changing while the agent gathers only what is actually missing. 

 What it does 

 Longevity is a privacy-first WebMCP workspace in which a person and their agent build a visible Life Function together. The agent reuses structured facts already available in its context, asks only for gaps, and submits those facts directly into the open page. Longevity then visualizes parental trajectories, the client’s observed trajectory, influence coefficients, a hereditary model, and conditional life-extension scenarios. 

 When context is sparse, the agent runs a live four-chapter interview: family and influence, ancestors, parents, and the client’s trajectory. It asks one short question per message, accepts text, voice, approximate answers, or “I don’t know,” and stops the required interview as soon as the first calculation is ready. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Longevity exposes seven client-side WebMCP tools. The agent can read the intake and privacy contract, submit known facts, inspect completeness, request exactly one next interview step, add a structured answer, and retrieve scenario comparisons. Every accepted tool call updates the same in-tab state the person is looking at. 

 This creates an experience that was difficult before WebMCP: private context can be reused without forcing the person to re-enter everything, while the browser remains the shared visual source of truth. The person can inspect sources and assumptions, adjust father, mother, and environment coefficients, and watch the Life Functions recalculate immediately—without the agent scraping or clicking through the UI. 

 Privacy by architecture 

 The deployed static page has no intake server, account, analytics, cookies, database, or persistent storage. It accepts structured facts only, never raw chat, audio, or transcripts. Personal facts remain in JavaScript memory inside the open tab and disappear on reload, tab close, or Clear. A restrictive Content Security Policy uses connect-src 'none'. The WebMCP manifest also states that retention of the external agent conversation is controlled by that agent platform, not by Longevity. 

 How we built it 

 
 React 19, TypeScript, and Vite 
 Imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool() 
 Strict JSON Schemas and structured tool results 
 Abort-scoped re-registration when the locale changes 
 Fully client-side calculations and state 
 English-first interface with a complete Russian UI and WebMCP contract 
 Netlify static deployment with restrictive security headers 
 Automated coverage for intake flow, privacy, calculations, charts, tool registration, and localization 
 

 Challenges and lessons 

 The hardest design problem was balancing completeness with a conversational interview. Too few questions produced a weak model; a conventional questionnaire felt endless. The four-chapter policy, one-question rhythm, explicit unknowns, and separate preliminary/refinement phases made the flow both bounded and useful. 

 A second challenge was making strong privacy language technically true. That led us to keep all personal state inside the tab, forbid raw conversational media, expose the privacy boundary to the agent before submission, and distinguish page storage from the agent platform’s own retention policy. 

 Finally, the model had to remain legible and epistemically honest. Longevity shows completeness, provenance, assumptions, and uncertainty, and presents its calculations as a conditional Androphysics model—not medical advice, a biological forecast, or a prediction of a person’s death.

title: RoomDex
pitch: A shared room canvas where people and agents plan, measure, and refine the same space through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared room canvas where people and agents plan, measure, and refine the same space through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates RoomDex began with one concrete request: move only the floor lamp to the other side of the chair. Room design is iterative, but an agent working from a screenshot has to guess at scale and translate intent into mouse movements. A generated image leaves nothing precise to refine. RoomDex is a client-only room-planning workspace where a person and an agent work on the same measurable 3D room. The visible room exposes 21 native WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect the room, compare three arrangements without changing anything, measure clearances, apply a layout, place wall art, move or style named furniture, analyze spatial constraints, review recent work, and undo a specific change. WebMCP is central because it exposes product meaning rather than screen coordinates. A tool such as move_furniture accepts a named object, real measurements, a relationship, and an expected revision. Every successful write updates the visible room, records whether a person or agent made it, and creates an undoable revision. Reads do not mutate the room. RoomDex checks collisions, boundaries, clearances, circulation paths, and fixed openings. The demo shows the agent inspecting the room, comparing arrangements, applying a reading corner, creating measured procedural wall art in opening-safe space, moving only the floor lamp to exact coordinates, analyzing the result, reviewing recent changes, and undoing only that move. React and TypeScript provide the interface and state boundary. Three.js renders procedural furniture. A serializable domain engine owns room geometry, spatial validation, activity, and history. One declarative WebMCP registry supplies the native document.modelContext.registerTool path and the local evaluation bridge. Writes are serialized and wait for the matching rendered revision before completing. Codex supported research, implementation, testing, native-browser verification, accessibility, security, performance, deployment, and release QA. The final release includes 211 deterministic tests across 19 files. All 21 native tools were verified on the public Vercel deployment in Codex's in-app browser. To test it, open https://roomdex.vercel.app/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled and confirm the toolbar says 21 agent tools . Ask the agent to inspect the room and compare all three built-in arrangements without changing it. Then ask it to apply the reading-corner arrangement, add a warm geometric print, move only the Floor lamp, analyze the layout, review recent changes, and undo only the lamp move. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Decision Passport
pitch: Keep the reason. Change the store.
about_excerpt: Keep the reason. Change the store. Like Comment Story Updates Decision Receipt: explain the winner, losses, accepted trade-off, and counterfactual. One Question Engine: ask the smallest human-owned question that can change first place. Common Room: import the checksum-bound Passport and rank 24 samples down to three. Form House: capture and edit explicit evidence before export. Answer reversal: H01 flips the winner while the carried evidence stays visible. Inspiration Shopping agents can search faster than people, but speed does not solve the harder problem: preferences are fragmented across stores, and recommendations rarely show which trade-off decided the outcome. We wanted an agent that remembers only what a person explicitly approved—and knows when to stop and ask. What it does Decision Passport is a two-store WebMCP journey. At Form House , a person records why a sample chair was a yes, maybe, or no. The agent turns those explicit reasons into an editable decision-passport-v1 ; the person can correct or remove any rule before export. The agent carries that checksum-bound envelope to Common Room , where it reduces 24 fictional sample chairs to three evidence-backed options. A deterministic One Question Engine simulates both sides of the unresolved trade-off and asks the smallest question whose answer can change first place. The final Decision Receipt explains why the winner won, why the alternatives lost, which trade-off was accepted, and what would reverse the result. Why WebMCP is the right interface WebMCP is the product boundary, not a decorative integration. It lets the agent operate each store's live, inspectable state and carry an exact user-approved object across origins. Dynamic registration exposes only the next valid tool. Tool annotations distinguish read-only operations and untrusted text. The same E01 – E04 evidence trace remains visible from the corrected rule, through checksum handoff and shortlist, to one human-owned H01 answer and the final receipt. People stay in control of meaning; the agent handles the tedious transfer and comparison work. How we built it We used React, TypeScript, Vinext, Tailwind CSS, Zod, and the WebMCP imperative API. Nine single-purpose tools span two store-specific deployments. Form House changes its exposed tool set as evidence becomes reviewable; Common Room exposes exactly one next tool at a time. Strict Zod contracts and a deterministic checksum validate transferred data. Scoring, hinge simulation, ranking, and receipt generation are deterministic, so judges can reproduce the same result without an API key, model call, account, or live commerce data. Challenges we ran into The central design challenge was preserving human agency without reducing the experience to a chatbot. Every preference needed to remain traceable to an explicit statement. The final question also had to be genuinely consequential, so the engine simulates both answers and asks only when the winner changes. Technically, we kept every tool bounded, every state reproducible offline, and the two origins cleanly separated while preserving one coherent visual protocol. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete two-store WebMCP journey with nine bounded tools A visible, editable, portable decision contract A question whose two answers provably produce different winners A deterministic receipt with a counterfactual Responsive, keyboard-visible, reduced-motion-aware interfaces No login, payment, tracking, browser history, hidden behavioral inference, or model API required A public 77-second captioned demo of the working flow What we learned Agents become more trustworthy when their action space shrinks as the task progresses. Portable context is also more useful when it is explicit, editable, checksum-bound, and visibly distinct from the one decision that remains human-owned. What's next The hackathon prototype intentionally stays narrow. A future version could standardize portable decision contracts across participating merchants and add other considered-purchase categories while preserving explicit consent, source evidence, and the human-owned decision hinge. Try it Open Form House in ChatGPT's in-app browser and complete the evidence-to-export flow. Copy the exact exported envelope. Open Common Room , import it, and follow the one-tool-at-a-time sequence. Watch the 77-second demo or inspect the MIT-licensed source . New-work disclosure All application code, copy, catalogs, WebMCP contracts, tests, and documentation were created for this challenge beginning September 1, 2026. Product names and attributes are fictional sample data. Openly licensed Pexels photographs, the local Kokoro demo voice model, the Montserrat caption font, and open-source packages are disclosed in the repository. The four quiet demo accents are procedurally generated; no stock music is used.
