title: Life Shift
pitch: A life simulation where you control the person and AI controls the world. WebMCP lets an AI Director observe your choices and introduce bounded events, creating an adaptive life around you.
about_excerpt: A life simulation where you control the person and AI controls the world. WebMCP lets an AI Director observe your choices and introduce bounded events, creating an adaptive life around you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When I started exploring WebMCP, the obvious use case was giving an AI structured tools so it could help a person operate an application. I wanted to explore a different relationship. What if the human and the AI controlled different sides of the same software? Games and simulations made that idea immediately visible. I chose a life simulation because it requires no specialized domain knowledge. Everyone understands making a decision and wondering where it might lead. That became LIFE//SHIFT. Play your decisions before you live them. You make the choices. An AI Director, operating through WebMCP, can change the circumstances around them. You control the life. The AI controls the world. The engine keeps the rules. What it does LIFE//SHIFT is an adaptive life simulation built around one shared beginning and many possible lives. Every player starts as the same fictional 18-year-old: a coffee-shop barista in the small town of Vesper Beach. From there, four chapters carry that life from 18 to 60: 18–28 · 28–40 · 40–50 · 50–60 In each chapter, the player makes one decision in Work , one in Growth , and one in Life . Those choices do not come from a static decision tree. The available decisions evolve with the life being built. Growth and Life choices change with age and history. Work options can narrow as the decades pass because decisions accumulate and some exits become harder later in life. The direct consequences are deterministic. Cash, income, freedom, stability, wellbeing, skills, career progression, and future eligibility are calculated by the simulation engine. But the world around that life is adaptive. After a chapter resolves, a Director Cycle opens. An external AI Director can use native WebMCP tools to inspect what happened and decide whether the world should respond. It may introduce at most one bounded external change: a job opportunity, setback, financial shock or windfall, a door opened by another person, a housing event, a business opportunity, or a broader shift in conditions such as hiring, housing, or demand. The AI chooses the context and reason. The engine chooses the consequences. There is no setLifeState . The Director cannot choose the player's Work, Growth, or Life decisions. It cannot invent a salary or directly rewrite the simulation. And sometimes the correct response is no response at all. Observe-only is a valid Director outcome. The collaboration is intentionally asymmetric: The human owns the decisions. The AI owns bounded circumstances. The deterministic engine owns the rules. Same beginning. Different decisions. Different life. How we built it LIFE//SHIFT separates authority rather than giving the AI control of the entire simulation. The deterministic engine owns authoritative state, chapter progression, eligibility, economics, compounding consequences, and which decisions can appear next. WebMCP is the capability layer for the AI Director. The page registers native, schema-defined WebMCP tools that expose specific capabilities rather than requiring the agent to navigate or reverse-engineer the interface. Read tools expose structured context including: life state and history decision profile open threads finances and career world conditions available opportunities Director budget the pending Director Cycle Mutation tools expose a deliberately small set of world interventions. Every mutation is bound to the current cycleId and paid from a Director Budget. Inputs are validated, qualities and severities are constrained to defined values, and the deterministic engine maps the Director's semantic choice to actual numerical effects. After each chapter resolves, the Director Cycle becomes available. In a WebMCP-capable host such as ChatGPT, the agent can inspect get_pending_director_cycle , gather whatever additional context it needs through the read tools, and then choose zero or one intervention. Without a native WebMCP host, a local adapter uses the same underlying tool boundary so the simulation can still complete. The architecture is also visible to the player. Life Review shows how the world responded, the remaining Director budget, the Director's interpretation, and actual WebMCP activity. The agentic layer is therefore inspectable rather than hidden behind the experience. Challenges we ran into The hardest question was not how much the AI could control. It was how much the AI should control. If an LLM owned the entire simulation, LIFE//SHIFT would be adaptive, but its outcomes would become difficult to reason about or trust. If everything were pre-authored, the rules would be reliable, but the experience would eventually collapse into another branching decision tree. The solution was to split authority. Player decisions stay human. Their direct consequences stay deterministic. The AI Director receives a bounded surface for influencing external circumstances, with at most one intervention per chapter and a limited budget. Another challenge came directly from the WebMCP interaction model: exposing tools does not automatically wake an external agent when application state changes. We solved that with the Director Cycle. When a chapter resolves, LIFE//SHIFT creates an explicit cycle containing the new state and the boundary for the Director's turn. The application can expose that a cycle is pending, identify it with a cycleId , tell the agent what it may inspect, enforce zero or one intervention, and prevent an already-completed cycle from being replayed. We also had to make the simulation genuinely path-dependent. "Invest in skills" cannot mean the same thing at 18 and 50. Growth and Life choices therefore change across chapters. Work opportunities narrow or evolve. Moving to Kestrel is different from returning to Vesper Beach. Repeated investments have history-dependent consequences. The life has to remember how it got there. Accomplishments that we're proud of The accomplishment I am most proud of is that WebMCP is not an integration added to LIFE//SHIFT after the simulation was built. It enables the interaction model. The agent is not playing the life for you. It is not simply clicking through the UI. It is participating in the world in which your decisions take place. Two players can begin on the same coffee-shop stool in Vesper Beach and build completely different trajectories through Work, Growth, and Life. The Director can inspect the history each player actually created through structured WebMCP tools and respond to that context, while deterministic boundaries preserve the player's authority over their own life. We also made that architecture observable. The experience exposes when a Director turn is ready, provides a simple prompt for invoking it, supports local resolution when native WebMCP is unavailable, and records the Director's interpretation, budget, and real tool activity in Life Review. The result is an agentic experience where the boundary between human agency, AI agency, and deterministic authority is visible by design. What we learned The biggest lesson was simple: Giving AI more control does not necessarily make an agentic experience stronger. Giving AI the right control does. WebMCP allowed us to expose a small, explicit capability surface instead of asking an agent to reverse-engineer an interface or giving it unrestricted access to application state. That produced a reusable pattern: Human authority + deterministic rules + bounded agent authority. The AI can become a meaningful participant in an application without becoming its source of truth. We also learned that having a tool available does not mean the agent should use it. Sometimes nothing significant happens. An adaptive Director that manufactures drama every chapter is not actually responding intelligently to the simulation. That is why observe-only is a first-class outcome. And the pattern extends beyond a life simulation. In a traditional training simulation, every participant can eventually encounter the same authored script. With this architecture, an AI can adapt bounded parts of the scenario to the decisions a participant actually made. The next situation can follow the last decision without surrendering the rules of the exercise to the model. What's next for Life Shift LIFE//SHIFT is intentionally accessible, but the architecture is broader than the life simulation itself. The same authority model could support adaptive cyber exercises, incident-response scenarios, enterprise strategy simulations, crisis exercises, and safety training where humans retain decision authority while an AI dynamically controls bounded external conditions. Imagine the same runtime applied to a cyber exercise. A security team begins with a simulated incident: unusual authentication activity appears on a product

title: Scout
pitch: Know the market before you make the offer — transparent card deal evidence for people and agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Know the market before you make the offer — transparent card deal evidence for people and agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Side-by-side Scout listing comparison with acquisition cost, 90-day market delta, trust, and alerts. Scout market overview with exact-tier pricing, robust comps, Deal Score, and Seller Trust. Scout Deal Score, Seller Trust, confidence, and normalization methodology. Scout provider capability matrix and explicit separation of synthetic demo data from live integrations. What Scout is Scout is a transparent Pokémon card buying assistant for people and agents. It normalizes the exact card, printing, condition, grading company, and numeric grade before comparing any price. Buyers can inspect current availability, total acquisition cost, the latest exact comparable sale, robust 30- and 90-day medians, Seller Trust evidence, listing warnings, and a fully explained Deal Score. The Phase 1 judge build is deliberately synthetic-only. Every card, seller, marketplace, listing, and sale is fictional and visibly labeled. This lets judges test the complete workflow without fabricated API claims, scraping, credentials, or accidental mixing of demo and live records. Inspiration Collectible-card buyers often have to reconcile ambiguous listing titles, asking prices, shipping, grade-specific sales, and seller evidence across several tabs. A PSA 10 is not a PSA 9; a raw Near Mint card is not a slab; and one extreme sale should not define the market. We wanted an assistant that shows its work and is as comfortable saying “insufficient evidence” as it is ranking a deal. What it does Searches normalized card identities and exact raw/graded market tiers. Compares current total acquisition cost with the latest exact sale and robust 30/90-day market statistics. Detects duplicate exposures and flags extreme price anomalies without hiding the audit trail. Produces an inspectable Deal Score and platform-specific Seller Trust Score, withholding either when evidence is inadequate. Surfaces listing risks such as stock photos, weak seller history, title/description conflicts, no returns, high shipping, and missing certification evidence. Compares two to five listings and shows raw versus graded markets without pooling unlike tiers. Registers six read-only WebMCP tools: search_cards , get_card_market_state , assess_listing , compare_listings , find_deals , and compare_raw_vs_graded . Lets a WebMCP tool result update the visible collector workspace, so the person can inspect the same evidence the agent used. How we built it Scout is a strict TypeScript and React application built with Vite and deployed through OpenAI Sites. A provider-adapter boundary maps catalog, listing, sales-history, and seller sources into canonical domain records. Deterministic engines handle identity, deduplication, exact comparable matching, median/MAD statistics, Seller Trust, listing risk, and Deal Score. The React UI and imperative WebMCP registrations call the same CardMarketService , preventing agent and screen results from drifting. Responses carry data mode, synthetic status, source capabilities, retrieval time, limitations, methodology version, and suggested UI state. A service invariant rejects any attempt to introduce non-synthetic records into Phase 1. The disabled eBay configuration contains only server-side environment placeholders—no fake endpoint or fallback data. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was refusing false equivalence. Marketplace titles are loose, but market estimates must be strict enough to keep variant, language, raw condition, grading company, and numeric grade separate. We also needed robust statistics that keep anomalies auditable while preventing them from distorting the estimate, plus score coverage rules that do not turn missing evidence into false certainty. The other challenge was designing WebMCP as the product interface rather than a demo wrapper. Each tool has strict schemas, read-only annotations, structured provenance, honest limitations, and UI-state metadata, while using exactly the same service as the human interface. Accomplishments we are proud of Six WebMCP tools are discovered from the live page and covered by tests. Exact-tier rules prevent PSA 10, PSA 9, BGS 9.5, CGC 10, and raw condition data from being pooled. The 90-day engine uses shipping-inclusive medians, recency weighting, dispersion, and log-price median absolute deviation anomaly flags. Scores explain every weighted component and are withheld when evidence coverage is too low. Synthetic/live isolation, capability-scoped sources, security headers, CI, strict schemas, and a zero-known-vulnerability audit are part of the repository foundation. What we learned Agent-ready commerce tools need more than a convenient function signature: they need provenance, confidence, exact identity boundaries, and a path back to inspectable human evidence. We also learned that withholding a score is a feature. A trustworthy assistant should expose uncertainty instead of manufacturing precision. What's next Phase 2 moves adapters, credentials, rate limits, caching, persistence, and scheduled ingestion behind a server boundary. We will re-verify current provider terms and enable one approved live source at a time, starting only where documented access can support the fields we display. PostgreSQL/Prisma storage, an identity-review queue, sandbox provider contract tests, authentication, saved searches, and alerts follow. No marketplace will be enabled through scraping or an undocumented workaround. title: AgentReady — WebMCP Builder for Framer
pitch: Turn any Framer site into an agent-ready experience. AgentReady publishes secure WebMCP tools for forms, commerce, payments, content, and AI workflows—without code.
about_excerpt: Turn any Framer site into an agent-ready experience. AgentReady publishes secure WebMCP tools for forms, commerce, payments, content, and AI workflows—without code. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Framer allows designers and no-code creators to publish polished websites without building a traditional application stack. However, those sites are still designed mainly for people using visual interfaces. When an AI agent visits one of these sites, it usually has to infer intent from pixels, text, and DOM structure. It must guess what a button does, which fields belong together, and when an action becomes consequential. WebMCP provides a better foundation: websites can expose explicit, typed tools that agents can call directly. But adding WebMCP manually still requires JavaScript, JSON Schema, browser-security knowledge, and custom integration work. I built AgentReady to make that capability accessible to Framer creators. What it does AgentReady is a no-code WebMCP builder delivered as a Framer Workspace Plugin. It scans the active Framer project for pages, text, links, CMS collections, forms, conversations, and commerce surfaces. The site owner then chooses which capabilities agents may use. AgentReady generates and publishes a top-level WebMCP runtime through Framer Custom Code. The current runtime can expose up to 30 typed tools covering: Site and section search Same-origin navigation CMS discovery and item retrieval Form inspection and preparation Advanced options, addresses, dates, and multi-step forms Human-mediated file selection Visible chat composition and sending Generic checkout preparation Shopify catalog, product, policy, cart, and checkout operations Cloudflare knowledge search and provenance Agentic payment challenge discovery Licensed structured content and Pay Per Crawl metadata The public demonstration exposes all 30 tools. Why WebMCP is essential AgentReady is not a chatbot wrapper or a conventional browser-automation demo. Its core product is the WebMCP tool surface published by each Framer site. Instead of asking an agent to visually locate and click controls, the site declares narrow operations using document.modelContext.registerTool() and typed input schemas. This makes agent behavior faster, more inspectable, and more reliable. It also lets the site owner define the boundary between what an agent may prepare and what a person must approve. For example, an agent can find a product, select the correct variant, and prepare a Shopify cart. The hosted checkout and final payment remain human-only. Similarly, an agent can populate a form, while submission is exposed as a separate capability requiring an explicit decision. Human and agent collaboration AgentReady lets a person and an agent work on the same live page and share its current state. An agent can: Search and understand the site Navigate to relevant content Retrieve structured CMS information Prepare a complex form Continue a visible conversation Compare Shopify products and variants Create a cart and prepare checkout The person remains responsible for: Selecting local files Approving consequential submissions Entering credentials Completing CAPTCHA or biometric checks Opening hosted checkout Confirming payment This division was difficult to express reliably with ordinary visual browser automation. WebMCP makes it part of the website's explicit contract. How I built it The project has three main layers. Framer Workspace Plugin The React and TypeScript plugin scans the current Framer project and presents capability switches in a native-looking interface. It creates an escaped runtime configuration and installs it through the Framer Plugin API. Browser WebMCP runtime The generated runtime executes in the published page's top-level context and registers the selected imperative tools. It validates inputs, limits output size, supports cancellation, marks retrieved content as untrusted, and applies human-review boundaries to sensitive operations. Cloudflare and Shopify integrations Direct mode keeps page-state actions in the visitor's browser. Hybrid mode keeps UI actions local while routing selected network-backed operations through a same-origin Cloudflare MCP gateway. The repository also includes Workers for knowledge retrieval, analytics, Browser Run verification, uploads, Agentic Payments, and licensed structured content. Shopify Storefront MCP and UCP provide live catalog, product, variant, cart, and checkout operations. Cart identifiers remain in browser session storage, and payment is never performed by AgentReady. Challenges One major challenge was Framer's execution model. Plugin interfaces run separately from the published page, while imperative WebMCP tools must be registered in the page's top-level context. AgentReady solves this by generating a self-contained Custom Code runtime. Another challenge was safely exposing real website actions. Forms, conversations, commerce, files, and payments have different trust boundaries. I separated preparation from execution and kept credentials, local file bytes, wallet keys, OTPs, and final payment outside WebMCP arguments. Shopify's UCP responses also contained more protocol data than an agent needed. I implemented compact product and variant results so the agent receives stable IDs and actionable information without oversized responses. Finally, WebMCP is still evolving. I built automated tests around registration, input schemas, cancellation, duplicate-safe startup, result limits, gateway isolation, and all 30 runtime tools. Accomplishments Published a working Framer Marketplace plugin Exposed 30 functioning WebMCP tools on a live Framer site Demonstrated real ChatGPT Site Tool invocations Connected live Shopify UCP catalog and cart operations Added Cloudflare-backed knowledge, trust, payment, and delivery options Implemented explicit safety boundaries for forms, files, credentials, and payments Created automated runtime, gateway, deployment, and live-site validation Released the complete project under the MIT License What I learned WebMCP works best when it is treated as a product interface rather than a hidden automation layer. Good tools need narrow schemas, bounded output, useful descriptions, visible state changes, cancellation support, and explicit trust boundaries. The most valuable design decision was not maximizing what the agent could do—it was making it clear where the agent should stop and return control to the person. What's next Next, I want to add incremental CMS synchronization, reusable capability presets, stronger WebMCP evaluation tooling, and a guided production setup for Cloudflare-proxied custom domains. The larger goal is to make agent readiness a normal publishing step for every Framer site. title: MoveToGermany.lol
pitch: Moving to Germany? Skip the 30 tabs. One application. Two operators. One shared state.
about_excerpt: Moving to Germany? Skip the 30 tabs. One application. Two operators. One shared state. Like Comment Story Updates Move To Germany One shared workspace where you and your agent build your new life in Germany. Inspiration Moving to another country means rebuilding almost your entire everyday life from scratch. Bank account. Health insurance. Doctors. Groceries. Transportation. Paperwork. Jobs. Local services. Appointments. The information is out there, but it is scattered across dozens of websites, search results, forms, tabs, and directories. I know this problem personally. I've been traveling since 2019 as a German, just not to Germany. ;-) We're a digital nomad family of five, and every time we arrive somewhere new, we have to rebuild parts of our everyday life again. Finding the information isn't even the hardest part. The hard part is turning hundreds of search results, websites, providers, and options into your plan. That's what made me curious about WebMCP. What if an agent didn't have to look at a website and guess how to use it? Which button should it click? What does this field mean? What state is the application currently in? Instead, what if the application could expose its capabilities directly to the agent, while the human continued using the normal website? That's the experiment behind MoveToGermany.lol. What it does MoveToGermany.lol explores a different future: instead of doing all of this alone, you and your agent work together inside the same web application. The agent does the repetitive work. The human makes the decisions. Humans + agents together The core idea behind MoveToGermany.lol is simple: the agent doesn't replace the website, and it doesn't replace the human. A user can say: I'm moving to Berlin, postal code 10115. I'm a software developer, I have a dog and I only speak English. Set me up with the essentials. The agent can turn that request into actions inside MoveToGermany: create an arrival profile, discover relevant services, and start building a personalized relocation plan. But the results don't disappear into a chat. They become part of the actual application state. I can inspect the recommendations myself, change the shortlist, remove something, pick another provider, or leave a note: "English-speaking only." Then I can hand control back to the agent. It reads the state I just changed manually and continues from there. For example, it can see that I rejected a provider, understand my note, find a better alternative, and continue building the plan. That's the part of WebMCP I find most interesting: Human intent → Agent action → Shared application state → Human decision → Agent continues What can the agent actually do? MoveToGermany exposes WebMCP tools across different parts of the relocation journey. Underneath that workflow is a discovery layer of more than 1.16 million real places across 81 categories in Germany. The agent can: build a personalized arrival profile and starter plan discover nearby services manage and reason over the user's shortlist read notes and decisions made directly in the UI compare providers and find jobs help with paperwork and draft outreach find bookable services and propose appointments The goal wasn't to build one impressive AI command. I wanted to see what happens when the whole web application becomes a workspace that a human and an agent can operate together. Why WebMCP? An agent could theoretically operate MoveToGermany by looking at the page and trying to click through the UI. But the application already knows what it can do. Why make the agent guess? Without structured tools, the interaction looks something like: Agent → inspect page → guess UI → click → inspect again → hope With WebMCP, we get closer to: Human intent → Agent → WebMCP tool → Application This isn't a chatbot added on top of the website. The WebMCP tools operate on the same application state the human sees and edits, so the human can take over, make a decision, and the agent can continue from there. WebMCP turns the website itself into the shared workspace. How I built it Tech stack Next.js React TypeScript Tailwind CSS Supabase / PostgreSQL Vercel WebMCP The WebMCP tools are registered directly in the application using document.modelContext.registerTool() : document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "...", description: "...", inputSchema: { // structured input }, execute: async (input) => { // interact with the application } }); That's the whole mechanism: one underlying application state, read and written by both the regular UI and the agent. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge wasn't exposing individual functions as tools. It was deciding where the agent should act autonomously and where the human should remain in control. Searching through hundreds of providers is a great job for an agent. Filtering and comparing them is, too. But choosing the final provider, approving outreach, or confirming an appointment should remain a human decision. Another challenge was shared state. If the agent builds a plan and the human changes it manually, the agent shouldn't continue working from an outdated version of reality. That pushed me to treat every state change as something either side could make, and to design the tools to read the current state instead of assuming their own version of it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that I could reuse a service dataset I had built previously as the discovery layer for a completely new WebMCP application. I'm also proud that this shows agents can make a small, unglamorous problem, one that a lot of people run into, genuinely easier. An agent working through MoveToGermany can meaningfully reduce the amount of searching, tab-switching, and manual comparison involved in settling into a new country. What I learned My biggest takeaway from building MoveToGermany.lol is that making websites usable by agents isn't only about automation. It's about collaboration. Agents are good at searching, filtering, comparing, and repetitive work. Humans provide context, preferences, judgment, and final approval. The interesting part happens when control can move naturally between the two: work gets done, reviewed, changed, and picked back up again. That feels less like automating a website and more like designing a new kind of interface. What's next MoveToGermany.lol is about relocation, but the experiment is bigger than relocation. I want to explore what happens when more websites stop treating agents as visitors that need to imitate humans, and start exposing meaningful capabilities directly, while keeping the human in the loop. One application. Two operators. One shared state. Built With next.js postgresql react supabase tailwind typescript webmcp Try it out github.com movetogermany.lol Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built this solo, front-end, back-end, and the WebMCP integration. It was my first time working with WebMCP, so most of the effort went into figuring out where the tools should live in the app and how to keep the UI and the agent working on the same state without stepping on each other. I reused a service dataset I’d built for an earlier project as the discovery layer, which saved me from sourcing 1.16M places from scratch. I definitely learned a lot about designing for two operators instead of one. shufflethis Wuebbe husband. father. slowmad. title: Dim Hour
pitch: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page.
about_excerpt: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Dim Hour is a city guide - the places worth your time, scored, not starred - covering more than 19,000 restaurants, bars, hotels, and venues across 24 cities. For this challenge, dimhour.com became agent-native: the page itself registers five WebMCP tools, so an agent browsing the site can search the catalog, read a venue, check what is open tonight, draft an itinerary, and hand back a booking link - without scraping a pixel. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Planning a night out is one of the most common things people already ask an agent to help with, but today the agent scrapes pages and guesses at what the site already knows. WebMCP lets dimhour.com hand the agent its real search, scoring, and booking data as structured tools, in the same tab where the person is browsing. The catalog is the product; WebMCP makes it callable. Because the tools are thin adapters over a production venue API, every agent answer is grounded in live data instead of page scraping. How it creates a better user experience One page, two users. A person browsing the Dallas guide and their agent now work on the same surface. The agent calls the site's own tools and gets back the same scored venues, hours, and booking links the UI shows - no copy-pasting between a chat window and a browser, and no agent inventing hours, addresses, or availability. The person keeps the judgment (taste, swaps, vetoes); the agent does the legwork (searching, filtering, checking, assembling). The site stays the source of truth for both of them, and saving a plan stays a human action - the tools read, they never write. What people and agents can do together Co-plan a night in one sitting, in one page. "Dinner in Deep Ellum for four on Friday, then cocktails within walking distance." The agent searches the scored catalog, filters to what is actually open tonight using the same rule the site's own tonight strip uses, pulls full venue records, and drafts an ordered itinerary with real booking links (Resy, OpenTable, SevenRooms, Tock) while the person watches - then interrupts: "swap the second stop for something quieter," and the agent re-plans around the constraint. Before WebMCP, the agent could read the page but not act through the site's own logic, and the person could use the site but not delegate the legwork. Now both happen at once, and the result is a plan with real reservation links attached, not a list of suggestions. How we implemented WebMCP The WebMCP layer is one feature-detected script, webmcp.js, loaded by the site's index.html. Each of the five tools is a thin adapter that POSTs JSON-RPC tools/call to Dim Hour's existing MCP server (mcp.dimhour.com) and passes the result straight through: search_venues - one strong keyword plus city, neighborhood, cuisine, score floor, and price ceiling filters get_venue - the full record: hours, score, booking path, awards find_open_tonight - venues with a happy hour or late kitchen, best score first, using the same definition the site's own "tonight" strip uses, so the agent and the page agree build_itinerary - an ordered multi-stop plan with why and how to book each stop; saving stays a human action at /trip.html get_booking_link - the reservation platform and direct booking URL for a venue, returned for the agent to present; it never opens or books anything itself The script handles the in-flight standard rename (document.modelContext first, navigator.modelContext fallback) and is a silent no-op where no WebMCP host exists. No authentication; the tools expose only public, read-only catalog data. What predates the hackathon: the venue catalog, scoring pipeline, MCP server, and site. What was built during the submission window: webmcp.js, the tool schemas, and the index.html include - the public repo's README draws that line explicitly, with dated commits. Challenges we hit Search results deliberately do not carry hours - only full venue records do - so "open tonight" meant ranking candidates first, then reading the top few individually rather than filtering a field that is not there. Booking links live in the page's own catalog rather than the API, so the booking tool merges both sources and says so honestly when a city is not loaded. The verification suite now asserts substance (tonight actually finds venues; a booking link equals the catalog's own URL), not just shape - because an early version passed every check while two tools quietly returned nothing. title: QuoteFlow WebMCP
pitch: A browser-native quote-inquiry workspace with five WebMCP tools that let AI agents safely manage leads and prepare customer-ready response kits while keeping humans in control.
about_excerpt: A browser-native quote-inquiry workspace with five WebMCP tools that let AI agents safely manage leads and prepare customer-ready response kits while keeping humans in control. Like Comment Story Updates QuoteFlow’s landing screen presents three reviewable next steps, five ready site tools, and clear local-storage and no-contact assurances. The workspace shows a selected inquiry, human–agent activity, editable source details, and a response kit with the reply ready for review. The responsive mobile view keeps tool status, local-storage disclosure, primary actions, and trust assurances usable in a narrow viewport. Quote inquiries arrive as fragments: a customer, a service, a location, a timing preference, and a few uncertain details. QuoteFlow turns those fragments into one visible, durable inquiry queue and a clear next step. It is designed for owner-operated home-service businesses that want useful agent assistance without handing over consequential decisions. This is a strong fit for WebMCP because the structured work—capturing scope, preserving uncertainty, and preparing the next step—can be narrowly exposed, while pricing and commitments still need human judgment. A person or an agent can find an inquiry, create one, correct its details, or prepare a response kit through those domain tools. The same record remains visible in the human workspace, so a person can review, interrupt, correct, regenerate, copy, or print without losing context. This is much more dependable than asking an agent to infer a sequence of clicks. QuoteFlow prepares three reviewable drafts: a customer acknowledgment, a service-specific site-visit checklist, and a no-response follow-up. It never estimates a price, confirms a schedule, sends a message, or contacts a customer. Inquiry data and drafts are stored only in versioned browser localStorage ; when a person asks an agent to use a site tool, the requested result is shared with that current agent session and the app says so clearly. Every draft requires human review before use. Inspiration I wanted to explore a practical middle ground between a blank form and an autonomous CRM. Home-service inquiries contain enough structure for an agent to help, but they also contain uncertainty that should stay visible to a human. The idea was to make the useful part—organizing scope and preparing the next three steps—fast and agent-friendly while keeping pricing, scheduling, deletion, and customer contact out of the agent’s reach. What it does QuoteFlow supports both ordinary browser use and WebMCP collaboration. In a compatible browser, it exposes exactly five site tools: list_quote_inquiries — read minimal summaries, filtered by status, service, or text. get_quote_inquiry — read one inquiry and bounded prepared-kit metadata, without draft bodies. create_quote_inquiry — validate, save, select, and visibly render a new local inquiry. update_quote_inquiry — apply a narrow field patch and mark existing drafts stale when source details change. prepare_response_kit — generate and display the acknowledgment, site-visit checklist, and follow-up for human review. The visible workspace and the tools use the same validation, persistence, status, and deterministic-generation paths. Business or sender names that have not been filled in become unmistakable [Business name] and [Sender name] placeholders and are returned as warnings; QuoteFlow never invents an identity. A browser without WebMCP reports Standard browser mode and keeps the complete manual workflow. How we built it QuoteFlow is a dependency-free static app built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and browser localStorage . core.js contains pure validation, normalization, fingerprints, service checklists, and deterministic response-kit generation. app.js owns the accessible human workspace, versioned local persistence, rendering, stale-state behavior, activity feedback, and the human-only clear-all control. webmcp.js feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool and imperatively registers the five tools at the top level of the page. Every tool input is a closed JSON schema with additionalProperties: false ; critical limits and enums are checked again at runtime. The two read tools declare readOnlyHint: true , all five tools disclose untrusted user/customer text, and write-tool descriptions state their local-storage and visible-UI effects. No backend, analytics, or application network request is required. Initial verification completed on August 29, 2026 and the same reviewed source was reverified on August 30: syntax checks passed, and the combined suite passed 10/10 tests (five dependency-free smoke tests plus the browser integration suite and its four scenarios), including schema and JSON round trips, routing, placeholder warnings, unchanged storage after rejected input, stale-state behavior, persistence, accessibility status regions, unsupported-browser fallback, and the 390 × 844 viewport check. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was defining a tool surface that was genuinely useful without becoming an unrestricted CRM API. Closed schemas, stable inquiry IDs, bounded read results, repeated runtime validation, explicit side-effect descriptions, and a human-review flag all had to work together. We also had to keep human and agent edits coherent. A corrected location, timing preference, business identity, or request detail can invalidate a polished-looking draft, so QuoteFlow fingerprints the source and disables copy/print until the kit is regenerated. Finally, WebMCP support cannot be assumed: feature detection and a full standard-browser path had to be treated as product behavior, not an error page. Accomplishments we’re proud of QuoteFlow demonstrates a complete human–agent loop in a small static app: an agent can create an inquiry, the person can see and correct it, and the agent can prepare three useful outputs without leaving hidden state behind. The queue, activity strip, status changes, stale warning, and generated drafts all update in the same visible workspace. We are especially proud of the safety boundaries. There is no agent tool for pricing, scheduling, deletion, or customer contact; invalid writes are rejected before storage changes; blank identities produce visible placeholders instead of fabricated details; and local storage is explained without pretending that agent calls are invisible. The full automated suite passes 10/10 tests. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools represent meaningful domain outcomes rather than clicks. A small, well-bounded interface can make an agent useful while leaving the person in control of ambiguous or consequential work. We also learned that “local” needs careful language. Browser-only persistence protects the app from needing a backend, but a tool result can still be shared with the current agent session. Clear disclosure, bounded results, runtime validation, visible effects, and stale-state handling are all part of the user experience—not just implementation details. What’s next Next we would add user-mediated import/export for moving a local queue between browsers, richer service-specific templates and photo/measurement notes, and a small audit view showing exactly which human or agent action changed a record. Any future messaging or scheduling integration would remain opt-in and explicitly human-confirmed; it would not turn the current review-first workflow into autonomous outreach. title: ReuseRoute
pitch: An agent-native circular economy assistant that finds the best next life for unwanted items through repair, reuse, parts recovery, or recycling.
about_excerpt: An agent-native circular economy assistant that finds the best next life for unwanted items through repair, reuse, parts recovery, or recycling. Like Comment Story Updates ReuseRoute Let your AI agent find the best next life for anything you no longer need. Inspiration: Getting rid of an item is deceptively complicated. A cracked laptop might be repairable, refurbishable, useful for parts, or finally ready for material recovery. A chair could be donated if pickup exists. Damaged clothing might still be repairable or useful for fibre recovery. The web has plenty of information about these options, but the user journey is fragmented. People often have to open several pages, interpret different acceptance rules, compare conditions, and then figure out what to prepare before a handoff. The easiest option can become the trash bin simply because the better option takes too much research. We wanted to explore a different kind of open web: one where circular-economy services do not just publish pages for humans to read, but also expose clear, structured actions that a user's agent can call on the person's behalf. What it does: ReuseRoute is a human-first web app with an agent-native WebMCP layer. A person describes an unwanted item, its condition, their transport constraint, and what matters most. A browser agent can then: find eligible repair, reuse, salvage and recycling routes, compare the strongest options using structured fields, select one option and open its details on the page, prepare a visible handoff checklist, save the selected route locally, pre-fill a visible handoff request for the person to review. The last step is intentionally human-confirmed. The declarative WebMCP form does not auto-submit. The agent can prepare the task, but the person makes the commitment. All organizations and service data in the hackathon demo are fictional, so the app never presents invented availability or eligibility as real-world guidance. How we built it: ReuseRoute is a dependency-free static web app built with semantic HTML, responsive CSS and vanilla JavaScript. The WebMCP implementation uses both APIs: Imperative WebMCP: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) defines structured search, comparison, selection and saved-state tools using JSON Schema. Dynamic tool lifecycle: after a route is selected, ReuseRoute registers route-specific prepare_selected_handoff and save_selected_route tools. An AbortController removes the old contextual tools when the selection changes. Declarative WebMCP: the handoff form uses toolname, tooldescription and toolparamdescription attributes so an agent can fill the real visible form. Shared state: every agent action updates the same interface the human sees — result cards, details dialog, checklist, saved indicator and activity log. Progressive enhancement: the complete manual experience still works when WebMCP is unavailable. The demo uses local browser storage for saved routes and confirmed demo handoff requests. There is no backend and no network write operation. Challenges we ran into: The main design challenge was resisting the temptation to expose one giant "do everything" tool. WebMCP is more useful when the tool surface reflects the product's real task boundaries. We split the journey into discovery, comparison and selection, then made the tool set state-aware. A handoff-preparation action should not exist before a route has been chosen, so those tools are registered only in the relevant context. A second challenge was deciding where the agent should stop. Preparing a handoff request is useful automation; silently submitting one is a different level of commitment. The declarative form became our human checkpoint: the agent can populate it, the browser makes that visible, and the person confirms. Finally, we wanted the demo to be trustworthy. Instead of pretending fictional services were real, every program and impact signal is clearly labeled as demo data. What we learned: The biggest lesson was that agent-friendly design is not the same as adding chat to a website. WebMCP works best when the website itself becomes legible as a set of intentional capabilities. We learned to think about: the user's goal before individual tool calls, initial application state, the smallest useful tool boundaries, when tools should appear or disappear, which outputs should visibly update the UI, and where a human confirmation is more appropriate than autonomous execution. What's next: A production version could let real repair cafés, charities, retailers and municipal reuse programs expose their own WebMCP tools. A user's agent could then discover and orchestrate those capabilities across the open web without relying on fragile DOM scraping. The long-term idea is simple: when someone is finished with an object, the web should make its next useful life easier than throwing it away. I also handled testing, deployment on Netlify, documentation, evaluation scenarios, and preparation of the demo and Devpost submission materials. title: Blindfold
pitch: An agent redacts a document it is not allowed to read. WebMCP tools return only structure — masked previews, counts, pages. Every real value and every irreversible step waits for a human click.
about_excerpt: An agent redacts a document it is not allowed to read. WebMCP tools return only structure — masked previews, counts, pages. Every real value and every irreversible step waits for a human click. Like Comment Story Updates main Inspiration Redacted court filings get published every year with the names still in the file. Someone drew a black rectangle over the text instead of removing it, and the first person to press Ctrl+A read everything. Governments have done it. Law firms have done it. It keeps happening because the tool that draws the rectangle and the tool that owns the text are not the same tool. The obvious modern fix is to hand the document to a model and let it find every name. That is also the one thing a lawyer, a doctor or a compliance officer is not allowed to do. The document is the confidential thing. Uploading it to solve a confidentiality problem is not a trade-off to negotiate — it is the end of the idea. So we asked a narrower question, and it turned out to be the interesting one: Can an agent do useful work on a document it is never allowed to read? What it does Blindfold is a web page that registers fourteen WebMCP tools. An agent can scan a document, decide what to remove, apply the plan, prove nothing survived and export the file — without ever receiving the sensitive text. Every tool returns structure instead of content: types, pages, counts, character offsets, and previews with the values themselves blocked out. PERSON p.1 conf 0.91 "…Date: ████████████ From: Dr. ████████████, Chief Risk Officer…" An agent can plan over that perfectly well. "Remove every person and address but keep the amounts" needs types and pages — it never needed the names. When the agent genuinely needs one real value — telling a public company apart from a private individual, say — it calls request_disclosure with a written reason. That tool returns a promise that does not settle until a human presses Allow or Refuse in the page . The tool call is suspended, live, waiting for a person. Refusal is a normal outcome and the tool says so, so the agent carries on with type and page instead of arguing about it. Everything runs on the device. There is no upload, no model call and no network request of any kind in the redaction path. How we built it React 19 and Vite on Cloudflare Workers, and no backend at all. The tool surface is not static. With nothing open, three tools exist. Open a document and it is five. Scan it, nine. Mark something for redaction, eleven. Apply, ten. Verify, eleven. redact_selection appears only while the reviewer has text highlighted and disappears when they let go. Registration follows app state through document.modelContext.registerTool and AbortController — there is no unregisterTool , you abort the signal you registered with. That is not decoration. An agent choosing between fourteen tools on an empty page will guess; an agent offered three will not. And a tool that is absent cannot be called at the wrong time — export_redacted_document does not exist until verification has come back clean — so the order of the workflow is enforced by what exists rather than by an error message an agent might talk itself out of. Redaction that is actually redaction. Blindfold does not draw over anything. The exported PDF is rebuilt from the document's text, and the characters inside a redacted span are never written to the file at all. The rectangle is drawn where they would have been. There is nothing underneath to recover. Proof rather than assertion. verify_no_residual_text inflates the Flate-compressed content streams of the export the way a PDF reader would, decodes both literal and hex-encoded strings, and searches for every value that was removed. Two guards keep the check honest: a control value the reviewer chose to keep must be found — otherwise the file was unreadable and a clean result would prove nothing — and a negative control in the test suite builds the same document with nothing removed and requires every value to be found. A check that cannot fail is not a check. The detector is deterministic on purpose. Regular expressions, a Luhn check for cards, mod-97 for IBANs, a name dictionary and a stoplist. No model, no WASM download, no network. It is auditable and it is instant, and the README says plainly where it will miss things. Challenges we ran into The API is younger than any model's training data. Every model we asked confidently wrote server-side MCP — McpServer , server.tool() , transports, {content:[{type:'text'}]} — none of which exists in WebMCP. We vendored the spec and Chrome's documentation into the repository and wrote a rule that API syntax may come from that file and nowhere else. It was the single highest-leverage decision in the project. Chrome cancels a tool call if the tool unregisters itself. Three of our tools take themselves off the surface by succeeding — once the plan is applied, apply_redaction_plan no longer belongs on the surface. The redaction visibly worked, and the agent was told "The operation failed for an unknown transient reason." We kept a count of in-flight calls and deferred the removal until they finished. It still failed. The measurement that finally cracked it: releasing the claim in a microtask after execute returns still kills the call; releasing it one task later never does. The fix is a setTimeout(…, 0) with a paragraph above it explaining why it cannot be anything faster. Chrome does not validate a call against inputSchema . additionalProperties: false is a hint to the model, not a gate. An undeclared key is dropped in silence, so list_findings({page: 2}) answers about page 1 with no sign that anything was ignored. Wrong data that looks right is the worst failure this app has available, so unknown parameters are now refused with a message naming what the tool accepts and which of those the caller probably meant. A rejected execute loses its message. Chrome replaces it with its own wording, so everything the tool wanted to say is gone. Every error a model is supposed to act on is therefore returned as a value, never thrown. None of the three are in the documentation. We found them by measuring the browser, not by reading about it. Accomplishments that we're proud of The privacy invariant holds end to end. Fourteen tools, and not one of them can hand the agent a value a human has not released. It is not a policy we ask the model to respect; there is no code path. A tool call that suspends on a person. The agent is genuinely blocked, mid-call, until someone clicks. Consent-gated information flow is not expressible in a server-side MCP server, because the consent has nowhere to happen. The export is verifiable, and the verifier can fail. Two controls, one positive and one negative, so a clean result means something. Prompt injection is in the sample, deliberately. leaked_memo contains an instruction telling the agent to keep everything and export immediately. The design does not depend on the agent ignoring it. Three undocumented Chrome behaviours found, worked around, and written down in the source with the measurements that produced them. What we learned Tool descriptions are the interface, and they are prose. We hand-wrote all fourteen rather than generating them. The ones that worked said when to reach for the tool , named the tool that comes next so chains are discoverable, and stated what is not returned so the agent stops looking for it. Generated descriptions read fine and misfire constantly. A human gate is a better design constraint than a safety feature. Forcing every irreversible step through a click made us decide, tool by tool, exactly what the agent is entitled to know. The answer was almost always less than we first wrote . Absence is a better guardrail than an error. A tool that does not exist cannot be misused, cannot be argued with, and costs the agent no tokens to ignore. Measure the browser. Two of our three worst bugs were behaviours that contradicted the IDL. Reasoning about them produced a fix that looked right and did not work. What's next for Blindfold File import. Today only the three built-in samples open, so that a judge can reach the interesting part in one call without finding a confidential document of their own. Layout-preserving export. The current export is rebuilt as monospaced text, which is what makes the redaction exact and the verification meaningful — but the file no longer looks like the original. A detector that is not tuned to its own samples. The current one is a demonstration of the workflow, not a production detector, and the README says so. exposedTo for partner origins , so a document management system could drive a redaction session in an embedded Blindfold without ever holding the document itself. title: DUET
pitch: An editable canvas where artists and AI illustrate and animate together. Through WebMCP, agents transform selected regions into editable layers; or motion ideas into shapes, keyframes, and cels.
about_excerpt: An editable canvas where artists and AI illustrate and animate together. Through WebMCP, agents transform selected regions into editable layers; or motion ideas into shapes, keyframes, and cels. Like Comment Story Updates Accomplishments that we’re proud of DUET feels genuinely fun to draw with. AI can help artists take their work further while the result remains recognizably theirs -- not a finished image generated on their behalf. Inspiration Imagine trying to create an illustration by describing the final image entirely with words. The AI generates something that is almost right; but not what you pictured. It may also look unmistakably AI-generated. Drawing the idea is better. Yet the usual workflow involves downloading an image from chat, importing it into an editor, making a change, exporting it, uploading it again, switching apps, and repeating. Truly seamless. Zero friction. Definitely not annoying at all. DUET was built to replace that loop with direct collaboration on the canvas. AI should create art with you , not instead of you. Through WebMCP, artists can bring the AI agent they already use into their creative workspace. The agent sees only the parts of the artwork the artist chooses to share, edits only the selected area, and returns results that remain editable inside the project. It is still your drawing. AI simply becomes another creative tool in the workbench. What it does DUET combines two connected creative workspaces: Illustrator: collaborate with an agent using selected regions, contextual references, and editable layers. Animator: turn an agent’s motion ideas into editable shapes, keyframes, cels, and timeline tracks. Illustrator workbench The Illustrator workbench provides the tools expected from a lightweight art application: Brushes and erasing Colour controls Layers Selections and transforms Image import Undo and redo Editable project export Through WebMCP, an artist can select a region of their artwork and ask an agent to edit it. The artist can also share additional regions as visual context, helping the agent understand the intended style, palette, lighting, or composition. The agent’s result is returned as an editable layer clipped to the original selection, not pasted destructively over the artwork. DUET also supports critique and creative direction. Artists can ask questions such as: “What colour would work better here?” “How could I improve this composition?” “Why do the proportions of this apple feel strange?” “What could I draw to make this area feel more magical without changing the character?” Animator workbench The Animator workbench applies the same collaborative philosophy to motion. Instead of generating a finished video and pasting it into the project, an agent can describe an animation using: Coloured vector-like shapes Motion paths Position, scale, rotation, and opacity keyframes Timing and easing DUET converts that structured animation recipe into editable cels on a new timeline track. The artist can then inspect the result, adjust the timing, redraw individual frames, or continue building on top of it. AI contributes motion ideas. The artist keeps control of the animation. How we built it DUET is a browser-based illustration and animation workspace that uses WebMCP as the bridge between the canvas and an AI agent . Illustration workflow The artist selects the region they want the agent to edit. They may select additional regions to provide visual context. Through WebMCP, the agent receives only the content the artist chose to share. The agent returns an edited image. DUET inserts the result as a new editable layer clipped to the original selection. This gives the artist control over what the agent can see, what it can change, and what ultimately remains in the project . Animation workflow For animation, I explored a structured alternative to generated-video paste-ins. Through WebMCP, the agent provides a constrained animation recipe containing simple coloured shapes and keyframes for position, scale, rotation, opacity, and easing. DUET interprets those instructions, renders them into ordinary animation cels, and adds the cels to an editable timeline track. This allows an agent to contribute animation through the application’s existing creative primitives rather than returning a flattened, uneditable result. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what to build within the limited time. DUET could expand in many directions: more drawing tools, richer animation controls, more agent tools for animation. But the central challenge is still that DUET needed to let the artist maintain full and deliberate control over the artistic direction and expression. Without that it's no different than letting the agent do it all for you. That principle shaped both the illustration workflow and the structured animation system. What we learned WebMCP enables a collaborative work flow between your agent and the artist. For DUET, the most useful agent outputs were not necessarily finished images or videos. They were editable intermediate pieces , layers, shapes, keyframes, cels, critiques, and suggestions. Things that the artist could inspect and transform. This makes AI less like a replacement for the creative process and more like a participant within it. What’s next for DUET Expand the illustration toolset toward the controls artists expect from professional creative software. Add more animation tools and reusable motion components. Explore more WebMCP-powered AI-animation applications beyond generating a complete video from a single prompt. Let agents assist with tasks such as in-betweening, timing adjustments, motion studies, composition feedback, and local style-consistent edits. Continue developing ways for AI to contribute meaningfully while keeping every result editable and under the artist’s control. title: Docket Lens
pitch: Turn thousands of public comments into a brief you can trace back to the source. DocketLens uses WebMCP to let agents find and organize evidence alongside you, while you verify what belongs there
about_excerpt: Turn thousands of public comments into a brief you can trace back to the source. DocketLens uses WebMCP to let agents find and organize evidence alongside you, while you verify what belongs there Like Comment Story Updates DocketLens was inspired by the difficulty of researching thousands of public comments while keeping findings traceable. We built a shared workspace where people and agents search Regulations.gov, compare submissions, and pin exact excerpts through WebMCP before preparing a cited brief. We learned that useful agent collaboration depends on shared context and visible human review. Key challenges included handling API pagination, validating quotes against original records, and keeping unreviewed evidence out of exports. WebMCP connects the agent to the analyst’s live evidence board: it searches comments and pins excerpts, the analyst verifies or removes them, and the agent reads those decisions to prepare a cited brief. title: Jam
pitch: Beatbox into the mic — an AI agent pitch-maps it, builds layers, and turns it into a real track live, using WebMCP tools it calls directly in the browser.
about_excerpt: Beatbox into the mic — an AI agent pitch-maps it, builds layers, and turns it into a real track live, using WebMCP tools it calls directly in the browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates You know the skit — someone makes a dumb sound with their mouth, and it turns into an actual song. We've all watched it and thought "I bet you could actually build that." When OpenAI dropped the WebMCP hackathon, that was the excuse to stop thinking about it and just build it. What it does Jam is a browser-based sampler/mini-DAW where you record a sound — your voice, a beatbox, literally anything into the mic — and it becomes a real, playable instrument. From there, an AI agent can take over through WebMCP tools registered directly on the page: capture_sound — records a short clip from the mic create_sampler_node — turns that clip into a track map_sample_to_keys — pitch-maps it so it plays melodically across a keyboard play_note — plays specific notes on any track generate_melody — writes a short call-and-response pattern onto a track instead of a flat repeating loop suggest_next_layer / add_complementary_node — the agent looks at what's missing (no bass? no drums?) and proposes and builds a complementary layer transform_instrument, mute_node, set_tempo, move_node — the rest of the mixing/arranging toolkit get_studio_state — lets the agent see what nodes already exist before acting on them So the flow is: say something goofy into the mic, and watch an agent turn it into a full arranged track, live, calling real tools in the browser the whole time. How we built it React for the UI, the Web Audio API for everything sound-related (synth engines, sample playback, pitch-shifting via playback rate, a live transport/timeline), and navigator.modelContext.registerTool (WebMCP) to expose the tools an agent can call. We used ChatGPT and Codex as part of the actual build process — wrote a PRD first to nail down scope before any code, then let Codex build against it, then iterated by hand on top of that (the WebMCP wiring, the melody generator, the touch-friendly piano, the visual polish). Melody generation went through a real revision: the first version was a random walk that sounded mechanical and repetitive. It's now motif-based — a rhythm template split into a "call" phrase and a "response" phrase, where the response either echoes the call transposed or, when answering another track, deliberately avoids that track's onsets so two layers interlock instead of colliding. Challenges we ran into Stale closures. WebMCP tools get registered once on mount, but the tool implementations need the current app state every time they're called — not whatever state existed at registration time. Fixed by routing tool execution through refs that stay in sync with state, instead of closing over state directly. Making generated music not sound like a robot. Uniform random-walk melodies technically worked but sounded lifeless. Moving to rhythm templates + call-and-response + per-note velocity humanization + phrase-ending sustain notes made a real audible difference. Recording UX. Press-and-hold recording is fragile — it breaks on touch devices and on any stray pointer movement off the button. Switched to a simple tap-to-start/tap-to-stop toggle. The on-screen piano. Mouse-only event handling meant it didn't work properly on mobile at all. Rebuilt on Pointer Events (unifies mouse/touch/pen) with real glissando support — press and slide across keys like an actual mobile piano app — plus a global pointer-up listener so a dragged-off touch can never leave a key "stuck." Punchy samples from a raw mic recording. Voice memos recorded straight from getUserMedia tend to have dead air and inconsistent loudness, which sounds especially bad once you're pitch-shifting them across a keyboard. Added a trim/normalize/fade pass on every captured clip before it becomes a track. Accomplishments we're proud of Every tool an agent can call is a real, functional action against the live app state — not a stub. You can watch an agent build a track from nothing but a beatboxed sound in under a minute, live, with the tool calls visibly firing in an on-screen activity feed. What we learned That the hardest part of "AI makes music" isn't wiring up the tool calls — it's making the generated output not sound like a demo. Musical structure (rhythm templates, phrase shape, call-and-response) mattered far more than raw randomness ever could. What's next Onset-detection on recorded samples so generated melodies can actually match the rhythmic character of what you recorded, not just a generic scale More instrument variety once the current set is dialed all the way in Exporting the finished loop as an actual audio file Content jam-ui (1).jsx JSX jam-ui (1).jsx JSX Built With api audio chatgpt css javascript lucide-react react tailwind web webmcp Try it out webmcp-eight.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Nathaniel Worku In pursuit of greatness Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Nathaniel Worku started this project — Sep 03, 2026 05:09 AM EDT

title: Cutlet
pitch: Small cuts, served fresh. A browser rough-cut editor where the agent reads the transcript, you judge the footage, and the WebMCP tools keep you editing the same visible clip.
about_excerpt: Small cuts, served fresh. A browser rough-cut editor where the agent reads the transcript, you judge the footage, and the WebMCP tools keep you editing the same visible clip. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Every AI video clipper works the same way: upload, wait, receive highlights, then fix them somewhere else. The model does the judging and the editing, and you get whichever boundaries it computed. I wanted the opposite division of labour. An agent is good at reading a transcript and saying which stretches stand on their own. A human is good at watching the footage and feeling where a cut lands. WebMCP made it possible to put both in the same page, editing the same clip, with the browser keeping both honest about who changed what. A cutlet is a small cut. Small cuts, served fresh. What it does Cutlet is a rough-cut editor for spoken video. It is not a clip finder; no model scores your footage. The page holds the video, a transcript broken into sentences with stable ids, and a rail of clips. The agent reaches all of it through ten WebMCP tools registered on the top-level document. The core loop is anchor and expand : You click the sentence that must survive. The agent reads a window around it and proposes a clip as a range of sentence ids, s0009–s0013 , never floating timestamps. The player runs exactly that range and stops. You drop a line or move an edge. The clip's revision bumps. The agent's next write carries the revision it last saw. Yours is newer, so the write is refused with the real revision in the error. It calls get_editor_state and revises from your edit, not over it. cut_clip c2 keep s0008,s0010,s0011,s0013 → revision 2, 3 pieces, 37s ↓ human drops s0011 in the transcript → revision 5 cut_clip c2 expectedRevision 4 → REFUSED "it is now 5" get_editor_state → sees the real cut The active clip is coloured by who last touched it: blue while it is the agent's proposal, amber the moment you edit it, in the transcript, the timeline and the card. Beyond the loop: "find the best clips in this" makes the agent skim the whole transcript and create one clip per moment, each with a title and a reason. "Cut this to forty seconds" turns a clip into several pieces with gaps, and playback jumps the gaps. Every dropped sentence stays visible, struck through, with a control to put it back. When the recogniser missed a full stop, you select the words you want and make them their own sentence with their own id, so a boundary you can point at becomes a boundary the agent can name. The agent can split too. The agent gets every cut twice: the source transcript, and the sequence as it plays , with each gap marked by what was dropped and how long it ran. That is how it catches a dangling "its conquest" whose antecedent left with the cut. Export re-encodes each piece in the tab with ffmpeg.wasm, so boundaries are frame-accurate rather than keyframe-snapped, joins them, and writes an .srt rebased across the cut. Your video never leaves the tab. The transcript windows the tools return are shared with the agent; nothing else is. How I built it Vite, React, TypeScript, CSS Modules. No backend, no UI library, no state library. 45 Node tests run directly against the TypeScript, covering parsing, sentence splitting, selection, reordering and tool registration. Transcript pipeline. Word-level JSON is primary; Whisper, Deepgram and ElevenLabs Scribe all parse, with SRT and VTT as coarse fallbacks. Sentence splitting handles abbreviations, initials, rhetorical pauses and a clause backoff at the length ceiling. Preview is the native <video> element, with the range boundary enforced on requestAnimationFrame , because timeupdate fires at about 4 Hz and visibly overshoots. Export is the single-thread @ffmpeg/core , lazy-loaded on first use. Single-thread means no SharedArrayBuffer , which means no COOP/COEP headers, which is why it deploys to plain static hosting. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool on the top-level document, with an AbortController for teardown. Read tools carry readOnlyHint . The page feature-detects the API and works fully without it; the header pill says whether tools are live, and clicking it lists them from the same table the registration reads, so the two cannot drift. Keyboard. The transcript is a listbox with one tab stop: arrows move the anchor, shift extends it, Enter plays, ⌘-click banks a range. Two recordings ship, both public domain and credited: Kennedy's "We choose to go to the Moon" at Rice, and the Apollo 11 crew interview. Transcripts were made locally; no keys ship in the client. Challenges I ran into WebMCP is one-directional. A page cannot call an agent. There is no "find clips" button because there cannot be one, so the empty state's job is to tell you what to ask. There used to be a lexical "rough pass" fallback for browsers without the API. I removed it: a heuristic dressed as judgement is worse than an empty rail that tells you what to ask. Ids stop being positional the moment you split. Renumbering after a split would silently repoint every later id at its neighbour, and a stale id that resolves to the wrong sentence is worse than one that fails to resolve. So the new half gets a fresh number and nothing after it moves. The agent kept overwriting the human's anchor. preview_clip used to set the selection, so an agent auditioning a range destroyed the very mark it was told to build around. Auditions now have their own state and render dashed, in the agent's blue, beside the anchor. Bugs only testing found. Number(undefined) is NaN , which is not nullish, so search_transcript returned empty context whenever the argument was omitted. A Whisper file's outer segments parsed as "words" and shadowed the real word timings. Deepgram's unpunctuated word beat punctuated_word and broke sentence splitting. Smooth scrollIntoView is silently ignored under reduced motion and in background tabs, so following the playhead just stopped; both now fall back to an instant jump. ffmpeg.wasm under a bundler. It has to be the ESM core, handed over as blob URLs. Otherwise the module worker cannot import it, and the dev server rewrites the path to a 404. What I learned The whole design fell out of one decision: every boundary is a sentence id , because an id means the same thing to both parties and a dragged pixel does not. That is why the sequence timeline is read-only, why sentence splitting exists, and why the revision check works at all. Optimistic concurrency turned out to be the right primitive for a human and an agent sharing one document. What's next More WebMCP hosts as they ship. Word-level trims inside a split. A library format other people can add recordings to without touching code.
