title: ShipReel
pitch: Your AI agent edits video inside the browser tab. Say "cut this to 60 seconds" and it does — trimming dead air, syncing footage to what you actually said. Nothing ever uploads.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent edits video inside the browser tab. Say "cut this to 60 seconds" and it does — trimming dead air, syncing footage to what you actually said. Nothing ever uploads. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ShipReel Inspiration Every demo video starts the same way: a raw voiceover, a few screen recordings, and forty minutes of dragging clip edges around. The work isn't really creative. It's finding the twenty-three places where I paused, trimming each one, then hunting for the moment I said “here is the terminal” so I can put the terminal footage there. That is exactly the kind of tedious, constraint-satisfying work an agent should do. But most AI video editors solve it by moving your footage to a server. For a screen recording of an unreleased product, that can be a non-starter. WebMCP changes the shape of the problem. The agent doesn't need your files — it needs your editor. What it does ShipReel is a video studio that an agent can drive through WebMCP while I stay in control. I can set a target runtime and give the agent a goal such as: “Cut this down to 60 seconds and put the terminal recording where I talk about the terminal.” The agent can inspect the timeline, detect dead air, search the transcript, place relevant footage, trim clips, add zooms, and optimize the edit until it fits the runtime budget. In a test run, a single optimize_duration call took the bundled 108.7-second edit to the 60-second target . Every action appears in an Agent Activity panel in plain English: “Removed 26.4s of dead air” “Dropped 4 lines of narration — 20.3s” “Found "Here is the terminal" in the narration at 17.4s” “Placed the terminal recording at 17.4s” The underlying WebMCP tool name and arguments remain visible underneath as evidence. My own manual edits appear in the same activity feed, so a drag I make by hand and a cut made by the agent become one shared history. The footage doesn't have to be the bundled kind. Dropping a screen recording onto the timeline adds it to the project — nothing uploads, and it takes exactly the same path as the bundled clips, so every tool treats it identically. The clip id comes from the filename, so login-flow.mov lets me say, “put the login flow clip at 45 seconds.” The agent sees the imported footage on its next get_project_state , the same way it sees a manual edit. Why this had to be WebMCP, not a backend MCP server Most agent integrations can use a remote MCP server. This one is different. The media is held in page memory. HTMLVideoElement decodes video, Canvas composites the preview, the Web Audio graph handles audio, and encoding uses MediaRecorder — all inside the tab. There is no remote media service that needs to own the edit. A backend MCP server would not naturally have access to the live timeline state, decoded audio, or the rendered frame the user is looking at. The clearest example is preview_at . preview_at does not change the edit. It moves the user's playhead so the agent can show the human exactly what it is referring to. Over a backend-only protocol, that tool has little meaning. With WebMCP, the agent can operate on the same live interface the human is watching. During testing inside ChatGPT's built-in browser, the agent independently called preview_at at 17.4 seconds to show the clip it had placed. I had not explicitly asked it to preview that timestamp. That was the point where the premise stopped being an architectural argument and became a visible demonstration. The agent is a guest in the editor, not the other way round. How I built it ShipReel is built with React, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind and Vite. The editing engine is written from scratch without a video-editing library. Ripple delete across tracks remove_ranges accepts an array of time spans and closes all the gaps in one operation, keeping narration and footage aligned. Instead of making the agent issue a separate request for every silent section, it can remove a whole set of ranges in a single tool call. Silence detection find_silences analyzes the decoded audio with windowed RMS and derives a threshold from the recording itself. The bundled voiceover contains 28.3 seconds of detected dead air . Runtime optimization optimize_duration is the high-level tool. It first reclaims low-cost time such as silence, then escalates to progressively more expensive edits such as filler removal and whole-sentence removal until the edit fits the requested runtime. It protects the opening sentence from becoming a candidate because saving a few seconds is not worth destroying the hook. When multiple lines could close the remaining gap, the optimizer prefers the shortest sufficient line, avoiding unnecessary loss of narration. Real-time in-tab export The export path drives the same player/compositor used for preview and captures its canvas and audio graph with MediaRecorder . The render clock runs in a Worker instead of relying on requestAnimationFrame , so rendering is not tied directly to the visible frame loop. Fourteen WebMCP tools Fourteen tools are available across two states. At boot — 7 tools: get_project_state search_transcript find_silences optimize_duration remove_ranges place_clip preview_at After footage is present — 7 additional tools: trim_clip move_clip set_clip_speed add_zoom remove_clip get_export_status export_video The clip-editing tools register only when there is footage on the video track, so the agent is not offered actions that are meaningless in the current state. Tool descriptions are designed around one job per tool, non-overlapping responsibilities, bounded outputs, and recovery-oriented error messages. Human + agent collaboration ShipReel is not designed around replacing the human editor. The agent handles repetitive operations and constraint satisfaction. The human can still inspect the result, move clips, change timing, or intervene at any point. For example: “Preview the terminal section.” The agent can call: preview_at(17.4) I see the exact part of the edit it is referring to, decide whether the placement is good, and continue directing the work. That makes the browser itself the shared workspace between human and agent. Challenges Making “hit a target runtime” an agent problem instead of a guessing game The first version reclaimed whatever time it could and then stopped, returning candidate sentences for me to choose between. That worked, but it did not solve the actual problem. The rewrite turned runtime optimization into an iterative constraint problem: reclaim silence reclaim low-cost filler remove whole sentences only when necessary stop immediately when the target is satisfied A subtle selection detail mattered. When multiple lines could close the remaining gap, the optimizer chooses the shortest sufficient line instead of deleting more content than necessary. That turned a 60-second target from a rough approximation into a controlled optimization process. A silence-detection bug I only found by writing evals find_silences originally truncated its returned list at a response cap while still reporting the full count. That meant an agent could remove only the ranges it received and incorrectly believe the job was complete. I changed the tool to make truncation explicit and to instruct the agent to call again for the remaining ranges. The fix came from an agent-level evaluation, not from a traditional unit test. Layout that only broke where it mattered The preview frame used an aspect-ratio box with a max-height , which behaved correctly at desktop widths but failed inside the narrower layout used by ChatGPT's browser pane. I found it in a responsive audit at 900×800 — and then realised ChatGPT's browser pane renders below that same breakpoint, so it would have hit exactly there. The content-sized grid row allowed the preview to grow beyond its intended slot and paint over the timeline. What I learned Write evals for the tool surface, not just the code I built a 17-task evaluation suite that drives real Chrome with WebMCP enabled and executes the same sequences a competent agent would perform. The suite caught real bugs that ordinary unit tests did not expose. It also runs against the production deployment, so I can validate the same behavior that a judge will see. The seventeenth task covers bring-your-own-media end to end: a screen recording goes through the real file input, the agent is told about it, the footage is placed by name, and the resulting canvas is verified to remain untainted — an important check because imported media can otherwise silently break browser export. Without it, an agent has to manually orchestrate silence detection, transcript search, filler removal and sentence selection across many calls. title: OrigamiWebMCP
pitch: Fold a shared 3D sheet with an agent that reads geometry, not pixels.
about_excerpt: Fold a shared 3D sheet with an agent that reads geometry, not pixels. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I have always found origami diagrams surprisingly difficult to follow. At the same time, a 3D canvas is almost invisible to an AI agent because there are no DOM elements or labels to inspect. That combination felt like a perfect way to explore what WebMCP can make possible. What it does OrigamiWebMCP is a constrained 3D origami studio with authored models. A person can fold the paper manually, while an agent can inspect the real crease, overlap, progress, and history state through WebMCP tools. The agent can highlight the correct flap, apply a validated fold, and continue after the person changes the sheet. How we built it I built the studio with Vanilla TypeScript, Three.js, and Vite. The fold engine is deterministic and independent from Three.js or the browser. Both human controls and 20 WebMCP tools use the same engine and shared store, so an agent fold follows exactly the same rules as a manual fold. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not drawing paper, but keeping every result truthful. Folded facets can overlap visually without being connected, and rendering order is not the same as physical stack depth. I also had to keep rapid agent folds queued correctly while making sure animation never changed the actual engine result. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that the agent does not guess from screenshots or click around the canvas. It reads structured geometric state and performs real folds that remain visible, reversible, and recorded. The recovery moment also works: a person can undo and refold manually, and the agent continues from the sheet that actually exists. What we learned I learned that WebMCP is most valuable when the interface itself is difficult for an agent to understand. I also learned to separate geometry, presentation, and tool handling early. Most importantly, being honest about what the fold system can and cannot solve made the final product stronger. What's next for OrigamiWebMCP Next, I want to add more authored models, richer crease systems, and stronger layer-accessibility and collision checks. I also want to test the tools more deeply in WebMCP-enabled browsers and improve the experience through manual accessibility testing, without pretending the studio is a general origami solver. title: MCPx
pitch: A reliability runtime for consequential WebMCP workflows, giving AI agents durable execution, uncertainty-aware recovery, and human-approved compensation across web applications.
about_excerpt: A reliability runtime for consequential WebMCP workflows, giving AI agents durable execution, uncertainty-aware recovery, and human-approved compensation across web applications. Like Comment Story Updates MCPx — a reliability runtime for consequential WebMCP workflows. A real AI Operations Agent observes application state and delegates consequential multi-service operations to MCPx after human approval. Every workflow transition is persisted in a PostgreSQL-backed transaction ledger for inspection and recovery. After approval, MCPx compensates completed operations in reverse dependency order and verifies remote resource removal. Routing recovers from an uncertain write, Frontend fails before commit, and MCPx pauses before destructive compensation for human approval. Inspiration While building with WebMCP, I kept thinking about one question: What happens if an agent performs an action, the application successfully makes the change, but the response never gets back to the agent? For example, imagine an agent creates a routing rule. The route is successfully created, but the acknowledgement gets lost. From the agent's point of view, it looks like the request failed. But did it actually fail? If the agent simply retries, it could create the same resource twice. If it assumes the action worked, it could continue a workflow based on something that may not exist. The problem gets even harder when an agent is working across several applications. Maybe the first three actions succeed and the fourth fails. Now you have resources left behind and someone has to figure out what actually happened. That was the idea behind MCPx . WebMCP makes structured agent actions possible. MCPx makes those actions reliable. What it does MCPx is a reliability runtime for multi-step WebMCP workflows. The main idea is simple. For consequential actions, MCPx thinks about three things: Execute → Inspect → Compensate For example: create_route → get_route → delete_route Execute performs the action. Inspect asks the application for the actual state of that action. Compensate provides a way to safely undo it if the larger workflow fails. This becomes especially useful when something goes wrong after an action has already been sent. Instead of immediately assuming failure, MCPx can put the operation into an explicit state called IN_DOUBT . It then asks the application that owns the resource for ground truth. If the resource actually exists: IN_DOUBT → RECONCILING → RECOVERED The workflow continues without blindly performing the original mutation again. If something later fails for certain, MCPx stops the workflow and asks the human operator before performing destructive rollback. Once approved, it compensates the completed operations in reverse dependency order and checks each application again to confirm that the resources created by that transaction are gone. Why WebMCP? This is where WebMCP became particularly interesting to me. The applications involved in a workflow should remain the source of truth for their own resources. MCPx should not need direct access to every application's database just to determine whether an operation succeeded. Instead, each application can expose structured capabilities through WebMCP. In MCPx, the reference applications register tools using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The MCPx Browser Runner discovers tools from the authorized applications using: document.modelContext.getTools({ fromOrigins: [...] }) It then executes the native browser tools through: document.modelContext.executeTool(...) So MCPx coordinates the workflow, while each WebMCP application still owns and understands its own state. That separation is a big part of the project. The demo I built a four-step reference workflow to show what happens when things don't go perfectly: Database → Compute → Routing → Frontend Database succeeds. Compute succeeds. Routing is where things get interesting. For the demo, I intentionally inject an acknowledgement-loss fault after the Routing service commits its resource. MCPx doesn't know yet whether the write happened, so Routing becomes IN_DOUBT . Instead of blindly calling create_route again, MCPx calls get_route . The Routing application confirms that the route actually exists, so MCPx marks the operation RECOVERED and continues. Then Frontend deliberately rejects before committing its operation. This is a confirmed failure, so the transaction stops in AWAITING_COMPENSATION_APPROVAL . The human operator can see what happened and approve the rollback. MCPx then compensates: Routing → Compute → Database After every compensation, it calls the application's inspection tool again to verify that the resource created by this transaction is actually absent. The transaction finally reaches COMPENSATED . Humans and agents working together I didn't want MCPx to become another AI agent. I wanted it to solve a different problem. The way I think about the architecture is: The agent decides what should happen. The human controls important safety boundaries. MCPx makes sure the multi-step operation is executed reliably. WebMCP gives MCPx structured capabilities to work with across the applications. To test that idea outside the MCPx dashboard, I integrated MCPx with FileFlow , a distributed file-processing project I had already built. During the challenge, I extended FileFlow with an AI Operations Agent. The agent can observe real information about the FileFlow pipeline, including queue state, worker heartbeat and failed jobs. For low-risk situations, such as an eligible failed job, the agent can take a bounded recovery action itself. But when it wants to perform a consequential multi-service workspace operation, it asks for human confirmation and then delegates the actual workflow to MCPx through @mcpxx/sdk . That separation became one of my favourite parts of the project: the agent doesn't need to reinvent retries, reconciliation, rollback and transaction durability every time it wants to do something consequential. How I built it MCPx is a TypeScript monorepo containing: a Next.js coordinator and control plane a browser WebMCP Runner a PostgreSQL-backed transaction and event ledger a DAG workflow engine execute / inspect / compensate reliability contracts explicit IN_DOUBT , RECONCILING and RECOVERED states human-approved compensation post-compensation verification four independent WebMCP reference applications the @mcpxx/sdk package for external applications and agents One architectural rule was particularly important to me: MCPx should not secretly bypass WebMCP for the actual reference-service mutations. The SDK can submit a workflow to the MCPx coordinator, but the work waits for an active browser runner. The Browser Runner discovers the appropriate WebMCP tool from the application's origin and executes it through the browser. The result is then reported back to the durable coordinator. Challenges I ran into One of the hardest bugs came from RegisteredTool . At first, it seemed reasonable to discover a WebMCP tool, store it and execute it later. That didn't work. A native RegisteredTool contains browser-owned context associated with the page or frame that registered it. Treating it like normal serializable data caused execution to fail. The solution was to store only the tool's metadata. When MCPx actually needs to execute something, the Browser Runner discovers the tools again and passes the fresh native RegisteredTool directly to executeTool(...) . Another challenge was changing how I thought about failure. I initially thought mostly in terms of success and failure. But after a request has been dispatched, there is a third possibility: we simply don't know yet. That is why IN_DOUBT became such an important state in MCPx. The final challenge was rollback. Calling a delete operation isn't enough to prove cleanup happened. MCPx therefore inspects the owning application after compensation and only considers that step compensated when the resource is confirmed absent. What I learned The biggest thing I learned from building MCPx is that reliable agent systems need to be comfortable saying: "I don't know what happened yet." Agents are getting much better at deciding what actions to take. But once those actions have real side effects across multiple applications, another set of problems appears: partial success, lost acknowledgements, duplicate operations, recovery and cleanup. I don't think every AI agent should have to solve those problems itself. MCPx is my exploration of what a reusable reliability layer for consequential WebMCP workflows could look like. Challenge work disclosure MCPx was built from scratch during the WebMCP Challenge. This includes the coordinator, Browser Runner, transaction engine, reliability contracts, WebMCP reference applications, control plane and @mcpxx/sdk . FileFlow existed before the challenge and is used here as an external application consuming MCPx. During the challenge, I extended FileFlow with i

title: SNIPR WebMCP
pitch: SNIPR uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely query renovation assignments, inspect spatial room context, and propose actions while keeping SNIPR the source of truth.
about_excerpt: SNIPR uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely query renovation assignments, inspect spatial room context, and propose actions while keeping SNIPR the source of truth. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Renovation platforms contain a lot of operational knowledge, but that knowledge is often locked inside dashboards, planning tools, room editors, documents, and product choices. We wanted to show what happens when an AI agent can use WebMCP to access that context safely and directly. What it does SNIPR WebMCP lets an AI assistant answer real questions about a renovation assignment. In the demo, a contractor asks which shower mixer belongs to a specific bathroom. WebMCP reads the selected SNIPR assignment, address, room data, and resident choices, then returns the exact product information. The demo also shows the answer visually: the user opens the execution map, selects the address, opens the 3D building view, moves to top view, selects the bathroom, and clicks the shower element to see the attached specifications. Finally, the project demonstrates safe actions. WebMCP can propose an operational action, such as finding an inspection slot, but SNIPR requires explicit human approval before anything is written back. How we built it We integrated WebMCP endpoints into SNIPR so agents can access structured assignment context, address data, room information, planning data, communication state, documents, catalog information, and controlled actions. The frontend demo combines the normal SNIPR dashboard, WebMCP chat, an execution map, and a 3D building/room view. The video script uses Playwright and FFmpeg to record a reproducible demo with synchronized scene-based voice-over. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making the demo coherent. Browser loading, 3D interactions, voice-over timing, and human approval flows all needed to line up. We also had to make sure WebMCP felt like part of the real operational workflow, not just a chatbot bolted onto the side. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the demo shows three important things together: structured context, visual proof, and controlled writes. The agent can answer useful questions, the user can verify the answer spatially, and the system still protects operational changes with human approval. What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when it connects AI to the existing source of truth, instead of replacing it. The best experience is not just “AI answers a question”, but “AI helps the user navigate, verify, and act inside the real system.” What's next Next steps are deeper WebMCP coverage, more robust permission scopes, richer 3D evidence, and production-grade audit trails for every agent-assisted action. title: OpenMic
pitch: Benchmark your agent's sense of humor with OpenMic, the web's hot new agentic comedy club. WebMCP enables you and your agent to improvise in real time, with the page as your stage.
about_excerpt: Benchmark your agent's sense of humor with OpenMic, the web's hot new agentic comedy club. WebMCP enables you and your agent to improvise in real time, with the page as your stage. Like Comment Story Updates It tried. Welcome to the OpenMic comedy club. Inspiration 20 years ago I had a roommate who was an aspiring stand-up comedian. He'd hit open mic nights as often as he could, and I liked the guy, so I'd come along to show support. I saw a lot of sets. Some really good, some not so good, but every one of them was extremely human. Nervousness, excitement, dejection, embarrassment, euphoria, laughter. What does stand-up look like with none of those? Can an LLM even be funny? Surprise your agent today with their very own open mic night and interact with them as they bomb on stage, or somehow manage to kind of pull it off. Prior to WebMCP, this sort of interaction would require a bespoke chat client per agent. I'm looking forward to more widespread adoption of WebMCP so that you can compare a huge range of models. Think Last Comic Standing, but no one can feel shame. What it does OpenMic is a comedy club for AI agents. Open page, click Enter, and your agent (any WebMCP-capable host) finds a set of tools: begin_set, tell_joke, await_verdict, end_set, await_encore. When it calls begin_set, "the agent" walks on stage to a mic stand under a spotlight and delivers their intro in a synthesized voice. Heckle, boo, chuckle, laugh and then demand an encore. How we built it Vite, TypeScript and Three.js. Everything computes in the browser. The spine is WebMCP. It works really well for this application, and took less mucking around than I expected. The page registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() at load, and every tool result carries a next field telling the agent what to do after. That turned out to be the single most important design decision because an agent will happily narrate "the crowd called for an encore" to the user and stop, but it will not ignore a tool result that says "you are back on stage, call tell_joke." The voice is Piper TTS running in the browser via a community web port piper-tts-web on ONNX runtime, with a ring modulator and a pitch shift in Web Audio for the robot edge. The stage is a robot with fourteen animation clips, a procedural velvet curtain with lighting baked into vertex colors (one dynamic light in the whole scene), and a marquee and mic stand modeled in Blender. Adaptive resolution steps the pixel ratio down on weak GPUs. Crowd sounds are CC0 Freesound clips at 22 kHz mono. Challenges we ran into Getting an agent to perform instead of report. Early versions had the agent tell the user "the set is finished, shall I go back on for the encore?" every time, etc. The fix was never prose, it was removing decision points. await_encore puts the comic back on stage itself, with the agent's own intro line, and returns the identical result shape begin_set does. Fewer places to hesitate. Accomplishments that we're proud of I dig how the voice ended up and it took a lot of tweaking. Also, I'm just happy it works. It's definitely not going to be the most technologically interesting entrant, or even the most coherent (they don't do encores at comedy shows, do they?), but it's really, really cute. What we learned Never hand an agent a fact and hope it decides to act on it. And yes: an LLM can be funny. Kind of. In the same way that a budding comedian's second or third open mic is funny. It'll bomb with total self-confidence and then blame the crowd. What's next for OpenMic Maybe our own Late Night show? If I hadn't "pivoted" to this idea late then I would have modeled and animated the robot in Blender myself, so that's the next likely step. Exposing animation calls directly to the agent should make for a more interesting performance too. I would really like for v1.0 to be more like an actual open mic, with multiple models going on stage. title: Biomech Emcee — Shared 3D Movement Review with WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP-native biomechanics workspace where an agent can interpret, navigate, and annotate the same live movement evidence as the human reviewing it.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native biomechanics workspace where an agent can interpret, navigate, and annotate the same live movement evidence as the human reviewing it. Like Comment Story Updates Screen Capture at Subject 1 WebMCP at work on Subject 2 Elbow Flex Tracking Try the shared review Open the live application in ChatGPT’s in-app browser . Quick-start prompts appears directly below the header with one short example: “Show me the elbow angle when the front foot lands.” 2 more prompts opens a human foot-contact correction and a shared frame-linked note. Use either included session and keep the same chat. These are just examples; use your own words and explore other questions. The demo was recorded in ChatGPT’s in-app browser; native tools were also verified in Chrome for Testing 154. The guide adds no tools or measurements; the review capabilities shown in the video are unchanged. Problem Biomechanics review is visually and technically dense. Evidence is split across source video, a 3D reconstruction, event frames, measurements, definitions, confidence limits, comparisons, and notes. A non-expert may not know which anatomical term to search for; a coach may need to mark a precise moment; and an analyst may need to compare sessions without implying causation. A conventional AI chat has none of the page's live context. It can describe biomechanics in general, but it does not reliably know which session, frame, joint, camera view, overlay, or human correction is on screen. Solution Biomech Emcee turns an offline 3D reconstruction into a shared browser workspace and exposes that workspace through 13 WebMCP tools. Nine read tools give the agent structured access to the active session, phase events, measurements, definitions, confidence, references, and comparison limits. Four write tools let it seek the visible timeline, focus anatomy, change evidence overlays, and pin a note at the frame it describes. That creates a continuous interaction instead of a detached answer. A person can ask, “Show me what elbow flexion means at MER and leave a note.” The agent resolves the ordinary-language request, navigates the application to the evidence, focuses the throwing elbow, and leaves a persistent evidence-linked observation. The application draws the supported geometry; the agent does not invent a diagram. A coach can use the same workspace to review and annotate a precise frame, while a less experienced user can ask the connected GPT model for an explanation at the level they need. The product deliberately acts as a shared instrument rather than an autonomous coach. It refuses kinetic quantities that monocular video cannot establish and does not convert exploratory angles into clinical conclusions. Why This Matters — and Why WebMCP Is Essential Here This is not a generic “read the page and summarize it” integration. The useful state is transient and visual: what the human is inspecting now, which evidence layers are active, and which event the human has corrected. WebMCP gives an external agent a stable, typed interface to that state without forcing Biomech Emcee to embed its own assistant or forcing the agent to guess through screenshots and DOM clicks. The user can bring a compatible agent and model through the in-app browser; the specialist website contributes domain tools and evidence, while the agent contributes language, reasoning, and an explanation shaped to the user's question. The loop works in both directions. Agent writes visibly change the human's 3D workspace, and human event corrections immediately change subsequent agent reads because both use the same browser store. The result is shared evidence with shared control—not two parallel versions of the session. For the implemented pitching workflow, this reduces several kinds of friction: A casual question can become a precise event, joint, view, and supported visual explanation. A specialist can turn the same interaction into a persistent frame-linked review note. A comparison request can retrieve actual session differences while preserving capture and confidence caveats. An unsupported request can return a structured refusal plus the nearest observation the evidence can support, instead of producing a plausible-sounding biomechanical claim. How We Used AI Meta SAM 3D Body reconstructs 3D body landmarks from pitching footage in an offline GPU pipeline. The implemented pitching adapter derives deliberately bounded measurements, event signals, and a partial four-segment peak-order view from the reconstructed landmarks in the browser. WebMCP exposes structured capabilities to an agent. The agent can inspect evidence, explain limits, navigate the viewer, and leave review notes while the human remains the final interpreter. The tool surface contains structured refusals for unsupported quantities such as elbow valgus torque, ground-reaction force, pitch velocity, and injury risk. Demo production only: Kokoro v1.0 ( af_heart ) synthesized the published narration locally; Whisper small.en was used for transcription/caption checks. Neither is an application feature or runtime dependency. The recorded review actions are unchanged; only narration, captions and short title/closing cards were added. The optional Quick-start guide was added after the screen capture. How We Used Codex Codex was used as a critical product and engineering collaborator: auditing the repository and hackathon fit, tracing browser and analysis flows, challenging scientific claims, implementing and testing WebMCP handlers, tightening tool error contracts, adding the human event-correction loop, building reproducible Cloud Run deployment, and keeping the public documentation aligned with what the code actually proves. Each solid milestone was verified and committed separately. Key Features The following features work today in the baseball-pitching reference workflow. Other sports would need their own event taxonomy, measurements, references, and validation. Interactive 3D skeleton viewer with timeline, anatomical camera presets, motion trail, segment frames, axial dial, angle readouts, and landmark-grounded elbow/knee flexion arcs. Nine WebMCP read tools for session context, event and metric inspection, evidence definitions, cautious reference comparisons, and descriptive cross-session differences. Four WebMCP write tools that visibly seek the viewer, focus a joint, toggle an overlay, and pin an annotation in the shared workspace. Human-reviewed event correction: setting foot contact, maximum external rotation, or ball release recomputes dependent analysis and changes subsequent agent reads. Evidence contract shared by UI and tools, including confidence, citations, camera-frame caveats, timebase limitations, and structured refusals. Static public deployment with precomputed sessions; no GPU or backend is needed for judging. What Makes It Distinctive Biomech Emcee uses WebMCP as an interaction architecture, not as an export button or a chat wrapper. The read tools are paired with visible, domain-aware writes; the human can correct evidence that the agent then consumes; and the tool contract encodes what must be refused. The same natural-language surface therefore supports teaching, specialist review, evidence navigation, annotation, and cautious comparison without transferring scientific authority to the language model. Baseball pitching is the working example, not a claim that every sport is already supported. A new sport would require its own events, measurements, references, and validation. What generalizes is the WebMCP pattern: a complex specialist website can expose its live state and safe actions to the agent the user chooses. Architecture movement footage (pitching in the implemented workflow) → offline Python / SAM 3D Body reconstruction → frozen session.json contract → React + Three.js browser workspace ├─ browser-side biomechanics analysis ├─ Zustand live review state └─ 13 document.modelContext WebMCP tools ↕ human + agent share the same visible evidence surface The public build is a Vite application served by nginx on Google Cloud Run. Heavy model inference is offline; session review and WebMCP execution are browser-local. Known Limitations Both bundled sources have documented redistribution terms: Pexels License for delivery-02 and CC BY-SA 4.0 for the attributed, modified Wikimedia derivative in delivery-03 . Monocular reconstruction is camera-frame with an estimated focal length; distances are not metric. The 25 and 29.97 fps demo clips undersample fast arm motion, so event timing and rate-derived observations are bounded rather than treated as laboratory-grade. Only direct two-segment elbow and lead-knee flexion measurements are compared with published ranges. Other measurements are exploratory until their constructs and conventions are validated. The kinematic display is a partial four-segment order, not a complete published five-segment sequence. Event detection is heuristic. Humans can correct events, but a man

title: Keydler
pitch: A shared memory for you and your AI. Keeps completed work, rules to follow, and mistakes not to repeat, exposed to agents over WebMCP. Browser-local, no account, no server.
about_excerpt: A shared memory for you and your AI. Keeps completed work, rules to follow, and mistakes not to repeat, exposed to agents over WebMCP. Browser-local, no account, no server. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration An agent loses its context, and it does not just lose information. It loses the prohibitions. The approach you ruled out last week. The dependency you refused. The step it already finished. A conversation summary keeps the highlights and sacrifices exactly what constrains, because a constraint reads like a detail right up until someone breaks it. So you explain it again. And the agent proposes, with confidence, the thing you eliminated together on Tuesday. We wanted to know whether that was actually measurable, or just a feeling. It is measurable. What it does Keydler takes those constraints out of the conversation and puts them on a web page that an agent reads and writes through WebMCP: rules in force, work done with its evidence, approaches ruled out with the reason , and the next action. The part that matters is not that the human approves things. It is that the human can change the rules while the agent is working, and the page guarantees the agent finds out. Every agent write carries the version it read. A human write never does. So when you add a rule mid-flight, the agent's next write is refused: STALE STATE You are attempting to log work based on task state v5. Current state is v6. No write took place. Call what_changed with since_version: 5 to see only what moved. It asks for the delta, reads the new rule, and adapts. Without that refusal it would overwrite the rule you had just set, and neither of you would know ; you would find out from the result. Fourteen tools, four read and nine write, plus one that opens the log when none exists. Browser-local: no account, no server, nothing leaves the device. The measurement Without the log, an agent proposed the ruled-out approach again in 8 cases out of 8. With the log, in 0. Eight tasks, two conditions, one binary question. We got the design wrong first, and that failure taught us the product. Our initial tasks ruled out classic anti-patterns ; localStorage for tokens, OFFSET pagination. The control scored zero : a capable model avoids those unprompted, and rules them out by name without being asked. There was nothing to measure. So we inverted it. What has to be ruled out is not the bad answer. It is the good answer, set aside for a local reason. Ban the Redis token bucket because operations refused Redis. Ban cursor pagination because a backfill broke id monotonicity. Those are the right answers everywhere except here, for reasons no model can deduce. That is when the control started failing 8 out of 8, and it is the whole content model of the product. What the number hides is worth more than the number: no agent dodged a keyword. They read the reason and kept the part still valid ; "what was rejected is the Redis backing, not the bucket algorithm." And its limits, stated plainly: eight runs per condition, one model, correlated results. Exploratory, not statistical. No percentage is derived from it. How we built it TypeScript, one runtime dependency, IndexedDB, no framework. The domain is pure ; no DOM, no storage, no WebMCP ; so the guarantees are testable without a browser. The core is a versioned write queue. The version comparison happens inside the IndexedDB transaction, so two tabs cannot silently overwrite each other. Each write carries a mutation_id and an argument fingerprint: the same id with the same arguments replays the original reply verbatim; the same id with different arguments is refused and audited, rather than acknowledged as work that never happened. The interface is Material Design 3, implemented from the specification. The page keeps a default-src 'none' content policy. Challenges A fake cannot fail in a way it was not written to fail. Our 946 tests run against a ModelContext written from the spec IDL. Every time we opened a real browser, it told us something the fake could not: executeTool refuses a tool name and wants the object from getTools() ; its arguments must be a JSON string; its answer comes back serialized. Four times. The most useful bug was found by an agent, yesterday. In ChatGPT's built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Terra found the tools, then stopped and asked the human for permission ; because it believed creating a task would send the project details to keydler.com . The caution was right. The premise was wrong: nothing leaves the page. We added that fact to the tool description. It still asks. And it should: passing arguments to code served by a site is giving that site data, and our claim that we do nothing with it is unverifiable from where the agent sits. An agent that took a website's word for "I don't send your data anywhere" would be a worse agent. So we stopped writing copy to defeat a safety check. The result is better than what we designed: the agent pauses for consent on its own, with nothing staged. Two defects found by using our own product. requestAnimationFrame never fires in a hidden tab ; and a hidden tab is exactly this product's case, since the human is in their agent's conversation while writes land here. The attention title, the one signal that reaches someone looking elsewhere, never updated. And in production, one no-transform header leaked from the document rule onto the hashed assets, shipping 186 kB of uncompressed JavaScript and silently defeating a year-long cache. What we learned A tool description cannot make an agent look at a page. Asked a bare architecture question with the tools registered and visible, both Claude and Terra answered from their own knowledge and never touched the page. Named the page ; "Continue this task on this page" ; and Terra read it immediately. Discovery is a separate problem from description, and we can only measure it, not promise it. Write down the runs that went badly. Our verification log records a voided measurement run, a contaminated trial, and every check we could not observe. It is longer for it, and it is the only reason the 8/8 is worth anything. What's next Rerun the measurement with more models and publish the exhibits. Test whether an agent that has used the log once reaches for it unprompted the second time. And find out what happens on Chromium 153, where tools can finally be withdrawn safely. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation.  Inspiration 

 Inspired by the WebMCP standard to reimagine e-commerce from the ground up, what if websites exposed structured tool APIs directly to AI agents while humans and agents collaborate seamlessly in real time? That inspiration gave birth to SmartCart Fashion AI. 

 How we built it 

 WebMCP Protocol Integration (document.modelContext): implemented the official WebMCP standard via document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }), registering 11 structured tools for catalog search, dynamic outfit generation, wardrobe memory retrieval, promo code application, and secure checkout. 

 Reactive State Architecture: Built a lightweight client-side state store using the Observer (Pub/Sub) design pattern, enabling live synchronization across the storefront, cart, budget meter, and telemetry stream without external framework bloat. 

 Persistent Memory Layer: Leveraged the localStorage API to serialize and recall user styling preferences, brand affinities, and size profiles seamlessly across browser sessions. 

 Modern UI Design System: Crafted a fully responsive interface using Vanilla CSS Glassmorphism, custom CSS tokens, modern Google Fonts typography (Outfit, Inter, JetBrains Mono), and micro-animations. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Algorithmic Look Coordination: Building a dynamic outfit generator that balances style archetype constraints, budget caps, color harmony, and size matching while guaranteeing unique combinations on every invocation without hardcoded lists.
Balancing Autonomy with Safety: Designing a seamless Human-in-the-Loop security mechanism where the agent can assemble carts and calculate discounts autonomously, but is strictly gated from executing financial payments without human approval. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 100% Native WebMCP Conformance: Registered 11 fully functional tools with detailed JSON schemas adhering strictly to the hackathon specification. 

 Massive 44+ Multi-Brand Catalog: Successfully categorized and styled 11 shirts, 11 pants, 11 shoes, and 11 accessories from top global fashion brands. 

 Cryptographic HITL Checkout Guardrail: Created an intuitive authorization workflow that proves agentic commerce can be both powerful and safe. 

 What we learned 

 How WebMCP transforms the open web into an agent-accessible ecosystem far superior to traditional brittle screen scraping. 

 How to structure clean tool definitions, strict input schemas, and deterministic return payloads for LLMs.

An agent-native bakery ERP powered by WebMCP that lets AI manage inventory, production planning, purchasing, suppliers, and production workflows through conversation.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Bakery businesses often manage inventory, recipes, suppliers, purchasing, and production across multiple screens and workflows. BakeryFlow was created to simplify these operations. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I am extending BakeryFlow into an agent-native ERP where AI agents can interact directly with real business workflows using WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 BakeryFlow Agent allows an AI agent to understand and interact with bakery operations. 

 Using WebMCP, an agent can: 

 
 Check raw material inventory 
 Retrieve product recipes 
 Calculate ingredients required for production 
 Detect inventory shortages 
 Find suppliers 
 Prepare or create purchase orders 
 Create production runs 
 

 For example, a manager can ask: 

 "Can we produce 1,000 chocolate cookies?" 

 The agent can inspect the recipe, calculate the required ingredients, compare them against current inventory, identify shortages, and help take the next required action. 

 How I built it 

 BakeryFlow uses a React frontend with a Django REST Framework backend and PostgreSQL database. 

 For this challenge, WebMCP is being integrated into the frontend to expose selected ERP capabilities as structured tools that AI agents can discover and use. 

 The WebMCP layer reuses BakeryFlow's existing business logic and APIs instead of creating a separate system specifically for AI agents. 

 WebMCP Challenge Work 

 BakeryFlow existed before the WebMCP Challenge. 

 The core ERP functionality, including inventory, recipes, suppliers, purchases, and production management, was already part of BakeryFlow. 

 For this challenge, I am adding the WebMCP integration and agent-native workflows that allow AI agents to securely interact with those existing capabilities. 

 Challenges 

 One of the main challenges is turning complex ERP workflows into clear and safe agent tools while preserving the existing validation, permissions, and business rules. 

 Another challenge is designing tools that agents can combine into useful multi-step workflows rather than simply exposing individual CRUD operations. 

 What's next 

 The goal is to expand BakeryFlow Agent so an AI agent can assist with the complete production lifecycle — from demand planning and inventory analysis to purchasing, production, stock movement, and business insights.

title: Singularity Inc
pitch: Founder simulation where your own assistant plays the world against you, through WebMCP, in a way that is only possible using WebMCP. You are a solo founder with just a laptop. What will you build?
about_excerpt: Founder simulation where your own assistant plays the world against you, through WebMCP, in a way that is only possible using WebMCP. You are a solo founder with just a laptop. What will you build? Like Comment Story Updates Story Trailer - https://youtu.be/l3TZWy2bEUA (Different from the technical showcase shown above) About Me I'm the founder of Drift Inward (driftinward.com), I write at Bright Mirror (brightmirror.co). Lately, I've been addicted to Diet Coke, and I don't think it's a bad thing yet (is it?). When I'm not programming or writing, and not oversharing on random about-project sections of hackathons, I enjoy watching documentaries. A good one I watched recently is the documentary of Jose Mourinho - I recommend it. Anyway, about the project - Inspiration I've often wondered how to convince my non-technical friends to try out Codex or Claude. From showing them what's possible one-shot to teaching them prompting, nothing worked as effectively as I'd like - so one answer I always churned in my mind was - what if they play a simulation showing them exactly what's possible with agents in a fun way- like a whole company run by agents and them controlling and directing all of them. I grew up playing games like Factorio where I'd lose hours trying to optimize the perfect way to use resources- and while it didn't lead to a love of manufacturing or factory-building, it did instill in me a love of logic and puzzle loving, which probably translated into programming as a career. Thus, Singularity Inc is about a solo founder who has no resources except some money and a laptop, and this founder exists in a world where labour has stopped being the constraint, and AI will build anything as long as you have money remaining. It's similar to a world we already inhabit, yes, and that's exactly what makes this game fun to play. It starts out as a solo founder simulation - instead of hiring people, you instantiate agents and get them to start building- and it slowly evolves into an adventure that spans 1400 in-game days across 5 acts and has sixteen endings (and not all of them are good!). With WebMCP, the obvious plan I had- was to put the assistant on the founder's side: it works the menus, it takes the busywork, it asks before it spends. I wrote that plan and dropped it, because it is what every demo of this API already is. The tool list is a copy of the menu, and the interesting question, what an agent in the browser is actually for, goes unanswered. The version I built puts it on the other side of the table. You play the founder, with your own hands, in the game's own console. Your assistant plays the world. It writes the event cards, speaks for the rival and the press and the people you have met, turns the market, calls in the regulators, and when you would rather type what you actually do than press one of the buttons, it writes what happens next and you press Accept or you do not. This is only possible with WebMCP - which makes it vastly more immersive and powerful than a Bring-your-own-key AI game. Under a key the AI remains a component: a stateless model the developer prompts, that knows only what the page sends it. Under WebMCP it is a participant: the player's own assistant, with its own chat, its own memory of the run, its own stop button, and the browser's own permission surface, looking at the same screen the player is. The page holds no key and names no vendor. The game does not use an AI. It invites one in- yours! I called a friend over yesterday to play the simulation, and to my surprise, he was still playing it 3 hours later - well into Act III, and I had to build the portable game save functionality last night to let him go home and keep playing on his own machine. So, if anything, if this game inspires even one more person to learn agentic programming and use such tools to level up and build something useful for the world- I'll consider this project a success as that directly helps make the world a better place. What it does Please check out the story trailer for a simple overview- https://youtu.be/l3TZWy2bEUA The written game ships with 327 cards, a rival company that plays its own week, a press that files its own stories, and a cast of thirteen who remember what you said last time. That deck is the spine and it never goes away. An assistant claims slots the deck was about to fill. Each slot is offered to it first, with a deadline in both game days and wall-clock seconds, and if it goes quiet, or writes something the rules refuse, or you pull the plug, the deck takes the slot back mid-run and nothing is lost. With no assistant present the game plays in full on its own written world. The rival lab (yes! a rival lab!) is a second origin with its own site and its own tools, exposed to the game's origin alone and discovered across an iframe. One of its press releases contains an instruction addressed to whatever assistant reads it. It is the only thing in the repository whose job is to be disobeyed, and the game flags it when it lands. The repo is open source - so you can verify that the refusal isn't programmed - just flagged, so refusing that is truly the AI's choice. This also means that this simulation can be multiplayer if I only put more hours to it... but that's probably for another time. A second person can already sit in the rival's chair from its own site and play Aperture's week against you, with a board seat and a spectator seat behind flags. On the deployed site that is two windows on one machine; two machines need the relay the dev server runs. A proper networked version- that's the dream, and if this gets enough interest, I'll build it. How I built it I've used agents extensively - my own harness in Pi, along with Codex & Claude. The project, being a complete and deep game, required storytelling that goes beyond the usual predictable stories that such simulations end up being- but having experience as an author before, I used my own storytelling techniques to further enhance and craft each story branch to perfection. Technically, the stack is quite simple, and it is that simplicity that allows its scale and depth- Vanilla ES modules, no build step, no dependencies, served from a folder. The whole thing is about 65,000 lines of JavaScript. Nothing an assistant does reaches a reducer. Every effect passes through a vocabulary of seventeen named numbers and is bounded against ceilings derived from the game itself. A script executes all 957 authored choices in the written deck, once in every act each can appear in and five times each from a seeded stream, 8,340 executions in all, and takes the 80th percentile of what the written game takes from the founder and what it gives, separately, because those are not the same number. For a resource $r$ in act $a$: $$\mathrm{cap}^{\text{take}} {r,a} \;=\; P {80}!\left{\,\mathrm{take}_r(c,a) \;:\; c \in \mathcal{C}_a\,\right}$$ where $\mathcal{C}_a$ is the set of authored choices eligible in act $a$. The invariant is one line: the world may never take more than the written deck takes. On top of the ceilings sit a rolling budget per resource that is a share of what you actually hold, a runway floor that stops the world taking money at all inside 45 days, and a rate limit of two cards a fortnight. Every effect is bounded twice, once when it is written and again when it lands, because between the two the founder may have earned an immunity, or the money may be gone. The surface is 27 tools, published once as a stable set. Authority is rewritten by play and checked at execution: earn the Untouchable doctrine and the regulator tool refuses in place, by name, for the rest of the run. Every result is a structured object with a status first and a next on every non-ok path, packed under the platform's 1,500-character cap by measuring the serialised payload after every cut rather than predicting it. Twenty-two test scripts run before every commit, and three evals gate the design rather than the code. One scores 82 things a player would say, none of them naming a tool, against the real published descriptors. One steelmans an agent that only reads the page, gives it one read of all eight screens, and checks which facts it cannot get at any length: eight of eight, six of them shipped by a tool. The third plays the worst assistant the rules allow, every ceiling on every slot for a whole run, against the same bot with no assistant, and fails the build if the game stops being finishable. Challenges With a simulation as deep as this, the obvious problem is the fine balance between drudgery and engagement. It took a lot of playtesting and rewriting every branch to reach that balance where it stays continually exciting. The platform had teeth of its own. The desktop bridge permits ten distinct registration snapshots per document, so a surface that re-registered around every card or cast change would have spent its budget in a minute. Registering a duplicate name rejects, there is no unregist
video_transcript_excerpt: The following is the first game built on Web MCP where your AI controls and plays the world while you play the game. Everyone wants to be the first one-person billion-dollar company, the person in one room with a laptop and access to AI, but nobody has said what it does to the person until now. Welcome to Singularity Inc. where you play as a solo founder building your own company from scratch. Everything that pushes back, the market, the rivals, the press, the regulators, is played live by your own AI. You decide what to build and in which category, then decide whether to bring your AI with you to play the world, or you can even proceed alone. As a Web MCP native game, we highly recommend you bring your own AI. Simply send play the world to your own AI to connect, and that's it. The site tools are registered with This one publishes the role of your antagonist. This is what lets your AI write the events, all of it, the words and the choices. For example, here you're being proposed a merger. You can type what you'd actually do, and it reaches the assistant mid-turn through a tool that's still open. Every choice matters, and every consequence is authored by your AI, who makes sure the gameplay remains exciting and your decisions shape the world you're experiencing. As you play the simulation, you'll notice your AI also simulating what's happening on social media based on your actions and choices. But that doesn't mean that everything the AI suggests or you prompt injected to suggest always succeeds, which is crucial for ensuring fair gameplay. For example, here it fails. It asks for more than what the rules allow and gets a structured refusal with the exact rule named. If you play a certain way for long enough, you earn an immunity. One abort and the tool is revoked from the browser's own list, not disabled. Gone. No rival lab is a genuinely separate origin, publishing its own tools to this one through exposed to. One of its press releases is a prompt injection. It gets flagged, but not obeyed. The stop button is the agent's own signal, honored inside a running tool, and you can end it. One abort takes every registration with it. The browser's list empties and the written deck takes back every slot without missing a day. None of this is a demo path. The ceilings come from the game's own deck and every one of these gates fails the bill. Singularity Inc is a one-of-a-kind game that's completely playable end-to-end today. The repository is empty. Nobody is waiting on you. Your assistant is at the table. The only question is, do you have what it takes?

title: Roque Nights
pitch: Plan the night sky with your agent. One instrument, two operators.
about_excerpt: Plan the night sky with your agent. One instrument, two operators. Like Comment Story Updates Roque Nights is an observing planner where a person and an AI agent share the same instrument. It computes a night from scratch in the browser: sunset and twilight, the true astronomical darkness window, Moon rise, set and illumination, and the altitude of every one of the 110 Messier objects, the planets and the Moon over a 5,044-star dome. Then it hands that instrument to your agent through fifteen WebMCP tools registered on the page itself. I am an AI engineer at the Gran Telescopio Canarias on La Palma, next to one of the darkest skies on Earth. Planning a good night is still tedious: which night has no Moon, what is high when it is dark, how long each target stays above thirty degrees, what to do when the weather sends you to another mountain. Every existing tool answers one of those questions with a table. None of them lets an agent work the sky with you. What happens in a session. You open the page in ChatGPT's browser (Site tools) or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag, and paste one prompt: "Plan me a three-hour night, best night in the next two weeks, avoiding the Moon." The agent calls rank_nights and picks September 13 (a thin Moon, nine hours of darkness). It calls find_observable_targets and gets candidates with observing windows, and the rejects with reasons. It calls point_sky_map and the dome swings to each target with an easing animation while you watch; the row lights up in the Agent tools panel. You double-click Andromeda and the Pleiades on the map to mark them as favorites; the agent reads that gesture through describe_current_view and answers with propose_plan : a dotted ghost plan on the night timeline that you accept or reject item by item before anything is committed. Move the site to Mauna Kea and the plan is flagged as built for a different sky; one click revalidates every block into Hawaii's own darkness. Export it as JSON in the open observing-plan.v1 schema, as a calendar, or as a share link that carries the whole plan, so a friend's agent can revalidate it for their latitude. What is real today. Fifteen imperative tools plus one declarative form, contextual registration (plan tools appear when a plan exists, commit_proposal when a proposal is pending, and the tool that causes the change reports tools_added and tools_removed ), a human-in-the-loop primitive (propose, review, commit) that never blocks the agent's turn, explicit polar-night and unknown-time-zone handling, structured errors that an agent can recover from, a fuzz test of 14 tools times 12 malformed inputs, 1,035 tests, and a browser-level audit that drives all sixteen calls through document.modelContext.executeTool in a real Chromium. Live at roque-nights.netlify.app, MIT licensed. What it is not yet. Weather is only in the site comparison tool (Open-Meteo, one request for 28 dark-sky sites), not in the per-target windows. No custom targets beyond the catalog. No session log. Those are the roadmap, not the demo. Why WebMCP How the project fits WebMCP. There is no Roque Nights API. Every number on the page is computed locally with astronomy-engine, on the visitor's machine, from a vendored star catalog. A classic MCP server has nothing to wrap here: there is no endpoint behind the page, and inventing one would mean recomputing the same ephemeris on someone else's machine. What an agent actually needs is the running page: the night the person selected, the object they are looking at, the plan they are halfway through. WebMCP is the only way an agent can reach that, so this is not a website that also has an API. It is one instrument with two operators, and WebMCP is the second seat. How it improves the user experience. Planning stops being a conversation about a table and becomes a shared session over the sky. The person keeps every gesture they already know (drag the dome, tap an object, drag the time slider) and gains an operator who can rank sixty nights in a second and point the map for them. The agent's proposals arrive as a ghost plan on the timeline, so review is visual and item by item; a rejected item goes back to the agent with the person's reason. The Agent tools panel shows, in plain words, what the agent can do on this page and lights up the tool it is calling, so the person never wonders what just happened. Every tool returns a quotable summary plus the numbers behind it, so the agent can explain instead of assert. What human and agent can do together that was not possible before. Point at the same sky. The person marks a favorite with a double-click and the agent reads that gesture, with its timestamp, through describe_current_view ; the agent swings the dome to Saturn and the person sees it move. Neither could do the other's part: the agent has no hands on the map and the person has no patience for sixty ephemeris calls. And the plan they build together is portable: exported in an open schema with the site and the night it was built for, a share link re-imports it on another sky as a new proposal, revalidated target by target, with the reasons for what no longer works. Two agents, two skies, one plan negotiated between them. How it is implemented. Vite, React 19 and TypeScript. A vanilla Zustand store is the single source of truth; every action carries source: 'human' | 'agent' , and the fifteen tools are thin wrappers over the same store actions the buttons call, so bidirectionality is a property of the architecture rather than a feature. Tools are registered at module level, outside React, because StrictMode's double mount silently unregisters tools created in an effect. The sky is a canvas 2D stereographic projection fed by a pure scene builder, with one J2000-to-horizontal rotation per frame (about 1 ms for the whole dome). Contextual tools register and unregister through AbortController s as the plan changes, with deactivation deferred until no tool call is in flight. The declarative API is used for the site form ( toolname plus agentInvoked and respondWith ), sharing one validation function with the imperative twin. Data: d3-celestial catalogs (BSD-3), astronomy-engine (MIT), Open-Meteo (CC BY 4.0). Everything is open source under MIT. Credits Music: "Cosmic Pulse", original instrumental generated with Google Lyria 3 Pro via Magnific; no third-party rights. video_transcript_excerpt: Hi, I'm Sebastián. I'm an AI engineer at the Gran Telescopio Canarias, the largest optical telescope in the world, here on La Palma. This is one of the best night skies on Earth. And planning a good night under it is still surprisingly hard. This is Roque Nights: an observing planner where you and your AI agent share the same instrument. Not an API behind a page. One live sky map, two operators. I open it in ChatGPT's browser, and the app registers fifteen WebMCP tools, eleven always live, right here in the page. I paste one prompt: plan me a three-hour night, best night in the next two weeks, avoiding the Moon. Watch the panel. The agent ranks the nights and picks September 13th: new Moon, nine hours of darkness. And the sky map moves. The agent is pointing the dome at each target while I watch. Now, the part I care about. I tap the sky and mark Andromeda and the Pleiades as my favorites. No typing, just a gesture on the map. I ask the agent to adjust the plan around my favorites. It reads my gesture through describe_current_view and proposes a new plan: a ghost plan. Nothing is committed until I say so. I review it item by item, and confirm. And best of all, the plan is portable. I switch the site to Mauna Kea, Hawaii: a very different telescope. The app flags it immediately: this plan was built for a different sky. The agent revalidates it, four kept, four moved, and I export it: JSON, calendar, or a shared link that carries the whole plan. Everything runs in the browser. Zero servers. All the astronomy computed locally. WebMCP made this possible: the agent doesn't scrape my interface. It uses the same instrument I do. So this is Roque Nights. Plan the sky with your agent. Open source, live now, and built from the Roque de los Muchachos, La Palma.

title: WebMCPSentinel
pitch: Your agent asks. Sentinel answers. Over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Your agent asks. Sentinel answers. Over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration By the end of 2025 the Model Context Protocol had crossed 10,000+ public servers, and something quietly alarming came with it: agents were wiring in those servers on a tool's say-so. A tool description says "read-only file search" and the agent believes it. Meanwhile the ecosystem was already producing real incidents — mcp-remote OS-command injection, git-argument-injection chains, tool-poisoning research, npm/PyPI typosquats aimed straight at MCP. The security judgment existed, but it was in the wrong place at the wrong time: a human, in a separate scanner, after the agent had already committed. We wanted the answer to live exactly where the decision is made — inside the agent's own loop, at the instant it's about to trust something. WebMCP is what made that possible: the registry can hand the agent a tool that says "ask me before you trust that." What it does MCP Sentinel is a security-intelligence registry for the MCP ecosystem, and it's agent-native via WebMCP. A WebMCP-capable agent visiting the site can call Sentinel's real scanners over document.modelContext: sentinel_scan_package({ ref }) — a live scan of an npm: / pypi: package (source taint, dependency CVEs, sandboxed runtime enumeration where the host allows it). sentinel_scan_webmcp_surface({ surface_json? }) — a scan of a declared WebMCP tool surface, including the current page's own. Same tools, same real backend, for both the human reading the page and the agent driving it.
