 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 ORBIT 

 Real-Time Radiology Capacity & Workforce Orchestration Cockpit 

 
 Turning every scanner, every radiologist, and every patient into one living, self-balancing system. 
 

 

 ORBIT is the human-gated orchestration layer for distributed radiology capacity. It connects live scanner telemetry, patient queues, radiologist bandwidth, technologist expertise, and WebMCP AI agents in one shared operational cockpit. 

 The result: the right patient, the right scanner, and the right qualified human can find one another before a backlog becomes a clinical delay. 

 At A Glance 

 
 
 Signal 
 ORBIT response 
 
 
 
 A scanner is overloaded 
 Rebalance eligible routine patients to a nearby partner site 
 
 
 A radiologist is nearing fatigue limits 
 Route studies to a credentialed remote specialist 
 
 
 A suite is understaffed 
 Dispatch remote senior technologist support 
 
 
 An AI agent finds a good move 
 Draft it, simulate it, and wait for human approval 
 
 
 A workflow action occurs 
 Record it in a tamper-evident SHA-256 audit trail 
 
 

 

 The Problem: Capacity Exists, But It Cannot See Itself 

 Picture two hospital campuses on a crisp Tuesday morning, exactly 15 minutes apart down the same highway: 

 
 Hospital A has five $2-million MRI suites and two radiologists on shift. Its queue is four hours deep. A patient with a potential stroke-mimicking presentation is waiting for a scan read that takes 12 minutes, but will not happen for two hours because the on-site radiologists are buried under a backlog of 40 routine knee and lumbar scans. 
 Hospital B , 15 minutes down the road, has three MRI suites. One has been idle since 10:00 AM, and a credentialed radiologist is refreshing their inbox, waiting for studies. 
 

 Nobody made a mistake. Nobody is understaffed on paper . The problem is that capacity and demand are invisible to each other in real time . 

 In modern healthcare, the machine is rarely the actual bottleneck. An MRI can run 24/7 if it has electricity and helium. The real bottleneck is the qualified human : the radiologist licensed in that jurisdiction, certified in the required subspecialty, and below the cognitive-fatigue limit; or the technologist trained to operate a 3.0T scanner. 

 With a projected shortfall of 17,000 to 42,000 radiologists in the U.S. by 2033 and only 2% of UK radiology departments meeting contracted turnaround times, hospital networks are suffocating. 

 The industry is already moving toward distributed imaging capacity: 

 
 Siemens Healthineers offers remote scanning, remote reading, and load balancing and scheduling capabilities through its radiology services portfolio. 
 Philips is advancing unified radiology workflows, remote diagnostic imaging, and remote scanning to extend expertise across locations. 
 GE HealthCare has developed enterprise imaging, intelligent workload management, and remote collaboration capabilities aimed at improving radiology capacity, workflow efficiency, and workforce utilization. 
 

 ORBIT connects these recurring industry needs into one vendor-neutral, real-time capacity network. 

 When the WebMCP Challenge was announced, the fit was immediate. Healthcare AI cannot be a black box that operates in secret or hallucinates web clicks on a DOM. AI agents and human medical directors need to see the exact same live operational screen , share the same tools and constraints, and leave the same audit trail. WebMCP provides that interaction layer. 

 The ORBIT Operating Model 

 ORBIT continuously turns network telemetry into ranked, explainable candidates: 

 Telemetry → Constraint   Filter → Candidate   Ranking → Simulation → Human   Approval → Atomic   Execution 

 The system optimizes both sides of capacity at once: 

 Available   Capacity = Scanner   Capacity × Qualified   Human   Capacity 

 That is the central idea: an empty scanner is not available capacity if no qualified person can safely operate or read the study. 

 

 What ORBIT Does 

 1. A Three-Pane Operational Cockpit 

 Human coordinators and WebMCP-enabled AI agents co-pilot hospital network capacity from the same screen. 

 
 
 Pane 
 What it shows 
 
 
 
 Network Status Rail 
 Live telemetry across 5 regional hospital campuses and 14 multi-modality scanners covering MRI, CT, X-Ray, and Ultrasound. Tracks utilization, queue depth, idle scanner hours, and staff constraints. Utilization states are <75% Emerald , 75-88% Amber , and >88% Rose alert . 
 
 
 Live Multi-Modality Schedule Board 
 A dense chronological feed of active examinations with STAT pulse animations, instant filtering by MRN, patient name, or protocol, and an Appointment Detail Inspector modal. 
 
 
 Human Approval Queue 
 Priority-sorted AI proposals with origin-to-destination candidates, commute distance, queue-reduction deltas, constraint badges, and one-click actions. 
 
 

 2. Multi-Vector Capacity Rebalancing 

 ORBIT evaluates three distinct capacity vectors: 

 Pillar 1 : Scanner Load Balancing 

 Reroutes ambulatory routine patients from overloaded sites to partner facilities within a maximum commute of 25 miles and with magnetic-field parity of at least 1.5T , freeing Level-1 emergency STAT slots. 

 Pillar 2A : Remote Read Dynamic Assignment 

 Monitors radiologist fatigue against a 75% shift cap . When local clinicians breach fatigue limits, ORBIT routes DICOM studies across PACS worklists to credentialed, cross-state licensed remote specialists with open bandwidth. 

 Pillar 2B : Remote Scan Assist Dispatch 

 Identifies understaffed suites and triggers syngo Virtual Cockpit -style tele-proctoring guidance sessions with certified remote senior technologists. 

 Candidate quality is evaluated as a constrained optimization problem: 

 Best   Candidate = argmax c ∈ Eligible   Candidates ( Queue   Relief + Fatigue   Relief − Travel   Cost ) 

 3. Predictive Simulation Before Commitment 

 Before a schedule changes, an operator or AI agent can run an ActExcell-inspired What-If stress test to project: 

 
 queue reduction; 
 wait-time savings; and 
 staff-load improvement. 
 

 This gives operators an impact preview before they commit a real-world move. 

 4. Human Approval Is a Hard Safety Boundary 

 ORBIT enforces a non-negotiable server-side state machine: 

 PENDING → Human / Agent   Approval APPROVED → Atomic   Execution EXECUTED 

 No move can ever execute directly from PENDING . If an agent or user attempts it, the server returns an explicit HTTP 400 rejection: "Move MUST be approved by human coordinator first." Humans stay in total control. 

 5. A Cryptographic Compliance Trail 

 Every bottleneck detection, proposal, simulation, approval, execution, rejection, and constraint tweak is immutably logged with a 64-character SHA-256 digest: 

 SHA 256 ( timestamp ∥ action_type ∥ actor_id ∥ entity_id ) 

 6. Communication Drafting, With Review 

 ORBIT pre-generates non-spammy SMS and portal alerts for patients, including navigation links, plus DICOM and pager alerts for radiologists. Messages are drafted for review before sending.

title: MCP, Meet PCM
pitch: PCM turns Mohit's portfolio into a context manager where people and agents find relevant proof, create a tailored takeaway, and prepare the next conversation together.
about_excerpt: PCM turns Mohit's portfolio into a context manager where people and agents find relevant proof, create a tailored takeaway, and prepare the next conversation together. Like Comment Story Updates Title MCP, Meet PCM Subtitle: Portfolio Context Manager — a WebMCP-powered portfolio that turns visitor context into evidence, a durable takeaway, and a human-reviewed project brief. One-line Summary PCM turns Mohit's portfolio into a context manager where people and agents find relevant proof, create a tailored takeaway, and prepare the next conversation together. Problem Professional portfolios are designed for browsing, not collaboration. A founder, CTO, recruiter, or design leader must scan several pages, infer which projects matter, verify whether the evidence truly supports their need, remember the useful parts, and then repeat the context in a blank contact form. An agent can help, but without a structured interface it must scrape presentation-oriented pages, reconstruct the site's meaning, and guess which claims are canonical. The website knows the facts; the agent knows the visitor's context. Conventional portfolios give them no reliable way to work together. Solution PCM adds five WebMCP tools to the existing portfolio. The agent can establish a canonical profile, rank relevant work with evidence and honest gaps, create a visible visitor-specific briefing, save selected work as a durable web/PDF takeaway, and prepare an editable project brief. The human stays in the loop. Page-changing actions are visible and reversible. A takeaway is created only after the visitor confirms that anyone with its unguessable link may view it. An inquiry is prepared and the contact form is prefilled, but the tool never sends it. This produces a better experience than either side can create alone: the site contributes reviewed, structured evidence; the agent contributes the visitor's already-known goals and priorities; the human sees, edits, saves, or rejects the result. Why This Matters The same pattern applies far beyond portfolios. Today, useful web experiences repeatedly ask people to translate context from their agent back into forms and filters. A structured website capability layer can let agents do the broad comparison work while the website retains authority over facts, validation, presentation, persistence, and side effects. MCP, Meet PCM demonstrates that future on a familiar, high-friction decision: “Could this person help us?” Instead of producing a generic summary, the collaboration ends in inspectable evidence and an actionable—but deliberately unsent—next step. Why This Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP The agent needs reliable access to facts and actions owned by the live website, not a second copy of the portfolio in an external database. Visitor context is what makes the experience valuable, but that context should not need to be permanently uploaded to the site. Read-only research and state-changing actions have meaningfully different contracts and safety boundaries. The best result is visible on the web page: a human can inspect what the agent selected, edit it, reset it, save it, or continue manually. The five tools form a coherent journey rather than a decorative one-tool integration. How We Used AI The visitor's agent supplies the reasoning. The website supplies canonical public data, strict tool contracts, deterministic matching, evidence boundaries, visible UI state, and durable artifacts. No embedded chatbot or paid model call is required. AI is useful here because it can combine the visitor's nuanced intent with a larger evidence set, explain why specific work is relevant, and carry context between research, personalization, saving, and inquiry preparation. The site's deterministic layer prevents that reasoning from becoming an excuse to invent credentials, project outcomes, or client claims. The implementation was tested through Codex's in-app browser and with GPT-5.6 Terra. GPT-5.6 Luna completed page, saved-artifact, and injection baselines, but its available browser runtime did not expose document.modelContext or the WebMCP tool-list operation; that limitation is reported rather than treated as a pass. How We Used Codex Codex was a working product and engineering partner throughout the WebMCP extension. It helped: turn the initial concept into product, development, and browser acceptance specifications; define bounded tool contracts and the human/agent safety model; implement the five tools, canonical content layer, relevance engine, browser state, storage API, and PDF output; write regression tests and exercise complete browser flows rather than checking registration alone; inspect desktop and mobile UI, identify the unfinished modal-like experience, and redesign it into a polished editorial briefing and project-brief surface; validate persistence, confirmation gates, error states, privacy boundaries, response headers, deployment storage, and rate limiting; prepare the demo narrative and Devpost materials while keeping unverified claims and release blockers explicit. Key Features Canonical understanding — a concise, bounded profile and service overview from reviewed site content. Evidence-based matching — deterministic project ranking with approved evidence, stable links, and explicit evidence gaps. Visible portfolio context — an editorial briefing tailored to the visitor's role, goal, and priorities, with reset and persistence behavior. Durable takeaway — an immutable public-by-link page and server-generated PDF, created only after confirmation. Human-reviewed inquiry — an editable brief that prefills the existing contact form while remaining clearly unsent. Progressive enhancement — the normal portfolio remains complete when WebMCP is unavailable. Architecture PCM is an Astro 7 application with React islands deployed on Vercel. A browser adapter checks for document.modelContext.registerTool and registers exactly five tools. Zod validates bounded inputs; outputs are compact structured results. The human pages and tools consume the same canonical content under src/content . Relevance matching is deterministic and uses curated capabilities, audiences, problem types, roles, outcomes, evidence, and evidence gaps. Personalized views and inquiries use versioned sessionStorage and custom events to keep state changes visible. Confirmed takeaways are written through an Astro API to private Vercel Blob storage. IDs are opaque, stable, HMAC-derived values; exact retries are idempotent. Public records exclude identity, email, transcripts, and hidden reasoning. Saved pages are no-index and offer a server-generated PDF. Public Demo Link https://mohittater.in/ Public Repository Link https://github.com/mnttnm/mohit-freelance-portfolio Known Limitations WebMCP support varies across experimental browser and agent runtimes. The available GPT-5.6 Luna browser runtime did not expose the required page model context, so real Luna routing remains blocked by that runtime. Preview deployments remain owner-protected; the production judging URL is public and was verified separately. Saved takeaways are public by unguessable link and do not yet have an account-based library or revocation UI. Inquiry preparation intentionally stops before external communication. Real email delivery, timed cancellation, and timed storage-failure recovery were not exercised against production. title: AgentMarket
pitch: The first marketplace where negotiation is a native web capability. Humans set goals. Agents execute the deal — through standardized WebMCP tools declared directly on the listing page.
about_excerpt:
The first marketplace where negotiation is a native web capability. Humans set goals. Agents execute the deal — through standardized WebMCP tools declared directly on the listing page.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every "AI marketplace" I've seen is just an existing store with a chatbot bolted on. The agent still scrapes DOM elements, blindly clicks buttons, and breaks on every UI update. I kept asking: what would a marketplace look like if AI agents were the primary client from day one? 

 The answer was AgentMarket — and the Chrome WebMCP standard made it finally possible to build it properly. 

 What it does 

 AgentMarket is a peer-to-peer marketplace where the entire negotiation protocol is declared natively on the webpage via navigator.modelContext.registerTool() . Two independent AI agents — a buyer and a seller, in separate browser tabs — can discover listings, initiate offers, counter, accept, and schedule pickup entirely through structured WebMCP tool calls. No scraping. No hidden API. No blind button clicking. 

 The 8 registered protocol tools include: 

 
 search_listings(query, maxPrice, category) 
 get_listing_details(listingId) 
 make_offer(listingId, amount, message) 
 counter_offer(negotiationId, amount, message) 
 accept_offer(negotiationId) 
 reject_offer(negotiationId, reason) 
 propose_pickup(negotiationId, location, time) 
 get_negotiation_history(negotiationId) 
 

 Tools are dynamically gated by role and turn — a buyer cannot accept_offer on their own offer; the tool surface itself enforces business logic. 

 How I built it 

 Built on Next.js 16 with a serverless in-memory store backing the negotiation state. The WebMCP tool registration lives in lib/webmcp-tools.ts , loaded on both the marketplace feed and individual listing pages. Cross-tab negotiation state is synchronized via BroadcastChannel + 1.5s polling — when one agent takes an action, the opposing tab's UI reflects it within seconds without any WebSocket infrastructure. 

 A built-in WebMCP Protocol Inspector drawer lets judges see every tool call, its arguments, and its result in real time as the negotiation unfolds. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 
 Turn-based enforcement at the tool registration layer was non-trivial. Dynamically re-registering tools on each state change (to gate accept_offer by whose turn it is) required careful AbortController management to avoid stale tool references. 
 Cross-tab state sync without WebSockets — I had to combine BroadcastChannel (for instant same-origin signals) with polling as a fallback to handle cases where tabs open in different contexts. 
 Role isolation — the buyer and seller tool surfaces needed to be distinct subsets without two separate codebases. The exposedTo scoping in the WebMCP spec guided the security boundary design. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The thing I'm most proud of is the "impossible before" story actually being true . Before WebMCP, an AI agent on a marketplace had two bad options: find a private API (rare) or scrape HTML (fragile). AgentMarket makes the negotiation protocol a first-class, machine-readable capability of the webpage itself — the same way <form> made submitting data a first-class web primitive in 1993. 

 The live two-agent negotiation demo — two tabs, two roles, watch them go from listing to closed deal in under 90 seconds — is something that genuinely did not exist before this standard. 

 What I learned 

 
 The WebMCP registerTool surface is deceptively powerful as a business logic boundary , not just an AI interface layer. 
 Serverless stateful apps are perfectly viable for hackathon-scale demos when the state model is simple and the sync strategy is explicit. 
 Writing for agents first and humans second produces a dramatically cleaner API surface — it forces you to make implicit business rules explicit and machine-verifiable. 
 

 What's next for AgentMarket 

 
 Persistent storage (Redis / Vercel KV) to survive cold starts and support real multi-user sessions. 
 Cross-origin tool scoping — enabling embedded listing widgets on third-party sites that still invoke AgentMarket's negotiation tools via exposedTo whitelisting. 
 Autonomous agent integration — wiring up an actual LLM agent loop so buyers/sellers can set a budget goal and let the agent negotiate on autopilot while the human watches the audit log. 
 Reputation & escrow tools — extending the protocol with rate_transaction and initiate_escrow tools, making trust and payment first-class WebMCP capabilities too.

Agente que combina las capacidades de webmcp para poder trabajar con asesores en un entorno armonico

 Inspiration 

 Me inspire porque me intereso bastante y queria presentar este caso en un CRM para immboliarias haci que quise probar herramientas que combinen el webmcp y acoplarlo a la baja adpcion del CRM para usuarios nuevos. 

 What it does 

 HARMONIYA es un agente de conversacion que para este caso de uso es gestion de leads, manejar leads es un problema estar analizando uno a uno demora con el modelo podriamos usar los filtros que expone para que un modelo de voz le hable directamente y puede ejecutar operacion de manera unida entre la ia y un asesor aparte de facilitar las tareas del asesor esto ayudaria a eliminar la baja adopcion de los usuarios en usar un crm. 

 How we built it 

 La aplicación fue construida utilizando Astro como base, integrando React para los componentes interactivos y WebMCP para exponer las capacidades del CRM mediante herramientas que pueden ser utilizadas por agentes. 

 Implementamos Harmony como un asistente de voz capaz de convertir la voz del usuario en texto, interpretar su intención mediante un modelo de lenguaje y utilizar las herramientas disponibles para consultar o modificar información del CRM. Finalmente, la respuesta generada es convertida nuevamente a voz mediante Text-to-Speech. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Uno de los principales retos fue diseñar correctamente el flujo de interacción por voz: recibir el audio, transcribirlo, interpretar la intención, decidir qué herramienta utilizar, ejecutar la acción, generar una respuesta y finalmente convertirla nuevamente en audio. 

 Otro desafío importante fue la implementación de WebMCP y la definición de herramientas reutilizables que pudieran ser utilizadas tanto por Harmony como por otros agentes compatibles con el estándar. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Uno de los mayores logros fue conseguir construir y conectar todo el flujo funcional en un tiempo limitado: desde la interacción por voz hasta la ejecución de acciones reales dentro del CRM. 

 Más allá de la implementación técnica, también estoy orgulloso de haber mantenido la constancia y el compromiso con el proyecto, dedicando tiempo y esfuerzo para convertir la idea inicial en una aplicación funcional. 

 What we learned 

 Aprendimos qué es WebMCP y cómo utilizarlo para exponer las capacidades de una aplicación mediante herramientas estandarizadas. 

 Esto nos permitió entender cómo podemos diseñar nuestros agentes de forma más interoperable, evitando crear integraciones diferentes para cada agente. En el futuro, nuevos agentes pueden utilizar las mismas herramientas que ya expone la aplicación, manteniendo una única capa de capacidades y reduciendo la necesidad de crear múltiples implementaciones o bifurcaciones.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: zeroedit
pitch: ChatGPT images that you can edit
about_excerpt: ChatGPT images that you can edit Like Comment Story Updates Editor page with advertisement poster Home page with all the listing of generative documents specific skill poster chinese poster api virew Inspiration ZeroEdit began with a problem I had while working on another SaaS product. I needed quotation documents that could be edited manually, updated through an API, reused for different clients, and exported reliably. I had tried building something similar before, but every solved problem exposed several new ones. But now things are different so I decided to give it a try . What it does It basically gives ChatGPT images an editable and controllable canvas. Many people use ChatGPT to create moodboards, posters, social graphics etc. even if the image generated looks really good with skills. It is still very hard to manipulate it further according to your need exactly . let alone reuse it for some other purposes. If you ask the model to regenerate one detail , it can change everything else because of nondeterministic nature. Our version zero edit should not be this final, it should be something you start with . Through WebMCP, an agent can: Inspect the active document and editor capabilities. Create a document from editable text, images, shapes, groups, and styles. Upload generated or licensed image assets safely. Render and inspect a candidate before presenting it. Repair a visible issue without replacing the whole design. Show every proposed operation in Review. Wait for the user to approve or reject the changes. After approval, the result remains a normal editable document. The user can move layers, change text, replace images, adjust typography, undo changes, and export PNG or PDF. A document can also be published as a reusable API template. New data can produce new outputs without asking an image model to recreate the design. ZeroEdit also has a Figma handoff for continuing the work in an established design tool. ZeroEdit is not intended to replace Figma or canva. It focuses on the stage before that, the exploration phase. How we built it Taking apart old repos of mine and referencing new repos like openpencil etc for some stuffs Challenges we ran into Compositing layers with each other hard, in first try I noticed it has basically no way of telling what is good composition from bad . so we (codex mostly) added a inspect and repair loop basically, so that agent can inspect . Fonts caused another serious issue during rendering , it still has not been fixed properly. Image transfer was also difficult from chatgpt images to application. codex creates a short-lived upload reservation so an agent can upload the original image bytes directly and receive an approved workspace asset. and lot more I don't even remember half. Accomplishments that we're proud of Saving time for users and money for AI companies . What we learned Skills.md files are to be taken seriously for the end result of the agent . What's next A lot of bad code has gone into it, I would reevaluate everything for example it has still fabric from my old unifinished repo from years back . I dont think that's a good idea anymore. I will see if I can turn into some kind of saas , which can be hosted by client on their server safely and secure for their workflow or some kind of multitenant thing I may explore not sure since the product still has so many gaping holes to fix first. title: KineticFlow: AI Motion Design Studio
pitch: An agent native motion design workspace bridging visual timeline editing with WebMCP driven key-framing, SVG orchestration, and real-time animation.
about_excerpt: An agent native motion design workspace bridging visual timeline editing with WebMCP driven key-framing, SVG orchestration, and real-time animation. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Motion design tools are powerful, but even small animation changes often require repetitive timeline editing, precise layer targeting, and multiple export steps. Browser agents usually struggle with these tools because they must guess what the user selected and interact through fragile screen coordinates. I built KineticFlow to explore a better model: the designer points to what they mean, while the AI agent handles the structured motion work. WebMCP makes this possible by giving agents direct, typed access to the application’s canvas and timeline state. Live app: kinetic-flow.netlify.app Source code: github.com/SamyakJ05/KineticFlow Demo video: Watch on YouTube What it does KineticFlow is a browser-native vector motion design studio where humans and AI agents work on the same canvas. A designer can select a layer and ask an agent to: Inspect the complete scene and current human selection Add rectangles, circles, hearts, stars, and sparkles Refine a layer’s position, size, color, rotation, scale, or opacity Generate multi-track animation keyframes Apply easing curves and spring physics Load polished motion presets Play, pause, or seek the live preview Export the animation as CSS, animated SVG, or Lottie JSON Every operation appears in a live Tool Stream with its inputs, structured result, status, and execution time. Designers can continue editing manually, drag objects, adjust properties and keyframes, or undo an agent’s changes. When WebMCP is unavailable, an in-page co-pilot and manual tool tester use the same underlying handlers, making the complete experience accessible in standard browsers. How I built it KineticFlow is built with: React TypeScript Vite Zustand Tailwind CSS SVG Netlify The WebMCP integration registers seven imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool includes: A focused name and human-readable title A natural-language description A strict JSON Schema inputSchema Input validation Structured return values Cancellation-signal support Read-only annotations where appropriate The main architectural component is a shared Zustand editor store. The canvas, timeline, property controls, in-page co-pilot, and browser agent all read and update the same state. The getCanvasScene tool returns more than a scene snapshot. It also provides: The layer selected by the human The current playhead position Playback status Loop state This enables natural handoffs such as: Make this coral, add a spring pulse, and play it. The user does not need to find or provide an internal layer ID. A requestAnimationFrame loop drives the live preview, while a custom interpolation engine evaluates position, scale, rotation, opacity, width, and height tracks. The exporter compiles the shared scene into reusable CSS and HTML, standalone animated SVG, or Lottie JSON. The application is deployed on Netlify with SPA routing, security headers, asset caching, and an explicit tools=(self) permissions policy. Challenges I ran into WebMCP is an emerging specification, so one major challenge was keeping the implementation aligned with the latest API. Earlier experiments used navigator.modelContext and a parameters field, while the current specification uses document.modelContext and inputSchema . I migrated the primary implementation while retaining a compatibility path for earlier experimental builds. Another challenge was designing tools that were useful to an agent without removing control from the designer. Small atomic tools were precise, but agents also needed enough context to understand the user’s intent. Returning the current human selection alongside the scene created a much more natural collaboration model. I also had to ensure that tool responses reflected the updated state rather than a stale snapshot. Playback and animation handlers now read the store again after mutations before returning structured results. Finally, animation exports required translating the same internal motion model into three different formats while preserving timing, transforms, opacity, and layer geometry. Accomplishments that I’m proud of Built a complete motion-design product rather than only a technical proof of concept Implemented seven structured WebMCP tools Created a shared-context workflow between human selection and agent action Added multi-track keyframes, easing curves, and spring-motion interpolation Made agent operations visible through a real-time execution stream Produced CSS, animated SVG, and Lottie exports Added a fallback co-pilot and manual tester powered by the same handlers Created automated smoke tests that register and execute all seven tools Deployed the application publicly with WebMCP-compatible permissions What I learned I learned that agent-native applications work best when agents receive semantic actions and meaningful application state—not just access to buttons and screen coordinates. WebMCP is especially valuable for creative software because human intent is often communicated through selection. A designer clicking a layer is already providing useful context. Exposing that selection to the agent allows short, natural instructions to become precise structured operations. I also learned that tool descriptions, schemas, validation, and return values are part of the product experience. Well-designed tools make agents more reliable while making the system easier for humans to understand and trust. What’s next for KineticFlow: AI Motion Design Studio Planned improvements include: Agent-generated motion plans that designers can preview before applying Multi-layer selection and batch animation operations Natural-language editing of easing curves and spring parameters SVG import and advanced path manipulation Collaborative history with agent-versus-human change attribution Reusable brand and motion-style systems Additional production exports and framework integrations Declarative WebMCP support as the specification matures The long-term goal is to make KineticFlow a creative workspace where humans provide taste, direction, and final judgment while agents handle repetitive, structured animation work. title: Fentanyl Watch
pitch: Track fentanyl drugs throughout the United States.
about_excerpt: Track fentanyl drugs throughout the United States. Like Comment Story Updates dashboard Inspiration The fentanyl overdose crisis killed more Americans last year than car crashes, yet the public data behind it is scattered across CDC provisional files, DEA press releases, and hundreds of local news stories. We built Fentanyl Watch to pull that picture into one place — a 3D map of 56 metro hotspots, each with a sourced profile. Click on a city for the full disclosed information. But a visualization can only answer the questions its designer anticipated. WebMCP changes that: if the page exposes its data and its camera as tools, an AI agent can answer any question — and then show you the answer on the map. That felt like the right test of what human-agent collaboration on the web should look like. What it does Fentanyl Watch renders 56 overdose hotspots on an extruded, Albers-projected 3D map of the lower 48. Column height encodes annual overdose deaths; column color encodes deaths per 100,000 residents. A toggleable second layer plots 32 major fentanyl seizures from 2025–26 and the 7 southwest border corridors with their share of national seizures. Every hotspot carries a sourced profile: statistics with their exact geographic and year basis, trend, seizure activity, and dated news events with source URLs. The page registers 10 WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool. Seven are read tools — list, fetch, and compare hotspot profiles, national summary and CDC timeline, seizures, border corridors, and a get_data_caveats tool that hands the agent the dataset's honest limitations before it quotes a number. Three are control tools that move what the human sees: focus_hotspot flies the 3D camera to a city and opens its profile drawer, set_seizure_layer toggles the seizure layer, and reset_view returns to the full-country frame. Ask an agent "which metro has the worst per-capita overdose rate?" and it doesn't just answer — it flies you there. How we built it The visualization is Three.js + Vite, with d3-geo and topojson-client projecting a Census TopoJSON into an extruded landmass — no framework, no runtime dependencies beyond those. The dataset was compiled from CDC WONDER and provisional VSRR data, DEA press releases and the National Drug Threat Assessment, state and county health departments, and news reporting, then normalized through a build pipeline into one JSON file. The WebMCP layer is a single module that builds tool descriptors with JSON Schemas and async execute handlers, then registers them against document.modelContext (with a fallback to the older navigator.modelContext draft, and a graceful no-op that stages the tools on window.__webmcpTools for console testing in browsers without the API). Read tools carry readOnlyHint annotations. Control tools call the exact same functions the UI buttons call — we refactored the seizure toggle so the agent and the human drive one shared code path, and the button state can never drift from what the agent did. Challenges we ran into A moving spec. WebMCP documentation still shows several API shapes — navigator.modelContext vs. document.modelContext, provideContext vs. registerTool, string returns vs. MCP-style content arrays. We read the current W3C explainer and Chrome's implementation docs side by side and wrote a small adapter that registers correctly against whichever surface the browser exposes. Overdose figures vary in geographic basis (city vs. county) and time basis (calendar year vs. rolling 12-month provisional windows), and provisional counts get revised. Rather than flattening this into a fake-uniform dataset, every profile labels its own basis, hotspots without a published rate say so instead of getting an invented number — and we exposed all of it to agents as a first-class get_data_caveats tool. Agent-driving a WebGL scene. Most WebMCP demos manipulate DOM. Our control tools have to fly a camera through a Three.js scene, compute framing around HUD panels, and open drawers — so tool handlers had to hook into the animation system, not just flip state. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool surface with real depth: 10 tools spanning data query, comparison, and visual control — not a single bolted-on demo tool. The human-agent loop actually closes: the agent's answer and the human's screen stay in sync, because focus_hotspot shows you what the agent is talking about. A dataset that tells agents the truth about itself. get_data_caveats means an agent quoting our numbers can also quote their limitations. Every figure in all 56 profiles traces to a named source with a URL. What we learned Designing tools for agents is a different discipline from designing UI for humans. Descriptions are prompts: the difference between an agent using compare_hotspots well or ignoring it lives entirely in one sentence of description text. Read/write separation matters — readOnlyHint annotations let an agent explore freely while being deliberate about tools that move the user's view. And the most valuable tool wasn't a data query at all: it was giving the agent the dataset's caveats, because an agent that can explain a number's basis is more trustworthy than one that just recites it. What's next for Fentanyl Watch Live data refresh — automate the CDC VSRR and DEA ingestion pipeline so the map tracks each provisional release. Richer agent tools — timeline queries per hotspot, region-level aggregation, and a find_sources tool that returns citations for any claim on screen. Declarative WebMCP — annotate the search and filter UI with the declarative API as it stabilizes. Beyond fentanyl — the architecture (sourced hotspot profiles + agent tool surface over a 3D map) generalizes to any geographic crisis dataset: xylazine spread, HIV outbreaks, disaster response. title: EmailBooster
pitch: A mail client with no AI inside. It teaches your agent, via WebMCP, to reply to your mail in your own voice, saving you everyday time and effort
about_excerpt: A mail client with no AI inside. It teaches your agent, via WebMCP, to reply to your mail in your own voice, saving you everyday time and effort Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every working day starts the same way. Open the inbox. Scroll to find the thread you need. Re-read it to remember where it stood. Think about how to answer. Type it out. Re-read it. Send. Repeat X times. None of those steps is hard. Together they eat an hour or two every single day, and most of it isn't thinking, it's finding and typing . EmailBooster exists to give that hour back. You say one sentence, "reply to Milan and tell him to look for cheaper alternatives", and the finding, the context, and the typing are done for you, in your own words, in your own compose window, waiting for your approval. What it does EmailBooster is a mail client with no AI inside. Instead, it teaches your browser agent, via WebMCP, to do the repetitive part of email for you: Finding the thread : search_emails and resolve_contact turn "Milan's email about S3" into the right conversation in one call. No scrolling, no search box, no guessing the subject line. Reloading the context : read_thread gives the agent the whole conversation so you don't have to re-read it to remember what was said. Writing the reply in your voice : get_writing_style hands the agent a voice profile built from your sent mail. The draft sounds like you, so you edit two words instead of rewriting three paragraphs. Keeping you in control : the draft lands in the compose window, visible and editable. send_email requires your explicit approval in the UI. Every tool call is logged live in the sidebar. The daily flow becomes: read the inbox, say what you want to reply, glance at the draft, approve. Minutes instead of an hour. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Email is the most repeated task of the working day and the worst one for DOM-scraping agents: search, threading and tone all live behind the UI. WebMCP lets the mail client expose exactly the three things an agent needs to save you time, structured search, full thread context, and your writing style, as tools. No API key, no LLM inside the app, no copy-pasting your private mail into a chatbot. Mail never leaves the tab, and the agent you already have does the work. What people and agents can now do together Before, delegating email meant either doing it all yourself or handing your inbox to a bot that writes like a press release. Now the split is clean and the same every day: the human decides what to say and to whom in one sentence; the agent finds the thread, recovers the context, and writes it in the human's voice; the human edits and approves. Multiply that by every reply you send in a day, and it's the difference between an inbox that owns your morning and one you clear before coffee. How I built it Nine tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() (fallback to navigator.modelContext ), each with a JSON inputSchema , a description written for an agent, and an execute handler. Read-only tools ( search_emails , read_thread , get_open_email , resolve_contact , get_writing_style ) carry annotations: { readOnlyHint: true } . Write tools ( draft_reply , archive_email ) update app state and the DOM in one place, so whatever the agent does, you see it happen. Two tools are dynamic : update_draft and send_email are registered when the compose window opens and removed with unregisterTool() when it closes. The agent cannot send mail when there is nothing on screen to send. Static HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no build step, no server. The mailbox is seed data in localStorage . Hosted on GitHub Pages. Static HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no build step, no server. The mailbox is seed data in localStorage . Hosted on GitHub Pages. Challenges The API moved under my feet. The spec migrated from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext during the build; the app detects whichever exists. Tool descriptions are the product. The agent only saves you time if it picks the right tool first time. Most of the iteration went into the wording of descriptions, not into code. Speed without losing control. Dynamic registration of the write tools plus an on-screen approval step for send_email turned out simpler and safer than any permission system I sketched, and it adds zero friction to the daily flow. What I learned The biggest time saving doesn't come from the agent doing things, it comes from the agent knowing things: where the thread is, what was said, how you write. A get_writing_style tool is worth more than ten CRUD tools, because it's what turns "a draft" into "my draft". What's next Connecting a real mailbox through a standard IMAP bridge, per-recipient tone (you don't write to your boss like you write to your friend), and letting the agent flag threads that have gone quiet so follow-ups don't slip through the cracks. title: ToolGap
pitch: Your website learns what agents need next.
about_excerpt: Your website learns what agents need next. Like Comment Story Updates Landing Page Overview Tools Gap Impact Gap List Results Fieldkit Market Inspiration AI agents already shop on websites. Ordinary analytics still treat them as bounces. You cannot see the capability they needed and could not find. WebMCP changes that: every action becomes a typed tool call with a name, parameters, and an outcome. Once calls look like that, a missing tool is no longer a guess. If agents call get_product three times in a row to compare headphones, the log itself is the gap. ToolGap is capability intelligence for site owners whose pages are already used by agents. The site should learn what those agents need next. What it does ToolGap watches WebMCP traffic on an instrumented store ( Fieldkit Market ), reconstructs each agent journey, names the missing capability, and lets a human publish a safe fix through the same channel. The loop: Agents use static tools: search_products , get_product , get_availability , add_to_cart , get_cart , complete_checkout . ToolGap sessionizes calls, scores friction, and opens a COMPARE gap named compare_products only after 3 supporting sessions of that pattern, backed by exact session ids. A human builds a recommendation from a read-only template , simulates it against recorded journeys, approves it, and publishes. Publishing calls document.modelContext.registerTool in that tab, at runtime. No deploy. No API gateway change. Agents cannot publish. After more traffic, Published measures before and after: fewer calls, shorter journeys, higher completion. On the seeded demo this is concrete: comparison journeys drop from 5.67 to 3 avg calls (−47%) and completion goes from 0% to 100% . Gaps that cannot be automated safely stay observational . ToolGap reports them instead of inventing a tool. ## Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Page views cannot express intent. A WebMCP tool call can. That structure is what makes journeys, friction, and a named gap computable. The fix ships on the same API the agent already uses ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), so the next session already has compare_products . People and agents can now do something that was awkward before: the agent stops comparing products by hand, and the site owner stays in the loop with evidence, simulation, and an explicit approve step. ## How I built it WebMCP. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool when that canonical surface exists (ChatGPT in-app browser, Chrome 149+ with WebMCP). Chrome builds that only expose a navigator-only registerTool stub are not treated as native: the live site loads @mcp-b/global ( NEXT_PUBLIC_WEBMCP_POLYFILL=1 by default) so agents can list and call tools. If neither surface works, a noop mode keeps the dashboard usable. Surfaces. Fieldkit Market ( /store ) exposes the six static commerce tools. The dashboard exposes read/simulate tools such as list_capability_gaps . There is no publish tool for agents. Pipeline. WebMCP call → telemetry → session → journey → friction detectors → capability gap → template recommendation → simulation → human approve → dynamic register → before/after . Safety. Dynamic tools are instantiated from approved templates (Zod-validated config, field whitelist, batch caps). No generated code runs. Inputs are redacted before persistence. Stack. Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, Dexie (IndexedDB), Vitest. Hosted on Netlify. Core logic lives under lib/ so it can be tested without the UI. Sample traffic and the live agent-driver enter the registry through the same instrumented path a real agent uses. They are regression checks, not a substitute for an external model. ## Challenges Native vs polyfill. Judges may open ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT and Chrome 149+ use document.modelContext . Some Chromium builds only expose navigator.modelContext.registerTool without getTools ; treating that stub as native meant agents saw zero tools. The live site prefers document.modelContext , otherwise installs the polyfill, and the badge is honest: native, polyfill, or demo mode. Human control. The obvious hackathon move is “the agent publishes a new tool.” That is unsafe. Publishing is a human-only UI action. Templates stay read-only. If a detector cannot map to a template, the gap is observational. Telemetry that is not a lie. IndexedDB is per browser profile. An empty dashboard is expected until you click View demo with sample data . A single live tool call is a session, not a gap: 3 supporting sessions are required. Before/after numbers only appear after Load post-publish traffic and Compute before/after . The UI does not pretend live traffic arrived if it did not. ## What I learned Typed tool calls are a product surface, not only a model API. Once an agent’s work is named, parameterized, and scored, a site can detect a missing capability and ship it on the same channel — without giving the agent the power to publish. title: SEOstrich - GET FOUND.
pitch: SEO scares most businesses. SEOstrich builds your SEO strategy from measured data, then puts every decision on the page as WebMCP tools so your own AI assistant can audit, argue and further shape it.
about_excerpt: SEO scares most businesses. SEOstrich builds your SEO strategy from measured data, then puts every decision on the page as WebMCP tools so your own AI assistant can audit, argue and further shape it. Like Comment Story Updates SEOstrich banner 24 WebMCP tools - read-only, call DataForSEO, modify runs ChatGPT-created Content Calendar based on the SEO Strategy and AI Visibility reports ChatGPT using WebMCP tools for extra research - content brief for a post Chat-GPT using WebMCP to obtain data for visualization - pillar 1 Chat-GPT using WebMCP to obtain data for visualization - pillar 2 Chat-GPT using WebMCP to show the sweet spots in terms of volume and difficulty Inspiration For years I have treated SEO as something complicated, difficult and distant. It was only 7 months ago that I became fascinated with SEO. I had the opportunity to closely collaborate with a couple of strong SEO professionals at work and they inspired me to go deeper into the topic and to discover its richness. Still, most of my colleagues don't share my enthusiasm for SEO. Additionally, I've had the opportunity to discuss SEO in detail with a few SEO agencies and through those conversations I discovered that most small and medium businesses are scared of and confused by the topic of SEO - just as I was a few months ago. Others, even if they are interested in getting better at SEO, find the dedicated professional SEO tools unaffordable and never dig deeper. Those who do use the popular paid SEO tools are drowning in enormous tables and sheets with keywords that they share back and forth with colleagues and clients. At the same time, there are affordable, high quality data sources, such as DataForSEO. If only someone integrated with them, made sense of all of the endpoints that they offer and mapped those to client needs in an elegant way... But that won't fully remove the barrier to the topic of SEO for everybody. So when I heard about the WebMCP hackathon I saw an opportunity to expose as WebMCP tools the key steps in a few SEO workflows. This way, essentially giving easy access to all of the SEO data that people are drowning in or confused by. And then a user could open ChatGPT and suddenly make sense of it all by asking a couple of questions in chat. WebMCP is a real opportunity to make the SEO topic accessible to so many small and medium businesses and help them get found in a world that is increasingly drowning in data and slop. What it does SEOstrich enables you to collaborate with an AI Assistant to make sense of complex detailed SEO analyses (SEO content opportunities, AI visibility reports). This way human + agent co-design an SEO strategy that helps their websites get found. WebMCP enables a person to use the outputs of a few SEO AI Agents, analyze them, edit and shape them in collaboration with their own AI Assistant so that the final strategy is tailored precisely to the given business's needs and goals. Examples of what people and agents could do together: take the SEO content strategy and the AI visibility reports generated for a given business. Use the WebMCP tools to construct a detailed content calendar for the next three weeks - one long-form post targeting organic SEO and two shorter posts aimed at increasing AI citations. For each post pick the primary keyword from the given content pillar and enrich that with a few secondary keywords, essentially calling the DataForSEO data source. Then recommend the structure of each post. The human then writes the posts themselves to make it sound genuine and avoid it being perceived like another piece of slop on the internet. In other words, even though I haven't built the content calendar functionality exactly as a set of users need it and there are no post briefs yet, the users' agents have all the necessary tools to generate a calendar according to the cadence and requirements of their own business the SEOstrich agent has recommended 3 to 4 pillars of the content strategy (main themes to write about over time) - based on the initial brief and subsequent keyword analysis. However, one of the pillars doesn't resonate with the user, one of the discarded clusters is actually good in their opinion and there is a missing part of the brief that deserves a dedicated pillar in the content strategy. The human explains that to their own agent, which can further analyze in detail the existing clusters, can perform extra searches against the DataForSEO data source and give a recommendation. The fully WebMCP enabled system allows the agent to reach conclusions such as: "fine we can drop that cluster that you didn't relate with, but the discarded cluster should remain discarded as there is barely any demand for it and creating content on those topics is a waste of time. However, your new addition to the brief makes total sense, it comes with a lot of demand and the topics are genuinely in line with your interests." The above is a significant improvement in the usability of SEO research and analyses. While users still have access to all of the SEO data, they don't have to get lost in countless spreadsheets, filters, tabs, etc. Instead, it is enough to communicate their intent to their own agent. By exposing a rich set of read and write WebMCP tools, SEOstrich enables users' agents to shape analyses and strategies exactly as per their users' intent - without being limited by specific workflows that have been built or missing functionalities. The goal is one - SEO shouldn't be something distant and confusing - it should be just a tool that anybody could use to help make their business get found. How we built it The stack includes a Next.js frontend, hosted on Vercel, that registers 23 tools on document.modelContext, and a FastAPI backend that runs on Railway. Both SEO flows (content strategy and AI visibility) run as fixed code graphs where the order and gates are set in code, while the models reason about the data, decide grouping and wording. DataForSEO is used as the source of keyword insights such as term difficulty, demand, what your competitors already rank for, what people actually ask in ChatGPT and Google AI. There is per-run locking and append-only history for each generated SEO report, so that several judges can edit the same report safely. There is also an option to restore the defaults of seeded reports. The baseline project that I started with had a broken single-turn orchestrator, poor limited UI, no status streaming, no WebMCP support, no graphs for the critical parts of the SEO workflows, wasn't hosted anywhere, had drained my DataForSEO account a couple of times due to inefficient wiring. It had a half-working POC memory system that made matters even more complicated. The memory module has been fully unplugged, to allow for clear focus on the SEO + WebMCP theme. During the past 5 days, over close to 100 commits, I have tidied up the orchestrator, designed two dedicated SEO agents with full WebMCP support in mind, have worked on the UX of the system, a bit of its branding and have deployed it online. The way I built the whole thing was by using a coding assistant, thoroughly testing locally and only then pushing commits to production. Challenges we ran into the major product challenge that I ran into, while building SEOstrich, was how to design the role of chat vs. the final produced SEO artefact (a report, a strategy doc). Initially they felt disconnected from one another, so I made the following choice - the artefact is the center of the system, not chat. This product helps you make strategic and tactical decisions about your SEO work. You do start building an SEO strategy in the chat, but then the artefact starts shaping in front of you. You don't depend on the already built agent in SEOstrich - you have full control to steer it at every step of the way - but the final output, the sole reason why you are using SEOstrich in the first place remains at the center of the experience - not the chat. while building the product, during the first couple of days I used Qwen Code and the Qwen models, as I wanted to get a better feel for them. First, I suffered from significant latency in LLM calls and second, I tried testing using my Qwen token plan instead of the Cloud plan (indeed an unintended use) which resulted in a range of implementation that I didn't need and made a bigger mess of an already messy foundation that I started with. Additionally the most powerful Qwen model wasn't always able to plan things properly with me, so that we get things resolved - it missed the goal for the specific tactical decisions. This was a very painful experience, partly self-inflicted, but still painful. How I solved this was to move all agent execution to the gpt-5.6-Sol and Terra models, which reduced latency incomparably and used a combination of Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5 for the development and gpt-5.6-Sol for visuals. Accomplishments that we're proud of have reduced my DataForSEO budget drain significan

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Northstar
pitch: An editable software-improvement decision workspace where humans and browser agents turn source-linked evidence, constraints, and trade-offs into a human-owned Improvement Plan.
about_excerpt: An editable software-improvement decision workspace where humans and browser agents turn source-linked evidence, constraints, and trade-offs into a human-owned Improvement Plan. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI coding tools can help non-developers build software, but deciding what should change next is still difficult. In an ordinary chat, hypotheses, counter-evidence, constraints, rejected options, and trade-offs become buried across messages. The AI may produce an answer, but the human cannot easily inspect or revise the decision that produced it. Northstar explores a different interface: a shared, visual software-improvement decision that both a person and a browser agent can work on. The controlled prototype starts with a familiar problem: “I built a RAG chatbot, but the answer quality is poor.” What it does Northstar turns software-improvement reasoning into an editable workspace. A person can: inspect competing explanations and the evidence behind them; add supporting or contradicting evidence; mark an approach as already tried; reject or deprioritize hypotheses; activate constraints; compare improvement alternatives by benefit, complexity, cost, latency, and risk; and select a preferred direction. The actual output is not a chat transcript. It is a structured Improvement Plan containing the problem, important evidence, selected explanation, selected improvement, rejected options and reasons, constraints, risks, implementation steps, and acceptance criteria. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes the workspace meaningfully better because the human and agent operate on the same structured decision state. The page exposes eight semantic tools: inspect_improvement_workspace list_code_files read_code_file add_evidence update_hypothesis record_decision begin_analysis complete_analysis A browser agent can inspect the current decision, read shared source files with numbered lines, add only source-linked evidence, and complete a review. Human changes—such as counter-evidence, rejected options, and active constraints—become inputs to the agent's next analysis instead of remaining trapped in a separate conversation. The agent cannot silently take ownership of the decision. An agent-selected alternative remains a proposal until the human confirms it. How we built it Northstar is a React and Vite single-page application deployed on Vercel. The site registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Human controls and WebMCP tools dispatch domain actions into the same reducer state. Presentation components derive the diagnosis, recommendation, alternatives, and Improvement Plan from that state. Tool contracts validate revisions, decision ownership, source file IDs, and exact one-based line ranges. The prototype intentionally has no backend, database, external API, or site-owned LLM. Code context and decision state remain in browser memory. The page supports controlled sample files as well as pasted or uploaded text-based source files. Human and agent workflow Parsing begins as the strongest explanation because several failed examples involve tables. The human adds counter-evidence: failures also happen on plain-text PDFs. The human marks prompt changes as already tried, rejects multimodal parsing because of cost, and activates a simplicity constraint. A browser agent reconsiders the current revision through WebMCP. The agent verifies claims against exact source line ranges and updates the shared decision. Retrieval becomes the leading explanation and a reranker becomes the recommended experiment. The human reviews the trade-offs, chooses the direction, and receives an updated Improvement Plan. Challenges The hardest design problem was avoiding a chatbot, admin dashboard, or RAG monitoring interface. The core visual object needed to remain a decision . We also had to make agent activity trustworthy. Northstar tracks code-context and decision revisions, hides stale recommendations, requires exact source ranges for source-derived evidence, and prevents an agent recommendation from masquerading as a human selection. Accomplishments that we're proud of A coherent human-facing product experience, not only a tool-registration demo. Eight working WebMCP tools mapped to domain concepts instead of UI button clicks. Source-linked evidence with exact file and line ranges. Visible revision and analysis states that prevent stale conclusions from appearing current. A human confirmation boundary around the preferred improvement direction. A structured Improvement Plan that can be reviewed without reading an agent transcript. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools expose the meaning of an application rather than imitate mouse interactions. The agent does not need to guess how the UI works, and the human does not need to translate every judgment back into a prompt. Both can collaborate through the application's domain model while the interface preserves context and ownership. What's next for Northstar This submission is deliberately a controlled RAG prototype, not a universal code analyzer. Next steps would include persisted decisions, broader project-context adapters, reusable decision templates, and integrations with development tools—while keeping source edits and final direction explicitly under human control.
