title: MapTruth
pitch: MapTruth lets people and browser agents turn a real OpenStreetMap view into AI-generated map artwork—without letting the model invent the geography.
about_excerpt: MapTruth lets people and browser agents turn a real OpenStreetMap view into AI-generated map artwork—without letting the model invent the geography. Like Comment Story Updates Same brief, prompt-only versus map-grounded New Orleans. Real OpenStreetMap geometry locked for Lower Manhattan Ten typed WebMCP tools exposed directly by the page Six native calls completed with visible execution receipts The agent stops before paid image generation Editorial montage made from authentic production captures Inspiration AI image models can draw maps that look authoritative while inventing streets, landmarks, and spatial relationships. That is harmless as wall art, but dangerous when somebody might plan from it. I built MapTruth to make the real place—not the model—the source of geographic truth, while still letting an AI do what it is good at: interpreting intent and styling evidence. What it does Ask an image model for a map of a real place and it can draw something beautiful, confident, and geographically false. MapTruth changes the input to that process. A person chooses a place and writes a brief; MapTruth locks a live OpenStreetMap view, resolves requested features against OpenStreetMap, and generates two images side by side: one from the prompt alone and one grounded in the sourced map. The comparison makes the failure mode visible. In the New Orleans demo, the ungrounded result invents a plausible city. The grounded result preserves the large-scale relationship among Lake Pontchartrain, the city, and the Mississippi River, and marks only places resolved within the locked view. Why WebMCP The page—not the model—owns the map and its invariants. Through document.modelContext.registerTool , MapTruth exposes ten typed browser tools for focusing a place, navigating, inspecting and locking the live map, marking features from OpenStreetMap, verifying geography, and staging a comparison. An agent calls those tools directly instead of interpreting a screenshot or scraping UI text. That changes what an agent is allowed to invent. The model may decide what kinds of places a brief needs, but it never supplies their coordinates. OpenStreetMap locates them. Anything that cannot be resolved inside the locked view is dropped and reported rather than approximately placed. The app's visible six-step assistant walkthrough uses WebMCP's native executeTool() path when it is available, so judges can watch the agent call the same registered tools that another browser agent discovers. It leaves a receipt for each action and stops at the human approval gate before any paid image generation. A better user experience Without WebMCP, an assistant would have to guess from pixels or automate fragile controls. Here it receives named, typed capabilities and compact structured results. A person can see the same state, source attribution, verification counts, geometry hashes, and approval boundary the agent sees. The interface also has a manual fallback, so the product remains usable in a browser that does not yet expose WebMCP. What people and agents do together The person chooses the real place, states the purpose, and approves cost. The agent turns that intent into a sequence of explicit browser-tool calls. OpenStreetMap supplies locations and geometry. MapTruth rejects unsupported places, verifies the locked evidence, and records tool receipts. The image model styles the evidence; it does not supply the evidence. How it was built MapTruth is a React and TypeScript application built with Vite. MapLibre GL JS renders the live map. Nominatim resolves the requested city; Overpass provides nearby OpenStreetMap features. The browser integration registers ten WebMCP tools with JSON schemas, annotations, bounded outputs, and untrusted-content hints. Vercel Functions proxy the external services and image generation. Examples use checked-in snapshots captured from the same live pipeline so a demo does not stall on a public service. A separate verification script launches installed Chrome with WebMCP enabled, discovers all ten tools through document.modelContext.getTools() , and executes inspect_map_context through the browser's own document.modelContext.executeTool() . Challenges The difficult part was not drawing a map. It was defining a trust boundary an agent could not casually cross: the model can name candidates but cannot set a coordinate; geometry must belong to the current locked place; stale locks must be rejected; and paid generation must require visible human approval. Public geocoding and Overpass services also vary in latency, so the experience needed deterministic examples without pretending they were a separate data path. Accomplishments Ten discoverable WebMCP tools operate a real map workflow rather than a toy counter or hidden demo route. Native discovery and execution are tested in installed Chrome, with no mocked model context in the production verifier. Every generated comparison has a visible source line and OpenStreetMap inspection link. Agent activity is legible to the person and stops before cost. The same app remains usable manually when WebMCP is unavailable. What I learned Reliable agent UX comes from moving important guarantees out of prompts and into the page's tool contract. Structured tools make collaboration clearer, but the strongest result comes from deliberately limiting each participant: the model names, OpenStreetMap locates, the page verifies, and the person decides. What's next Next I would add saved, shareable evidence bundles; compare OpenStreetMap changes over time; and support more source layers while keeping the same provenance contract. The most useful extension is not more autonomous drawing, but better ways to inspect why a place was accepted or rejected. Honest limits MapTruth verifies that generation received geometry derived from the current OpenStreetMap view. It does not claim that every generated pixel is cartographically exact or that OpenStreetMap is perfectly complete or current. The prompt-only image is deliberately untrusted. Example snapshots are marked as snapshots; typing a new city exercises the live service path. Built during the challenge The repository was created on August 26, 2026 and its first commit is dated the same day, after the challenge submission period opened on August 25. The full implementation history is visible in the public commit log. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: SynapTable
pitch: A local-first visual canvas where people and agents turn connected ideas into structured, reversible workflows.
about_excerpt: A local-first visual canvas where people and agents turn connected ideas into structured, reversible workflows. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration SynapTable began with a problem my girlfriend encountered as a medical student. She regularly creates concept maps to understand how ideas relate and tables to compare dense information, but her workflow required constantly moving between ChatGPT and Google Docs—copying responses, rebuilding tables, and manually turning explanations into visual structures. One day, she complained that the generated table and concept-map experience did not match what she actually needed. The AI could suggest an organization, but it could not work directly inside the editable workspace where she was studying. That conversation gave me the idea for SynapTable: a visual canvas where people can think freely, organize concepts into tables, and move between both formats without leaving the workspace. WebMCP made the next step possible. Instead of building another isolated chatbot, I could introduce an AI copilot that operates through bounded, transparent tools inside the same canvas. The person remains in control while the agent helps transform ideas into useful, editable structure. What it does SynapTable is a local-first visual thinking canvas with connected concepts, rich notes, images, semantic tables, multi-project persistence, undo/redo, and exports. Its WebMCP integration exposes six bounded tools: Get a privacy-minimized workspace summary. Find visible layers by name and kind. Create a concept. Create a structured table. Organize explicit canvas layers into table rows. Create canvas concepts from explicit table rows. Agent changes appear directly on the same canvas used by the person. They remain visible, editable, reversible, and persisted in IndexedDB. Why WebMCP The useful context already lives in the web interface: spatial layout, connected concepts, and structured tables. WebMCP lets an agent collaborate through precise product actions instead of scraping the DOM or returning instructions the user must perform manually. A person can brainstorm freely, ask an agent to structure visible ideas, inspect and edit the result, undo it as one operation, and continue using normal canvas controls. How we built it The human UI and WebMCP adapter share a typed editor-command facade. Every mutation validates the active project and expected revision, creates one undo entry, persists before returning success, and rolls back on failure or cancellation. The six tools use closed JSON Schemas with generated CSP-safe validators, typed errors, a 1,500-byte output budget, cancellation handling, remount protection, and untrusted-content annotations. Hidden and locked layers cannot be mutated through WebMCP. Table discovery exposes dimensions and header status without exposing cell contents. The integration is progressive enhancement: the normal editor works when document.modelContext is unavailable. The approved Cloudflare preview enables WebMCP on the same origin and returns Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) with restrictive CSP and cross-origin headers. What we added during the challenge SynapTable existed before the challenge. During the submission period we added the WebMCP command facade, six tools, schemas and generated validators, lifecycle and cancellation controls, project/revision guards, content budgets, persistence-before-success, same-origin policy headers, native browser validation, and public index-based table-row conversion. We also expanded regression, security, accessibility, and cross-browser coverage. Validation The audit passed 173 unit/integration tests and 234 applicable production-browser tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. The native Codex in-app browser completed all six tools on the public Cloudflare origin. It created a concept, found it, organized it into a table, created a second table, converted two rows into concepts, and preserved the resulting eight-layer workspace after reload. No account is required. Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Ask the agent to summarize the workspace, create concepts, find them, organize them into a table, create another table, and convert data rows back into canvas nodes. Challenges and learning The hardest parts were maintaining one consistent mutation boundary for humans and agents, handling stale revisions without partial writes, making strict schemas work under CSP, and validating the experimental native API rather than relying only on mocks. We learned that agent-facing product design works best when tools describe user-visible capabilities instead of mirroring internal data structures. Small schemas, explicit revisions, reversible commands, and minimized outputs make human-agent collaboration easier to understand and safer to debug. What's next The next phase is a purpose-built study copilot—not a generic chat sidebar. Students could attach their own lecture notes, slides, PDFs, and approved references, then ask SynapTable to propose concept maps, comparison tables, study guides, and missing connections. Every generated claim should remain traceable to its source. Agent changes would follow a propose → preview → approve flow and continue through SynapTable's bounded WebMCP commands, so the result is visible, editable, reversible, and never silently written to the canvas. Near term: the Study Copilot I plan to explore Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) to orchestrate focused study workflows: a structure assistant that turns material into maps and tables, an evidence assistant that preserves citations and flags unsupported claims, and a review coach that finds knowledge gaps and suggests what to revisit. AG-UI could stream progress, tool activity, state changes, approvals, and cancellation between that agent backend and SynapTable. A2UI could provide safe, declarative controls for tasks such as choosing comparison criteria, resolving ambiguous concepts, confirming a table schema, or configuring a quiz—without executing arbitrary agent-generated UI code. Next: structured study knowledge SynapTable could add previewable actions such as “organize these concepts,” “cluster by body system,” “compare these conditions,” and “summarize this branch.” Tables could gradually gain typed study properties, tags, filters, and reusable views—for example topic, source, confidence, exam date, and review status—without turning the free-form canvas into a spreadsheet. An optional user-controlled database could add authenticated cross-device sync, version history, source provenance, reusable course workspaces, and study-group collaboration while preserving a local-first/offline mode. Shared maps could support comments and instructor or peer review, with clear ownership and permissions for every project. Later: move from organizing to remembering Students could turn selected concept nodes or table rows into editable flashcards that stay linked to the original map and source. SynapTable could then build review queues, surface weak areas visually, and let a learner jump from a missed card back to the surrounding concept map. Cloze cards and image-occlusion review would be especially useful for anatomy and other visually dense subjects. The longer-term goal is a learning workspace where trusted source material, visual understanding, structured comparison, and active recall reinforce one another. These capabilities would support education and study; SynapTable would not present them as clinical diagnosis, patient-care guidance, or medical advice. title: Ladder
pitch: An agent calls a tool on your page. Ladder runs it against a copy first, shows the person who owns the records what will change, lets them cut it down, then commits under a guard that rolls back.
about_excerpt: An agent calls a tool on your page. Ladder runs it against a copy first, shows the person who owns the records what will change, lets them cut it down, then commits under a guard that rolls back. Like Comment Story Updates Before WebMCP the tool ran on a server and the operator stood outside the room. With WebMCP it runs in the tab they already have open. The guarded path: fork and record, proof, cut down, then replay the same execute() under a guard that rolls back. A tool wrote a field the proof never showed. Requested 27, applied 0, refused 27, and the agent is told to replan. Four tools on the page. Two read, two write. Only the writes take the fork-and-proof path. The same engine on a second product: edge infrastructure rollout, built in a day, with no shipment anywhere in it. What Ladder is A human control plane for consequential WebMCP actions. WebMCP gives agents the ability to act on websites. Ladder gives humans the ability to decide exactly what those actions are allowed to change. Before an agent changes real data, Ladder runs the exact same tool against a clone of the page's state, records every write, and turns them into a proof the human can edit. The human approves or narrows it. Ladder then reruns the same tool against real state under a guard, and anything outside the approved proof rolls the entire commit back. Why this matters WebMCP settled how an agent acts on a page: a tool is registered, the agent calls it, the page does the work. That is the hard part and it is solved. What it did not settle is what happens when the agent is wrong. The operator sees a function call and a name. A call that is ninety per cent right can only be taken whole or thrown away whole. Freight operations run on legacy systems built around human operators: screens, workflows, permissions, manual decisions. The next generation of these systems will be AI-native. Agents will search records, propose actions and execute operational workflows directly. That creates a new problem. How do humans and agents collaborate when an agent can change the operational system itself? An agent may correctly identify 27 shipments that need a remedy, and the right answer is almost never "do all 27". One carries lithium-ion batteries and cannot go on a passenger flight at all. One has twelve hours of temperature-control endurance left and cannot wait until morning. One is ordinary freight whose customer will not notice. The operator needs to apply that judgment to the agent's proposal without taking the whole task back by hand. As legacy operational software becomes AI-native, the interface between human judgment and agent autonomy becomes part of the operating system itself. Ladder is a pattern for building that boundary. The freight story below is the proof, not the identity. What it does Ladder executes the same WebMCP tool twice: once as a shadow transaction, once as the guarded commit. The shadow run calls the tool's real execute() against a structuredClone of the page's state, behind a Proxy that records every write. Nothing real is touched. What the tool would do becomes a diff. The person sees the blast radius: how many records, how much money, how many of the actions are irreversible, and a bar showing that share against the whole dataset. They untick what they do not want, and every figure moves as they do it. The button they press says "Apply 20 · Refer 4 to duty manager". Then the same execute() runs again, against real state, through a Proxy that lets the approved writes through, silently skips the ones that were narrowed out, and throws a ScopeViolation if the tool goes anywhere the preview never showed. A violation rolls the entire commit back. The developer writes one function, the way they already do. Ladder runs it twice. Nothing disappears into "success" One run, accounted for end to end: Agent requested: 27 Above the operator's authority, referred: 4 Left for the operator to decide: 23 Operator removed: 3 Applied: 20 Every requested action is accounted for. applied plus every rejected count equals requested on every path the app can reach, including the ones where nothing lands. There is a test for it. What people and agents can now do together The person's edit reaches the agent as data it can act on. When someone cuts 27 down to 20, the tool does not return "success". It returns what actually happened and why the rest did not: { "status": "partially_applied", "requested": 27, "applied": 20, "rejected": [ { "reason": "the operator removed these from the change", "count": 3, "ids": ["HAWB-70003", "HAWB-70005", "HAWB-70007"] }, { "reason": "above the gateway operator's authority, referred to a duty manager", "count": 4, "ids": ["HAWB-70001", "HAWB-70002", "HAWB-70023", "HAWB-70025"] } ], "replan_required": true } Different refusals carry different reasons and the agent can tell them apart. A row the tool itself declined comes back with the rule that declined it. A record the person removed comes back as its own bucket. A record that changed while they were deciding says so. The agent is never left guessing which kind of no it received, so it can ask again about the four only instead of re-proposing all twenty-seven. Autonomy works the same way. After a run of clean approvals Ladder drafts a standing rule with caps and an expiry, and a person ratifies it the way they would approve a pull request. A person can also set one up front. When a rule is ratified, Ladder calls unregisterTool() and re-registers the tool with a description that states the rule, so the agent's own toolset changes as trust is granted . When the rule expires, the tool reverts. Irreversible tools can never carry a rule at all. The case it was built on Thursday, 19:40. A flight from Frankfurt to Chicago is cancelled. Two consolidations were on it, so 42 shipments belonging to 31 different customers are now unbooked. Nobody assembled that list. The cancellation did. There are ninety minutes to the first cutoff, and three ways out. Rebook on the same carrier tomorrow morning, which is free and costs eighteen hours. Put it on a competitor's freighter tonight, which recovers the time and costs money. Truck it to another airport and fly from there, which lands one day late instead of two. The person responsible has to decide which shipments are worth which remedy, against consequences, in the ninety minutes they have. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite. Two products ship from one engine to prove the engine is not the domain: index.html . Air freight recovery. Four tools: search_shipments and get_shipment read, propose_remedy and notify_customers write. edge.html . Edge infrastructure rollout. Four tools: list_pops and inspect_pop read, roll_config and page_oncall write. Eight tools across two pages. Neither product's engine knows what a shipment or a POP is. The second product took a day. That is the evidence that the engine is an engine. The core is about 900 lines. runShadow() forks state with structuredClone and records writes through a Proxy. runCommit() replays the same function against real state under a write guard that throws on anything the preview never showed. Reads carry readOnlyHint and skip the whole path. No fork, no prompt, no proof. 394 tests cover it. What we learned Chrome's own guidance for gating a consequential step is to not register the tool and let the user do it by hand. An action is either fully automatic or fully manual, with the decision made at tool-registration time, before the change is understood. Ladder is the in-between. The tool stays registered, the agent still calls it, and the human decides against consequences at the moment those consequences exist. What's next Persistence and a durable audit trail. Standing rules, history and the activity log are in memory today and a reload clears them. Per-field approval instead of per-record. Widening the recorder past two levels. And an honest answer for concurrent commits against one store, which is not supported today. Implementation and limitations agent.requestUserInteraction() does not exist yet. The spec defines this hook for pausing execute() to ask the user. Measured directly against Chrome 151's WebMCP testing build on 26 August 2026: execute receives only its first argument. There is no agent object, so there is no requestUserInteraction to call and no AbortSignal to listen on. Ladder feature-detects for the hook and renders its approval surface in the page. Both paths are written and both are spec-conformant; only one is exercised in the runtime a judge will open. We are not claiming to mount on the platform's own hook and we are not listing AbortSignal handling as delivered. We also measured that a pending execute survives 96 seconds and returns its structured result intact, which is why the approval can take as long as a person actually needs. The write recorder is two levels deep by design. Rather than let an unpreviewed write land quietly on real state, objects read below

video_transcript_excerpt: Frankfurt to Chicago is cancelled. 42 shipments, 31 customers, one operator to rebook them. The first move is not a right. It sets what she is looking at. When an agent calls a tool on your page, the person who owns those records sees what is about to change and keeps only what they want. Before Web MCP, the tool ran on a server somewhere else. It could reach the records, but the person answerable for them only found out once the change had landed. Web MCP moves it into the page she already has open. title: Estro
pitch: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking.
about_excerpt: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Projects Page ChatGPT Browser Window with Estro Before vs After Project Open within Estro Inspiration Everyone has a friend who takes the same photo on the same phone and it comes out like a poster. When you finally ask how, they send you a recipe: exposure +0.95, tint -18, an S-curve, blacks +52. You understood the word "photo." Every editor puts Saturation, Temperature and Tint in front of you and assumes you already know what they mean. Most people don't, so they never touch them, and the picture stays as it came off the phone. That's the gap Estro is for. The sliders were never the problem. The words were. WebMCP fits this problem unusually well because the thing a beginner needs isn't a smarter filter, it's someone beside them who can move the control, say the word out loud, and explain it in one sentence. An agent driving the real editor through the same commands a person uses can do exactly that, and the person keeps the Undo button. What it does Estro is a photo editor that runs entirely in the browser and registers 56 tools with document.modelContext . Open it in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and the agent next to the page can use the editor the way you would. Hand it your friend's recipe and it works through the steps. Every edit lands as a card in the interface naming the control, the value, a plain-language explanation of what that word means, and an Undo button for that one step. Mine and the agent's edits sit in one History, so I can undo its saturation without undoing my crop, and it can see what I did. Where Estro doesn't have a control the recipe names, the agent has nowhere to hide it. There is no Dehaze tool, so it has to say so and tell you what it used instead. Ask it where the contrast slider is and it points at the real control without touching it, so you can drag it yourself. Ask for a before-and-after and it puts the canvas in split view. Ask it to match your other three photos from that evening to this one and each project gets its own Undo, because each keeps its own history. Underneath, it's a real non-destructive editor: layers, groups, crop, transform, masks, curves, levels, colour balance, selective colour, vibrance, sharpen, blur, grain, lens correction, presets, batch export, and a live per-channel histogram that names which channel is clipping. Nothing is uploaded. There is no server and no account. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite on the front. Dexie over IndexedDB for project history, the origin private file system for original photos, a dedicated worker for thumbnails, resampling, histograms and hashing, and Canvas compositing on the main thread with a 256 MB LRU cache for derived previews. Zod validates every command at the boundary. WebMCP was treated as an architectural layer, not a feature. The interface and the tools call the same validated domain commands, the same history, and the same transaction path, so a dragged slider and an agent's apply_color_adjustment produce identical history entries. Tools register at module load, before first paint, via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every result is a JSON envelope carrying ok , the previous and resulting revision IDs, a transactionId , an undoToken , affectedIds , warnings, and a plain-language summary . Colour and layer commands also return an explanation of the term in ordinary words, so an agent can pass it straight back to someone who didn't know it. Every mutation accepts an optional expectedRevisionId and is refused with HISTORY_CONFLICT if the project moved on, checked immediately before the commit. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint , destructive ones destructiveHint , and anything that can return user-authored text carries untrustedContentHint . Errors carry a code , a fieldPath , a recoverySuggestion , and whether the project was preserved. The agent side is never invisible. Every tool call surfaces a card in the Activity Center, every committed revision carries its Undo, and History distinguishes the person's edits from the agent's. Challenges we ran into An agent cannot open a file. Browsers grant file access only from a user gesture. Rather than fake it, the tool focuses the Import control, reports whether an editor was open to receive that focus, and says why. A manage_project operation draws a three-frame sample scene and imports it through the same path a real file takes, so an agent arriving at an empty browser still has something to edit. Import had to be atomic across two stores. A project revision in IndexedDB and original bytes in OPFS can't share a transaction. A persisted intent record moves through prepared, committed, and deleted, and startup recovery finishes or undoes whatever a crash left, so History can never point at a file that isn't there. Adjustments bled. Brightening a rotated cut-out was brightening the background behind it, because the adjustment read a padded rectangle off the shared canvas. Each adjusted layer now renders alone on an isolated surface and is composited afterwards. WebMCP can't be tested in jsdom. 940 unit tests cover the domain, commands and persistence, but tool discovery only exists in a real WebMCP-capable browser over HTTPS, so every registration check was manual. Cutting video. Estro started as a photo and video editor. Ten days in, the video half doubled the surface and carried the least-verified code. It was removed, not hidden: roughly 12,500 lines, 14 tools, five panels, and one LGPL dependency. One thing done properly beats two things done partly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The person never loses control. Every agent action is a real, named, individually undoable edit in the same History as their own, and the explanation of the word travels with it. The honesty holds under pressure. Out-of-range values are clamped and the clamp is reported. Unavailable formats are disabled with a reason. A stale revision is refused rather than silently overwritten. There's no path by which the agent can do something to your photo that you can't see and can't reverse. Fifty-six tools, one command system, zero servers. What we learned Describing side effects in the tool description matters more than clever schemas. When a tool said exactly what it would change and what it would return, the model called it correctly first time. When it didn't, the model guessed. Returning an explanation from the tool, rather than trusting the model to write one, was the right call. The product's whole promise is that the word arrives attached to the effect. That only holds if the explanation comes from the same place the effect did. And the most useful tool in the set turned out to be one that changes nothing: the one that points at a control and explains it. Teaching isn't editing on someone's behalf. It's showing them where the thing is. What's next for Estro Local model support so the explanations can be spoken aloud for people who'd rather listen than read. Voice as an input, for the same reason. Bringing back a narrower video treatment once the photo side has been used by real people for a while. And a proper accessibility pass with screen-reader users, because a photo editor that explains itself in plain words should also work for people who can't see the slider it's explaining. video_title: Estro: The AI Photo Editor That Explains Itself
video_transcript_excerpt: Photo editors expect you to know exactly what saturation, tint, and exposure curves mean. Most people do not. Estro completely changes this dynamic. It is a powerful photo editor that runs entirely in your browser and actually explains itself. You open a project and tell the agent exactly what you want to achieve. Here we ask it to make a cold street photo look like a golden hour shot. We also tell it to explain every control it touches. You just talk to it like a normal person. The agent immediately gets to work. It moves the sliders for you. Every single edit drops a visible card right on the screen. The card names the specific control, shows the exact numerical value, and explains what the term means in plain English. If you do not like a specific adjustment, you just undo that single card without losing your other work. You always keep total control of the image. You do not always want the agent to do the heavy lifting. Sometimes you just want to learn where things are. Here we ask the agent to simply point out the contrast slider without making any changes to the photo. The agent immediately highlights the exact slider in the right panel. It gives you the clear location and the current value. You then drag it yourself. This is how you actually learn the interface and become a better editor. You can also ask it to perform an audit of the image. We ask if any of our recent changes ruined the fine details in the photo. The agent reads the live histogram and tells you exactly what is happening with your pixels. You click the split view to see the final result in comparison. 56 tools, one unified command system, and zero servers. Everything happens locally on your machine. Your photos always stay yours.

title: Scopebox
pitch: Turn human intent into the live capability boundary for web agents. Scopebox lets agents act only inside explicitly framed fields and request the smallest scope expansion when needed.
about_excerpt: Turn human intent into the live capability boundary for web agents. Scopebox lets agents act only inside explicitly framed fields and request the smallest scope expansion when needed. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP gives web agents a powerful new ability: websites can expose native tools that agents can call directly. That raises a second question: Who decides what the agent is allowed to change right now? Scopebox explores a simple answer: The agent can only touch what the human frames. Instead of giving an agent a fixed set of write capabilities, Scopebox turns a human visual selection into the live capability boundary. The demo uses a deliberately small six-field launch board so that this interaction is easy to see, but the pattern is meant to generalize to CMSs, CRMs, admin dashboards, forms, and internal tools. What it does Scopebox separates broad visibility from narrow write authority. The agent can inspect the whole page, but initially has no write capability. A human can frame specific fields, such as Headline and Description. The page then dynamically exposes WebMCP write tools that are valid only for that exact scope. If the agent discovers that another field must change, it cannot expand its own authority. It requests the smallest necessary scope expansion and waits. The human can either keep the current scope or explicitly expand it. When the human approves an expansion: the capability boundary changes, only the newly granted field becomes writable, the pending WebMCP request resolves, and the agent continues automatically in the same turn. No extra chat message such as “I pressed it” is required. When the bounded changes are ready, the agent can submit them for review, but it cannot accept its own review, publish, or deploy. The final decision remains human. How we built it Scopebox is a small JavaScript WebMCP prototype built around a canonical application state. The visible Launch Board is intentionally not an ordinary editable form. Agent mutations must pass through the registered WebMCP capability surface. The main control mechanisms are: Dynamic WebMCP capabilities The tools exposed to the agent change with the current human frame. At Scope v0, the agent can inspect the workspace and active scope. After the human frames writable fields, write and scope-expansion capabilities become available. Exact scopeVersion binding Write capabilities are bound to the exact scope version under which they were granted. A stale capability fails closed with HOLD / SCOPE_STALE . Mixed in-scope and out-of-scope updates fail atomically rather than partially applying. Human-gated scope expansion request_scope_expansion creates a visible Human decision surface and remains pending while the human decides. Approval resolves the same Site-tool call and lets the agent continue automatically. Denial preserves the existing scope. Timeout, cancellation, replacement, and stale-request paths fail closed. Exact reviewId binding Human review actions are bound to the exact active review ID. Missing review identity fails with HOLD / REVIEW_ID_REQUIRED . A stale or mismatched review fails with HOLD / REVIEW_STALE . Review submission also closes the write tools until the human either returns the change set to draft or accepts it. Canonical field surface Normal browser editing does not create hidden or “ghost” agent edits. The canonical application store wins over DOM-only mutations, and the agent must use the scoped WebMCP write capability to change canonical state. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not creating a tool call. It was preserving the meaning of human authority across a live interaction. A scope-expansion request originally behaved like a normal short-lived tool call. Refreshing the registered capability surface could cancel the very request that was waiting for the human. We changed the continuation model so that capability registration is deferred while the Human decision is in flight. The pending call now resolves with the exact Human decision, after which the agent re-inspects the new scope and continues in the same turn. Another challenge was separating what the browser can display from what the agent is actually authorized to mutate. Making the Launch Board canonical and non-editable through ordinary browser form interaction closed that gap. Accomplishments The final prototype demonstrates: dynamic WebMCP capabilities driven by a Human visual frame exact scope-version binding atomic failure for out-of-scope edits Human-only scope expansion automatic same-turn continuation after Human approval exact review-ID binding stale review and stale scope fail-closed behavior write-tool closure during Human review Return to Draft and Accept flows canonical protection against browser-only ghost edits a live public deployment tested through ChatGPT's in-app browser The final validation suite passes 21 tests with 0 failures . What we learned WebMCP is not only a way to give agents more tools. Because tools can be registered dynamically, the capability surface itself can become part of the user interface. That makes it possible to treat human intent as something operational rather than merely conversational. The Human gesture does not just tell the agent what the user wants. It changes what the agent is technically capable of doing. What's next The Launch Board is only one example. The same interaction pattern could be applied anywhere a web application contains actions that should remain bounded by explicit Human intent: CMS content fields CRM records and deal stages administrative permissions internal operations tools structured forms approval workflows Different interfaces can expose different capability surfaces while keeping the same rule: The agent can only touch what the human frames. title: CommitWeb
pitch: When an AI plan succeeds across three services but fails on the fourth, CommitWeb keeps what worked, finds a safe replacement, and asks for your approval-without starting over.
about_excerpt: When an AI plan succeeds across three services but fails on the fourth, CommitWeb keeps what worked, finds a safe replacement, and asks for your approval-without starting over. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration You ask an AI assistant a simple question: "I'm moving to Bengaluru. Can you arrange my electricity, movers, mail forwarding, and internet? Keep it within my budget and make sure the appointments don't clash." You want the AI to handle the details, so you do not have to manage every booking yourself. But what happens if it confirms three services and then the internet booking fails? The first three bookings still exist. Starting over could repeat them. Picking another internet slot could clash with the movers. And your approval of the first plan should not become permission to make any change. That question inspired CommitWeb. WebMCP gives AI agents tools to act inside web applications. We wanted to explore what comes next: how those actions can work together, and how an agent can recover when only part of your request succeeds. The moving scenario is our way of making that problem easy to see. The bigger idea is simple: if we trust AI to take action for us, it also needs a careful way to handle what happens when something goes wrong. What it does CommitWeb brings several service actions into one plan. It checks that they work together, asks for your approval, and helps recover when only part of the plan succeeds. Our demo follows a move from Hyderabad to Bengaluru using four services: electricity, movers, mail forwarding, and internet. You set the rules. Keep setup costs within 5,000 rupees. No appointments before 10 AM. No overlapping visits. Have electricity ready before the internet installation. Before booking anything, CommitWeb checks the whole plan. If two appointments clash, it shows the problem and offers a repair. You review the corrected plan and approve it. Then comes the important part. Three services confirm their changes, but the internet slot expires. CommitWeb keeps those three confirmations and looks for a new internet slot that still fits your original rules. It shows why an unsuitable option is rejected. It checks the replacement against the bookings that already exist. And because the plan has changed, it asks for your approval again. Only the replacement internet booking runs. The other three are not repeated. At the end, you get a record of what happened, including the failure and the recovery. That record survives a page refresh and can be downloaded. How we built it We built CommitWeb with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and native WebMCP. Each demo provider has its own browser document, saved state, and WebMCP tools. The coordinator discovers and calls those tools to prepare bookings, check the combined plan, and carry out approved actions. WebMCP is part of the working system, not just a label on the interface. Seven checks decide whether a plan meets the user's rules. These checks run in code rather than relying on an AI to guess. For example, the budget rule is: Total setup cost must stay within 5,000 rupees. Approval is tied to a fingerprint of the exact plan. A changed plan cannot reuse the old approval. Retry protection prevents the same approved action from creating duplicate bookings. We used Codex throughout planning, implementation, debugging, and testing. We built in phases, checking the core behavior before moving on to the next part. The current demo uses four independently stateful provider documents inside one same-origin application. They model separate services, but they are not live electricity, moving, postal, or internet companies. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was handling what had already happened. After three services succeed, showing a single "failed" message is not enough. The system needs to remember which bookings exist, which step failed, and what can still change. Recovery also had to respect the original request. A new internet slot is not a useful fix if it overlaps with the movers or breaks the budget. Another challenge was keeping approval meaningful. We had to make sure approval for the first plan could not quietly authorize a different one. We also worked through browser compatibility and tool lifecycle issues while testing native WebMCP. We checked the flow in a supported Chrome browser, not only through automated tests. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud of the recovery sequence. Three services commit. The fourth fails. CommitWeb preserves the successful bookings, rejects an unsuitable replacement, gets fresh approval, and completes only the missing booking. We built 38 automated tests covering the core rules and recovery behavior, including expired holds, invalid approvals, duplicate retries, and saved state. We also captured native browser evidence showing the completed recovery and the receipt after a refresh. What we learned A successful tool call is not the same as a successful outcome for a person. Four bookings can each look reasonable on their own and still make a bad moving plan together. We also learned that recovery should not hide failure. People need to see what worked, what did not, and what they are being asked to approve next. That changed how we designed both the system and the interface. What's next for CommitWeb Our next step is to test the same approach with real providers across separate websites. We also want to support more situations, such as travel bookings, where a failed step can leave someone with several confirmed arrangements and one missing piece. Today, CommitWeb demonstrates recovery by finding a replacement. It can also prepare a fallback proposal for undoing supported actions, but it does not yet automatically carry out that process across providers. We want to extend recovery carefully, while keeping the user informed and in control. The goal stays simple: one failed step should not make you start over. title: GymDeck
pitch: A gym webapp that lets ChatGPT build, adapt, and improve your workouts as you use it.
about_excerpt: A gym webapp that lets ChatGPT build, adapt, and improve your workouts as you use it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When I started looking into going to the gym, getting a workout plan was easy. ChatGPT could make one in seconds. The problem was actually using it: the routine stayed in the chat, my workout logs lived somewhere else, and ChatGPT had no way to know what I completed or how much weight I used. I built GymDeck to connect those steps. ChatGPT can create the plan directly inside the workout tracker, while GymDeck records what actually happens in the gym. That history gives the agent enough context to recommend what should change next. And the best part of all, it's free! Training should still be a routine. The agent is most useful when it helps improve that routine over time or adapt it when something changes. For example, when equipment is unavailable, time is running short, or the user wants to have a change of scenery. ## What GymDeck does GymDeck is a mobile-first workout tracker designed for human-agent collaboration through WebMCP. A user can: Create and edit a multi-day workout plan Load a saved training day as today’s workout Track sets, reps, weight, effort, notes, rest time, and cardio Replace or reorder exercises during a workout Preserve completed work when a workout changes Review training history, volume, consistency, and personal records Receive clear progression recommendations based on previous performance Accept, edit, ignore, or apply those recommendations to the saved plan Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can read and update the same workout state shown in the interface. It can create a plan, add or replace unavailable exercises, shorten a workout, log sets, review history, recommend a new weight, and apply that change directly to the next session. Every human and agent change is visible in GymDeck’s activity history and recent changes can be undone. ## How I built it GymDeck is built with React and TypeScript and hosted as a browser-based application without a built-in application server. The app exposes 23 tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools are separated into focused read and write actions, including: Reading the athlete profile, current workout, saved plan, and exercise history Creating or editing training plans Adding, replacing, or reordering exercises Logging and correcting completed sets Adding timed cardio Reviewing progress Generating progression recommendations Applying accepted recommendations to the saved weekly plan The normal interface and WebMCP tools call the same underlying state functions. This keeps the visible workout, history, recommendations, and agent actions synchronized. All important data is stored locally in the browser using versioned persistence. GymDeck works after a refresh and supports JSON import and export, demo data, and a fresh-workspace option. It does not require authentication, an external database, an OpenAI API key, or a chatbot embedded inside the app. ## Challenges I faced The biggest challenge was designing tools that an agent could use reliably. The first versions were too ambiguous. An agent might update only today’s workout when the user meant to change the saved plan, or interpret creating a first plan as replacing existing data. I separated these actions into clearer tools for first-time plan creation, explicit plan replacement, editing saved days, and loading a plan day into today’s workout. Another challenge was keeping history accurate across both human and agent actions. Correcting a completed set now updates its persisted history entry, repeated logging does not accidentally reopen a set, and replacing an exercise preserves work that was already completed. Progression also needed to be more than a generic message. GymDeck now compares recorded performance with the saved prescription, explains why it recommends increasing, maintaining, or reducing a weight, and can apply the accepted change back to every matching exercise in the plan. Finally, WebMCP support depends on the browser hosting the site. GymDeck’s manual workout interface works on mobile, but the complete agent workflow currently requires a WebMCP-capable desktop browser such as ChatGPT’s in-app browser. ## What I learned I learned that WebMCP is not about placing a chatbot inside a website. The important part is giving an external agent a clear and dependable interface to the product’s real state. Tool names, schemas, descriptions, safety boundaries, and return messages matter as much as the visual interface. Small, focused tools were much more reliable than broad actions that tried to handle every possible request. I also learned that a useful agent experience needs visible results. When ChatGPT changes a workout, the user should immediately see what changed, understand why it changed, and remain able to edit or undo it. GymDeck demonstrates how an agent can move beyond giving workout advice and directly help maintain a training routine that improves with the user. It is also licensed under the MIT license for all to use and develop. title: magpie
pitch: Magpie remembers where capabilities live and how they are wired into reusable workflows.
about_excerpt: Magpie remembers where capabilities live and how they are wired into reusable workflows. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets a site hand an agent typed functions instead of a page to scrape. The limit shows up immediately: document.modelContext is per document . The agent sees the page it is on and nothing else, while every task I actually wanted spanned sites. Find the delayed orders here, open a ticket there, email me a summary. Then the less comfortable realisation: agents could already do that. They browse, they navigate, some remember. What was missing was not capability. What it does The extension is three parts, and only the last is impossible outside a browser extension: Discovery : a modelContext polyfill installed in the page's MAIN world at document_start, or a native implementation wrapped in place, mirroring every registration out to the service worker. Registry : one list across tabs and sessions: live page tools, remembered sites that are closed right now, and nine action tools of its own, each with a status (AVAILABLE, SITE_CLOSED, AUTH_REQUIRED, TOOL_CHANGED, TOOL_MISSING) . A public crawler can catalogue which sites expose tools, but it is always signed out, so it never sees the ones behind your login. Cross-site execution : the extension runs each step on the site that owns that tool, in your own logged-in tab. The site exposes 13 capabilities of its own through registerTool() , and is where a run stops being something that happened and becomes something you can repeat: every step the agent took, the capability each one used, and a button that runs the whole thing again. Reach on one side, certainty on the other. What I actually built Not a smarter agent, a layer that makes an agents actions accountable and repeatable. Four things it refuses to do: Refuses to invent. A fabricated capability is rejected with the real names listed. Refuses to self-approve. The write prompt takes no approved argument an agent could set for itself, and fails closed where it cannot ask. Refuses to guess. Where judgement is needed, a reason step stops and hands the question back with the data attached. A gate fails closed rather than compare against data that never arrived. Refuses to take the agent's word. The engine writes the run record, so a step marked ok genuinely ran. Steps are JSON only, never generated JS, validated, then checked against the registry. Challenges I ran into Half of real WebMCP tools navigate instead of returning data. Pointed at real commerce sites, I found tools that move the browser rather than return values ,and a navigation drops that tab's tools from the registry, so a site read as "closed" seconds after its own tool had run. The agent may bypass you entirely. One posting straight to the extension's page API got a run id back while nothing was saved. Recording had to become a property of the bridge rather than of how a prompt was phrased, because you do not control the prompt. What I learned Magpie is not a new capability. Neither was WebMCP. Agents operated websites long before the spec scraping the DOM, driving a mouse. What WebMCP added was a contract: the site declares what it supports, with types, instead of the agent inferring it from markup. This project does the same thing one layer up, a contract across pages rather than within one. What's next Watch jobs, where the hard part is not the timer but pre-approving a write with limits validated in code rather than at a prompt. Remote MCP servers feeding the same registry. And a manual builder, so aworkflow can be assembled from proven steps with no agent involved at all.  Inspiration 

 Resolvia was inspired by a personal experience I had while trying to get a subscription refund. What should have been a simple process became difficult because I had to contact different parties, repeat the same information, and deal with inconsistent responses.
I realized that many disputes become complicated not because the information does not exist, but because it is scattered across different systems and people.
That experience inspired me to build Resolvia: a system that keeps evidence, context, and actions connected throughout the entire resolution process. 

 What it does 

 Resolvia is an AI-powered dispute resolution platform that helps investigate and resolve cases using evidence.
When a dispute is created, Resolvia keeps it as a persistent case. The AI can collect evidence, review claims, identify inconsistencies, and help determine the next step.
With WebMCP, Resolvia can also interact with supported web applications to retrieve information and perform structured actions. Important evidence and actions remain recorded so the final resolution is easier to understand and review. 

 How we built it 

 Resolvia is built around a case-based workflow. Each dispute has its own status, evidence, investigation history, and resolution.
Instead of asking AI to immediately make a decision, the system guides the case through several stages such as evidence collection, investigation, and resolution.
We use WebMCP to give the AI a structured way to interact with web applications, while keeping the process transparent and traceable. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the main challenges was deciding how much control the AI should have. Disputes may involve important customer or financial decisions, so we did not want the AI to act without clear evidence.
Another challenge was handling incomplete or conflicting information from different sources.
We also wanted WebMCP to be a meaningful part of the product, not just something added for the competition. It needed to genuinely help Resolvia collect information and move cases forward. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am proud that Resolvia became more than a simple AI chatbot.
Each dispute can keep its evidence, history, and progress over time, making the system more suitable for real-world resolution workflows.
I am also proud that WebMCP fits naturally into Resolvia by allowing AI agents to interact with web applications while keeping important actions traceable. 

 What we learned 

 Building Resolvia taught me that many disputes are caused by fragmented information rather than a lack of information.
I also learned that giving AI more abilities is not enough. A good agentic system also needs clear workflows, persistent context, evidence tracking, and human oversight.
WebMCP showed me how websites can become easier and more reliable for AI agents to interact with through structured capabilities. 

 What's next for Resolvia 

 Next, I want to expand Resolvia beyond subscription refunds into other cases such as billing disputes, marketplace transactions, delivery problems, and service complaints.
I also want to add more WebMCP integrations, improve evidence tracking, and introduce stronger human approval for sensitive actions.
The long-term goal is for Resolvia to become a reliable resolution layer that helps users and businesses turn fragmented information into clear, evidence-backed resolutions.

title: Relay Room
pitch: A cooperative escape-room game where a human and an AI agent use WebMCP tools to investigate a mysterious facility, solve its puzzles, and unlock the exit.
about_excerpt: A cooperative escape-room game where a human and an AI agent use WebMCP tools to investigate a mysterious facility, solve its puzzles, and unlock the exit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most WebMCP demos focus on task automation. I wanted to test a different use: making the tool interface part of a game. Relay Room is an asymmetric escape room. The player can see the room and use its controls, but cannot access the remote systems. Relay can operate those systems through WebMCP, but cannot see the room. Progress depends on the information they exchange through an AI agent connected in the browser. What it does Relay Room is played by one person and Relay (the AI agent, as in ChatGPT or Gemini in WebMCP in Chrome). The player reads visual clues, connects cables and activates controls. Relay receives a private manual and eight WebMCP tools to inspect the facility, decode signals, operate remote systems and release the exit door. This version has only one simple level to understand the game mechanics. The game has three stages, randomized puzzles, scoring, saved progress, voice lines, a solo test mode and offline support as an installable PWA. How I built it I used Next.js, React and TypeScript. The WebMCP integration uses the imperative API, with eight tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The interface and the WebMCP handlers share the same game state. Visual clues stay in the interface. WebMCP only exposes the manual, system state and remote actions that Relay is allowed to use. Local storage keeps the current mission and best score. Challenges The first problem was deciding what each participant was allowed to know and do. If a tool reveals the visual clues, the player is no longer necessary. If the tools expose too little information, Relay cannot reason about the puzzle. I also had to account for two connection paths: Chrome with a compatible WebMCP extension and the built-in browser in ChatGPT Desktop. They have different setup and permission flows, so the onboarding explains both options and verifies that the eight tools are available before starting. I think we are still in early stages of user experience for doing these kinds of interaction. What I learned WebMCP tool descriptions are part of the interface. Relay needs to know when to call each tool, what it changes and what to do with the result. Capability detection is not enough. The page also needs to explain which browser or client to use, where it must remain open and which permissions the player needs to approve. There is a need for a future version of WebMCP to register listeners, so the page can also send messages to connected agent. title: Ringlight
pitch: Your browser agent traces a fraud ring across a live money map, and you freeze it with one click.
about_excerpt:
Your browser agent traces a fraud ring across a live money map, and you freeze it with one click.

 The webMCP integrated setup for the fraud ring assessment.

 The webMCP integrated setup for the fraud ring assessment. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Human in the loop firing up, asking for permission to block the account. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Following dirty money is slow and manual. An investigator clicks through accounts one at a time, building the picture by hand, while the money keeps moving. We wanted the person's own browser agent to do that tracing with them, live, on the page in front of them, and to keep the human in charge of the one irreversible action. 

 What it does 

 Ringlight is a fraud-ring investigation console that runs in the browser. You ask your agent to trace a suspicious transfer, and it follows the money account by account across a live money map, scores the risk, pulls a hidden ring of mule accounts out of the noise, and puts a dollar figure on the exposure. Then it proposes to freeze the ring. Freezing is irreversible, so it stops and asks: one human click approves it, and the ring goes dark while every clean account stays untouched. A time scrubber replays the whole investigation, every step recorded. It opens with a seeded case so it works instantly, and you can drop in your own transfers as CSV or JSON to investigate real data. 

 How we built it 

 Ringlight is built on WebMCP. The page registers about ten tools with document.modelContext.registerTool: traceFlow, scoreRisk, detectRing, dollariseExposure, buildCaseTimeline, freezeAccounts, fileSarReport, replayInvestigation, and more. The user's in-browser agent (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with WebMCP) discovers those tools and calls them with structured arguments; our handlers run inside the page, do the real graph traversal and risk math, and mutate the live map. The agent is not clicking pixels or scraping a screen, it is calling real, typed functions we exposed, which is the whole point of WebMCP. freezeAccounts is registered as irreversible, so our substrate intercepts it and requires an explicit human approval before the handler runs. Everything is vanilla HTML, CSS, and ES modules, no framework, no build step, no runtime network, so it deploys as a static site and runs inside ChatGPT's browser. A small polyfill of document.modelContext lets the same tools run from a button when no WebMCP host is present, so it is always demoable. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Making the agent operate a rich, live UI safely, not just answer questions. Designing the human-gate so an irreversible action always pauses for a person, on top of ordinary WebMCP tool calls. Rendering a readable force-directed money map by hand in SVG with no library, so the app stays self-contained. Keeping it keyless and offline so any judge can run it, while still accepting real bring-your-own data. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 An agent and a human co-investigating a fraud ring on a shared, live surface, with the irreversible action human-gated and every step replayable. A genuinely load-bearing use of WebMCP: remove it and there is no agent-to-page channel and no demo. It runs with zero setup in the browser and is covered by a real test suite. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP flips the usual direction: the agent calls the page, not the other way round, which makes agent actions typed, permissioned, and inspectable instead of brittle screen-scraping. The most valuable safety primitive is a human-gate on the one action that cannot be undone. 

 What's next for Ringlight 

 Richer graph analytics, more bring-your-own formats, and a shareable case file so an investigator can hand a frozen ring to a colleague.
