title: Crepusculum Dream: A Playable WebMCP Portfolio
pitch: An explorable HD-2D portfolio where visitors and agents share one live interface—walking the world, building goal-specific tours, and inspecting page-aware work through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An explorable HD-2D portfolio where visitors and agents share one live interface—walking the world, building goal-specific tours, and inspecting page-aware work through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Playable HD-2D home world—explore by keyboard, mouse, touch, or a WebMCP agent sharing the same live page state. A goal-specific tour appears in the live UI, giving visitor and agent a shared route through the portfolio. Research tools expose publication metadata and paste-ready BibTeX; copying stays an explicit human action on the shared page. The sanitized Mods page keeps the case study and external links while replacing bundled third-party artwork with coarse mosaics. The WebMCP interface separates global and page-specific tools and explains their shared visible state. Inspiration Most portfolios give every visitor the same menu, even though a recruiter, research collaborator, technical reviewer, and creative visitor are looking for different evidence. Agents also tend to receive a detached data view that the person cannot see. I wanted both participants to inhabit the same place: a playable portfolio whose visible page, navigation, and tool surface move together. Crepusculum Dream began as my personal HD-2D hub world. For the WebMCP Challenge, I meaningfully extended it into a shared human-agent interface and packaged the result as a separate, rights-safe competition edition. What it does Visitors explore a dusk-lit pixel world with keyboard, mouse, or touch controls. Landmarks lead to Projects, Research, Mods, Zine, and About. A WebMCP-capable agent can operate the same live interface through tools registered for the current route: Five global tools list pages, retrieve my biography, navigate, change language, and create a personalized portfolio tour. Home adds tools for walking the on-screen traveler to a landmark and reading its position. Every content page supplies its own version of get-page-overview and focus-page-section; the same tool name has page-specific sections and effects. Projects exposes the fluid-simulation work, Research exposes publications and a read-only, paste-ready BibTeX result, Mods exposes project details and a Workshop action, Zine exposes individual pieces, and About exposes photography captions. There are 16 distinct tool names. The live registry contains 7 tools on Home and 8 / 9 / 9 / 8 / 8 on Projects, Research, Mods, Zine, and About respectively, so an agent sees only actions that make sense on the page shared with the visitor. Human-agent collaboration The challenge-period centerpiece is create-portfolio-tour. The agent translates a visitor goal—recruiting, research collaboration, technical review, creative exploration, or a complete tour—into a visible liquid-glass route panel. Both participants see the same stops. Choosing one uses the site's real router; first arrival opens at the page introduction or abstract, while choosing a deeper stop centers and highlights that section below the persistent top bar. This is not a static API beside the website. Tool calls act on the mounted DOM and the same router used by the visitor. The URL, visible page, focused section, browser metadata, and registered tools change together. On Home, agent-driven movement controls the same traveler that the person can move directly. Information-retrieval tools can spare an agent from reading and re-grounding against an entire long page when the visitor needs one precise fact. Interaction tools provide semantic actions for navigation, movement, and focus instead of relying on fragile coordinate-based UI operations. Together, these tools can reduce unnecessary context and token use while lowering grounding and execution errors, potentially improving task-completion reliability. How I built it The application uses TypeScript and Vite without a frontend framework. Home is rendered in Canvas 2D at a low internal pixel-art resolution and scaled with nearest-neighbor rendering, combining procedural sprites and tiles with lighting, fog, embers, ash, depth blur, and color grading. Content pages reuse the animated dusk backdrop. Tools are registered through the standards-track document.modelContext.registerTool() API. Global tools stay registered for the session. Each route owns an AbortController; mounting registers contextual tools and unmounting cancels their work and removes them. This prevents stale tools after rapid navigation and lets shared tool names have route-specific schemas, results, and visible behavior. Every tool has a human-readable title, a strict JSON schema with additionalProperties: false, concise descriptions and results, trust/read annotations, and cancellation-aware execution when the host provides a signal. get-citation is a read-only information tool that returns a complete, paste-ready BibTeX entry for Overleaf; copying remains an explicit control in the shared page UI rather than an agent tool. The production build targets Chrome 149 or later. What I added during the challenge The playable world and an initial set of global, Home, and Research WebMCP tools predated the submission period; I do not claim them as new work. The latest public pre-challenge baseline is 5acdbc7 , dated August 17, 2026. Challenge-period work added the page-aware registry and route lifecycle, contextual overview/focus tools, exclusive tools for every content area, the Workshop action, a read-only paste-ready BibTeX retrieval tool with copying left to the visible page UI, strict schemas and annotations, cancellation support, Chrome 149 compatibility, route-specific metadata, structured WebMCP documentation, the visible goal-specific tour, shared-state focus behavior, and a repeatable six-route smoke test. The dated evidence is the original repository's 5acdbc7...5052cf2 comparison and the competition repository's CHALLENGE.md . Competition-safe edition The submitted repository is a clean export with new Git history so removed third-party source files are absent from both the tree and its history. It uses an anonymous blue-and-white pixel identicon, nonrepresentational coarse mosaics for redacted previews, CSS-only card/relic grids, and optimized runtime media only. Identity-specific game names, source artwork, a research PDF, the original publication teaser, and adapted literary mascots are not bundled. The Mods page retains ordinary external links to the separately maintained project and Workshop listing; their target content is not copied or proxied here. The audit compared all 31 retained image/vector/video files against 27 restricted baseline originals and found zero SHA-256 matches. Details and licensing boundaries are documented in ASSET-AUDIT.md , PROVENANCE.md , and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Challenges The hardest engineering problem was making page lifecycle part of the tool contract. An asynchronous registration can finish after its page disappears, so route cancellation and ownership must be explicit. Stable tool names also need page-specific schemas so an agent cannot request a section absent from the visible UI. The hardest experience-design problem was keeping collaboration observable: navigation, scroll positioning, fixed-top-bar clearance, highlighting, transition timing, and the tour panel all have to agree. A separate challenge was drawing a clear provenance and licensing boundary without weakening the working demo. Accomplishments One live router and DOM are shared by human and agent rather than parallel representations. Page-aware registration keeps the available actions precise across all six routes. Native Chrome and Codex in-app-browser checks pass, as does the automated WebMCP smoke suite. get-about-me is genuinely read-only; visible focus remains a separately modeled interaction. The public deployment, source, tests, metadata, and submission documentation describe the same sanitized build. What I learned WebMCP is most compelling when tools express capabilities of the interface currently in front of the visitor. Page scope reduces ambiguity, visible effects build trust, and stable semantic actions let an agent help without taking the experience away from the person. Team Yunhao Luo led the overall site design and implemented the application, WebMCP integration, testing, rights-safe packaging, and submission materials. abcdefgJack contributed only through idea exploration and design discussion. What's next I would add evaluation datasets for tool selection, visitor-authored tour goals, deeper accessibility testing, and richer collaboration cues while following the evolving WebMCP standard. License and provenance The application source is MIT-licensed. Original site content and the limited third-party fonts/profile-link marks retained by the competition edition are separately documented. The original personal site and repository are linked only as the transparent pre-challenge baseline; the submitted live build and source are the sanitized competition edition. title: Redini-Atelier
pitch: A WebMCP design studio where agent actions arrive as editable ChangeSets you can preview, amend and undo before the canvas changes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP design studio where agent actions arrive as editable ChangeSets you can preview, amend and undo before the canvas changes. Like Comment Story Updates How it works—agent intent→one editable ChangeSet→human negotiates→receipt & history. Atelier is the product Redini is the transaction layer Inspiration Most AI agent demos mutate your app silently. You ask for a change, it happens, you hope it was right. Approval dialogs are binary — yes or no — while real design work is never binary. I wanted the opposite: what if every agent action arrived as a set of related, negotiable changes you can actually see together? A title, a background, a logo position — proposed at once, previewed as one coherent poster, edited one by one. That question became Atelier, powered by Redini . ## What it does Atelier is a WebMCP design editor where agent actions arrive as editable ChangeSets instead of silent mutations. ONE agent intent → ONE WebMCP call (design_update) → ONE ChangeSet → derived preview → amend / skip → atomic commit → receipt → Undo ↔ Redo One call can propose 3 or 6 operations at once. Before anything touches the live canvas you can preview the full result, amend any parameter with typed controls, skip any operation, and commit only the accepted subset. The receipt preserves the distance between what the agent intended and what you authorized: INTENDED / AMENDED BY YOU / SKIPPED BY YOU / APPLIED — STATE v0 → v2 Redini is the small, app-agnostic transaction layer underneath. Every commit, undo and redo advances the version — \( v_{n+1} > v_n \) — so a proposal that was staged on an old state becomes stale instead of being silently applied elsewhere. Live: https://redini-atelier.netlify.app — Try ?clean=1 for the focused agent path. ## How we built it Stack: TypeScript + Vite, native DOM/CSS, Netlify static hosting. No framework, no snapshots — forward operations + compensating inverses only. WebMCP: We use the native surface — document.modelContext.registerTool() , getTools() , executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(args)) . The public app exposes 5 focused tools: design_update , list_templates , get_current_design , filter_templates , get_vendor_content . design_update stays pending while you negotiate and resolves with a concise result like {"status":"committed","appliedCount":2} . Undo/Redo are intentionally human-side only. Verified like a product: 104 tests, tsc --noEmit clean, production builds, and a real Chrome 149+ E2E that drives the true executeTool path — including PREVIEW — not applied yet , amend, skip, Commit N changes , receipt, Undo, Redo, keyboard ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z , and stale proposals. Deployed with explicit Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) so the experimental browser gate is unambiguous. ## Challenges we ran into WebMCP is still experimental. executeTool expects the tool object + JSON string , Chrome needs --enable-features=WebMCP , and documents must be origin-keyed or registerTool must reject with SecurityError . We found all three with a real Puppeteer spike on Chrome 149. Product challenges were harder: Preview without double-render: simulate() already gave the right derived state, but we rendered it as a translucent overlay on top of the committed poster. Fix: hide the committed canvas while previewing. Honest atomicity: if runtime.apply() mutates then throws without returning an inverse, the world may be partially changed. Redini never claims “nothing happened” in that case — it surfaces stateUncertain instead. Derived bounds: move {x:640,y:400} passes a per-field check but puts the logo fully outside the 640×400 canvas. Bounds are now validated on the sequential derived logo state and re-validated at commit. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, demo-ready loop that holds together under verification: agent proposes 6 changes in one call → you amend one, skip one, commit 2 of 6 → receipt → Undo → Redo → provenance shows Agent proposed vs You staged Template "..." , all with 0 console errors . We are proud of the small things judges can falsify: the badge names the proposal that owns the preview, Commit is disabled at 0 ops, templates are real <button> s, and the 104-test suite includes the exact repros from our external audits. And it works inside the real ChatGPT in-app browser — our final smoke was there, on the Netlify URL, with frame-ancestors allowlisted for it. ## What we learned A transaction layer does not need snapshots. Set-semantics + idempotent inverses are enough, and the hardest part is not the algorithm but making the UI tell the truth. We also learned to keep the agent surface small — 5 tools and one negotiable ChangeSet are more legible than a toolbox of approvals. Built solo for my first hackathon, it was also a crash course in reading specs before building. ## What's next for Redini-Atelier Redini stays a small, reusable guard. Next we want to make it a tiny npm module with a cleaner validate(op, priorOps?) contract, add opt-in persistence for history, and try the same pattern on other domains — dashboards, forms, planning tools — where one agent intent naturally touches several related fields. Code is MIT at https://github.com/cioffiAI/redini-atelier — v1.0.0-challenge is frozen, main stays open. title: Adaptive WebMCP
pitch: Using WebMCP to let AI agents adapt public sector websites in real time for people who experience cognitive overload, distraction, or difficulty navigating the web.
about_excerpt: Using WebMCP to let AI agents adapt public sector websites in real time for people who experience cognitive overload, distraction, or difficulty navigating the web. Like Comment Story Updates Healthcare site State Gov site Local Gov site ChatGPT session Inspiration The web has made real progress on accessibility, but cognitive accessibility still gets overlooked, and it's genuinely hard to design for. WCAG gives us solid guidance on consistent navigation, understandable content, motion, focus, and giving people enough time to complete tasks. Those standards matter, but they don't cover every way someone might struggle to process what's happening on a page. A site can check every accessibility box and still feel like a lot. Picture a typical homepage: a promotional banner scrolling across the top, a popup asking you to subscribe, several competing calls to action, maybe a video, and a nav menu with a dozen choices. None of that is necessarily inaccessible on its own. Put it all together, though, and it becomes hard to process, especially for someone with a cognitive or learning disability. Some sites offer controls that help, and browsers and operating systems provide preferences too. But if a site is already overwhelming, asking someone to hunt down another menu, parse a list of settings, and figure out which combination might help just adds more burden. WebMCP gave me a different way to think about the problem. What if I could just tell my AI agent, "There's too much happening on this page," and the site could tell the agent what it's actually capable of changing? What it does I built Adaptive WebMCP to explore that idea. It includes three demo experiences modeled after a state government site, a county government site, and a healthcare site, three categories where digital accessibility is especially important and often legally required. Each site can adapt in several ways: text can get larger, contrast can increase, spacing can change, movement can stop, and navigation can simplify. I also built in plain-language content, since cognitive accessibility isn't only a visual concern. Government and healthcare sites lean heavily on legal, institutional, or medical language that's genuinely hard to process. The experience can also reorganize around a person's goal. If someone needs to renew a driver's license, find urgent care, or pay property taxes, the agent can focus the whole site on that task and clear away the unrelated information competing for their attention. All of this is exposed through WebMCP. Someone might say, "The movement is distracting me," "I don't understand what this means," or just, "Make this easier to use." The agent discovers what the site supports and picks from the adaptations I've made available. The person doesn't need to know the name of a setting or where to find it. They just describe what's getting in their way, in their own words. How I built it Adaptive WebMCP runs on React, Next.js, and TypeScript, deployed through ChatGPT Sites. All three portals share the same adaptive interface, with their capabilities registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . I built nine WebMCP tools in total. Some help the agent understand the experience first, like what adaptations are available and which settings are already active. The rest handle changing readability, simplifying navigation, focusing on a task, applying a preference profile, resetting the experience, or opening a mobile viewport for QA testing. I was deliberate about what these tools are allowed to do. The agent isn't handed broad control of the page to generate CSS or rewrite the DOM on the fly. Every tool maps to something I've already defined in the application. The site decides what's possible; WebMCP just gives the agent a structured way to use it. Plain language is a good example of this restraint. Instead of letting AI rewrite government or healthcare information on the fly, the site holds publisher-controlled plain-language content. The agent can surface that version through WebMCP, but the organization stays responsible for what it actually says. I also built reusable profiles like low-vision , reduced-distraction , and comfortable-reading , so someone can ask for a whole experience without knowing which individual settings need to change underneath it. Traditional controls still work too. WebMCP is another door into the same adaptations, not a separate "AI version" of the site. I took this a step further and experimented outside the visitor experience entirely. A developer or tester can ask the agent to open an in-page mobile preview on an iPhone 15 or Pixel 8, which let me apply the same WebMCP model to responsive QA, not just accessibility. Across all of it, the principle holds: the site defines what can change, the person describes what they need, and WebMCP connects the two. Challenges I ran into The hardest question here wasn't technical. It was deciding how much the agent should decide on the user's behalf. Accessibility is personal. Two people can experience the same interface completely differently, and I didn't want an agent diagnosing someone from a prompt or deciding what their "accessible mode" should look like. The user's request stays the source of truth. The agent can help interpret it, but the site controls which actions are actually possible. Cognitive accessibility is also much broader than reducing motion or enlarging text. The adaptations in this demo are examples, not an attempt at a complete solution. Persistence raised its own question too. Display preferences are useful across visits, but task focus is contextual. So I store display preferences locally while keeping task focus session-specific, so nobody comes back later to find the site still organized around a task they finished months ago. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud this turned into more than an accessibility panel bolted onto AI. I ended up with nine WebMCP tools working across three distinct public-service environments. The agent can inspect an experience before changing anything, combine adaptations through reusable profiles, and even reorganize a whole service portal around what someone is trying to accomplish. At the same time, the traditional accessibility controls keep working with no agent involved at all. That balance matters to me. WebMCP isn't replacing accessible design or WCAG. It's opening another path into capabilities that should already exist. What I learned I started this project thinking about WebMCP mostly as a structured way for agents to perform tasks on websites: search, retrieve information, submit something, change some state. Somewhere along the way, I started thinking about the interface itself as part of that state. A site can tell an agent not just what a user can do , but how the experience can change for that user. That ended up being the most interesting idea in the whole project. It also reinforced why the person needs to stay at the center of this. An agent shouldn't be the one deciding whether someone needs an accommodation. The person already knows when something isn't working. The agent's job is just to translate that need into capabilities the site actually supports. What's next for Adaptive WebMCP The bigger opportunity here is interoperability. Accessibility and personalization controls work differently from one site to the next. What happens if some of those capabilities become predictable to agents through WebMCP, everywhere? A person could eventually set preferences with their agent once and have every supported site respond to them, instead of configuring each site from scratch. My prototype doesn't do that yet; preferences are still stored locally in the browser. Getting from this demo to something truly portable raises real questions around consent, privacy, standards, and how these capabilities should complement WCAG rather than compete with it. But that's the direction I want to keep pushing: a web that adapts to the person using it, instead of asking that person to relearn how to adapt to every website. title: Diamond Control
pitch: A human-gated agent workspace where WebMCP lets agents read, recommend, and prepare actions without taking the final decision away from the person.
about_excerpt:
A human-gated agent workspace where WebMCP lets agents read, recommend, and prepare actions without taking the final decision away from the person.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI systems are becoming more capable very quickly. But greater capability also creates a new problem. 

 As tasks become longer and the amount of context grows, it becomes harder for an AI system to maintain reliable reasoning across everything it has to process. Important details can be missed, reasoning can drift, and hallucinations can become harder to detect. 

 That is why I believe greater AI capability should be paired with clearer Human Gates. 

 Diamond Control started from this idea: let the agent do as much useful work as possible, but keep explicit Human checkpoints at the decisions where correctness, authority, or risk really matter. 

 I did not want the Human to approve every small step. I wanted the AI to be able to work independently until it reaches a decision that genuinely belongs to the person. 

 What it does 

 Diamond Control is a human-gated agent workspace built with WebMCP. 

 It gives an AI agent a structured way to understand the current workflow, identify what needs attention, recommend a bounded next move, prepare that action, and request Human review. 

 The application exposes five WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_workspace_state 
 get_attention_items 
 recommend_next_move 
 prepare_action 
 request_human_gate 
 

 The first three tools read or recommend without changing the workflow. 

 prepare_action can create a reversible proposed action, and request_human_gate can move that proposal into AWAITING_HUMAN . 

 But no WebMCP tool can approve or reject an action. 

 The final decision remains in the visible Human Gate. 

 In the demo, the agent identifies the proof-repair lane, recommends Review and run proof validation , prepares the proposal, and requests Human review. 

 The workflow enters AWAITING_HUMAN , where the agent stops. 

 The Human then chooses Reject, and Diamond Control produces a NO_ACTION proof receipt showing that the decision was made by the Human. 

 How I built it 

 Diamond Control is a browser-based application built with TypeScript/JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and WebMCP. 

 The main design goal was not simply to connect an AI agent to a web interface. I wanted the workflow itself to expose enough structure that the agent would not have to guess what the page means from buttons and text alone. 

 WebMCP provides explicit tools for: 

 
 reading workflow state 
 discovering items that need attention 
 recommending a next move 
 preparing a bounded action 
 requesting Human review 
 

 Behind those tools is a small state model that separates agent preparation from Human authority. 

 A proposal can move through states such as PROPOSED and AWAITING_HUMAN , but only the visible Human controls can produce an APPROVED or REJECTED decision. 

 I also added a fail-closed rule: if one proposal is already waiting at the Human Gate, the agent cannot silently replace it with another proposal. The Human must resolve the existing decision first. 

 The project is intentionally browser-side and small. It does not depend on a backend, database, authentication system, private user records, or an automatic approval service. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The main challenge was not making the agent more capable. 

 The harder problem was deciding exactly where that capability should stop. 

 I had to separate several concepts that can easily become mixed together in an AI workflow: 

 
 reading information versus changing state 
 recommending an action versus executing a decision 
 preparing work versus authorizing it 
 agent capability versus Human authority 
 successful automation versus correct execution 
 

 Another challenge was making the boundary visible and testable rather than keeping it as an instruction written only in a prompt. 

 That is why Diamond Control uses explicit workflow states, a visible Human Gate, and a proof receipt after the decision. 

 I also learned that long AI workflows need clear checkpoints. If every small action requires Human confirmation, the system becomes too manual. But if the AI is allowed to continue without clear boundaries, it becomes difficult to know when Human judgment is actually required. 

 Finding that balance became the central design problem of the project. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I am proud that Diamond Control demonstrates a complete agent-to-Human workflow rather than only exposing a collection of WebMCP tools. 

 The demo shows a natural-language request moving through the entire process: 

 
 the agent reads the workspace 
 identifies what needs attention 
 recommends one next move 
 prepares the action 
 requests Human review 
 stops at AWAITING_HUMAN 
 the Human makes the final decision 
 the system produces a proof receipt 
 

 I am also proud that the authority boundary is enforced by the application itself. 

 The agent cannot approve or reject an action, and it cannot replace another proposal while an unresolved Human Gate is open. 

 For me, this is important because Human control should not depend only on asking an AI model to behave correctly. The workflow should make the boundary explicit. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that WebMCP becomes much more useful when it gives an AI agent a flexible, structured way to understand and interact with a workflow, instead of limiting the interaction to a small set of rigid buttons. 

 A good agent interface should expose meaningful state, available actions, constraints, and decision boundaries. 

 This allows the AI to adapt its help to the situation while still operating inside explicit rules. 

 For me, the value of WebMCP is not just automation. 

 It is making the collaboration between the Human, the interface, and the AI more flexible without losing control. 

 I also learned that giving an agent more autonomy does not necessarily mean giving it more authority. 

 Those are two different things, and separating them can allow an AI system to do substantially more work while still preserving the decisions that should remain Human. 

 What's next for Diamond Control 

 The next step is to make the boundaries between autonomous AI work and Human authority much more complete and explicit. 

 With stronger boundaries, agents should be able to run longer tasks on their own, carry work across multiple steps, and automatically bring the workflow to the correct Human Gate when a real decision is required. 

 The goal is to reduce unnecessary manual coordination. 

 Humans should not have to supervise every small step. They should be asked to intervene only at clear checkpoints where judgment, authority, or risk actually matters. 

 Over time, I would also like to extend the same pattern to more complex workflows, more types of actions, stronger proof and recovery mechanisms, and multiple agent environments. 

 If these boundaries are designed well, AI agents can become more autonomous while execution still remains aligned with the correct level of Human authority.

title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: Easel
pitch: Design alongside your agent on the same live canvas! Easel uses WebMCP and context from across your life through your connected apps to help you create website mock-ups, posters, and graphics.
about_excerpt: Design alongside your agent on the same live canvas! Easel uses WebMCP and context from across your life through your connected apps to help you create website mock-ups, posters, and graphics. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A problem I’ve often faced when designing is that everything I need is scattered across different apps. The details might be in Notion, assets in Google Drive, feedback in Slack or Gmail, and references in Canva or Figma. Bringing it together means constantly switching apps, copying information, and making changes manually. I wanted an agent that could work alongside me—not just generate a design and hand it over. That’s why I built Easel: a shared canvas where we can collaborate through WebMCP and use context from the apps I’ve already connected in Codex. What it does Easel lets you create website mock-ups, posters, and graphics with an agent while still editing everything yourself. Select a title and ask the agent to make it bigger. Annotate a paragraph you want rewritten. Ask it to find a photograph in Drive, apply feedback from Gmail, or use confirmed details from Notion to update matching information across your designs. The demo follows a book-club organizer working on a website mock-up and poster. It starts with small edits, brings in context as needed, and ends with an exported poster. Everything stays editable throughout. How I built it I used React, TypeScript, and Vite, with Vercel for hosting and browser-local file storage. Human edits and agent actions go through the same command system, with shared validation and undo history. WebMCP exposes operations for inspecting selections, editing layers, placing assets, updating shared fields, and exporting. Codex handles the connected apps; Easel receives the relevant information without needing their credentials. I used Codex for planning, implementation, and debugging. Challenges I ran into The hardest parts were the everyday interactions: moving an entire frame, selecting an image rather than its placeholder, and making text wrap correctly. These details matter when a person and an agent are both editing. I also worked on reducing unnecessary agent calls. Named layers, selection-aware targeting, and batch updates make a small change more direct. What I’m proud of The agent doesn’t just look up information or produce a separate result. It uses that information inside the design I’m already working on, and I can keep making changes myself. What I learned Useful agent tools need clear targets and reversible changes, not just lots of functions. Sometimes selecting a layer and saying “change this” communicates more than a long prompt. What’s next I want to improve layout handling, accessibility, and performance on larger files. For now, website frames are deliberately mock-ups, not fully functioning websites: I want to get the collaborative design experience right first. title: Pit Wall
pitch: A WebMCP-powered racing strategy game where humans and AI share the pit box—analyze live race conditions, make strategy calls together, or hand the race to an AI Crew Chief.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered racing strategy game where humans and AI share the pit box—analyze live race conditions, make strategy calls together, or hand the race to an AI Crew Chief. Like Comment Story Updates Pit Wall — A WebMCP-powered racing strategy game built around shared human + AI race control. Track & Control Selection — Choose the circuit and control model: Human, Co-Crew Chief, or a fully delegated AI Crew Chief. WebMCP Site Tools — 8 structured tools give ChatGPT live race intelligence plus controlled race actions. AI Race Analysis — ChatGPT reads live race state, evaluates strategy tradeoffs, and recommends a call without acting. Live Pit Wall — Position, fuel, tire age, running order, field strategy, and decision context evolve throughout the race. Shared Pit Wall — Human and AI Crew Chief calls coexist in one persistent race, with control passing between them. Decision History — Every Human and AI Crew Chief strategy call is attributed, timestamped by lap, and preserved. Race Recap — Stage results, strategy history, and major events create an auditable record from green flag to finish. Inspiration Race strategy is a constant sequence of decisions: tires, fuel, track position, cautions, pit timing, and when to sacrifice position now for an advantage later. Most AI experiences put an assistant beside an application. I wanted to explore something different: what happens when the AI has an actual role inside the experience? Pit Wall turns the player into a stock-car crew chief competing against autonomous rival pit walls. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can join that same pit box. The human can ask the AI to analyze the race, make one strategy call, manage a stage, or take responsibility for the entire race. Delegation itself becomes a game mechanic. What it does Pit Wall is a browser-based stock-car strategy game built around human-agent collaboration. Players race across five differentiated environments: Daytona International Speedway Bristol Motor Speedway Darlington Raceway Pocono Raceway Watkins Glen International The simulation models fuel, tire age, pit service, cautions, stages, track position, pace, strategy splits, and autonomous opponent pit walls. Players can interact with the race at several levels of autonomy. Observe ChatGPT can inspect the live race without changing anything. Advise The agent can analyze position, fuel, tires, stage context, field strategy, recent events, and deterministic Race Intelligence, then explain the strategic tradeoffs while leaving the decision to the human. Act The player can delegate exactly one strategy decision to ChatGPT. Delegate The player can hand over a bounded portion of the race—or the entire race through the checkered flag. Every strategy call records its provenance, so the interface shows whether a decision came from the Human or AI Crew Chief. The result is not a chatbot layered on top of a game. The agent and human participate in the same simulation, operate against the same race state, and can exchange control as the race develops. Why WebMCP Pit Wall is designed around a problem that ordinary browser automation does not solve particularly well. A visual agent would have to inspect the interface, infer what each control means, extract race state from rendered text, and manipulate UI elements. WebMCP gives the agent a semantic interface to the same live race the human is playing. Pit Wall registers eight Site Tools: get_race_state get_my_car_state get_field_state get_current_decision get_recent_events get_decision_history commit_strategy advance_to_next_decision Six are read tools and two can mutate the race. The read tools expose structured information about the race, player car, field, current strategic decision, recent events, and decision history. The write tools allow an authorized agent to commit a strategy call and advance the simulation to its next meaningful decision point. This means ChatGPT does not need to infer application state from pixels or simulate mouse clicks. It can reason over explicit race state and perform defined actions through the application's own interface. Human UI actions and WebMCP actions operate against the same canonical race session. Human + agent collaboration The central idea is not simply that AI can play the game. The player determines how much authority the AI receives. Ask: Analyze this situation and recommend a strategy, but don't execute anything. ChatGPT can inspect the race and act as an analytical crew chief while the human retains control. Or: Take this strategy call for me. ChatGPT can make exactly one decision. Or: Take the pit box through the end of this stage. The agent can manage a bounded portion of the race and return control at the stage boundary. Or: Take the pit box and call this race through the checkered flag. The AI Crew Chief can operate the race autonomously through successive strategic decisions. Control is therefore not binary. A player can move between Human, Co-Crew Chief, and AI Crew Chief behavior during one continuous race. Human and AI decisions remain attributed separately even as control passes between them. This creates an interaction model where a human and an agent can observe, reason, collaborate, transfer authority, and take control back inside the same stateful application. Race Intelligence Pit Wall calculates deterministic Race Intelligence for both the player and agent. It includes context such as: fuel margin to the next race boundary tire age relative to the field position trend stage context observable opponent strategy recent strategy consequences The simulation calculates the facts. ChatGPT interprets them. This separation is important. The agent does not invent the underlying fuel state, tire age, position, or field behavior. Pit Wall provides deterministic race information, while ChatGPT reasons about what that information means strategically. This allows the AI to explain why a decision matters instead of merely selecting an action. Strategy has consequences Pit Wall does not guarantee that either the human or AI will win. Pit service can sacrifice substantial track position. Staying out can gain immediate position while creating future tire or fuel problems. Short-pitting can create an undercut opportunity while temporarily sending the car backward through the running order. Different race environments also create different strategic conditions. The player's position, tire state, fuel state, pit history, field strategy, and race circumstances evolve as decisions are made. Completed WebMCP-controlled races have produced everything from victories to difficult finishes. Every decision remains visible in the strategy history, including: who made the call the lap on which it occurred the selected strategy the resulting position consequence Stage winners and the player's Stage 1 and Stage 2 results are preserved through the final race recap. The checkered-flag screen therefore becomes more than a finishing position. It provides a record of how the human and AI managed the race together. How I built it Pit Wall uses a React/Vite frontend, FastAPI backend, and deterministic Python race simulation. The architecture is: Human + ChatGPT → React/WebMCP interface → FastAPI → Pit Wall adapter → deterministic race simulation → user car + autonomous field The browser interface presents the same race state used by the agent. WebMCP tools are registered through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The application exposes eight WebMCP Site Tools directly from the live browser experience. The FastAPI layer provides the race-session API, while the simulation owns the canonical race state and advances the user car and autonomous field. The submitted application is self-contained and does not require an external database at runtime. The production build is packaged as a single-origin Docker application and deployed on Render. Reliability and integrity Giving an AI permission to mutate a stateful application introduces a different engineering problem from simply asking an AI for advice. A strategy call must apply to the correct decision. It must not execute twice. An agent managing a bounded portion of the race must stop at the requested boundary. And once the checkered flag falls, neither the human nor agent should be able to continue mutating the completed race. Pit Wall therefore includes protections for: stale decisions duplicate decisions decision-boundary overrun stage-boundary handling post-finish mutation actor provenance Human/AI control state Human and AI actions travel through the same underlying simulation rules rather than separate gameplay paths. A dedicated simulation exploit and strategy-integrity audit was completed before submission. The standalone test suite currently passes 46 focused tests covering the simulation, API behavior, WebMCP integration, decision handling, and race integrity. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. pitch: Naviquest is SDK for creating research friendly websites. It can be customized for better results, and it creates a smart research layer within the browser for agents for efficient web research.
about_excerpt:
Naviquest is SDK for creating research friendly websites. It can be customized for better results, and it creates a smart research layer within the browser for agents for efficient web research.

 1 2 3 



 
 What inspired me to build Naviquest 

 Naviquest began with a frustration I kept running into while working with web agents. An agent could need a small piece of information from a page, yet the only way to give it that information was often to hand it the whole page. It felt wasteful, but more importantly, it felt unreliable. The useful detail could disappear inside navigation, repeated controls, boilerplate, and markup that was never meant to explain anything to a person. 

 I kept thinking about the browser sitting in the middle of this process. The browser has already loaded the page. It knows what is visible, what is interactive, where the headings are, and how a control relates to the surrounding content. Asking a model to reconstruct all of that from a large page dump seemed backwards. I wanted the browser to do the work it is already good at, then let the agent ask for the small piece of evidence it actually needs. 

 That is where Naviquest came from. I wanted an agent to be able to arrive on a page, understand what kind of place it had reached, find the relevant information, and keep track of it after the page changed. The goal was never to make an agent sound more certain. I wanted it to have a more honest relationship with the page: to point to the evidence it used, to know when it had lost its place, and to say when an answer was not there. 

 My work on Octocode shaped that instinct. I learned that research becomes much stronger when an agent can orient itself before it starts searching, recover the exact source for a claim, and separate what it knows from what it is guessing. I wanted to bring that discipline into the browser. A web page should not be treated as an unstructured wall of text. It has meaning in its layout, accessibility information, controls, and changes over time. 

 Accessibility became an important part of the project for that reason. Names, roles, headings, landmarks, and state often explain a page better than its raw markup does. At the same time, I learned not to pretend that the page reveals everything. There are parts of the browser environment that a page script cannot truly see. Rather than hide those gaps, I wanted Naviquest to name them. That choice matters to me because a tool that is confidently wrong is much less useful than a tool that can clearly describe its limits. 

 The project also grew out of a practical question: what does it mean for an answer to stay grounded after someone interacts with a page? Pages move. Routes change, menus open, content loads late, and controls update without a full navigation. A reference to a DOM node can become meaningless quickly. I wanted a way for an agent to return to the meaning of what it found, rather than cling to a brittle pointer from an earlier moment. 

 I have tried to keep the foundation simple. Naviquest starts with deterministic page understanding and retrieval because that gives me a path I can inspect and trust. Browser AI can be useful for tasks such as checking a grounded response, shortening it, translating a query, or describing content that is otherwise hard to reach. But I do not want AI in the project merely because it is available. It has to earn its place by making the research experience better without weakening the connection to evidence. 

 Building this has made me more interested in the difference between having less context and having better context. A smaller payload is not automatically a better answer. The real challenge is preserving the detail that matters while leaving behind the noise. That is still the question I am working on: where does browser-side research genuinely help an agent understand a page, and where does it not? 

 Naviquest is my attempt to explore that question in a practical way. I want browsing agents to be better, more precise, and easier to trust. I want them to ask the page for help instead of swallowing it whole. And I want their answers to remain connected to something a person can inspect for themselves, and most importantly, tokes consumption is something that I truly bellieve that can be improved, give the APIs we are having today (including Chromium AI beta features https://developer.chrome.com/docs/ai/built-in ) 

 P.S 
The biggest challenge was the demo video, which wasn't able to showcase all of Naviquest's capabilities the way I intended
