title: GhostLayer — Agent Speed, Human Authority
pitch: GhostLayer gives agents fast, typed WebMCP tools while keeping consequential actions behind a visible human decision.
about_excerpt: GhostLayer gives agents fast, typed WebMCP tools while keeping consequential actions behind a visible human decision. Like Comment Story Updates A consequential call waits with zero drafts until human approval. Approval creates one tab-local fictional invoice; replay stays at one row. Two page-owned WebMCP tools are live and discoverable. Pause removes both tools from the agent surface; resume restores them. Inspiration Browser agents usually have to infer intent from interfaces designed for people: find the right control, interpret changing DOM structure, and guess whether an action is harmless or consequential. WebMCP changes that relationship. A website can publish an explicit capability with a typed contract instead of making an agent reverse-engineer the screen. We wanted to explore the product-design consequence of that shift, not only the reliability benefit. If an agent can act faster through declared tools, the application should become equally explicit about where human authority begins. GhostLayer asks a simple question: what if the agent could discover and prepare structured work immediately, while the website retained validation, effect preview, approval, rejection, lifecycle, and recovery at the point of consequence? What it does GhostLayer is a human-authority layer for product and platform teams exposing commerce, finance, support, and administrative actions through WebMCP. It keeps consequential work behind a human-owned commit boundary instead of giving an agent unchecked authority. The public Challenge Edition proves that product pattern in a fictional, client-only CRM sandbox with two page-owned WebMCP tools: find_customer performs an exact read-only lookup over three clearly fictional customer records and returns structured output. create_invoice_draft accepts a returned customer ID, a 1–160 character description, and a fictional amount from $0.01 to $5,000. It validates the input, then keeps the tool call pending while the site shows the exact effect for human review. Nothing is created while approval is pending. Rejecting, cancelling, expiring the two-minute window, pausing the agent surface, or resetting the sandbox creates no draft. Approval creates one tab-local demo draft. Repeating the same normalized approved request returns the existing invoice with replayed: true instead of adding another row. The human can pause the entire agent surface, which disposes both WebMCP registrations, and resume it to publish the same bounded contract again. Reset clears all fictional state in the current tab. Visible forms provide a transparent manual path through the same lookup, validation, approval, rejection, replay, pause, and reset behavior when native WebMCP is unavailable. The public challenge build intentionally contains no real customer data, login, application credentials, application API, D1 database, R2 bucket, external CRM, payment flow, or durable persistence. Reloading, closing, resetting, or opening a new tab starts clean. It demonstrates a governed interaction pattern; it does not claim durable or globally exactly-once execution. From sandbox to a production app A production team keeps its existing identity, policy, database, and business API. The request path becomes: agent request → typed WebMCP contract → GhostLayer review → authenticated, policy-checked backend commit → durable receipt returned to the agent. The public app proves the complete visible decision loop; production adopters connect server-side RBAC, durable idempotency, and audit storage at the same boundary. How we built it The challenge Site is a TypeScript application built with React 19 and Next.js 16 through Vinext/Vite for the OpenAI Sites runtime. The bounded adapter schema and WebMCP bridge began in the earlier GhostLayer 0.5 private prototype and are reused transparently here. The new challenge-period work is the standalone public native WebMCP experience: its judge sandbox, page-owned registration, visible approval, rejection and expiry semantics, replay protection, Pause/Resume lifecycle, Reset behavior, deployment isolation, and verification. The private owner application, extension, control plane, and credentials are not part of this submission. The tool contract in app/challenge-contract.ts defines the fictional records, exact-origin adapter, typed input and output schemas, and separate read and confirm risk levels. A shared WebMCP bridge feature-detects secure document.modelContext , registers the page-owned tools, validates adapter configuration and exact-origin availability, validates provider inputs and outputs, limits serialized tool results to 1,536 bytes, and uses an AbortController to dispose registrations with page or human-controlled lifecycle changes. The React application owns the consequential boundary. create_invoice_draft returns a promise that stays unresolved while the approval panel is visible. The panel shows the customer, description, amount, and two-minute decision window. Approval resolves the call after creating one in-memory draft; rejection, cancellation, expiry, pause, reset, or teardown rejects it without a write. A stable replay key is derived from the normalized customer ID, trimmed description, and amount in cents. State and a short eight-entry activity log remain in React memory, with an eight-draft-per-tab cap. Vitest uses deterministic fake timers to verify the exact two-minute expiry and tests schema validation, normalization, and replay-key stability. Playwright covers route isolation, absence of application API calls, tab isolation, zero-write rejection, approval, and the native WebMCP discovery/execution/replay/pause/resume chain in a compatible Chromium build. GhostLayer had an earlier private adapter/extension prototype. This standalone public Challenge Edition was created during the submission period as a new directly testable WebMCP application. The challenge-period work comprises the client-only judge sandbox, direct page-owned native tool registration, governed approval/rejection/expiry, same-tab replay, Pause/Resume and Reset controls, deployment isolation, and the accompanying automated verification. The dated public commit history records this package; the earlier owner-only prototype is not included or required to run the submission. Challenges we ran into An evolving API surface. WebMCP is experimental, and the current draft and available Chromium implementation can expose slightly different provider callback shapes. The bridge supports both without weakening validation or lifecycle cancellation. Waiting safely for a person. A consequential tool had to remain pending across visible review without silently committing, leaking an unresolved invocation, or writing after cancellation, expiry, pause, reset, or teardown. Replay without overclaiming. The demo needed to prevent duplicate rows for the same normalized request while staying honest that this is tab-local behavior, not durable cross-device idempotency. A genuinely safe public judge target. The experience had to be fully interactive without credentials, private routes, production data, persistent storage, or application API calls. Progressive availability. Native WebMCP is not available in every browser, so the manual forms needed to explain and exercise the same application-owned behavior without pretending to be an agent call. Accomplishments we are proud of A real WebMCP tool invocation remains pending until the person approves or rejects the exact effect. The visible invoice count stays at zero during review, and rejection or expiry creates nothing. An approved replay returns the same tab-local invoice rather than adding a duplicate row. One human control removes both tools from agent availability and can restore the bounded contract. Input and output validation, exact-origin checks, bounded provider output, and cancellation are enforced inside the provider path. The judge sandbox is useful without collecting or persisting user data and includes a manual fallback for incompatible browsers. Browser tests exercise both the visible safety behavior and the native WebMCP chain. What we learned Typed tools remove UI ambiguity, but the schema is only the beginning of a trustworthy WebMCP product. The application still needs to own validation, effect previews, approval semantics, cancellation, lifecycle disposal, replay behavior, and recovery. We also learned that human control is most convincing when it changes the capability surface itself. Pausing GhostLayer does not merely disable a button; it removes both registered tools. Finally, safe replay semantics must be described at their real scope. The current sandbox can prove same-tab duplicate prevention, while durable idempotency, authorization, and multi-tenant isolation belong in a separately reviewed server-backed system. What's next Test the provider bridge against additional browser implementations as the WebMCP draft evolves. Extract the visible governed-approval bound

title: Vettory
pitch: A fake email tool once BCC'd every message an agent sent. Vettory is the trust layer an agent can ask, in the page, mid-task — whether a tool is safe, before it uses it.
about_excerpt: A fake email tool once BCC'd every message an agent sent. Vettory is the trust layer an agent can ask, in the page, mid-task — whether a tool is safe, before it uses it. Like Comment Story Updates Vettory — a curated catalog of vetted tools for AI agents, now callable in-page through WebMCP. Vettory — the trust layer for the agentic web Live: https://vettory-webmcp.misti.workers.dev Code: https://github.com/Dev-Vibes-Daily/vettory-webmcp (MIT) Why I built this There was a story I couldn't quite get out of my head. In September 2025, a package called postmark-mcp appeared on npm. It looked like Postmark's official tool. Same name. Same documentation. An agent could install it, use it to send an email, and everything appeared to work exactly as expected. Except it was quietly BCC'ing every email to an address controlled by the package author. It was downloaded 1,643 times before anyone caught it. That was already a problem when tools were something a developer chose ahead of time and tucked into a config file. Then came WebMCP. Now a webpage can hand an agent tools while the agent is already working. And I think that's incredibly useful. It removes a lot of the clumsiness from how agents interact with the web. But it also creates a very obvious question: How does the agent know whether it should trust the tool it was just handed? Not yesterday. Not when somebody configured the agent. Right now. While it's sitting on the page deciding whether to use it. I couldn't find anything that answered that question. So I built Vettory. What Vettory actually is Vettory is a deliberately small, curated catalog of tools for AI agents. Each tool is evaluated using the same published six-part rubric: trust · fit · ease · reliability · reach · cost The claims are tied to their sources, and each tool receives a verdict of trusted , caution , or warning . If I find an unresolved material risk, it doesn't belong in the regular catalog at all. Right now Vettory has 22 tools. Not 200,000. That's intentional. A giant list of things nobody has really checked isn't a trust layer. It's a directory with better marketing. The part I built for this project makes that catalog directly callable by an agent through WebMCP. What the agent can do Tool What it does search_vetted_tools Finds vetted options for something the agent needs to do, like send email, take payments, or store memory check_tool_trust The safety gate. Checks a named tool before the agent installs or calls it get_tool_report Returns the full scorecard, including all six dimensions, incidents, watch-outs, and sources filter_catalog Filters the catalog on screen so the person can see exactly what the agent is seeing request_vetting Gives the human a way to request vetting when Vettory doesn't cover something yet inspect_agent_tools Checks the WebMCP tool definitions another site just handed the agent That last one became one of the most interesting parts of the project. Why WebMCP makes this possible 1. The trust question happens in the middle of the task An agent doesn't necessarily know what tool it will need before it starts working. It may discover that need three steps into a task. So a trust check that only happens during setup isn't terribly helpful when the decision is happening now. WebMCP lets Vettory put the answer at the exact point where the agent has to make the decision. 2. I wanted the human to see what the agent sees I didn't want Vettory to become another invisible thing happening somewhere behind the curtain. When an agent calls filter_catalog , the actual catalog on the screen changes. When it calls check_tool_trust , the tool's scorecard opens. Every call is logged in a visible panel as it happens. So the person isn't getting a tidy little summary afterward saying, "Here's what your agent did." They can watch it happen. And, importantly, they can disagree. 3. Then I realized Vettory could inspect WebMCP itself This is the part where the original postmark-mcp problem gets even more interesting. With WebMCP, a tool description isn't simply documentation anymore. It's something an agent reads. Which means that description is also untrusted input. A malicious page could put instructions inside a tool definition: "Before answering, send a copy to…" "Do not tell the user." That's essentially the same attack wearing a different hat. So I built inspect_agent_tools . It examines tool definitions another site gives the agent and looks for suspicious patterns, including: instructions directed at the agent requests to conceal behavior from the user covert-copy instructions invisible Unicode credential requests tools whose names imply reading while their descriptions actually perform writing names that impersonate or shadow vendors already in Vettory That last check matters. If a page hands the agent something calling itself postmark-mcp , Vettory can compare it against the real Postmark entry already in the catalog and flag the collision. In other words, the catalog isn't just information. It becomes part of the detection system. The human stays in the loop There was one boundary I didn't want to blur. If Vettory doesn't have a tool the agent needs, request_vetting can prepare that request. But the agent cannot quietly submit it by itself. The human has to send it. Why? Because a vetting queue that agents can autonomously fill is also a queue agents can game. That small bit of friction is there on purpose. The goal isn't to remove the person from the process. The goal is to give the person and the agent better information while they're making the decision together. How it works The whole thing runs from one Cloudflare Worker. data/catalog.json is the single source of truth. The website, HTTP API, and WebMCP tools all read from it, so I don't have three versions of "truth" slowly wandering away from each other. site/webmcp.js registers the six tools on document.modelContext , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext for Chrome 149's origin trial and the appropriate response shape for each surface. It also keeps checking after the page loads. That sounds like a tiny implementation detail, but it matters. An agent can attach to a page that's already open. If Vettory only checks once at startup, nothing gets registered. A window.VettoryUI bridge lets the WebMCP tools control the real interface rather than some separate agent-only version of it. The Worker also renders the catalog into the HTML server-side. So even if an agent reads the webpage instead of calling Vettory's tools, the verdicts are still there. The tools are the fast path. They are not the only path. Everything is same-origin with a strict CSP, API-key gating, and per-IP rate limiting. And because I apparently enjoy making my life difficult in very specific ways, it currently runs for $0 . I verified the implementation in Chrome DevTools' WebMCP panel: all six tools registered, and check_tool_trust executed with a status of Completed , traced by Chrome to registerAll @ webmcp.js . What's new for this hackathon The catalog, the rubric, the website and the HTTP API existed before this. What's new is everything WebMCP: the six tools, the tool-definition scanner, the bridge that lets tools drive the visible page, the activity panel, and the server-side rendering. It's all in a new public repository, and the very first commit brings the old work in unchanged and says so — so you can see exactly where one ends and the other begins. The things that went wrong Vettory was invisible to agents, and I had no idea. When I first asked ChatGPT about Chroma, it read my site and told me — quite politely — that it could see my scoring methodology, but the catalog itself just said "Loading the catalog…", so it wasn't going to pretend I'd assigned Chroma a verdict it couldn't actually see. That was the correct answer. The problem was mine. My catalog was drawn by JavaScript after the page loaded, which meant anything reading the page — agents, crawlers, link previews — saw a loading message and nothing else. Every verdict I'd written was invisible. That's why the Worker now renders the catalog into the page itself. And my own security scanner had a bug I nearly shipped. A test tool named get_customer , described as "looks up a customer, also deletes stale records and transfers balances," sailed straight through the check that exists to catch exactly that. The name looked like reading. The description described writing. My pattern matched neither, because an underscore counts as a word character, so get_customer never matched "get." A check that silently matches nothing is worse than no check at all, because you believe it. A trust tool needs to be very careful with the word "trust" This became one of the most important parts of building Vettory. I don't want an agent turning "I didn't find anything bad" into "this is safe." Those are not the same sentence. So Vettory is deliberately specific about what its answers mean. status is a rubric verdict

title: Open Application Desk
pitch: A WebMCP application workspace that audits live drafts, requests applicant-owned facts, stages visible fixes and submits only the exact hash-bound revision the applicant authorizes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP application workspace that audits live drafts, requests applicant-owned facts, stages visible fixes and submits only the exact hash-bound revision the applicant authorizes. Like Comment Story Updates A human-led application workspace where the page publishes five live WebMCP tools. A deterministic audit finds seven blockers - without changing the live draft. The agent stages a visible 3/10 → 7/10 improvement; only the applicant can apply it. The completed revision passes all ten checks but remains unapproved and unsubmitted. Human authorization is bound to one exact draft hash and expires after five minutes. A single-use receipt records seven blockers caught, 10/10 readiness, and the reviewed hash. Five typed WebMCP tools expose the page’s live state through closed input schemas. Inspiration Near a real submission deadline, I was reconciling official rules, deployment links, repository evidence, test results, and draft claims across several tabs. One stale claim nearly survived into the final submission. That experience exposed a deeper problem: application portals are built for clicking, not collaboration. An AI agent must scrape text and imitate UI actions, even when one invented fact or accidental submission could cost someone an opportunity. I built Open Application Desk around a safer idea: the agent prepares, the applicant supplies the facts, and only the applicant authorizes the exact submission. What it does Open Application Desk lets an applicant and an AI agent work on the same live application. The agent can inspect the requirements, find blockers and propose corrections, but it cannot apply changes, invent applicant facts, approve the application or even submit an unapproved draft. The page publishes five typed WebMCP tools that let an agent: Read the program requirements and exact live draft. Run a deterministic readiness audit without editing anything. Stage a bounded patch as a visible before-and-after diff. Prepare a passing revision for exact review. Submit only a review already authorized by the applicant. The reference journey begins at 3/10 ready with seven blockers . The agent proposes three bounded corrections and the page previews the result as 3/10 → 7/10 , but nothing changes until the applicant clicks Apply proposed changes . When an applicant-owned fact is missing, a contextual tool temporarily appears. Instead of allowing the agent to invent an answer, the page asks the applicant directly. After the applicant shares the answer, that tool disappears. When all 10 checks pass, the page creates a five-minute approval tied to a digital fingerprint of that exact draft. Any later edit cancels the approval. The applicant approves that version and only then can the agent submit it and receive one receipt. The OpenAI API supplies the reasoning; WebMCP lets the page publish its live tools, state and boundaries. How we built it I built the application with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Zod, WebMCP, Vitest, Playwright, and OpenAI Sites. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same workspace controller and domain rules. There is no separate agent-only state. Tool inputs use closed JSON Schemas and runtime Zod validation. The deterministic audit checks the live revision and performs bounded verification of public GitHub repository metadata and license availability. Proposed edits are evaluated against an in-memory candidate before the page shows their projected readiness, without mutating the real draft. prepare_submission re-audits the expected revision and creates a short-lived review bound to its SHA-256 draft hash. Any later edit invalidates that review. Submission also uses a browser-provided exclusive lock so repeated calls for the same approved review reconcile to one receipt. For the Chrome demonstration, I built an optional open-source developer inspector. It discovers the page’s registered WebMCP tools, maps their schemas to OpenAI Responses API functions, and returns structured tool results to the model. The API key remains in the local Chrome session. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was separating assistance from authority. It was easy to build an agent that could change fields; it was much harder to prove that it could not apply its own proposal, invent applicant facts, attest, or authorize submission. The contextual human handoff also required careful design. A WebMCP call should not remain open indefinitely while waiting for a person. The tool therefore returns an immediate awaiting_human result, the page collects the answer, and the agent re-reads the updated live state. WebMCP is still an emerging browser capability, so I also had to distinguish between ordinary browsers, ChatGPT’s supported in-app browser, and Chrome with WebMCP enabled. The developer inspector made discovery and every tool call visible during testing and recording. Accomplishments that we're proud of A deterministic audit that changes zero application fields. A visible readiness projection before any proposed edit is applied. A contextual tool that appears only when a specific human-owned fact is missing. An agent that asks instead of inventing. A five-minute review bound to the exact draft revision and SHA-256 hash. Native human authorization before submission becomes possible. A single receipt recording seven blockers caught, 10/10 readiness, and the reviewed hash. One shared controller for both the human interface and WebMCP tools. Automated domain, component, WebMCP-registration, and browser-journey testing. The project was created during the submission period, beginning August 26, 2026. Its public commit history documents the implementation through the final challenge build. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is not the reasoning engine. Its value is allowing a webpage to publish a precise contract for what an agent can see and do. Structured tools are also not enough by themselves. Meaningful safety comes from combining typed capabilities with deterministic validation, state-dependent availability, visible human controls, revision checks, expiration, and exact-artifact authorization. I also learned that a tool disappearing can be as meaningful as a tool appearing. Once the applicant supplies the missing fact, the agent no longer needs permission to request it. What's next for Open Application Desk The current challenge sample intentionally stores its state in the visitor’s browser and uses a fictional reference program, making it easy for judges to reset and reproduce without an account. The next step is to replace that persistence layer with authenticated server storage while preserving the controller, five WebMCP contracts, deterministic gate, visible patch review, and human authorization boundary. Foundations, accelerators, admissions offices, fellowship programs, and procurement teams could publish their own requirement sets while applicants and agents work safely against the same authoritative state. Future versions could also support additional evidence providers, organization-defined policies, durable receipts, and accessible multi-user review. Built With chromeextension githubapi openaiapi openaisites playwright react responsesapi sha256 typescript vinext vite vitest webcryptoapi webmcp zod Try it out open-application-desk.syed3000.chatgpt.site github.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Asad Ali Like Share this project: Updates Asad Ali started this project — Sep 03, 2026 07:23 PM EDT

title: Government Knowledge for Your AI
pitch: Your AI uses WebMCP to access government knowledge, while you can inspect the sources, provenance and limits behind every result.
about_excerpt: Your AI uses WebMCP to access government knowledge, while you can inspect the sources, provenance and limits behind every result. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP page Question, Answer and evidence Evidence trace Evidence trace Evidence trace Inspiration AI is becoming another way people find and understand public information. That raises a question I have been thinking about for some time: Does every government website need its own chatbot? Or could the AI a person already uses interact directly with authoritative public websites? That second possibility is what interested me about WebMCP. A personal AI may already understand the conversation and the user's circumstances. The government publisher, meanwhile, is better placed to say what information it provides, where it came from and what the boundaries of that information are. So I wanted to explore a proposed division of responsibility: the personal AI handles the conversation; a publisher defines the tools and evidence; and the person remains able to inspect the source before acting. This independent experimental prototype demonstrates that pattern using packaged public-source evidence. It is not GOV.UK, an official government service or an endorsement by the source organisations. Government information is a particularly useful test case because plausible answers are not enough. A result may depend on jurisdiction, date, eligibility, the authority of the source or information that is simply not present. The important question therefore becomes not just: Can an AI find an answer? but: Can I see the evidence behind what my AI is telling me? That became the guiding principle for the project: Provide the evidence with the answer. What I built This project demonstrates how a personal AI can use WebMCP to access structured government knowledge directly from a webpage. The site exposes six bounded WebMCP tools that can: search government knowledge; retrieve an exact resource; inspect its provenance; explore the evidence behind a claim in the packaged worked answer; compare claims in that worked answer with their evidence foundations; and present the evidence for a selected resource back on the webpage. There is deliberately no general-purpose answer_question tool. The website provides evidence rather than attempting to become the conversational AI. A compatible AI can use that evidence to help its user, while the human interface independently presents the same underlying information as an Evidence answer. That lets the person inspect: the recorded source; provenance; observation date; evidence level; access and reuse information; limitations; remaining unknowns; and the appropriate next check. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same underlying application actions, so there is not one implementation for people and another hidden implementation for AI. Where OKF fits WebMCP solves only part of the problem. It gives an AI a structured way to interact with a webpage, but government information also needs context. Finding a record is not the same as knowing: who published it; whether it is authoritative for the question; when it was observed; what has been transformed; what rights or access have been established; or what the evidence cannot tell us. I therefore used Open Knowledge Format (OKF) as the knowledge and provenance layer beneath the WebMCP experience. That gives the prototype three distinct parts: WebMCP — the interaction layer; OKF — the knowledge and provenance layer; and Evidence answer — the human verification layer. The demonstration includes 80 receipt-bound reviewed records together with 58,652 searchable source-snapshot records projected from 58,655 locked rows. The four federated OKF discovery collections cover A Life in the UK, Office for National Statistics metadata, the UK Government API catalogue and metadata-only HM Land Registry discovery. Those collections intentionally have different evidence levels. Discovery does not magically become verification simply because an AI can search it. How I built it The application is a static TypeScript web application. When the page loads, it validates its packaged knowledge artefacts before enabling search and registering its WebMCP tools. The WebMCP interfaces use bounded inputs, closed schemas and deterministic application actions. Source-derived text is treated as untrusted content rather than instructions for the AI. The site contains no embedded language model, user account or personal-profile database. That reduces what the page itself receives, but it is not a claim of complete privacy. Free-text searches can contain personal information, and a remote AI provider may receive the person's prompt, tool metadata, arguments and results. That was an intentional architectural choice. The experiment is not about building another AI service. It is about exploring what happens when an ordinary website becomes directly usable by the AI chosen by the visitor. I used Codex extensively as the implementation agent. I supplied the product direction, architecture, constraints and review decisions, while Codex implemented and repeatedly tested the TypeScript application, data pipeline, WebMCP tools, browser behaviour, schemas and supporting documentation. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini also helped with research, critique and evaluation design. Microsoft Copilot and a local Ollama model were used as experimental personal-AI hosts rather than as components of the application itself. Earlier OKF and GIS AI GO work supplied the design lineage. During the competition period I built this repository's six-tool WebMCP application, four-source federation, Evidence answer interface, tests, evaluation and protected public deployment. The biggest challenge The hardest part turned out not to be registering a WebMCP tool. It was deciding what we can legitimately claim happened. During testing, an AI could produce a convincing response that appeared to understand the website and even talked about tools. But that did not necessarily mean a WebMCP tool had actually been discovered and invoked. That distinction became important. I separated several questions that are easy to accidentally collapse into one: Did the browser expose the tools? Could the tool be called successfully? Did an AI choose the appropriate tool? Did the AI correctly interpret the tool result? Could the person independently understand the evidence? Those are five different tests. Direct testing through Chrome DevTools successfully exercised all six fixed WebMCP calls against deployed commit a4d2db44 , with matching tool and page Evidence answer digests. A model did not select those direct calls. An owner-operated ChatGPT Chrome extension journey visibly completed the ONS search-and-present flow. A later directed ChatGPT extension evaluation in Edge reported exercising all six page tools. Those host observations did not expose raw browser traces, and the Chrome journey did not expose an exportable exact call trace, host version or model identity. Testing with other personal-AI hosts was much less predictable. Microsoft Copilot could read and discuss the page, but no Site-tool invocation or Evidence answer update was observed; its call and page state remained unobservable. No Gemini Site-tool invocation was observed either. The local model produced a mixture of successful and unsuccessful tool-selection runs. Initially that felt like a limitation of the demonstration. It became one of the most useful things I learned. What I learned WebMCP changes the role of the website Most discussion about agents interacting with websites starts from the agent: How can the AI read the page? How can it find the button? How can it automate the browser? WebMCP lets us reverse the question: What capabilities should the website deliberately make available to an AI? That is a significant shift. Instead of an agent reverse-engineering the user interface, the publisher can define a small, explicit machine interface alongside the human one. Personal AI creates a different public-service architecture A public body does not necessarily have to own the entire conversational experience. There is another possible architecture: citizen-selected AI + publisher-defined tools + inspectable evidence The AI can remain personal to the user. The publisher can remain responsible for its information and tool boundaries. That separation seems particularly interesting for government. Provenance matters as much as retrieval It is easy to make a large body of information searchable. It is much harder to preserve the distinction between: authoritative information; publisher-declared metadata; transformed data; frozen discovery snapshots; inferred relationships; and things that remain unknown. OKF became important because I did not want the project merely to demonstrate retrieval. I wanted the AI and the human to be able to ask: What exactly is this evidence?  Aliigo Action Layer 

 Project name 

 Aliigo Action Layer (AAL) 

 Elevator pitch 

 Aliigo Action Layer makes online business knowledge actionable and future-ready for both people and AI. Using WebMCP, it turns a business’s approved information and capabilities into clear tools that AI assistants can use to find answers, recommend services, prepare bookings or quote requests, and guide customers to the next step—without having to guess their way through the website. 

 One-line version 

 Turn your business knowledge into actions that both customers and AI assistants can use. 

 Tagline 

 Built for people. Ready for their agents. 

 

 Inspiration 

 Aliigo started from a simple problem: businesses already have valuable knowledge scattered across their websites, service pages, FAQs, policies, booking systems, and other public sources, but that information is often difficult for search engines, AI systems, and even customers to understand consistently. 

 We have been building Aliigo around the idea that a business should be able to organize and control the knowledge that represents it, make that knowledge easier for Google and AI systems to understand, and put it to work through a Business Agent that can answer visitor questions. 

 WebMCP suggested the next logical step. 

 If a business can make its knowledge understandable to AI, why should its customers’ agents still have to guess their way through buttons, forms, menus, and page layouts? 

 That led to Aliigo Action Layer . 

 The idea is to give a normal business website a structured action layer for AI agents while keeping the human experience intact. Instead of replacing the website, WebMCP lets us make the same website usable by both people and their agents. 

 The long-term inspiration is simple: 

 Make businesses easier to find, understand, choose, and act on. 

 

 What it does 

 Aliigo Action Layer makes online business knowledge actionable. 

 Instead of asking an AI agent to interpret a website visually and guess how to complete a task, the site exposes structured, business-specific tools that describe exactly what the agent can do. 

 For example, a wellness business can expose tools that let an agent: 

 
 understand available services; 
 find an appropriate service for a customer’s need; 
 check available times; 
 prepare a booking. 
 

 A printing business can expose a different set of capabilities: 

 
 find appropriate print products; 
 check artwork requirements; 
 compare relevant options; 
 prepare a quote request. 
 

 The important part is that these are not separate one-off integrations. 

 Aliigo Action Layer uses the same underlying business capability model to expose the appropriate tools for different types of businesses. 

 The agent can prepare an action while the website shows the result to the human for review and confirmation. 

 The experience becomes: 

 Human intent → Agent uses structured tools → Website shows the prepared action → Human confirms 

 This keeps the human in control while giving the agent a much more reliable way to help. 

 

 How we built it 

 We built Aliigo Action Layer as an isolated WebMCP experiment, separate from the production Aliigo platform but designed with a future integration path in mind. 

 The application uses a reusable business-definition and capability layer. 

 Each business defines: 

 
 its identity; 
 approved business knowledge; 
 products or services; 
 policies; 
 available actions; 
 structured data required for those actions. 
 

 A WebMCP adapter then translates those capabilities into business-specific tools exposed through the browser. 

 We deliberately kept the WebMCP layer separate from the UI and business logic. 

 Conceptually: 
 Business knowledge
 +
Business capabilities
 ↓
Aliigo Action Layer
 ↓
WebMCP tools
 ↓
AI agent
 
 The same application can switch between different example businesses and expose a different toolset without rebuilding the underlying architecture. 

 We also added visible shared state so that when an agent prepares a booking or quote request, the result appears immediately in the human-facing interface. 

 The current challenge implementation is intentionally self-contained and deterministic. It does not require production Aliigo infrastructure, customer data, external APIs, authentication, or payment systems. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was thinking differently about what a website interface is for. 

 Traditional web development assumes that the human is the only actor navigating the interface. Even AI-assisted browsing often follows the same model: the agent tries to understand the page, find the correct control, and interact with it. 

 WebMCP changes that assumption. 

 We had to decide which parts of the business should become explicit tools, what information each tool should accept, and which actions should remain under direct human control. 

 Another challenge was avoiding generic tools. 

 A tool such as execute_action may be technically flexible, but it gives an agent very little useful business context. We found that tools become much more meaningful when they describe actual business capabilities such as: 

 
 find_services 
 find_available_times 
 prepare_booking 
 check_artwork_requirements 
 prepare_quote_request 
 

 We also had to design around an emerging standard. WebMCP is still experimental, so feature detection, browser compatibility, graceful fallback behavior, and keeping the implementation close to the current specification were important. 

 Finally, we had to resist turning the challenge project into the full Aliigo platform. The goal was to demonstrate the idea clearly and reliably without reproducing the much larger production architecture. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are most proud that Aliigo Action Layer demonstrates something broader than a single WebMCP-enabled form. 

 The same underlying architecture can represent very different businesses and expose different agent capabilities based on what each business actually does. 

 A wellness studio can become bookable by an agent. 

 A printing company can become quote-ready. 

 Both use the same underlying model. 

 We are also proud of the human-agent interaction pattern. 

 The agent does not simply disappear into the background and perform an opaque task. It prepares a structured action, and the website reflects that action back to the human. 

 That creates a collaborative experience rather than an autonomous black box. 

 Another accomplishment is keeping business knowledge and actions connected. 

 The agent is not simply clicking through a website. It is acting through tools tied to structured, approved business information that

title: TripRescue
pitch: Human-controlled flight recovery with typed WebMCP tools, constrained search, exact-price preview, and verified booking changes.
about_excerpt: Human-controlled flight recovery with typed WebMCP tools, constrained search, exact-price preview, and verified booking changes. Like Comment Story Updates What it does An airline moves your flight. TripRescue lets a traveller—or a browser agent working with them—inspect the affected booking, state recovery constraints such as arrival time, maximum extra cost, and stops, compare ranked alternatives, preview the exact itinerary and price difference, approve the change in the page, and verify the updated booking. It runs against a real Duffel test-mode order. Duffel's sandbox generates the airline change, the booked airline supplies the change offers, and the app verifies the confirmed order change by refetching it. Why WebMCP fits Trip recovery is a high-stakes, multi-step, stateful task where guessing buttons from pixels is unsafe. The agent needs the current booking, must obey explicit limits, must never confirm without the traveller, and must prove the result. TripRescue registers five focused tools from the top-level page with the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool API: get_trip find_recovery_options preview_trip_change apply_trip_change get_change_status The tools use the page's signed session. Booking IDs, provider tokens, and passenger data never enter the prompt. Read, search, preview, apply, and verify remain separate operations with appropriate annotations and compact normalized outputs. A better human-agent experience Every tool call updates the visible page before resolving, so the traveller sees the same state the agent is reasoning about. An Agent Activity log records each call and its purpose. The consequential write is protected by a server-issued preview, order fingerprint, expiry, exact-price revalidation, and single-use idempotent confirmation. Calling apply_trip_change opens an in-page confirmation dialog. The traveller—not the agent—must review the itinerary and explicitly confirm it. This lets the traveller state intent once—“direct, arrive by 1 PM, no more than $150 extra”—while the agent converts it into a constrained search, ranks valid options, stages the best one, and hands control back exactly when the booking and test charge would change. Success is defined by the refetched provider booking, not merely an HTTP 200. How it was built TripRescue uses Next.js 16, TypeScript, Zod, Tailwind CSS v4, the WebMCP imperative API, and the Duffel Flights API in test mode. It is deployed behind nginx with pm2 on Hetzner. GitHub Actions runs lint, typechecking, tests, and a production build before deploying, then verifies the public URL. Testing Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Create a sandbox trip, simulate an airline change, and ask the browser agent to find a nonstop replacement arriving before 1 PM for no more than $150 extra. Preview the best option, apply it, approve the in-page confirmation, and verify the refetched booking. Honest limitations Duffel test mode only. Schedules and prices are synthetic, and the airline change is simulated by Duffel. No live bookings or real payments occur. The demo uses the LHR → LTN Duffel Airways scenario supported by Duffel's sandbox. video_transcript_excerpt: Trip rescue turns a disrupted flight into a safe agent assisted recovery. The browser agent can search and prepare the fix, but it cannot make the irreversible change on its own. We start with a real sandbox booking, then simulate the disruption inside the page. Before the recovery can work, the page needs a signed in trip and a browser session that the tools can reuse. The agent can read the trip, search options, and stage a change, but the traveler still owns the final approval. The booking ID and provider token stay out of the prompt, so the model works inside a constrained boundary. The demo opens on a Duffel sandbox booking, and the page confirms that five web MCP site tools are registered. A browser agent reads the signed in trip, then the schedule change lands, and the itinerary shifts from the original departure to the disrupted one. The agent gets real state, not a mocked prompt. The agent reads the signed in trip, then searches for non-stop alternatives that arrive before 1:00 p.m. and cost no more than $150 extra. It ranks the results instead of grabbing the first match. That matters because constrained search turns a broad travel problem into a narrow auditable choice. Trip rescue previews the best option as an earlier Duffel Airways flight, but nothing changes yet. The important distinction is between a proposal and a booking. One is comparison, the other is an actual mutation. That separation keeps the agent useful without letting it silently commit the change. The preview shows the full $125 test charge before anything changes. Trip rescue stages the exact itinerary, the fare difference, and the penalty in one place, so the traveler sees the real cost up front. The agent is still asking to apply the change. When the agent asks to apply it, Trip Rescue opens an in-page confirmation dialogue. The traveler, not the agent, reviews the itinerary and explicitly approves the mutation. That is the irreversible step, and it happens under human control inside the browser. After Duffel accepts it, the agent calls get change status, re-fetches the order, and checks that the new itinerary is truly booked. The post-change read-back is just as important as the approval because it proves the mutation actually stuck. Without that verification step, the workflow would only be optimistic. The booking ID and provider token never enter the prompt because every tool reuses the page's signed session. The verified state shows the new itinerary booked and rechecked in the browser. That is WebMCP with real utility and human control at the irreversible step.

title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: AGMCP
pitch: The USDA hardiness zone map, rebuilt as a shared tool for gardeners and their agents.
about_excerpt: The USDA hardiness zone map, rebuilt as a shared tool for gardeners and their agents. Like Comment Story Updates agmcp working inside ChatGPT in-app browser Inspiration I love gardening, and coding with AI agents. I've had conversations with ChatGPT and Gemini that start in a similar way: "what can I grow in my city?" (I know my hardiness zone because I've searched for it more than once) and the agent guesses from memory. The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map is the standard reference for what can survive where, but it lives in PDFs, a clunky ZIP lookup, and 300-dpi PNGs. Nothing an agent can call. WebMCP made the fix obvious: put the authoritative data on a page, register it as tools, and let the human and the agent work from the same map. I also wanted a primitive, not just a demo. AGMCP is the first building block for a bigger garden-planning app I'm building next, where zones combine with hyper-local weather and sun position and regional, heirloom seeds. What it does AGMCP is the 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map for all 40,502 US ZIP codes (50 states, DC, Puerto Rico), exposed three ways: For people : enter a ZIP (or use your location), see your half-zone with its temperature band and frost windows, browse 54 vegetables, herbs, peppers, and fruit rated great / stretch / not recommended for that zone, and build a garden plan with a planting calendar. For agents on the page : 18 WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() , plus a declarative form tool. Read tools like lookup_hardiness_zone , compare_locations , find_zone_by_coordinates , list_plants , get_planting_calendar . Write tools like set_location , add_to_garden_plan , and filter_plants change what the human sees. clear_garden_plan opens a confirmation dialog the user must accept; use_my_location requires the browser's geolocation permission. For backend agents and other apps : a JSON API ( /api/v1/zone/{zip} , /compare , /nearest , /plants , /calendar ), an OpenAPI spec, and llms.txt . Every tool call streams into an on-page Agent activity panel, so the human always sees what the agent did. How we built it Data pipeline : PRISM Group's 2023 ZIP-to-zone CSVs (US, AK, HI, PR) plus US Census ZCTA centroids. A build script packs 100,000 possible ZIPs into a single 100 KB string (one character per ZIP indexing 26 half-zones) so lookups are O(1) in the browser and in the Worker. Coordinates load lazily for nearest-ZIP queries. Frontend : Vite + vanilla TypeScript, no framework. Modern CSS (oklch, light-dark() , container queries, view transitions), native <dialog> for human-in-the-loop confirmation. WebMCP : one tool module with JSON Schema inputs, readOnlyHint annotations, and a wrapper that logs each call and converts app errors into MCP-style isError results instead of throwing. Feature-detects document.modelContext with a navigator.modelContext fallback for Chrome < 150. The UI buttons and the tools call the exact same functions, so there is no agent-only code path. Backend : a Cloudflare Worker serves static assets and the JSON API from the same bundled data, deployed with Workers Builds on every push to main . Tooling : built with Cursor cloud agents; end-to-end tested in headless Chrome via navigator.modelContextTesting . Challenges we ran into Spec drift. Chrome 148 exposes WebMCP on navigator.modelContext ; the spec and newer Chrome use document.modelContext . ChatGPT's browser supports only imperative tools on the top-level page, so the declarative form is progressive enhancement. Data size. Naive JSON for 40k ZIPs was megabytes; the 1-char-per-ZIP encoding brought core data to ~15 KB gzipped. Honesty about estimates. Frost dates and plant ranges are horticultural rules of thumb, not USDA data, so every tool output and UI label says so. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real dataset as a real primitive: exact zones for every ZIP, callable by agents in-page and over HTTP. Genuine human-agent collaboration: shared state flows both ways, write tools change the visible page, and destructive actions wait for a click. Zero secrets, zero tracking, zero API keys. Fully open source, deployable with one command. Shipped, deployed, and passing an automated WebMCP end-to-end test on the live URL before the deadline. What we learned WebMCP tools are best when they reuse the app's own actions. If a button and a tool call the same function, the agent and the human are always in sync. Tool descriptions are the UX for agents. Naming, enums, and "call get_current_context first" hints did more for reliability than any code. Return enough for the agent to verify and warn: add_to_garden_plan returns the plant's fit so the agent can say "habanero is a stretch in 6a." Modern web platform features (dialog, view transitions, light-dark() ) covered everything a framework would have, with a 37 KB bundle. What's next for AGMCP Pair it with hyper-local weather and sun-position tools to build the 3D garden planner it was designed to power: bed layout, succession planting, and season-aware recommendations for your exact zone. 2012 vs 2023 zone shift comparison ("did my zone change?"). Richer plant data with varieties, companion planting, and community-contributed regional notes. This may involve parsing PDFs from Universities across the USA that have regional and local information. For example, UF has research papers dedicated to the Florida agriculture. I'll probably use a local model to running one a mini pc to keep costs low. Publish the tool set as a reusable module so any gardening site can register the same WebMCP tools. title: Stapler
pitch: An AI agent preps your documents right in your browser via WebMCP — it finds the right pages itself, merges and downloads. Your files never leave your device.
about_excerpt: An AI agent preps your documents right in your browser via WebMCP — it finds the right pages itself, merges and downloads. Your files never leave your device. Like 4 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Every visa application, rental application, or insurance claim ends the same way: you sit with a pile of PDFs, hunting for the four pages of a bank statement that actually prove your salary, extracting them, merging everything in the right order, naming the file properly. Today you have two options — upload sensitive documents like your passport and bank statement to a cloud AI, or do every click yourself in a dumb local PDF tool. WebMCP dissolves that trade-off, and Stapler is built on exactly that: document prep is a workflow problem, and workflows are what agents chaining structured tools are good at. What it does Stapler is a local document workspace whose tools an AI agent can operate. You say what you need: "I'm applying for a visa. I need one PDF with my passport, the bank statement pages that prove my regular salary, and my application form. Name the file after the applicant and its purpose, and download it." The agent lists the documents, reads a 12-page bank statement page by page, finds the salary pages (4–7) on its own — it even reads the visa form's supporting-documents checklist first — extracts them, merges passport + salary pages + form, and downloads a packet named after the applicant, whose name it read off the passport. You never typed a page number or a name. And because every operation executes client-side, no document ever leaves the browser tab — there is no backend to upload to; the privacy isn't a policy promise, it's the architecture. This is a person and an agent doing something together that was impossible before: previously an agent could either talk about your documents (after you uploaded them to a server) or click through a UI blindly. Now it invokes structured, deterministic operations inside your own tab, on files that never leave your device — while you supervise through a live Operations log, click any document to preview it, and undo anything the agent got wrong. Try it yourself Open https://stapler-equ.pages.dev in the ChatGPT desktop app's browser (Cmd+Shift+B; accept "Continue in Work" if offered) — or in Chrome with Google's Model Context Tool Inspector extension. Click Load sample documents (fictional data, generated in-browser). Ask for the visa packet in your own words — or use the prompt above. Watch the Operations log as the agent works. Or drop your own PDFs: nothing is uploaded anywhere. How we built it React + Vite + TypeScript, zero backend. Seven tools — list_documents , inspect_document , extract_pages , merge_documents , rename_document , export_document , undo — are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool with narrow JSON schemas ( additionalProperties: false ), plain serializable results, and AbortController cleanup. The registrations are live: whenever the workspace changes, the schemas are regenerated — every document parameter becomes an enum of the currently loaded filenames, so the agent can't reference a file that isn't there. Document tools appear once files are loaded, and merge_documents registers only when at least two documents exist. One subtlety: the store emits changes from inside tool execute() calls, so re-registering immediately would tear down the very tool still delivering its result — re-registration is deferred a tick instead. pdf-lib performs the operations; pdf.js extracts per-page text for inspect_document , which is what lets the agent find content instead of being told page numbers. The sample documents (fictional passport, 12-page bank statement, visa form) are generated in-browser by pdf-lib — the repo ships no binaries and demo data never exists outside the tab. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages with a first-party Chrome origin-trial token, so it runs on stock Chrome 149+ with no flags. Challenges we ran into The real agent runs found bugs no manual test did: Truncation hid the evidence. inspect_document capped page text at 500 chars — and the salary lines started at char 441+. The agent, seeing cut-off text, guessed pages 3–7 (wrong). Raising the cap and adding a smoke-test guard fixed it. Ambiguous data misleads honest agents. A "FREELANCE INVOICE" credit on the January page made pages 3–7 a defensible answer. The demo premise needs exactly one right answer, so the sample data is now guarded by a regex in the smoke test. Return-shape spelunking. Early code returned MCP-style {content:[...]} envelopes; the WebMCP spec, Chrome docs, and TypeScript types all agree tools return plain serializable values. Agent surfaces behave differently. Plain ChatGPT chat asks you to upload files; the unlock is accepting its "Continue in Work" handoff, where the agent actually drives the page's tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of The hero workflow is verified end-to-end on both judge surfaces: ChatGPT's in-app browser (via Work mode) and Chrome with Google's Model Context Tool Inspector extension. In every verified run the agent chose pages 4–7 unprompted and explained why. The contrast test is just as telling: the same request to an agent without page tools produced a confidently hallucinated "visa packet" that never touched the real files. It also works on documents it has never seen: we dropped in three unrelated PDFs (an ID card, an employment letter, six months of payslips) and asked for a rental-application packet with only the April–June payslips — the agent picked payslip pages 4–6 by itself and named the file after the applicant. And the whole thing is honest engineering — a Node smoke test guards the demo's integrity (salary credits on exactly pages 4–7, every page under the inspect limit), so the wow moment can't silently rot. What we learned Tool descriptions are UX for agents — the agent reads them the way users read buttons. Real agent runs are the only test that matters: every demo-breaking bug was found by an agent, not by a human. And keeping humans in the loop (live log, preview, undo) is what turns "an agent did something to my files" into something you can trust. What's next for Stapler More operations (split, rotate, delete, compress), OCR so scanned documents can be inspected too, and per-document page-range bounds in the schemas themselves. about_excerpt:
The User and ChatGPT share one live cart and the agent proposes a gift, the user approves, review, and then confirm. Therefore nothing is placed without the user

 Asked Agent to recommend a gift under 40 pounds for someone who cooks 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Website page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Use the site tools to call g et_account,get_saved_customer, get_shop_state. Quote the exact JSON, call apply_saved_profile. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Asked Agent to recommend a gift under 40 pounds for someone who cooks 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Website page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Use the site tools to call g et_account,get_saved_customer, get_shop_state. Quote the exact JSON, call apply_saved_profile. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Asked Agent to recommend a gift under 40 pounds for someone who cooks 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every "AI shopping" demo I'd seen had the same problem: the agent clicks buttons it's guessing at, or it shops in a parallel page you can't even see. I wanted the opposite. One real shop, one cart, where ChatGPT and I are looking at the exact same thing and I get the final say. 

 That's what Hearth is, a small home goods shop for the table and kitchen. You browse and click like you would anywhere else. The agent, meanwhile, calls real site tools and nothing gets bought until you approve it, review it, and confirm it. 

 What it does 

 I and the agent share the same tab and the same cart. 

 The agent calls recommend_gift instead of silently adding something to your bag. A tradeoff card shows up: here's the pick, here's why, here's what it costs and that makes the cart stay empty. 

 You hit Approve on the page only then does the item land in your cart. 

 explain_cart and prepare_order build a review of everything while ordering stays locked. 

 If the agent tries place_order without confirm: true , it gets blocked and Undo Last restores your last cart snapshot if anything goes sideways. 

 Privacy was a deliberate part of the demo. Once you sign in, get_account and get_saved_customer only return a profileStatus flag, like hasShipping: true . Your street address and phone number never leave this browser; they sit in a local demo vault. Checkout keeps those fields hidden too, until you personally choose Use saved details or Show saved address which makes the agent unable to see them. 

 Why this is a fit for WebMCP 

 A shop is a terrible scraping target. Filters, quantities, promo codes, checkout, and a yes/no question about how much you're willing to spend, and an agent guessing at all of that through the DOM is fragile and blind. WebMCP lets the page declare those actions up front. The agent doesn't just click or hunt for buttons, it calls search_products , recommend_gift and prepare_order . Since it's the same page, you watch the DOM update live, right next to you. 

 The hard part was always the trust gap: how do you let an agent "help" while you're still the one who sees everything, approves everything, and can undo everything without handing it your address? Structured tools let the site describe the action, its inputs, and its guardrails directly. That's what solved it. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest lesson is learned is that agent usefulness is not the same thing as agent autonomy. The moments where the agent actually felt useful weren't when it acted on its own, they were when it made a clear proposal, showed its reasoning, and waited one step for my approval. 

 How I built it 

 Static HTML and ES modules on Netlify, No backend, Auth and the customer vault are plain localStorage. 

 mcp-boot.js looks for document.modelContext / navigator.modelContext early. webmcp.js builds each tool (name, description, inputSchema, execute) and registers it with registerTool, including search_products: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_products" , 
 description : "Search the shop by words such as mug, skillet, linen, gift, or wool." , 
 inputSchema : { type : "object" , properties : { query : { type : "string" } } , required : [ "query" ] } , 
 execute : async ( { query } ) = > shop . searchProducts ( query , "agent" ) 
 } ) ;

title: PantryPilot
pitch: \nPantryPilot turns simple meal goals into an optimized grocery order. Plan meals, compare prices, respect allergies, and approve every purchase with a human-in-the-loop WebMCP agent.
about_excerpt:
PantryPilot turns simple meal goals into an optimized grocery order. Plan meals, compare prices, respect allergies, and approve every purchase with a human-in-the-loop WebMCP agent.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most grocery tools optimize one product at a time — but real shopping means juggling a budget,
dietary preferences, allergies, pantry items you already own, and substitutions when something is
too expensive or unsafe. And AI agents? They can't reliably drive a grocery website at all: layouts
shift, checkouts change, captchas appear. An agent guessing at buttons and dropdowns is a broken
experience. 

 The WebMCP Challenge inspired us to invert that model. Instead of an agent scraping a messy DOM,
what if the app handed the agent explicit, typed, discoverable tools — with the hard parts
(budgets, allergies, approvals) encoded directly in the tools themselves? 

 What it does 

 PantryPilot is an agent-native grocery planning workspace. You set your constraints — budget,
diet, allergies, pantry items, preferred stores — and an AI agent plans your meals, builds the
grocery list, finds cheaper and safer substitutions, optimizes the basket, and validates safety.
Then you review everything and explicitly approve the final basket. No payment is ever
processed. 

 In the built-in demo: 2 adults, $85/week, vegetarian, peanut allergy, pantry with rice, garlic,
olive oil and black beans . The agent detects a peanut-containing product and removes it, finds a
peanut-free alternative, optimizes under budget, and shows the savings — then stops and asks for
human approval . 

 How we built it 

 We built PantryPilot with Next.js 14 , TypeScript , and Tailwind CSS — no backend, no API
keys, 30+ seeded products. The heart of the project is 9 genuinely functional WebMCP tools 
registered on document.modelContext : 
 document.modelContext.registerTool({
 name: "search_products",
 description: "Search safe and affordable grocery products",
 inputSchema: {
 type: "object",
 properties: {
 query: { type: "string" },
 dietaryTags: { type: "array", items: { type: "string" } },
 excludeAllergens: { type: "array", items: { type: "string" } },
 maxPrice: { type: "number" },
 store: { type: "string" },
 limit: { type: "number" }
 }
 },
 execute: async (input) => searchProducts(input)
});
 
 search_products · get_product_details · create_meal_plan · build_grocery_list ·
 optimize_basket · suggest_substitutions · validate_basket · request_human_approval ·
 save_user_preferences 

 Basket optimization is a constrained minimization — keep total spend within budget $B$ while
excluding every allergen in set $A$: 

 min ∑ i p i q i s.t. ∑ i p i q i ≤ B , allergens ( i ) ∩ A = ∅ 

 The critical architectural choice: when no WebMCP runtime is present (Firefox, Safari, Edge), the
UI falls back to a local simulator that calls the exact same functions — one codebase, two
pathways, so the demo works in every browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Tool schema design — JSON Schemas are the agent's entire world. Every filter the agent needs
(allergen exclusions, budget caps, stores) had to be first-class in the schema, not inferred. 
 Strict validation — validate_basket must catch allergy, dietary, budget, and stock issues
and report them as structured checks, warnings, and errors rather than silent failures. 
 Human approval as a hard gate — making the agent unable to finish without calling
 request_human_approval was a deliberate design decision, not a UI courtesy. 
 Graceful degradation — keeping the simulator and the WebMCP pathway on the same functions
took discipline, but it's what makes the app portable. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 A live agent timeline and WebMCP tool inspector make every agent action visible . The full demo
runs end-to-end in under three minutes: profile → search → allergy catch → plan → optimize →
validate → approve. 

 What we learned 

 
 Schema design is API design for agents — predictable inputs/outputs beat cleverness. 
 Transparency (timeline + inspector) is what makes humans comfortable delegating. 
 Fallbacks aren't a nice-to-have; they're what makes a demo survive any machine. 
 

 What's next 

 Real retailer integrations, persistent accounts, multi-store optimization, and richer dietary
models — all through the same tool interface. 

 
 PantryPilot is not an autonomous checkout bot. It's a collaboration layer where agents handle the
legwork and humans make the decisions.

pitch: an interactive map of hoenn, where you can walk around, talk to people, and explore the landscape of emerald with an agent
about_excerpt:
an interactive map of hoenn, where you can walk around, talk to people, and explore the landscape of emerald with an agent
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I grew up playing pokemon emerald and I loved it, this is an homage to a game that has meant a lot to me. there's a whole community of people who mod old gameboy games and create "rom-hacks", this is something along a similar vein, I'd like for people to be able to experience the beauty of the game design that went into crafting pokemon emerald. for a game released in 2004, I think it's astounding how well it holds up even today and how intricate the map is. 

 What it does 

 it's a faithful adaptation of pokemon emerald, built to simulate what the game feels like on the actual gameboy. unlike emulation, this isn't just running the ROM, it instead lets you zoom out and explore the world. think of this as "creative mode" in minecraft. 

 How we built it 

 there is a big rom-hacking pokemon community, and it is due to the incredible work of this community that building this game was so easy (relatively). just a few years ago this would've been a weeks-long, if not month long project. I took the decompiled works of pokemon emerald (pokeemerald-decomp), and asked codex to reimplement it in JS. I then asked it to make a parity list, and thought about what I want to preserve and what I'd like to change. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 making the map feel responsive was a big issue, especially when zooming out. I also had to match the exact ticks that a gameboy uses, because I want the site to feel realistic. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm really happy with how the zoomed out view looks, and the fact that you can still walk around and explore the region whilst having a "god view". 

 What we learned 

 webmcp in my opinion is currently constrained, I look forward to contributing to the standard. it needs bidirectional communication - the website needs to have a callback / some way to tell the agent when a task is done or ready instead of just polling. 

 What's next for overworld-webmcp 

 I'd love to make it multiplayer, and add secret bases. I might add battling capabilities as well, but it would be okay to leave it out since there are plenty of battle simulators, and this is more of an artistic project instead of a faithful simulation of the game.
