title: AI Boardroom
pitch: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide.
about_excerpt: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide. Like Comment Story Updates One COO and 6 Ai Assistant Agents Inspiration Founders often need to make consequential decisions with incomplete evidence, changing constraints and too many disconnected conversations. AI Boardroom puts a founder and a browser assistant in one shared decision room where specialist perspectives, evidence and trade-offs remain visible. What it does AI Boardroom gives one browser AI six specialist perspectives: Product, Evidence, Commercial, Operations, Technology and Chair. WebMCP lets the assistant read the live brief, request named roles, post evidence-linked contributions, respond when constraints change, and retrieve the exact decision record. The central interaction is deliberately human-controlled. A fictional launch budget changes from R20,000 to R8,000; the previous recommendation becomes stale, the assistant reads the new revision, and a new recommendation can be prepared without rewriting the earlier record. The founder reviews alternatives and reservations, then approves, rejects or requests revision in the visible page form. This is stateful collaboration rather than a detached chatbot transcript. The app does not run six independent AI workers or call a model API. One browser assistant adopts the roles and the human retains the final decision. How we built it The app is built with the OpenAI Sites React and TypeScript scaffold, Vinext and D1. Native document.modelContext.registerTool exposes seven WebMCP tools: start_session, get_boardroom_context, update_agenda, request_perspective, add_contribution, prepare_recommendation and get_decision_record. UI actions and WebMCP tools share the same API and persistence logic. Mutation inputs use expectedRevision for optimistic concurrency and operationId for safe retries. Evidence is stored with the relevant contribution and rendered as untrusted text. The visible review channel is a workflow boundary, not proof of human identity. Challenges The design challenge was making an AI council useful without pretending that six hidden agents or automatic consensus exist. We made the roles explicit, preserved disagreement, invalidated recommendations when the brief changed, and kept approval out of the WebMCP tool surface. A second challenge was handling uncertain browser or network outcomes without duplicating or overwriting decisions. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the agent can operate on the same visible, stateful interface as the human. Structured tools make the collaboration legible, while revision checks, evidence snapshots and a human review stop make the limits legible too. What's next Production use would require stronger identity and access controls, consent design, privacy and retention rules, abuse and rate-limit controls, independent security review, and integrations governed by explicit human approval. Disclosure All briefs, budgets, evidence and decisions in this project are fictional. The app does not make purchases, send messages, or change external systems. Browser-generated council text is created at runtime and is not preseeded consensus. title: Mastery Gate
pitch: Your own ChatGPT becomes a Socratic exam coach — but the site decides what it may know, say, and be. Answer keys structurally redacted; mastery gates that register new tools when you earn them.
about_excerpt: Your own ChatGPT becomes a Socratic exam coach — but the site decides what it may know, say, and be. Answer keys structurally redacted; mastery gates that register new tools when you earn them. Like Comment Story Updates Track hub: two PL-400 objectives, the four-dimension rubric, and the live Tool Roster your agent sees. Gate opens at 3 or above on all four. Mastery earned: advance_module and start_exam just materialized in the agent's tool list. Capability is the guardrail, not a prompt. Exam mode: every coaching tool revoked in the live registry, only get_exam_status and submit_exam remain. Train aided, test unaided. A micro-lesson: scenario first, commit before the reveal, governing rule, exam clue, and the aim your coach opens every session by asking. Every distractor maps to one of 17 named misconceptions. A miss returns the diagnosis and routes you to the paragraph that repairs it. Inspiration Every AI study tool has the same fatal flaw: ask it nicely and it gives you the answer. That's homework theater, and the research says it's worse than useless. Learning science is unambiguous: retrieval practice beats re-reading , feedback works when it names why you were wrong, and desirable difficulties (the friction) are where retention comes from. The AI-tutoring RCTs agree from the other direction: constrained Socratic tutors roughly double learning (Kestin et al. 2025), while unguarded chatbot access makes students worse once the aid is removed (Bastani et al. 2024). The guardrails are the active ingredient, and prompts are guardrails an AI can be talked out of. WebMCP made a different kind possible: architecture . The page owns the tools, so the site decides what the AI may know, say, and be. I had already built this pedagogy once without AI, with deterministic scoring, named misconceptions, and repair routes, for my daughter's engineering statics course. Mastery Gate is what that pattern becomes when you hand it to an agent. What it does Your own ChatGPT becomes a Socratic coach for Microsoft's PL-400 exam, and the site is the referee it cannot overrule. A deterministic TypeScript engine grades, counts attempts, diagnoses named misconceptions (a miss returns "policy-precedence-instinct", never the key), scores a four-dimension mastery rubric (Recall, Connections, Application, Transfer, every dimension at 3 or above, never an average), and gates progression. The agent coaches through the page's WebMCP tools: Socratic questioning, an earned hint ladder, remediation routed to the exact lesson paragraph. Ask it for the answer and it refuses, leading with the reason (the answer is in no tool it can call), then asks one smaller question instead. Capability is the guardrail. advance_module does not exist until the gate opens; it materializes in the agent's tool list when mastery is earned. Exam mode revokes the coaching toolset entirely: train aided, test unaided. On screen, the Tool Roster reads 13 tools with the gate closed, 15 when it opens, 2 during the exam . The site's decisions are visible to learner and agent alike. The rubric interview is the centerpiece. The engine's own routing hands the mic to the AI to judge free-form teach-back explanations, then validates its scores against verbatim lesson-text evidence and clamps them. The AI does what only AI can; the site does what AI must not. Zero AI infrastructure: static site, no backend, no API keys. The visitor brings the intelligence; the site brings the authority. Everything also works agent-less. The coach is an interface, not a dependency. How we built it A pure-TypeScript engine (MIT, packages/mastery-gate ) under a Next.js static export on Cloudflare Pages; the learner's state lives in localStorage and never leaves the browser. The lesson content is instrumented deeply: 34 questions across two PL-400 objectives, every distractor tagged to a 17-misconception taxonomy, remediation anchors into the exact authored sections. Two evidence-graded research briefs live in the repo mapping each mechanism to the learning-science literature. And every layer was adversarially cross-reviewed by a different model family than the one that wrote it. Challenges we ran into We probed the runtimes before trusting documentation , live at /spike . ChatGPT's runtime has no toolchange events; Chrome does. The registry feature-detects, and gate-crossing responses announce new tools. When the protocol gives you no push channel, the payload becomes the push channel. getTools() and registerTool() return Promises in real runtimes; our lenient mocks hid that until production crashed. Chrome also enforces executeTool(RegisteredTool, jsonString) strictly. The mocks now tell the truth, and each crash shape is a named regression test. The subtlest bug was pedagogical. Early on we redacted so hard the coach had no curriculum. It refused to leak answers, then taught from its own pretraining, probing about scenarios the learner had never seen. The fix became our design law: the agent gets exactly what a learner reading the page gets, no more and no less. Redaction is symmetry, not secrecy. The host moved under us (Aug 28 to Sep 2). The ChatGPT desktop app's plugin update broke its own browser bridge (a missing scripts/ dir in the cached skill), then native page-tool injection into conversations turned intermittent, and a long session tripped an undocumented 10-changes-per-page-load budget on the tool surface, read straight from the app's browser-service.mjs ( max_tools 100, max_total_descriptor_bytes 65,536, max_registration_changes 10). None of it was the page; Chrome 152's reference runtime returned every tool throughout. But a coach that stalls on a host quirk is a bad coach, so the kickoff self-heals all three: it falls back to the app's own WebMCP bridge (same registered tools, different transport), corrects the tools.call(name, input) convention, and refreshes the tab when the budget is spent, saying so in one line each time. We surveyed five agent surfaces and found only two can invoke page tools today (ChatGPT's desktop browser, Chrome 152 with the flag); three read but cannot call. The ecosystem gap is real. See What's next. Accomplishments that we're proud of The first live coached session: the agent read its tool descriptions and volunteered "I will not reveal or submit the answer", unprompted. The descriptions are its employment contract, and it signed. In the demo it refuses on camera. Cross-family adversarial review found and sealed, before any judge could: five independent exam-escape paths, a self-serviceable mastery gate (an agent quoting the question back as "evidence" to award itself 4/4/4/4), and an answer-cache side channel through coaching notes. The site reacts to its own state instead of asking the agent to. A miss scrolls the page to the repairing paragraph, a gate change updates the roster, and start_exam mounts the exam where the learner is standing. The page moves; the chat stays put. And when the interview isn't unlocked yet, the referee says why : request_next_action returns the per-dimension coverage ledger, so "not yet" always comes with "here's what's missing." A Tool Inspector on the page: schema-generated forms for every registered tool, so anyone in any browser can invoke the real surface, with the same guards and the same redaction, and no agent at all. A "Your model" panel showing the learner exactly what the agent sees (the misconception ledger with its evidence) next to a one-tap erase. Glass box, both directions. What we learned You cannot make a chatbot answer-proof with a prompt; the learner can always rewrite it. You can make it answer-proof with a tool surface. We learned that the hard way on our own machine: a tutoring skill installed in ChatGPT quietly announced a "direct-answer mode" and handed over an answer, outranking the pasted contract. Host-level instructions beat prompts every time. But even then the engine leaked nothing. The skill could only read what the page shows every learner. The kickoff now claims precedence over installed coach skills; the gate never needed to. And starving the agent is not governing it: the coach teaches best when it holds exactly the learner's page, nothing more. The future of the open web isn't agents driving websites. It's websites that stay authoritative while agents make them personal. What's next for Mastery Gate The bridge (in-repo companion, tested; live pairing is roadmap): an MV3 extension plus a local MCP server so any MCP-speaking client, CLI agents included, can invoke a page's WebMCP tools. Three of the five surfaces we surveyed need exactly this. The remaining designed lessons and more certification tracks; spaced-review scheduling keyed to the misconception ledger; concept-level deep links. The Mastery Debrief : an end-of-module film assembled from the learner's own ledger, directed by the agent, validated by the engine, narrated live by the coach (backend shipped; the film is roadmap). When WebMCP's service-

title: WorkSpec Studio
pitch: Design an application with your agent, derive its infrastructure needs, compare Azure and AWS, record the ADR, and export the complete .workspec workspace.
about_excerpt: Design an application with your agent, derive its infrastructure needs, compare Azure and AWS, record the ADR, and export the complete .workspec workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Architecture decisions usually fragment across diagramming tools, spreadsheets, cloud pricing tabs, chat transcripts, and ADR documents. The diagram stops matching the estimate; the rationale disappears; and the final artifacts are trapped in somebody else's database. We built WorkSpec Studio to make architecture a shared, inspectable workflow between a person and an AI agent, with portable files as the durable result. What it does WorkSpec Studio takes a project through one connected journey: Design the application as an interactive C4 model. Derive an editable, provider-neutral infrastructure shopping list from its deployable elements. Map the same requirements to Azure and AWS and compare deterministic monthly planning estimates. Prepare and review the cloud-platform decision. Record the approved choice as an architecture decision record. Download the complete .workspec workspace as a ZIP. A user can start blank, load an example, or import an existing .workspec bundle. The C4 canvas supports context, logical-container, and deployment views. People can create, move, connect, and edit elements directly; the agent can propose or arrange the same model through WebMCP. The resulting workspace is schema-validated YAML that can be reviewed in the browser, committed to Git, used by WorkSpec command-line tools, or consumed by a hosted WorkSpec Enterprise installation. Why WebMCP Architecture work combines two different strengths. Agents are good at turning intent into a coherent first draft and tracing consequences across many artifacts. People are responsible for understanding the system, correcting assumptions, weighing trade-offs, and approving durable decisions. Without WebMCP, an agent must manipulate a complex infinite canvas with fragile pointer automation or edit files somewhere outside the UI the person is reviewing. WorkSpec's WebMCP tools connect both participants to the same live browser-local workspace. The agent can create a structured C4 proposal in one operation while the person immediately sees a real diagram they can drag and edit. The infrastructure list is derived from that same model, the provider comparison uses that same list, and the ADR is generated only from the visible draft the person has approved. Every successful agent operation appears in a collapsible Agent activity history. How we built it The workbench is a TypeScript and React monorepo composed from reusable WorkSpec packages for C4 schemas and rendering, infinite-canvas interaction, topology planning, provider mapping, decisions, ZIP workspaces, and the shared Studio shell. The page registers eleven bounded tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(). They let an agent inspect the workspace, navigate the gated workflow, control relevant sidebars, create a complete C4 architecture, inspect and pin diagram layout, update infrastructure requirements, compare providers, prepare an unsaved decision, record a reviewed decision, and export the workspace ZIP. All tool inputs use closed JSON schemas. Handlers resolve the current application state through stable action references, and registrations share an AbortController so React Strict Mode cannot leave duplicate tools behind. Human UI actions and agent tools operate on the same canonical MemoryWorkspace. The cloud estimates are deterministic planning figures rather than live quotes, keeping the comparison reproducible. Provider-specific choices do not leak into the source architecture or neutral requirements. Human review is part of the protocol The decision flow is intentionally split into two tools. prepare_cloud_decision opens the Decision page and fills a visible, editable provider and rationale draft. record_cloud_decision rejects calls until that draft exists and is used only after explicit human approval. This makes review a real product boundary, not a sentence in an agent prompt. The export tool returns the exact current workspace as a bounded base64 ZIP. That gives agents a reliable handoff even in browser environments where clicking a download button is awkward, while people retain the ordinary visible download control. Challenges we faced The biggest challenge was making an infinite visual canvas genuinely agent-operable without taking control away from the person. We added semantic architecture and layout tools rather than exposing cursor coordinates, while keeping every generated node editable and draggable. We also had to keep one canonical state across four routed stages, preserve unknown files during ZIP round trips, prevent stale React closures in registered tools, and make irreversible decision recording impossible before a visible draft exists. Accomplishments we're proud of One continuous Design → Infrastructure → Compare → Decision story. A real C4 canvas that supports both semantic WebMCP operations and direct human editing. Provider-neutral requirements with traceability back to architecture elements. Like-for-like Azure and AWS mappings and monthly estimates. A visible approval gate before ADR generation. Complete .workspec ZIP import and export. Eleven WebMCP tools plus a clear Agent activity history. More than two thousand automated tests across the WorkSpec packages and applications. What we learned The best WebMCP tools describe meaningful product operations, not DOM gestures. A tool such as "prepare a decision for review" is more robust and more understandable than a sequence of clicks, and it lets the UI enforce the same rules for both humans and agents. We also learned that shared visibility matters as much as capability. The strongest moments are not when the agent finishes everything invisibly; they are the pauses where a proposal appears in the real UI, the person edits or approves it, and both continue from the same state. What's next Azure and AWS are the first provider adapters. The provider-neutral model is designed for additional clouds, on-premises targets, live pricing catalogs, policy checks, and organization-specific mapping rules. We also plan to reuse the extracted Studio packages directly inside WorkSpec Enterprise. Try it Live app: https://studio.workspec.io/ Source: https://github.com/FieldstateNZ/workspec-studio Suggested prompt: Help me design Orderlight, an online ordering system that takes payment through an external gateway and fulfils accepted orders asynchronously. Build the C4 architecture, derive and review the infrastructure plan, compare Azure and AWS, and prepare a recommendation. Stop for my review at every stage and do not record the decision until I explicitly approve it. title: City for You
pitch: A city map that a browser agent reshapes around the preferences it already knows about you.
about_excerpt:
A city map that a browser agent reshapes around the preferences it already knows about you.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Sample profile personalization 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Sample profile personalization 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Sample profile personalization 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 City guides usually ask everyone the same questions: what they enjoy, how they move around, what their budget is, and what kind of day they want. We imagined a better experience where a browser agent can share only the relevant preferences, while the website keeps the personalization visible, optional, and reversible. 

 What it does 

 City for You is an interactive Santiago map that collaborates with browser agents through WebMCP. 

 The agent can inspect the map’s capabilities and propose a personalization using selected interests, mobility, budget, and an optional note. The website shows a preview before changing anything. After approval, it filters 80 curated places across 17 interests and creates a simple three-stop itinerary called “Your day in Santiago.” 

 Each recommendation includes a neighborhood, explanation, matched interests, suggested time, and contextual photograph. Users can ask the agent to explain the active personalization or reset the map at any time. 

 Three fictional profiles also make the experience testable without a WebMCP client. 

 How we built it 

 We built City for You with TypeScript, React, Vinext, Leaflet, OpenStreetMap, and OpenAI Sites. 

 The website registers five typed tools using document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 get_map_capabilities 
 preview_personalization 
 apply_personalization 
 explain_personalization 
 reset_personalization 
 

 Every tool has an explicit input schema and runtime validation. Previewed preferences are stored separately from the active map, preserving the approval step. 

 The itinerary uses a deliberately simple and inspectable ranking. It scores featured places by how many approved interests they match, gives free places a small boost for low-budget profiles, and avoids repeating neighborhoods when possible. 

 Codex helped us shape the concept, define the privacy boundary, implement and debug the WebMCP flow, expand the place catalog, build the responsive interface, write automated checks, and deploy the public site. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was designing personalization without suggesting that the website can directly read an agent’s memory. We solved this by accepting only a narrow, validated preference object and clearly showing what the site received. 

 We also had to keep preview and active state separate so an agent could not unintentionally change the experience before user approval. 

 Another challenge was making the result feel meaningfully personalized without introducing an opaque recommendation system. We chose a small deterministic ranking that is easy to explain and verify. 

 Finally, WebMCP is still an emerging browser capability, so we built fictional sample profiles as a reliable fallback for demos and unsupported clients. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that City for You demonstrates a complete WebMCP collaboration loop rather than a single agent-triggered action. 

 The final product includes: 

 
 Five working WebMCP tools 
 A visible preview-before-apply flow 
 80 Santiago places across 17 interests 
 Lifestyle-specific categories such as vegan, coffee, wellness, markets, pets, and live music 
 A ranked three-stop day plan 
 Explain and reset capabilities 
 A responsive public deployment 
 A complete fallback experience without an agent 
 

 Most importantly, personalization remains understandable and reversible throughout the experience. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP works best when the website and agent have clearly separated responsibilities. 

 The agent selects relevant context. The website validates it and owns the product logic. The person remains in control of whether the proposed change is applied. 

 We also learned that preview, explanation, and reset are not secondary privacy features. They are essential parts of a trustworthy personalized experience. 

 On the implementation side, we learned the importance of explicit tool schemas, runtime validation, lifecycle-safe tool registration, and deterministic behavior that can be tested without relying on model output. 

 What's next for City for You 

 Next, we would connect the map to live place data, opening hours, events, routing, accessibility details, and travel times. 

 We would also improve the ranking with distance, mobility, time of day, weather, and explicit user feedback while keeping every recommendation explainable. 

 Longer term, City for You could expand beyond Santiago and demonstrate the same consent-based personalization pattern across travel, commerce, education, and other agent-enabled websites.

title: Personal Data Rights Workbench
pitch: Turn a vague “delete my data” request into a transparent plan that shows what can go, what must stay, and why.
about_excerpt: Turn a vague “delete my data” request into a transparent plan that shows what can go, what must stay, and why. Like Comment Story Updates Delete What You Can, Explain What You Must Keep 1. What we built The Personal Data Rights Workbench makes a synthetic account's data footprint legible before consequential actions commit. A person or browser agent can inspect a 14-category inventory, read four consent choices and two retention constraints, simulate a complete data-minimization partition, understand feature trade-offs, and stage consent, erasure, or portability actions. The responsive data map reorganizes into Delete , Retained by rule , and Kept by choice . The headline fixture shows exactly 9 / 2 / 3 categories and an honest 92.6% reduction of deterministic demo bytes. The review matrix shows the exact staged action IDs and values. Commitment through the normal visible page control updates inventory and consent, clears staging, and creates an immutable synthetic receipt. 2. How we used WebMCP The top-level page registers nine imperative JavaScript tools for inventory, consent, retention, simulation, plan-bound staging, cancellation, and receipt reading. It prefers document.modelContext and retains navigator.modelContext only for older Chrome preview builds. Registration is scoped with an AbortController and atomic: all nine calls are initiated in one synchronous task, then awaited as a group. If any call throws or rejects, every attempted name is removed, the lifecycle is aborted, and readiness rejects. Tool callbacks use execute(input, { signal }) , while tolerating older callers that omit options. Inputs are validated in code, every non-retained category must be explicitly classified, plans receive unique IDs, and all staging is bound to the exact current plan. No consequential commit tool is exposed through WebMCP. Final commitment uses the normal visible page control and remains subject to Codex/browser safety confirmation; ordinary browser actuation may still reach visible controls. The read-only receipt tool returns only after commitment. 3. Why it matters Privacy controls often split one intention across opaque settings, retention language, and destructive forms. This workbench explores a more inspectable model: structured agent assistance for inventory and planning, explicit user intent for every category, visible consequences, version-bound staging, and a clear commit point. The demo does not determine legal rights or establish compliance. It demonstrates how WebMCP can make a complex workflow composable, visible, and truthful before and after commitment. 4. What we learned Tool quality is inseparable from visible state. The same domain service powers the UI, WebMCP tools, and deterministic rehearsal. A mutating callback rejects if already cancelled, then commits state, synchronously flushes the React subscription update, and returns without awaiting post-mutation work. Confirmed receipts also close every staging path. We also learned that schemas are routing guidance, not authorization; omitted categories must not be interpreted as user intent; every staged action needs a plan version; partial tool registration is unsafe; and receipts should describe only actions that actually committed. For compatibility with the client used in the demo, tools are registered imperatively in the top-level page. How we used AI and Codex This is a new project created during the challenge period. I used Codex while working on the project. The recorded walkthrough uses Codex Site Tools to discover the nine page tools, inspect the synthetic account, simulate and stage the plan, and read the receipt after visible confirmation. Codex also helped prepare the project write-up and testing instructions and run the automated checks. The application itself uses deterministic client-side logic, not an embedded language-model backend. Testing instructions No account, credentials, payment, or real personal data is required. Open https://webmaxru.github.io/webmcp-data-rights-workbench/ directly as the top-level HTTPS page in a WebMCP-capable client. The repository documents Codex Site Tools, ChatGPT's in-app browser, and Chrome with WebMCP enabled; client availability is environment-dependent. Verify the page reports nine native WebMCP tools ready. If native WebMCP is unavailable, the labelled rehearsal can illustrate the UI but does not establish native tool discovery or invocation. Ask the agent to inspect inventory, consent, and retention constraints. Request the deterministic headline plan: keep account_profile , tax_invoices , and saved_delivery_addresses ; delete the other nine non-retained categories; leave the two retained categories classified by their rules; and set sale_or_sharing to false. Have the agent simulate and stage that plan without committing. Verify 9 / 2 / 3, 92.6%, two feature effects, and the exact staged consent and erasure details. All staging must use the returned current plan_id . Review the visible staged actions and activate Confirm staged actions . Verify nine inventory records become erased, sale-or-sharing consent is false, and staging is cleared. Ask the agent for get_privacy_receipt . It should match the visible confirmed result. Additional staging, cancellation, or re-confirmation must fail until the synthetic demo is reset. Refresh for a fresh in-memory account. For negative cases and the consent-only/export-only paths, follow the testing guide . Known Limitations All records, identities, sizes, retention rules, dates, and receipts are deterministic synthetic fixtures. The 92.6% figure is demo-byte selection, not measured deletion from a real service or proof of privacy improvement. State and receipt immutability are scoped to the in-memory demo session. Refreshing resets the account. Portability is a staged synthetic export request, not a real downloadable data export. There is no identity proofing, legal eligibility engine, production deletion queue, external account connection, analytics, or persistent backend. Browser-preview support and agent safety behavior are outside this app's control; the visible confirmation button is not an authorization boundary that prevents all browser automation. title: Moirae Console
pitch: Moirae Console adds a governance layer to WebMCP, routing AI agent actions through The Fates so every request is allowed, denied, or escalated for human approval.
about_excerpt: Moirae Console adds a governance layer to WebMCP, routing AI agent actions through The Fates so every request is allowed, denied, or escalated for human approval. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Moirae Console Moirae Console Chrome Window Moirae Console in ChatGPT browser Inspiration WebMCP is incredible for letting websites expose structured capabilities directly to AI agents. But the moment I saw it, one question immediately jumped out at me: If an agent can discover what a website can do, who decides what it is actually allowed to do? Capability discovery and authority are two very different things. That distinction is the entire foundation of Moirae Console. I was already working on The Fates—a deterministic governance and control-plane project for AI systems. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to pull that architecture out of the backend and turn it into something visible and tangible. Moirae Console is the human- and agent-facing surface for that idea. I set a deliberately narrow goal: let an AI agent discover useful tools via WebMCP, but force an independent governance check before it can actually disclose protected data or trigger a host-side action. The central idea is straightforward: WebMCP exposes the capability. The Fates determines the authority. Moirae makes that boundary visible to the human. What it does Moirae Console exposes exactly two WebMCP tools on a fixed demonstration document: inspect_document and publish_document. Here is the catch: just because an agent discovers these tools doesn't mean it has permission to execute them. Instead of firing immediately, the request passes from the WebMCP browser surface to a trusted host boundary, and then hands off to Ananke, the Fates authority component. Ananke evaluates the request and returns one of three decisions: ALLOW, REQUIRES_APPROVAL, or DENY. For a simple inspection, Ananke returns ALLOW, permitting the host to disclose the document. For a publication request, it initially returns REQUIRES_APPROVAL. The agent cannot approve its own action—a human has to step in and perform a separate approval step before the host asks The Fates for fresh execution authority. (If you run the restricted-agent demonstration, the exact same publication attempt simply receives a DENY, and nothing happens on the host side). By showing the governance decision separately from the actual host effect, Moirae proves that authorization and execution don't have to be mashed together into a single, insecure step. For the human, that means fewer blanket permissions and fewer interruptions: low-risk actions can proceed automatically, sensitive actions pause for approval, and forbidden actions stop cleanly. Without a structured interface like WebMCP, this kind of collaboration tends to depend on application-specific automation or prompt conventions; here, the agent discovers real web capabilities while authority remains independently governed. How I built it The browser app is built with React, TypeScript, and WebMCP. The WebMCP surface is intentionally thin, strictly registering the two public tools via document.modelContext.registerTool(...). I explicitly locked down the browser. It isn't allowed to choose privileged parameters like governance actions, credentials, caller authority, or publication destinations. The host completely controls those values. The execution path looks like this: AI agent discovers tools via WebMCP. Moirae Console browser sends a bounded, same-origin API request. Trusted Moirae host authenticates the request and passes it to Ananke, the authority component used by this challenge runtime, within The Fates architecture. Ananke evaluates and returns ALLOW, REQUIRES_APPROVAL, or DENY. The host verifies the authority and finally executes the effect. Crucially, the host independently validates the authority returned by The Fates before doing anything. The protected document and the Fates credentials never even enter the browser bundle. Everything runs on public, pinned source checkpoints of Moirae Console, Project Ananke, and Project Adrasteia (Runtime Contracts 0.6.2). It's all open-source and Apache-2.0 licensed. Challenges I ran into The hardest part wasn't registering the WebMCP tools—it was preserving the strict distinction between an agent requesting something and the system having the authority to actually do it. Once I started testing that boundary aggressively, several thorny implementation problems popped up: Human approval leaks: Initially, there was a risk of sending too much approval context to the browser. I fixed this by giving the browser a short-lived, opaque handle. The real authoritative identifier stays strictly on the host. Clicking "Approve" just asks the backend to perform a new governed transition, rather than blindly trusting a local UI state change. Concurrency: I had to make sure a single human approval couldn't accidentally trigger multiple effects if a bunch of requests hit the server at once. The publication path now relies on bounded atomic installation and strict replay/idempotency controls. Canonicalisation & evidence binding: A governance system is useless if one layer authorizes a request but the next layer executes a slightly different version of it. The Console actively recomputes and verifies authority bindings rather than trusting values just because they came back in an HTTP response. Failing closed: If The Fates goes offline, returns corrupted evidence, or spits out something the Console can't verify, the system absolutely cannot default to granting permission. In the tested failure paths, it fails closed rather than treating uncertainty as permission. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Instead of treating this like a fragile hackathon demo, I treated it like a system that should be attacked. I'm incredibly proud of the testing rigor. The final candidate passed a fairly brutal test suite: 186 Moirae Console tests, 266 Ananke tests, and 407 Runtime Contracts tests, alongside strict TypeScript checks, dependency audits, and live testing of the approval flows, replay behaviour, and concurrency/race conditions I designed the system to withstand. I also verified the live Railway deployment in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, where ChatGPT discovered the two WebMCP Site Tools and successfully invoked the governed inspection flow. Even better, I ran a repository-aware adversarial review using an independent AI model. I gave it access to the actual repos, shell, and running services, and let it try to break the system. It attempted bypasses, credential confusion, replay attacks, and evidence substitution. The result? PASS WITH LIMITATIONS. It didn't find a single HIGH or CRITICAL blocking defect. I chose to thoroughly document the remaining known limitations rather than pretending I'd built a flawless production security system for a hackathon reference implementation. What I learned The biggest takeaway is that capability and authority fundamentally need different abstractions. It's fantastic that an agent knows a tool exists, and it's great that it knows how to invoke it. But neither of those facts means the resulting real-world effect should actually be allowed. WebMCP gives us a beautiful, clean way to handle the capability side. Building Moirae showed me how powerful it is to pair that with a hardened, independent authority layer. I also learned that "human-in-the-loop" design is broken when it's just a confirmation popup bolted on as an afterthought. Human approval has to be treated as a core part of the authority model—a separate transition that the agent cannot perform through the exposed WebMCP surface. Finally, adversarial testing proved that systems rarely fail because of a single "bad function." They fail at the boundaries: identity, freshness, canonicalisation, and replay. Hardening those boundaries changed my entire design. What's next Moirae Console is a small demonstration, but it points toward a much safer, broader model for agentic web applications. The agent can discover capabilities and propose useful work, while the human only steps in when their authority is actually required. Low-risk actions can continue automatically, sensitive operations can pause for a real human decision, and forbidden actions can stop cleanly at the host boundary. That creates a model where people and agents can collaborate without giving the agent unrestricted control. A production version would need stronger deployment identity, durable state, signed authority evidence, monitoring, and recovery guarantees. Those are deliberately documented as future work rather than hidden behind the hackathon demo. WebMCP doesn't just give agents more things to do. It makes those capabilities structured enough that we can finally govern them properly. title: PodHood — WebMCP for Podcasts & YouTube
pitch: Turn any podcast or YouTube library into a surface your agent can drive: 8 WebMCP tools that search, filter, read timestamped transcripts, and cue the player on the page you're both looking at.
about_excerpt: Turn any podcast or YouTube library into a surface your agent can drive: 8 WebMCP tools that search, filter, read timestamped transcripts, and cue the player on the page you're both looking at. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into* Live demo → https://aiengineer.podhood.com * — a real production library of 1,065 talks. Open it in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and just start asking. Inspiration Podcasts and conference talks hold an enormous share of what a field actually knows, and almost none of it is reachable. Search gives you an episode, not a moment. A transcript is a 20,000-word wall. "Where did she explain the eval harness?" is a question no podcast page can answer today. Agents don't fix this — they inherit it. An agent that lands on a podcast page can do one of two unpleasant things: swallow the entire transcript and burn its context on filler, or drive the UI by guessing at pixels. Either way it works around the page instead of with it. WebMCP changes where the agent is standing. It is already here, in the browser, next to the person, looking at the same screen. That turns out to change what a tool is even allowed to be. What it does PodHood turns any podcast or YouTube channel into a structured library — summaries, chapters, key moments, speaker-diarized and word-aligned transcripts, recognized people, companies and products — and then registers that structure as eight WebMCP tools via document.modelContext , across two surfaces. On the library page search_episodes — search the catalog by meaning or keyword; returns episodes with timestamped citation links filter_episodes — apply topic / person / company / product / collection / year filters; the visible list and the URL change list_episodes — read back exactly what the visitor is looking at right now, with IDs open_episode — navigate the visitor to an episode page On an episode page read_episode — summary, speakers, and the chapter + key-moment outline with timestamps search_transcript — find exact text and highlight it in the transcript panel read_transcript — speaker-labeled, timestamped transcript windows, by chapter or time range play_moment — seek the player to a moment and start playback play_moment is the whole thesis in one call. The agent is not handing you a link to go read later. It moves the playhead in the player in front of you, and you hear the thing. That is only possible because the agent shares the view with a human — which is exactly the shape WebMCP has and no other agent interface does. What a human and an agent do together here On https://aiengineer.podhood.com — 1,065 talks from the AI Engineer conference series, 86 collections, 1,033 speakers, 880 companies — the loop looks like this: "What's actually being said about evals at these conferences?" → the agent runs search_episodes , then filter_episodes on the Evaluation & Observability topic. Your screen changes. You are now looking at 83 talks, and so is it. "Only 2026, and only speakers from model labs." → filter_episodes narrows again. You watch it happen, and you can undo it by clicking, because they are the same filters you would have clicked. "Open the second one and find where he explains the harness." → open_episode , then search_transcript . The line lights up in the transcript panel. "Play it." → play_moment . The player seeks and starts. You ask a follow-up while it plays; the agent has read_transcript scoped to that chapter and answers with a citation that points at your domain, at the right second. No copy-paste, no tab-switching, no "here's a link, go find it yourself." The agent does the navigating; the human does the listening and the deciding. Why WebMCP is the right primitive for this We already run a hosted MCP server for podcast catalogs, so we can compare the two honestly. An external MCP connector is a good way for an agent somewhere else to query a catalog. It cannot touch the page a person is looking at. It has no playhead, no transcript panel, no filter rail. WebMCP inverts that assumption, and the tools change shape as a result. filter_episodes is not a query — it is a UI mutation the person watches happen. search_transcript is not a string match — it is a highlight. This is the only agent interface where "tell me" and "show me" are the same call. Three properties we deliberately locked in: Read and view-state only. No writes, no accounts, no purchases. An agent can only change what the visitor could already change themselves — filters, highlight, playhead — all visible on screen and reversible with a click. There is no state an agent can reach that a human cannot see it reach. Show-branded, not platform-branded. The tools present as belonging to the creator's show, on the creator's domain — not to PodHood. Domain-native citations. Every link an agent produces resolves to the creator's own domain with a timestamp. Agent traffic lands on the creator, which is the only version of this that is sustainable for the people making the content. Why this needs more than a transcript Every tool here is downstream of structure that has to exist before the tool can be honest: search_episodes needs a semantic index over the catalog, not ctrl+F. filter_episodes needs entities disambiguated — "Claude" the model versus a person named Claude, three different speakers named Chen. play_moment needs word-level audio alignment . A timestamp four seconds off makes the entire feature feel broken. read_episode needs chapters and key moments that were actually extracted, not guessed at read time. This is the part of WebMCP we think is under-appreciated: good tools are a consequence of good data modeling. You can bolt document.modelContext onto anything. You can only make it useful on top of a page that already knows what it contains. How we built it The tool layer registers on document.modelContext when each surface mounts, with JSON-schema'd inputs and compact, agent-shaped return payloads — never raw DOM, never a whole transcript. Tools are bound to the same client state store the UI reads from , so an agent's filter_episodes and a human's click on the filter rail go down one code path. There is no drift between what the agent believes is on screen and what is on screen — and list_episodes exists precisely so the agent can re-ground itself against the real view at any point. read_transcript is windowed by chapter or time range, because handing a model ninety minutes of speech is how you get a confident wrong answer. Tool names and descriptions were tuned hard. A model will reach for search_episodes when it wants search_transcript unless the boundary is stated explicitly in the description. Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. Our origins are registered for the Chrome WebMCP origin trial, so document.modelContext is available with no flags — including on creators' custom domains. Zero creator configuration. The tools ship automatically with every published PodHood library. Nothing to enable, nothing to write. Agents without WebMCP support see a completely normal page; nothing degrades. Challenges we ran into Sizing outputs. The first read_transcript returned everything and the agent drowned. Chapter-scoped windows plus a "next window" affordance fixed it. One state, two drivers. Making agent-driven and human-driven state genuinely the same object took a refactor. Anything less produced ghost states, where the agent was filtering a list the human was not seeing. Restraint. The tempting move is to expose thirty tools. Eight sharply-described verbs outperformed a larger surface every time we tested. Testing against a moving target. WebMCP is an origin trial. ChatGPT desktop plus Chrome flags plus a live registered origin is not a fast dev loop. What we learned The best WebMCP tools are not an API bolted onto a page — they are the page's own verbs, named. Everything that worked here was already something the site could do: filter, highlight, seek. WebMCP just let an agent do it on the human's behalf, in front of them. The tools that tried to be more than the page could do were exactly the ones models misused. What's next Cross-library tools, so an agent can work across a creator's entire network of shows at once. A compare_moments tool for putting two speakers' claims side by side with both timestamps. Publishing the WebMCP tool layer as a standalone open-source package, so any media site can adopt the same eight verbs. Prior work vs. work done during the submission period PodHood is an existing product. The ingestion pipeline, the Brief data model (chapters, key moments, diarization, entity recognition, word-aligned transcripts), the search index and the player all predate this hackathon. Everything in the WebMCP layer is new work built during the submission period (August 25 – September 3, 2026): all eight tool definitions and their schemas, the document.modelContext registration for both surf

title: CoShop: The Agent-Native Storefront
pitch: A WebMCP storefront where shoppers and AI agents collaborate in the exact same session, featuring live UI grounding and secure human-in-the-loop checkout validations.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP storefront where shoppers and AI agents collaborate in the exact same session, featuring live UI grounding and secure human-in-the-loop checkout validations.

 Inspiration 

 We realized that real agentic checkout,the kind large merchants will actually ship to production,needs a human sign-off gate for the same reason two-factor authentication exists. An agent should be able to do the tedious 90% (searching the catalog, comparing specs, filling the cart, applying discount codes) autonomously, but the final "place an order with real money" step requires a deliberate, visible human decision. CoShop was born out of the necessity to build a secure, collaborative, and beautiful environment where humans and agents can shop together without liability risks. 

 What it does 

 CoShop is a high-performance, stateless e-commerce storefront that exposes its entire architecture to AI agents via WebMCP. 

 
 Live UI Grounding: When the AI agent interacts with the store (e.g., searching or adding an item to the cart), the human shopper's screen visually reacts. The cart slides open, the product card pulses, and an accessible activity log narrates the action. The AI doesn't work in a black box; the human watches exactly what it is doing. 
 Human-in-the-Loop Checkout: When an agent attempts to check out, it is securely gated. The agent can only stage the checkout, which summons a live confirmation banner on the human's screen. The transaction is completely halted until the human physically clicks "Confirm Order." 
 

 How we built it 

 We built CoShop using Next.js 16 (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS v4, styling it with a premium "Midnight Violet" glassmorphism aesthetic and 8K photorealistic product assets. 

 The core of our WebMCP integration relies on the use-webmcp-tool React hook. We registered 11 distinct tools to document.modelContext . 

 The architectural magic happens in our state management. We used Zustand as a single source of truth. When an AI agent executes a WebMCP tool (like add_to_cart ), the callback fires a Zustand state mutation. Because the React UI is listening to that exact same store, the UI instantly animates via Framer Motion to reflect the agent's action to the human user. Furthermore, the cart state is persisted into secure, HTTP-only cookies, ensuring the app remains entirely stateless and scalable on Vercel's Edge network without requiring an external database. 

 

 The WebMCP Fit & User Experience 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP: 
Most agentic-commerce demos rely on brittle DOM-scraping or disjointed chat widgets that act on a storefront rather than with it. CoShop leverages the Model Context Protocol for Web (WebMCP) to expose 11 schema-defined tools directly to the agent's context window. This eliminates hallucination-the agent doesn't guess how to buy a shoe; it natively calls add_to_cart(productId, size, qty) with 100% deterministic accuracy. 

 What humans and agents can do together now: 
Before CoShop, you either shopped yourself, or you handed a task to an autonomous agent and hoped it didn't accidentally drain your credit card. CoShop introduces the Shared Session . A human can manually add a shirt to their cart, and concurrently ask their AI agent to find a matching pair of waterproof boots and add them to the same cart. They are no longer isolated; they are collaborating in real-time. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was bridging the gap between the agent's headless execution and the human's visual experience. Initially, when the agent added an item to the cart, the human wouldn't know it happened unless they manually checked. We had to heavily engineer our state synchronization so that WebMCP execution callbacks directly triggered UI animations, sidebars, and focus states, ensuring absolute transparency. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are incredibly proud of achieving true Live Agent Grounding . Being able to give an agent a complex prompt-
 "find me a waterproof running shoe under $120, add a size 10 to my cart, and stage a checkout" 
and then literally sitting back and watching the website's UI animate and scroll on its own as the agent executes the tasks is a magical experience. We are also proud of building this with zero external database dependencies, making it blazing fast and infinitely scalable. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the future of agentic web isn't just about giving AI access to APIs; it's about building secure hand-offs. The Model Context Protocol for Web proves that we don't have to choose between full autonomy (which is dangerous) and manual labor. We can have collaborative autonomy, where the AI does the heavy lifting and the human provides the final, secure consensus. 

 What's next for CoShop: The Agent-Native Storefront 

 We plan to expand the WebMCP toolset to include dynamic sizing recommendations (where the agent reads the user's past purchase history to determine the best shoe size) and real-time inventory negotiations. Ultimately, we want to open-source the "Human-in-the-Loop Checkout" component as a standalone NPM package so any e-commerce store can securely integrate agentic checkout.

title: CoHabby Living
pitch: A compatibility-first roommate finder where your browser agent does the structured work through six WebMCP tools, and you keep every human decision.
about_excerpt: A compatibility-first roommate finder where your browser agent does the structured work through six WebMCP tools, and you keep every human decision. Like Comment Story Updates The last click stays human: Confirm demo introduction moves the state to v9. Demo confirmed. No real message was sent. compare_shortlist lays two people side by side across six dimensions of daily life. Warm is the chosen tone for the first hello. Public proof: MIT license, public repository, immutable tag, and the live footer's exact deployed revision ba55c557358a. Six WebMCP tools registered on one page: five change what the person sees, one is read-only. READY · v1 is the state both of them share. prepare_introduction drafts a first hello from facts already on the page. The person edits every word; no site tool can confirm or send. Synergy Lens: explain_synergy_match opens Maya's 92 read, 88% profile evidence, and three practical reasons the household rhythms fit. Approval is not a tool. The agent stages the living plan; only the person clicks Yes, use these choices. State moves v2 to v3. find_compatible_rooms brings Maya, Jordan, and Sam onto the page, person first, home as context. Whole-card selection stays human. Inspiration Finding a roommate is easy. Finding someone you can actually live well with is hard, and it shapes daily life for a lot of people: traveling nurses, single parents, new graduates, retirees, interns. Rooms are easy to list. Compatibility is what nobody helps with. CoHabby puts the person first and the room second. I also believe good technology should make people more human, not more mechanical. WebMCP made that concrete: the page can hand an agent real tools and still keep the meaningful decisions on the human side of the screen. CoHabby is already a live product with real users on the web , iOS , and Android . This challenge build is a separate, new codebase, but the problem it targets and the people it serves are the same. What people and agents do together Six small WebMCP tools share one page with the person: get_living_context reads the visible state (the only read-only tool) stage_living_brief stages a living plan from everyday habits find_compatible_rooms brings Maya, Jordan, and Sam onto the page, person first explain_synergy_match opens the Synergy Lens: a 92 score, 88% evidence, three practical reasons compare_shortlist lays two people side by side across six dimensions of daily life prepare_introduction drafts an editable first hello from facts already on the page Three actions are deliberately not tools: approving the plan, editing the hello, and confirming the introduction. The public tests assert that apply_living_brief and confirm_introduction do not exist. The agent prepares everything. The last click stays with the person. Why WebMCP fits Roommate matching is structured work with a few consequential decisions in between. WebMCP lets the page describe each step precisely, so the agent completes it reliably instead of guessing at the UI, and every result renders where the person can see it. Agent and human read the same state, which advances visibly from v1 to v9. How I built it Next.js and TypeScript. Every tool has a strict JSON Schema input (bounded enums, patterns, additionalProperties: false ) and a separate output schema, so nothing reaches the agent that a person could not see. Each call runs under a combined abort signal: cancel it and it rolls back to its checkpoint and commits nothing. A tool resolves only after the page acknowledges the new state has rendered, so "done" always means "visible." The live footer prints the deployed revision, the repo is MIT, and the judged source is pinned to an immutable tag. Fixtures and Synergy scores are fictional demo data, and the film says so. This WebMCP app is entirely new work created during the submission period (repository started Sept 1, 2026; every commit is dated inside the window). It shares no code with CoHabby's existing web and mobile products. Only the brand, the mission, and the roommate-compatibility concept pre-date the challenge; CHALLENGE_WORK.md in the repo documents the separation. Challenges and what I learned The hardest call was the human boundary. Making everything a tool would have looked more autonomous. It also would have let an agent introduce you to a stranger without asking. The hardest engineering was render acknowledgement: agents move faster than browsers paint, and a tool that returns before its result is on screen creates a page the person and the agent disagree about. The lesson: small, bounded tools with visible results beat one clever tool, and the best agent-native page is the one where you can tell exactly what the agent did and what you decided. title: Serendipity
pitch: An AI-powered city planner that uses WebMCP to discover, combine, and book a personalized night out across independent local services.
about_excerpt: An AI-powered city planner that uses WebMCP to discover, combine, and book a personalized night out across independent local services. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I started Serendipity because planning a free evening in Tokyo kept turning into admin. I would find an interesting place, look for dinner nearby, check when both closed, open a map, and then discover that the route did not fit. A simple night out could leave me with ten tabs and no actual plan. The first version was a technical reservation-network demo. It worked, but it did not answer the question a normal user would ask: why would I use this? I kept the reliable parts and rebuilt the product around a simpler job. Give it the evening you have, and get back one plan whose times and prices you can check for yourself. What it does You choose Shibuya, Shinjuku, or Ikebukuro, then set the group size, time, per-person budget, walking limit, and the kind of night you want. Dinner can be included or left out. Serendipity builds one route with two or three stops. It shows when to visit, how long the walks are, what each stop should cost, and the estimated total for the group. If three stops do not fit, it says why it returned two. If nothing fits, it does not quietly loosen the request. It shows the closest option and waits for the user to approve the change. Each stop has a sources section with the publisher, checked date, published hours, official menu, and official link. This is planning from published information, not a live booking service. Serendipity does not claim a seat is available and does not send anything to a venue. Why WebMCP is a strong fit This kind of planning often starts as a conversation: “Plan a calm Ikebukuro evening for three, include dinner, and keep it under ¥4,000 each.” Then comes the follow-up: show me where the meal price came from, or change one stop. An assistant can try to operate the form like a person, but it has to interpret the layout and guess whether the page really changed. WebMCP gives it five actions instead: find a plan, show the evidence for a place, change one stop, save the plan, or delete it. Those actions use stable plan and place IDs, and the result appears on the same page the user is watching. I stopped at five tools. Finding a plan, checking evidence, and changing a stop are read-only. Saving and deleting are the only write actions, and they only affect this browser. Opening a restaurant or venue website is still a normal link the user chooses. How I built it The app is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript and deployed on Vercel. The planner is deterministic. It checks combinations of activities and meals against published opening hours, visit length, closing time, budget, and walking limits. Restaurant budgets use the highest price in the official menu range. Walking time is marked as a coordinate-based estimate. I reviewed 21 places across the three hubs: four activities and three meals in each area. Every place in a route needs support for its name, address, coordinates, hours, public access, and price. I wrote the short descriptions myself and used official pages instead of copying marketplace reviews or photos. Google enrichment exists behind a server flag, but it is off in the submitted version. The live app works from its reviewed data and official menu pages. The human controls and the five Site Tools call the same controller. I did not want an agent demo sitting beside a separate, less reliable product. If a request is stale, malformed, cancelled, or unsafe, both paths reject it in the same way. Challenges The hardest part was deciding what the app was allowed to say. It is easy to make a schedule look convincing. It is much harder to prove that a place is actually open at that time and that the displayed price came from a menu. I spent more time removing weak data than adding new places. Parks without published hours, prices inferred as zero, stale closure calendars, and unclear reuse rights all forced changes to the data model. The UI went through several bad versions. One was two dashboards side by side. Another had oversized type and decorative cards that made the route harder to follow. Feedback on those versions was blunt, but correct. I removed most of the explanation from the main path, gave the route the full page, and kept source details behind disclosures. The agent and the human also kept finding different edge cases. A late response could overwrite a newer search. Browser Back could make the URL disagree with the plan. A damaged saved record could break reopening. Fixing those bugs led to one shared state controller instead of two implementations. Accomplishments The live app covers three Tokyo hubs, with four reviewed activities and three official-menu meals in each one. Codex discovered all five Site Tools in the ChatGPT desktop browser and used them to build a real plan and open its meal evidence on the visible page. A strict request can return an honest no-result. The app only offers a relaxed search after the server has verified it and the user chooses it. What I learned A difficult technical demo is not automatically a useful product. The first version proved that several sites could coordinate, but people still asked, “What is this for?” Rebuilding it around one understandable job made the engineering choices much clearer. Good Site Tools are closer to product actions than UI controls. The agent does not need a tool for every button. It needs a few useful verbs, clear limits, and enough evidence for the person to check the result. WebMCP worked best when the agent and the user could look at the same updated plan, not when the agent disappeared into a background workflow. What’s next I would add more neighborhoods only after reviewing them to the same standard as the current three. The next practical improvements are transit-aware travel, shareable saved plans, and an optional live Google check controlled by the user. I would not add booking or payment until a venue provides real booking authority and there is a safe way to handle the transaction.
