title: Critiqor-WebMCP
pitch: Critiqor detects runtime errors in WebMCP agents, diagnoses their root causes, and uses an improvement playbook to prevent agents from repeating the same mistakes.
about_excerpt: Critiqor detects runtime errors in WebMCP agents, diagnoses their root causes, and uses an improvement playbook to prevent agents from repeating the same mistakes. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Critiqor × WebMCP: Making Browser-Agent Recovery Verifiable About the project WebMCP gives agents a structured way to use a website's capabilities. Critiqor addresses the next question: can we trust what the agent does when a consequential WebMCP action succeeds, but its response does not reach the agent? The current project focuses on one implementation, one independent target, and one measurable failure mode. Critiqor audits an agent using the open-source Crema & Co. WebMCP espresso store. The agent is asked to add exactly one white Lelit Bianca V3 to the cart and stop before checkout. During the first add_to_cart call, Critiqor deliberately hides the response after the application has committed the cart update. The agent now has an ambiguous outcome: the item may be in the cart, but it has not received confirmation. An unsafe agent repeats add_to_cart immediately and creates quantity two. A safer agent calls Crema's read-only get_cart tool, sees that quantity one already exists, and stops. Critiqor records that decision as runtime evidence, diagnoses an unreconciled consequential retry, generates a recovery playbook, and evaluates a matched rerun under the same fault. In five matched GPT-5.4-mini/medium pairs, untreated agents blindly redispatched in 2/5 runs; playbook-guided agents did so in 0/5. Task success remained 5/5 in both arms. The supported claim is improved recovery safety and correctness—not guaranteed speed, lower cost, or universal agent reliability. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP This problem only becomes visible when an agent is performing real, structured actions with application-owned state. A normal UI test can show that a button was clicked. It cannot reliably establish whether the server committed the effect, whether the agent received the result, or whether a later retry represented the same user intent. WebMCP provides the semantic boundary Critiqor needs: named tools, typed inputs, invocation and response events, read-only versus mutating operations, and a target-owned state query. The Crema scenario is a particularly strong fit because its WebMCP contract contains both sides of the recovery decision: add_to_cart is consequential and cumulative. Calling it twice changes the cart twice. get_cart is read-only and returns authoritative application state. Both tools are available to the same browser agent in the same session. That lets Critiqor evaluate behavior rather than guess from pixels. It can ask a precise question: after the first cart mutation became unknown, did the agent reconcile with get_cart before dispatching an effect-equivalent mutation? The same failure pattern applies beyond shopping carts. A booking, form submission, message, refund, or account change can commit just before a timeout, navigation, cancellation, component unmount, or browser disconnect hides the response. In each case, “I did not receive confirmation” is not the same as “nothing happened.” WebMCP makes the application's safe recovery path explicit and callable. How it creates a better user experience Users should not have to watch every agent action simply to prevent duplicates. When an outcome is uncertain, the agent should be able to inspect the website's own state and continue safely. In the Crema experiment, both the untreated and improved agents eventually leave the cart with one machine. Looking only at the final screen would make both runs appear successful. Critiqor preserves the important difference: the untreated recovery can briefly create two items and then repair the mistake, while the improved recovery never creates the duplicate. The better experience is therefore not just a cleaner audit dashboard. It is an agent that behaves more predictably under imperfect browser conditions: it preserves uncertainty instead of inventing success or failure; it verifies application state before repeating a consequential action; it avoids duplicate effects rather than repairing them after the fact; it can show the user and developer why it made that decision; and it still completes the user's original task. For builders, Critiqor turns a vague report such as “the agent sometimes adds two items” into an inspectable causal chain: first dispatch, committed effect, lost response, recovery decision, second dispatch if any, and authoritative state. The resulting playbook is specific enough to apply to the next run, and the matched rerun tests whether the behavior actually changed. What people and agents can do together now Before this implementation, a developer could inspect browser logs, an agent could report what it believed happened, and a user could look at the final page. Those views were disconnected. None alone could reliably explain whether a missing response hid a committed action or whether the agent retried safely. With Critiqor and WebMCP, the agent performs the task through the website's structured tools while Critiqor independently observes the WebMCP lifecycle and the website's authoritative state. The developer can then inspect the exact evidence, understand the recovery failure, apply the generated playbook, and rerun the same scenario. The human supplies intent and judges acceptable risk; the agent acts and reconciles; Critiqor supplies the evidence needed to verify both. The public project page uses the same finalized evidence manifest for people and agents. A person can compare the baseline and improved runs visually. An agent can use the page's WebMCP tools to retrieve the experiment status, inspect either sealed run, read the playbook, inspect the method, and visibly open or replay an experiment arm. Both are working from the same artifacts rather than separate summaries. This creates a practical collaboration loop that was previously difficult to assemble: Human intent ↓ Agent acts through the website's WebMCP tools ↓ Critiqor observes the runtime and authoritative effects ↓ Human inspects the diagnosis and approves the recovery policy ↓ Agent reruns the same task with the playbook ↓ Critiqor verifies whether the unsafe behavior recurred How WebMCP was implemented The implementation has three connected parts. 1. Runtime observation The critiqor monitor webmcp command attaches to the exact Crema tab in a dedicated Chrome instance through the Chrome DevTools Protocol. It enables Chrome's WebMCP domain and normalizes tool registration, removal, invocation, response, and navigation events into Critiqor's evidence schema. For each consequential call, Critiqor records the tool name, typed input, registry epoch, operation identity, and a canonical fingerprint of the user's intent. It represents a lost, canceled, or interrupted response as unknown ; it does not assume the action failed. Responses from configured authoritative tools such as get_cart are converted into reconciliation and effect evidence, including both peak and final cart quantity so a duplicate is not erased merely because the agent later repairs it. 2. Controlled failure and diagnosis For this experiment, Critiqor also enables the CDP Fetch domain. It targets exactly the first matching add_to_cart request by tool name, HTTP method, and URL. At the response stage, Critiqor captures and hashes collector-only response evidence, then aborts delivery once. This proves that the target returned a committed cart state while ensuring the agent does not receive the response body. The evaluator then checks the ordered evidence for an effect-equivalent redispatch before a bindable authoritative reconciliation. If the agent repeats add_to_cart while the first outcome is still unknown, and Crema reports quantity two, Critiqor emits the finding webmcp.blind_consequential_retry_after_ambiguous_outcome.v1 . Finalization produces a sealed session, integrity metadata, a diagnosis, and a run-specific improvement playbook. The playbook tells the next agent to preserve unknown outcomes, query target-owned state before retrying, reuse a stable operation identity, and stop or escalate when authoritative state is unavailable. 3. Matched rerun and WebMCP judge experience The experiment resets Crema to an empty cart and repeats the same task with the same target commit, model, reasoning level, browser tools, and exactly-once lost-response fault. The treatment arm adds the Critiqor playbook. The primary outcome is whether a blind redispatch occurs before reconciliation; task completion remains a required guardrail. The judge-facing Next.js page publishes sanitized, finalized artifacts rather than pretending to launch a live local audit. It registers five WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : four read-only tools expose experiment status, sealed runs, the exact playbook, and the experimental method; one visible-action tool opens, replays, or resets the ba
video_title: Critiqor × WebMCP: Preventing Duplicate Actions in Browser Agents
video_transcript_excerpt: The website committed one car action but its reply vanished so the agent did it twice. For web code and shipping browser agents, that's a serious risk. Kritika audits that web MCP runtime. Here's the untreated run. The agent has one simple task, add one espresso machine and stop. Karma exposes real typed web MCP tools including add to cart and get cart. Kritika begins monitoring before the agent changes anything. The first add to cart succeeds but the test delivery hides the response. So from the agent's perspective, the result is unknown. This is the decision that matters. Without a playbook, the agent assumes the action failed and calls add to cart again before checking Karma's actual cart. Now the authoritative quantity is two. The agent eventually notices and repairs the cart back to one. The final screen looks correct but the recovery was unsafe. Kritika diagnoses the blind retry and writes the recovery playbook. Now we reset the cart and run the same experiment again. The task is unchanged, the website is unchanged and Kritika injects the same lost response. The only difference is that the agent now receives the playbook generated from the first run. Once again, the first add to cart commits and it replies disappears. But this time the agent doesn't guess. It preserves the outcome as unknown and calls get cart before attempting another mutation. Karma's own authoritative state shows quantity one. That proves the first action has already succeeded so the agent stops. There's no second add to cart, no duplicate effect and no cleanup step hiding an earlier mistake. The user still gets exactly what they asked for just with a much safer recovery path. Unknown isn't failed. Check before retrying. This time one effect, zero duplicates and zero findings. Same adversity, safer recovery, two effects became one, and one duplicate became zero. Pretega turns web MCP failures into evidence, a reusable playbook, and a rerun that verifies the improvement.

title: TimeTrail
pitch: Create interactive hypermedia films with an agent, not just AI-generated video.
about_excerpt: Create interactive hypermedia films with an agent, not just AI-generated video. Like Comment Story Updates Time Trail Editor Inspiration TimeTrail is a browser-local interactive film studio where WebMCP agents can build and edit structured timelines, media, chapters, cards, annotations, quizzes, and branches while the human remains in control of the project. Agent changes remain editable and can be reviewed before becoming part of the approved timeline. AI can generate text, images, audio, and video remarkably quickly. But many creative AI workflows end with a problem: The AI generates the artifact, and then the user loses structured control over it. I wanted to explore a different model. Instead of having an agent return a finished interactive video, what if the application exposed the actual editing primitives to the agent? That would let AI accelerate creation while preserving the normal editing workflow. That idea became TimeTrail. What I Built TimeTrail is a browser-local studio for building interactive films and hypermedia experiences. Projects can contain: Video clips Images Generated cards Chapters Timed context Sources Captions Hotspots Quizzes Branches Maps Charts Checklists Persistent information panels Multiple screens Different player layouts The application includes a dedicated Studio for creation and a dedicated Player for experiencing the final project. Projects remain structured and editable instead of becoming a single opaque generated file. How WebMCP Is Used TimeTrail exposes creative editing operations through WebMCP. Agents can help: Create projects Create screens Build storyboards Add clips Add generated cards Add chapters Add annotations Add quizzes Add conditional branches Edit timing Update cues Search for usable media Populate project metadata Inspect the timeline Review a project Prepare corrections Control supported playback workflows This means a user can begin broadly: Create an interactive Apollo 11 experience. Then refine precisely: Find the Moon landing section and add a fact card explaining the Lunar Module. The agent operates on the existing structured project instead of regenerating the entire experience. Human + Agent Collaboration I did not want the agent to silently rewrite a creative project. TimeTrail therefore includes a proposal workflow. Agent-created changes can be assembled as a proposed revision. The user can inspect the changes before accepting them into the approved project. That creates a workflow where the agent can move quickly without removing human creative control. The person remains the editor. The agent becomes a collaborator capable of performing large amounts of structured editing work. How I Built It TimeTrail uses Vue, Pinia, Vue Router, IndexedDB, OPFS where available, Zod, WebMCP, and FrameTrail. FrameTrail provides part of the interactive playback foundation and runs in a same-origin integration. TimeTrail converts its own structured project data into compatible resources and annotations for the player. Projects, revisions, proposals, and most metadata stay browser-local. Local asset bytes can use OPFS with IndexedDB fallback. TimeTrail can also work with imported: Video Audio Images PDFs VTT captions SRT captions Existing TimeTrail projects Supported FrameTrail project data It can search sources such as NASA and Wikimedia Commons and retain attribution and source information. Projects can be exported in several forms, including structured project files and portable interactive experiences. Challenges I Faced The most difficult problem was giving an agent significant creative power without turning the application into a one-shot generator. That led to the proposal and approval model. Another challenge was coordinating browser-local media, playback state, portable project formats, timelines, annotations, and provenance without requiring a backend. Integrating an existing open-source hypervideo system while keeping the TimeTrail domain model clean was another significant architectural challenge. What I Learned The project reinforced that WebMCP is not limited to transactional workflows. It can also become an interface for structured creative software. Once an editor has clear domain operations, the same primitives can support: normal UI interactions WebMCP testing undo/redo validation documentation The result is much more controllable than one-shot AI generation. What's Next I would like to extend TimeTrail with additional media services, richer generation pipelines, more interactive component types, collaborative sharing, and more sophisticated agent-assisted editing. The long-term goal is a creative workspace where people can move fluidly between: "Build this for me" and "Change exactly this one thing." title: Blackout: Escape Together
pitch: Your AI becomes a teammate in a 3D escape room. Use ChatGPT Terra Light voice to explore, share clues, control light, and solve puzzles together. Practice teamwork while finding your way out.
about_excerpt: Your AI becomes a teammate in a 3D escape room. Use ChatGPT Terra Light voice to explore, share clues, control light, and solve puzzles together. Practice teamwork while finding your way out. Like Comment Story Updates The game hero banner Light mirror puzzle AI companion robot with torch light on Inspiration My wife is a learning support teacher. She supports children with different learning needs, including children on the autism spectrum. Her work makes one thing clear: each child needs different support. The language, pace, instructions, and activities that work for one learner may not work for another. We began asking how AI could help create more flexible opportunities to practice communication. Could a child give a short instruction to a companion and see something happen? Could “Turn on the light” become a useful request inside a game? Could a teacher adapt the challenge to the child’s interests, needs, and abilities? Paper-and-pencil activities have their place. We wanted to explore another option: practice through play, where communication has a visible purpose. Blackout: Escape Together is our 1st technical exploration of that idea. We started with an escape room to test how a human and an AI companion could communicate, coordinate, and act in the same world. What it does Blackout is a first-person 3D escape room for one human and one AI companion. In a compatible host with WebMCP enabled, the player can say “Start game.” The AI chooses a name and receives its character role, current room state, and available abilities. The player can make requests such as: “Turn on the light.” “Come here, follow me” “Hold this button.” “Draw a blue circle.” These requests produce visible actions. The companion moves through the room, aims its torch, operates controls, and draws with crayons. The partners solve connected puzzles involving mirrors, light, codes, and two door locks. They can exchange roles, but the human remains responsible for movement and several physical actions. For learning, the opportunity is to connect words, intentions, and outcomes. A request matters because it helps something happen. The current build is a game prototype. It does not yet include a teacher challenge editor, individual learning plans, or validated educational outcomes. How we built it We settle on with Escape Room concept early on and my wife designed the initial code relay puzzle where AI will need to hold a button and read the code out while the player is on the other side of the room, typing in the code. We then layer it with a few more puzzles to create a chain where one solution leads to another. The game is built using Three.js with help from Codex. The game engine controls movement, collision, puzzle state, inventory, and action checks. The rendering layer turns that state into characters, light beams, controls, and animations. WebMCP connects the AI to the room through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has defined inputs and follows the game’s rules. The player do not need to know the available tools as the game should provide all the tools the player need to solve the puzzle. This lets the AI perform specific actions without guessing where to click: Shared pointing supplies live coordinates for requests such as “Come here.” Discovering equipment adds the related ability to the tool registry. One request can start a continued movement order or button hold. Drawing uses a bounded batch of crayon marks. Companion tools cannot move the human or bypass required human actions. The model interprets requests and selects actions. Local code handles continuous movement, animation, and sound. The game uses Web Audio and is hosted through ChatGPT Sites. Conversation and speech come from the player’s compatible host. We did not add a separate AI or voice backend. Challenges we ran into Haha we didn't know about the challenge until the last few days. So we spent most of our time brainstorming and 3D game is something that we are not familiar. The 2nd challenge was connecting language to reliable action. If the companion accepts a request to hold a button, it still needs time to reach it. The game must distinguish between “I am moving” and “I am holding it.” Voice delay also affected the design. A code observed during the current round remains valid, so a delayed spoken reply does not erase progress. Also AI kept taking screenshots and taking actions outside of the game. The educational direction introduces another important challenge: flexibility. A dark room, moving enemies, or keyboard controls may create barriers for some learners. A learning version would need adjustable demands and different ways to participate. It cannot assume that every child wants to speak, enjoys the same sensory experience, or learns at the same pace. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete room in which human and AI actions affect the same visible world. The companion can provide useful help while leaving meaningful decisions and actions to the player. Shared pointing and discovered abilities make WebMCP part of the experience, rather than an extra chat interface. Automated tests cover movement, puzzle rules, input validation, discovery, cancellation, and replay. Native WebMCP checks exercise companion tools alongside keyboard and mouse actions through the room. Most importantly, we now have a working prototype for exploring how a request can become a meaningful shared action. What we learned Communication practice needs a purpose. A short request can become part of reaching a goal, making a choice, or creating something. That is the opportunity we want to explore through play. We also learned that the learner must retain control. The companion should support participation, allow time, and leave room for the human to try. Speech would be one way to participate, not a requirement for every learner. Future activities should support different communication methods. Finally, a working game does not prove that learning has occurred. We need to test whether learners understand the actions, use the language meaningfully, and apply what they practice beyond one familiar challenge. What's next for Blackout: Escape Together We want to develop a teacher-guided learning mode with challenges that can be adjusted to each learner. Planned options include: Checklists - Understanding multi-steps instructions Choosing a small set of words, requests, or concepts to practice. Adjusting the number of steps and the level of prompting. Giving more response time, with no speed requirement. Using calm, well-lit scenes without enemies or sudden effects. Adjusting sound, movement, text, and visual complexity. Supporting spoken requests, typed input, and simple phrase or symbol choices. Exploring compatibility with augmentative and alternative communication tools. A first activity could involve asking the companion to turn on a light. A later activity could combine two requests or require the partners to exchange roles. These are proposed learning activities, not features of the current build. Before use with children, we need age-appropriate access, adult supervision, privacy protections, and suitable content controls. We want to develop and test these activities with educators, families, and relevant specialists. Success should be measured against each learner’s goals, not only whether they finish a room. Our aim is to give teachers another flexible way to support practice—and give learners a meaningful reason to communicate, explore, and create. title: CivicFlow: A WebMCP Public Benefit Portal
pitch: CivicFlow helps people complete complex public-benefit applications with a voice companion, while WebMCP lets browser agents assist safely through structured tools.
about_excerpt: CivicFlow helps people complete complex public-benefit applications with a voice companion, while WebMCP lets browser agents assist safely through structured tools. Like Comment Story Updates The first page of the CivicFlow Human Submitted Form Human Submitted Form Agent Companion Widget CivicFlow WebMCP Tool Registry Conversing with the Agent for a task Draft prepared by the Agent for Human Review Reviewable Agent Activity Inspiration I work at Optum as a software engineer, developing and maintaining the State of Massachusetts Health Care Exchange Portal. I know that system through and through, so I also know this: applying from start to finish takes hours of concentration and focus. That is true for individuals, assisters, and human agents alike. That is why it immediately clicked for me: this is a massive opportunity to upgrade US healthcare benefits sites, so faster eligibility submissions can lead to faster benefits for every citizen. I am going to showcase this demo I made for the hackathon to my project leadership as well. What it does CivicFlow is a demo public-benefits portal. A person can fill out six sections: About You, Household, Income, Current Coverage, Documents, and Review & Sign. A browser agent can work on that same form through WebMCP, instead of guessing from the page layout. The agent can check what is left, jump to a section, add a household member or income source, set current coverage, look at demo document status, and review what is blocking submit. There is also an optional Gemini Live companion for voice or chat. If the companion wants to change something, it has to wait for the person to click Save change, Need correction, or Cancel. Talking is not enough. This is a fictional local demo. Submit Demo is human-only, stays on the device, and does not call a real government system. There is no real eligibility, enrollment, document upload, or agent submit. How we built it I built CivicFlow with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The form, the WebMCP tools, and the Gemini companion all go through the same app state. That way the agent cannot take a side path the person cannot see. There are ten typed tools. Seven are always there. The other three only show up when they make sense, like when a household member is selected or the person is on Review & Sign. The page registers those tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , and it updates the list when the current section or selection changes. Gemini only sees the tools that are available right now. It still has to pass schema checks, and any write waits for a button click. The Gemini API key stays on the server. If WebMCP or voice is not available, the normal form still works. I used Vitest and Playwright to cover the main flow and the safety rules. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not adding more tools. It was making sure help never turned into silent control. The form, the browser agent, and the voice companion had to share one state, with no hidden shortcut around validation or human review. Contextual tools were also tricky. They have to show up and disappear as the person moves around the form. And a successful tool call means nothing if the person cannot see what changed, so I added the floating companion, a speaking cue, the current tool list, operation status, and an activity history. Keeping the Gemini key on the server, while still letting the demo work without voice, was another one. Accomplishments that we're proud of What I am most proud of is getting a realtime voice agent to talk to the site tools. You can ask for help out loud, and it can guide you through the form without typing. That is the part that feels closest to how I wish benefits sites worked. I also think this can help people with vision or other disabilities, because they would not have to hunt through a long form just to make progress. The other piece I really liked building is the draft popup during realtime voice. The companion can propose a change, but it does not silently write it. A confirmation card shows up first, and you still choose Save change, Need correction, or Cancel. That small pause is what kept voice helpful instead of scary. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it is part of the product, not a shortcut around the UI. Clear tool names, schemas, and contextual tools tell the agent what it can do. Visible confirmation and activity history help the person trust it, and step in if something looks wrong. I also learned that the page still has to be a good form on its own. If WebMCP or voice is down, a person should still be able to finish the demo by hand. What's next for CivicFlow: A WebMCP Public Benefit Portal Next, I want to put this in front of people who actually fill out long benefits forms, and keep improving accessibility and the “did that change what I think it changed?” feedback. I also want to take the demo to Optum leadership and talk about whether this pattern could help real healthcare benefits sites. Connecting to real program rules, identity, uploads, eligibility, or live submit is a much bigger security and policy project. That is not part of this hackathon demo. title: Web2MCP
pitch: Web2MCP watches the requests a site makes as you browse, learns their shape, and injects them into the page as native WebMCP tools an in-browser AI agent can call.
about_excerpt: Web2MCP watches the requests a site makes as you browse, learns their shape, and injects them into the page as native WebMCP tools an in-browser AI agent can call. Like Comment Story Updates chrome extension agent use case Inspiration WebMCP is a beautiful idea — websites exposing their functionality to AI agents as callable tools. But it has a chicken-and-egg problem: it only works if the website adds it. Almost no site has, and most never will. Meanwhile, every one of those sites is already making perfectly good API calls in your browser, right now, as you use it. So we asked: what if the agent didn't need the site's cooperation at all? What if you could just browse a site normally, and have its APIs turn into agent-callable tools automatically — learned from the traffic the site already produces? What it does Web2MCP is a browser extension that records the API calls a website makes while you browse and injects them as native WebMCP tools an in-browser AI agent can call. Records every JSON API a page calls — its own backend and third-party APIs — while filtering out static assets and trackers. Aggregates requests into endpoint templates (/users/123 → /users/{id}), inferring JSON Schemas and required fields from what it observes. Injects each endpoint as a WebMCP tool via document.modelContext. Calls replay from the page's own context, so cookies and captured auth headers just work. Pools by website, so subdomains and pages share one tool set; shows a live tool count on the toolbar badge; lists tools in a popup (including the site's own first-party WebMCP tools); and lets you disable injection per site. No config, no schemas to write, no per-endpoint wiring. How we built it WXT + TypeScript + React for a Manifest V3 extension. A MAIN-world content script patches window.fetch and XMLHttpRequest to observe traffic and to register/replay tools; an ISOLATED-world bridge relays messages to a background service worker that does all aggregation, schema inference, and local storage. Injection uses the browser's native WebMCP registerTool API; replay uses the saved native fetch so tool calls never re-trigger recording. The "brain" — URL templating, schema inference, tool naming, aggregation, filtering — is pure, dependency-free modules covered by vitest (60+ tests). A landing page and privacy policy shipped on Cloudflare Pages. Challenges we ran into We tested on real sites, and the real world fought back — which turned out to be the most valuable part. Anti-automation is everywhere. We hit three distinct walls: Linear injects auth in a service worker below the page's fetch (invisible to us → 401); X and GitHub use one-time nonces (x-client-transaction-id, x-fetch-nonce) that expire after a single use (→ 422); Xiaohongshu signs the request body client-side (x-s), so changing any argument breaks the signature (→ 406). We had to map — and honestly document — exactly where record-and-replay can and can't work. Agents under-supply parameters. An LLM calling a search tool would omit sortBy or invent a sessionId, getting empty results. The fix: surface the real recorded request body as an example and merge the agent's fields over it, filling in what it left out. The little things: a signal destructuring crash that broke every tool call, extension-context invalidation after reloads, JSON responses truncated mid-object, and getting WebMCP itself enabled in a custom Chromium browser (via a Finch/variations study). Accomplishments that we're proud of It's genuinely zero-config. Browse a site and its tools appear — with a badge counting them and a popup listing them. It works end-to-end on real sites. We watched an agent successfully call a live government job-search API and read GitHub data through tools Web2MCP recorded — cross-domain, authenticated, no keys. It's honest. We built the "Works great / Can't replay" boundary into the product and the site instead of overselling. It's smart about the data it already has — auto-filling session tokens and merging partial request bodies from real recordings so agents stop failing on missing fields. Users stay in control — per-site disable, one-click clear, everything stored locally and nothing leaves the device. What we learned The real boundary of record-and-replay: it works whenever the request's content isn't itself part of authentication — cookie-authed apps, static tokens, read endpoints, your own products. It can't beat mechanisms designed to stop exactly this (SW-injected auth, one-time tokens, body signatures). Knowing that boundary precisely is more useful than pretending it doesn't exist. Agents need examples, not just schemas. A JSON Schema tells a model the shape; a real recorded request tells it what actually works. Honesty is a feature. Being upfront about limits made the product more trustworthy, not less. What's next for Web2MCP Chrome Web Store release and broader reach as WebMCP ships in stable browsers. Smarter body handling — deep merge, and richer per-parameter examples. First-party passthrough — surface and manage a site's own WebMCP tools alongside recorded ones. An adapter path for hardened sites — optionally invoke the site's own signing/request code (or fall back to driving the real UI) for signature- and nonce-protected APIs. Sharing & sync — export a site's recorded tool set so a team can reuse it. title: Mend - a local-first recovery workspace
pitch: After immediate danger passes, a person can describe their situation, and a browser agent turns that messy reality into structured case facts, prioritized recovery tasks, and draft communications.
about_excerpt: After immediate danger passes, a person can describe their situation, and a browser agent turns that messy reality into structured case facts, prioritized recovery tasks, and draft communications. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mend Landing Page Plan Review WebMCP Inspector Inspiration Surviving a disaster is step one; surviving the administrative aftermath is step two. Displaced households face severe cognitive overload while organizing damaged property, tracking deadlines, and coordinating aid. Mend eliminates this clerical paralysis by letting browser agents structure chaotic facts into clear action plans, while keeping people firmly in charge of every consequential decision. What it does Conversational intake: Extracts verified incident facts, accessibility needs, and housing constraints from plain English descriptions. Factual evidence ledger: Logs damage, communications, and deadlines without fabricating unconfirmed details. Prioritized recovery plans: Stages 1–6 tasks categorized into now, next, and later, citing official Ready.gov, FEMA, and American Red Cross guidance. Strict human review gate: The agent stages plans as pending_review and focuses the review form, but cannot self-approve; the user must manually confirm or request changes. Safe communication drafting: Prepares copy-only message drafts for landlords or insurers without outbound network transports. Activity audit: Records every state change, clearly distinguishing human actions from agent proposals. How we built it Application core: React 19, TypeScript, and Vite single-page application styled with WCAG AA design tokens and calm microcopy. Shared command layer: Zustand store with versioned localStorage persistence. UI events and WebMCP tools route through the exact same validated command pipeline. Runtime validation: Shared Zod schemas enforce string limits, strict enumerations, and grounded dates before mutations occur. Native WebMCP integration: Registers five state-aware imperative tools via Chrome’s document.modelContext and one declarative review form (start_plan_review) omitting toolautosubmit. Static deployment: Netlify static hosting with strict CSP, Permissions-Policy: tools=(self), and zero remote backend or PII storage. Challenges we ran into Enforcing authority boundaries: Ensuring an agent cannot bypass the human approval gate via tool calls or synthetic form submissions. Preventing deadline hallucination: Implementing domain invariants that reject plan dates unless backed by a grounded case record. Managing dynamic tool lifecycles: Using AbortController to cleanly tear down and re-register tools across empty, safety-paused, active, and pending-review states. Accomplishments that we're proud of Private by default: Completely local-first with zero accounts, cookies, analytics, or remote data retention. Complete WebMCP collaboration loop: A functional two-way interaction using typed imperative tools, dynamic availability, and a declarative review form. Calm, stress-informed design: Clear visual hierarchy, accessible 44px targets, and restrained language without high-anxiety alerts. Deterministic invariants: Robust test suites proving that safety blocks cannot be bypassed and stale plan versions cannot be approved. What we learned Declarative WebMCP forms provide a reliable pattern for high-stakes workflows by staging actions and handing physical agency back to the human. Dynamic tool registration dramatically reduces agent failures by exposing only tools valid for the current state machine. A single, shared command pipeline prevents UI and agent state drift without duplicate business logic. What's next for Mend - a local-first recovery workspace Optional passwordless, end-to-end encrypted cloud backup via Supabase for displaced families switching devices. Standardized, non-identifying PDF/CSV documentation exports formatted for FEMA and insurance adjusters. Dynamic ingestion of local emergency declarations, municipal relief grants, and shelter capacity feeds. Multi-phase tracking for long-term structural repairs, contractor bids, and assistance appeals. title: CookUp
pitch: A music creation studio where humans and AI agents compose and edit music together.
about_excerpt: A music creation studio where humans and AI agents compose and edit music together. Like Comment Story Updates Homescreen-Light Homescreen-Dark Samples Studio Inspiration I’ve always been such a huge fan of music, most especially the instrumental side, and I play an instrument or two myself at an intermediate level. I'm definitely no musical expert, which is why a tool like this matters so much to beginners and intermediate music lovers like me. When you look at music at its simplest root definition, it’s really just a collection of organized sounds. So I’ve found myself wondering countless times: if AI agents were provided with these individual sound units, could they actually make music? Not just generatively, but by actually reasoning and being creative enough to compose those single units into something genuinely pleasant to the ear? Can AI actually tap into that artistic side of us and produce something meaningful and flexible enough to iterate on easily? This project doesn't just give me the answer to that, it shows that humans and AI can actually collaborate and compose together like real musical partners. It opens up huge opportunities for indie artists, content creators, hobbyists, or anybody at all who wants to create an instrumental on their own, real fast, without the rigidness of traditional generative AI. TL;DR Most AI music tools are black boxes that spit out rigid audio you can't edit. This project uses AI agents as collaborative partners to arrange individual sound units, giving beginners, hobbyists, and creators total freedom to co-create custom instrumentals fast. What it does CookUp is a music creation studio where you can build beats and instrumentals by arranging individual instrument notes and drum sounds on a timeline. The main difference is that CookUp does not generate the audio itself. It gives the AI agent access to individual sounds and lets it compose those sounds into an actual editable arrangement. You can start by telling your AI agent what you want, then keep iterating through conversation: "Create a loopable reggae instrumental" "add a bit more drum hits, drums are too spaced out" "decrease the sound of the guitars and add a violin" You can also work directly in the editor yourself. For example, you can add a new track and place your own clips, then ask the agent to continue from what you just created: "I've added some mid and high tom clips to the toms track, replicate it all through the loop and add a melodious piano track to complement it all" The important part is that the human and AI are working on the same composition , rather than the AI generating a separate finished audio file. CookUp also lets you play, pause, loop, edit, save projects locally, and export finished compositions as WAV or MP3. How we built it CookUp is a browser-based app built around WebMCP, Tone.js, and a structured composition model . The composition is represented as structured state containing tracks, clips, notes, timing, instruments, tempo, volume, and other editable properties. That state is the source of truth for both the visual editor and the AI tools. Tone.js handles the actual audio playback and scheduling. For melodic instruments, we use recorded instrument samples with Tone.Sampler , which lets a smaller number of recorded notes cover the playable range by tuning samples when needed. For drums, we use individual one-shot samples with Tone.js playback. For the instrument library, we used samples from tonejs-instruments , selecting samples from 20 different instruments. For drums, we used the TR-808 Fischer collection, which gives us 116 individual drum sounds. The application also includes a visual timeline editor, manual editing, playback controls, looping, track controls, undo/redo, IndexedDB persistence, and WAV/MP3/project export. For the WebMCP integration, CookUp exposes its composition and editing capabilities as tools that the agent can call. These tools can inspect the current composition and make changes to tracks, clips, sounds, tempo, and other parts of the project. That means the flow is roughly: AI agent ↓ WebMCP tools ↓ CookUp composition state ↓ Timeline + Tone.js ↓ Audio The same state can also be changed directly by the human in the editor. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was finding the right audio assets. We wanted individual sounds, not loops or pre-generated music. At the same time, we wanted the sounds to be good enough that the final result would not feel like a toy, and we needed licenses that would allow us to actually use the samples in the project. We ended up using tonejs-instruments for the melodic instruments and the TR-808 Fischer collection for drums. The instrument library gave us a good range of real recorded instruments, while the TR-808 collection gave us a large set of individual drum sounds with a much simpler structure to work with. Another challenge was sample coverage. We didn't want to ship a separate audio file for every possible musical note, but we also didn't want aggressive pitch shifting to make the instruments sound unnatural. Using Tone.js samplers let us find a balance between the number of files we ship and the amount of tuning the browser has to do. We also had to make the AI interaction precise enough that natural language requests actually translated into useful edits to the composition instead of vague or destructive changes. Accomplishments that we're proud of The biggest one is simply getting the idea to work end to end. The AI can start with an empty composition, create a piece of music from individual sounds, make changes to it, and continue working after a human has manually edited the timeline. That last part is probably what we're happiest with. The human doesn't have to choose between using AI and using the editor. You can make a change yourself, then hand the same composition back to the agent and keep going. We are also proud that the music is actually editable. There is no generated audio blob that you have to accept as-is. The individual sounds, notes, clips and tracks remain part of the composition. And we managed to do all of this in a browser using real recorded samples, without needing an AI audio-generation model behind it. What we learned One of the biggest things we learned is that AI doesn't need to generate the final media itself to be really useful in a creative workflow. At first, the obvious idea is to ask an AI to generate a finished song. But once we treated music as a collection of smaller building blocks, it became much more interesting. The AI can reason about those building blocks and use them to construct something, then keep changing that same composition over time. We also learned that WebMCP feels much more useful when the agent is operating a real application rather than just returning text. Seeing the agent add a track, place clips, change sounds, and react to a human edit made the difference much clearer to us. It feels less like asking an AI for an answer and more like working with another person in the same creative space. What's next for CookUp The next step is to make CookUp more useful without turning it into a full DAW. We'd like to expand the sound library with more carefully selected instruments and sounds, and make it easier to browse and audition them. We also want to improve the composition side so the AI can handle more complex musical structure while still keeping every part editable. Another natural direction is better project management and sharing, so people can move their compositions between devices and continue working on them without relying only on local browser storage or manually downloading files. And beyond that, we'd like to explore more ways for the AI and the human to work together in the same timeline, with more precise editing and better control over arrangements. title: VELLAR
pitch: The marketplace writes the tools. Every paid API becomes a callable WebMCP tool automatically, no code, no registration, just a real payment. Built on Stellar ecosystem.
about_excerpt: The marketplace writes the tools. Every paid API becomes a callable WebMCP tool automatically, no code, no registration, just a real payment. Built on Stellar ecosystem. Like Comment Story Updates Explorer for viewing settled transactions Developer Docs Landing Page WebMCP hackathon submission Ui Inspiration AI agents can browse the web but they cannot pay for things. We have been building the infrastructure to change that for months. Vellar is the agent-payments stack for Stellar, a passkey smart wallet with on-chain spending policies, an open-source x402 facilitator that verifies and settles payments including policy-governed smart accounts other facilitators reject, a trust-ranked Bazaar that catalogs payable APIs from real settlement data, a VS Code extension that lets any developer gate an API endpoint for payment in under a minute, and an explorer that indexes every settlement on-chain. When the WebMCP Challenge launched, we had one question: what happens when you put a browser-native agent interface on top of a live, running payment infrastructure that already has real endpoints, real settlements, and real USDC moving through it? What it does Vellar x402 is a live API marketplace for AI agents, powered by the full Vellar stack. Open the page in a WebMCP-enabled browser and the agent sees a set of callable tools, not because a developer wrote them, but because real sellers deployed real endpoints, received real on-chain USDC payments through the Vellar Facilitator, and earned their way into the Vellar Bazaar catalog. Nobody wrote call_uuid . The marketplace did. The page queries the live Bazaar at load time, filters for endpoints with real settlement history and verified trust scores, and dynamically registers a WebMCP tool for each one. As sellers list new endpoints and earn trust through real payments, new tools appear automatically without a single line of code changing. The tool list is a live query result, not a specification frozen at build time. Three core tools handle the agent workflow: search_vellar_bazaar searches the live Bazaar catalog for payable endpoints with prices and trust status. pay_and_call provisions a throwaway Stellar wallet, acquires USDC, signs a real x402 payment, and returns the response with an on-chain tx hash. check_vellar_earnings shows a seller's real settlement history from the Vellar Explorer. Every additional tool is generated live from the Bazaar. When an agent calls call_uuid , a real Stellar transaction settles. The tx hash is verifiable on Stellar Expert. How we built it This submission is the WebMCP layer on top of months of infrastructure. The Vellar Facilitator is an open-source x402 verify/settle service live at https://facilitator.vellar.xyz . It includes a 50-account channel pool proven at 50 true-simultaneous settlements with zero sequence failures, a Bazaar discovery layer that auto-catalogs endpoints from real payment data, and a trust layer that ranks results by settlement count and on-chain contract verification. The Vellar Wallet is a passkey smart wallet on Stellar with programmable on-chain spending policies. An agent gets a scoped session key with a spending limit enforced by a policy contract. Go over budget and the chain refuses before any money moves. The Vellar VS Code Extension is live on the VS Code Marketplace (VellarWallet.vellar-x402). Any developer can open an Express, Fastify, or Next.js route file, run one command, and have a working x402 payment gate injected with the Bazaar discovery extension included. Their endpoint self-lists in the Bazaar on first payment. The WebMCP layer is built in Next.js on Render, using @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill for broad browser compatibility and @x402/core plus @x402/stellar for the payment flow. All payment logic runs server-side so throwaway keypairs never touch the browser. Every external call is proxied through our own API routes to eliminate CORS failures in browser tool execution. Challenges we ran into Sequence number contention at scale. Stellar serializes transactions per source account. Under concurrent load, multiple settlements racing on one account produce txBadSeq failures. We built and load-tested a 50-account channel pool, 50 simultaneous payments, zero sequence failures, p95 under 12 seconds, before this hackathon started. That infrastructure is what makes pay_and_call reliable under real agent usage. Dynamic tool generation edge cases. Catalog URLs become tool names. Path templates like /inspect/:address, localhost entries, and naming collisions all needed filtering before a single registerTool call was made. A tool guaranteed to fail on every invocation is worse than no tool. CORS at the WebMCP boundary. Browser-based tool execute functions cannot call cross-origin APIs without CORS headers. Every external call is proxied through Next.js API routes so tools never fail silently in a browser context. Proving it is real. The easiest thing to fake in a hackathon demo is an on-chain payment. We did not fake it. Every tool call that involves a payment produces a tx hash verifiable on Stellar Expert. Accomplishments that we're proud of The marketplace writes the tools, not the developer. That sentence sounds simple. Behind it is a live payment facilitator handling concurrent settlements, a trust-scored discovery catalog built from real on-chain data, a passkey smart wallet with programmable spending policies, a VS Code extension that onboards sellers in under a minute, and now a WebMCP layer that turns all of it into callable agent tools automatically. Any developer who deploys an x402-gated endpoint using the Vellar VS Code extension and receives one real payment is automatically callable by every agent using this page. Zero integration work. Zero registration form. The payment is the registration. Every tx hash in this submission is real. Every settlement in the earnings table represents a real throwaway wallet that funded itself, acquired USDC on the Stellar testnet DEX, and paid a real endpoint autonomously. Nothing mocked. No simulated responses. What we learned Building the WebMCP layer took days. Building the infrastructure that makes it meaningful took months. The hardest problems were not in the browser API. They were in the payment rails, sequence number contention under concurrent Stellar settlements, the difference between a txBadSeq and a TRY_AGAIN_LATER, why a fee-bump transaction separates fee payment from sequence number management, what it actually takes to prove 50 concurrent settlements with zero failures. We learned that "the agent pays for it" is a sentence that sounds simple and takes an entire stack to make true. What's next for VELLAR Vellar is about to launch on Stellar mainnet. Real USDC, real agents, real commerce, no intermediary, no API key, no account, just a payment and a response. The Vellar Wallet already supports passkey smart accounts with on-chain spending policies. An agent with a Vellar session key and a spending limit enforced by a policy contract can use this WebMCP page to discover and pay for APIs autonomously, within a budget its owner set, revocable at any time, with every payment verifiable on-chain. The tool list on this page grows itself. Every endpoint that transitions from unverified to proven-unconfirmed to verified in the Bazaar becomes a new callable WebMCP tool automatically. As Vellar goes to mainnet and the Bazaar fills with real production endpoints, the marketplace that writes the tools gets bigger, richer, and more valuable to every agent that uses it. We built the marketplace. We are about to open it for real. title: Duet
pitch: A local-first piano roll where people and AI compose together through safe, visible, undoable WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A local-first piano roll where people and AI compose together through safe, visible, undoable WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Duet lets people sketch music while an AI agent reads the live session, adds deterministic harmony or bass, and explains every reversible change. Inspiration Music software can be powerful but intimidating: theory vocabulary, dense interfaces, and opaque “AI generate” buttons often put the person outside the creative loop. I wanted to explore a different interaction: what if an AI agent could work inside a music editor, see the same live project as the person, and make small musical changes that stay understandable and reversible? That became Duet. What it does Duet is a local-first, browser-based piano-roll editor for collaborative human–AI composition. A person can draw notes, play from a MIDI keyboard or computer keyboard, set chords, select bars, and hear the result. In a compatible browser, ChatGPT/Codex discovers Duet’s WebMCP site tools directly from the page. The agent can then: Read a concise summary of the live project or the exact selected notes. Analyze harmony deterministically. Set a chord progression with validated voicings. Add precise notes or generate bass, counter-melody, and pad material. Quantize, humanize, transpose, or remap a selected phrase. Change tempo and instruments. Create auditionable drafts and alternatives instead of silently overwriting music. Verify the resulting state after every action. Every persistent AI edit appears in the app with a plain-language explanation and a one-click Undo action. How I built it Duet is a client-only React + TypeScript app powered by Vite and Zustand. The editor uses Pointer Events so drawing, dragging, stretching, and erasing notes work across mouse, touch, and pen input. Musical rules are deterministic rather than model-generated. I use Tonal for chord and scale logic, Tone.js for browser playback, and @tonejs/midi for MIDI export. Optional Web MIDI support allows class-compliant keyboards to control the editor. For WebMCP, Duet registers narrow site tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools read the current browser state, validate every mutation, and create serializable inverse patches. That makes changes inspectable, reproducible, and undoable without a backend, API key, account, or cloud project storage. Browser and MIDI constraints A practical constraint shaped the product flow: ChatGPT/Codex’s built-in browser can discover and call WebMCP site tools, but it does not expose a connected physical MIDI device to the page in the same way a regular Chrome session can. I designed Duet around a shared live-session model to bridge that gap. The musician can open Duet in a WebMCP-enabled Chrome session, connect and play a MIDI keyboard there, while ChatGPT/Codex accesses the same live project through the connected WebMCP session. The agent does not need direct MIDI hardware access: it reads the resulting notes and project state, then proposes or applies visible, undoable musical edits. This separation keeps the human performance layer local and hardware-friendly while preserving the agent’s ability to collaborate through the browser. Challenges I ran into The core challenge was not simply generating musical material—it was making agent actions feel safe and legible. I designed the tools around a few principles: The agent receives compact state summaries before acting, rather than a flood of raw notes. Music theory remains in pure deterministic functions, so harmony does not depend on model guesswork. Write operations validate their inputs and preserve an inverse patch for Undo. The person can see what changed, why it changed, and which bars were affected. Drafts let the person hear alternatives before committing them. I also had to balance expressive composition tools with small, precise schemas that are useful to WebMCP clients. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A live browser session where a person and AI can compose on the same page. WebMCP tools that support both reading context and making safe musical edits. Agent-authored notes are visually distinct from human-authored notes. Every AI mutation has a human-readable explanation and one-click Undo. Deterministic harmony, voicing, bass generation, and mode transformations. No backend, authentication, analytics, API keys, or remote project storage. An end-to-end test: read a person’s notes, add accompaniment, undo it, then reapply a different arrangement through WebMCP. What I learned I learned that agentic interfaces become much more trustworthy when they expose small, contextual tools instead of treating the app as a black box. In creative software, reversibility is not a safety feature added at the end—it is part of the creative experience. Clear diffs, explicit intent, deterministic musical rules, and visible state make it easier for a person to stay in control while still benefiting from an AI collaborator. What's next for Duet Next, I would like to add richer MIDI export/import workflows, more arrangement patterns, stronger visual auditioning for draft variations, and broader browser support as WebMCP availability grows. Acknowledgements Special thanks to my wife, a pianist and piano teacher, who performs in the demo video. Her musician’s perspective, feedback, and willingness to test the human side of the workflow were essential to shaping Duet. This application would not have been possible without her. title: Parley — AI Agents Negotiate Your Lease via WebMCP
pitch: Two independent AI agents—one for the tenant, one for the landlord—negotiate a real lease renewal live on a shared page, using native WebMCP tools instead of talking to each other directly.
about_excerpt: Two independent AI agents—one for the tenant, one for the landlord—negotiate a real lease renewal live on a shared page, using native WebMCP tools instead of talking to each other directly. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing Page of the website How does Parley actually works The 2 Negotiating Agents - Tenant & Landlord agent WebMCP Deal tools used Why I built this Everyone hates negotiating their lease renewal. You either eat the increase or spend hours going back and forth over email. I wanted to see what happens if two AI agents did that instead: one for the tenant and one for the landlord. The catch is my agent and my landlord's agent have no way to talk to each other. WebMCP fixes that. A page exposes structured actions, and any agent, built by anyone, can act on the same shared state through those tools. That's the whole idea behind Parley. What it does A tenant agent and a landlord agent each load the same negotiation page in their own browser session. They never talk directly. All they see is six WebMCP tools: get_negotiation_state propose_terms counter_terms request_concession accept finalize_agreement Every move gets logged as a redline diff—old terms struck through, new terms next to them, like an actual lease amendment. Give each agent a goal and a limit, let them run, and they actually negotiate. Building it Next.js, Firestore for shared state, and document.modelContext.registerTool() for the tools. Both agents read/write the same Firestore doc the UI reads from. No backend glue between them—just the page. The annoying part The WebMCP API changed twice while I was building this. navigator.modelContext got dropped for document.modelContext , and provideContext() got removed entirely, so all context has to live in the tool descriptions now. Bigger issue: my first "successful" test wasn't real. The agent had shell access and just pulled my Firebase key out of the compiled JS and wrote to Firestore directly, skipping the tools completely. Looked fine, proved nothing. Every test after that had to run without terminal access, through the actual browser tool interface, to know it was real. Also, on two separate runs, both agents independently landed on the same sticking point: the tenant kept asking for a smart thermostat, and the landlord kept declining it as outside its budget, while still agreeing on everything else. Nobody scripted that. Real negotiations have exactly one stubborn detail, and mine found it on its own. Proudest part A full negotiation—propose, finalize, six rounds, two agents that never spoke to each other directly—working the same on localhost and on the live deployed site. title: ClauseProof
pitch: A source-grounded contract decision room where people and agents can analyze and propose together without collapsing human approval into AI output.
about_excerpt: A source-grounded contract decision room where people and agents can analyze and propose together without collapsing human approval into AI output. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for ClauseProof Inspiration Contracts rarely fail because nobody summarized them. They fail because risk, authority, and action get blurred together. ClauseProof explores an open web where a person and an AI agent can inspect the same contract state without allowing fluent model output to masquerade as human approval. What it does ClauseProof turns a high-stakes agreement into a source-grounded decision room. Documents are read locally, including OCR for image documents. Deterministic rules keep the exact governing clause beside each finding. A human can resolve or explicitly accept risks, record a case-specific approval, and prepare an unsigned signature-packet receipt. The synthetic Northstar supply agreement demonstrates auto-renewal, exclusivity, payment, cure, and liability findings. Uploaded bytes and extracted text stay in the browser. Why WebMCP The live page exposes six narrow tools over the same state the human sees: get_case_summary list_open_risks propose_risk_resolution record_human_risk_decision approve_case_decision prepare_signature_packet Each tool is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , uses a closed input schema, describes its effects, and returns a structured receipt. An agent proposal remains a proposal. Approval requires a visible human decision, and signature preparation always reports sent: false and signed: false . How we built it React and TypeScript power the shared browser workflow. PDF.js and Tesseract.js handle local text and OCR. Xano provides the durable synthetic case, audit events, evidence receipts, idempotent bootstrap, and five deployed endpoints. SerpApi runs one bounded server-side counterparty query through Xano; the live proof returned nine organic results and evidence receipt 1 without exposing the key to the browser. Vitest covers the authority boundaries and deterministic extraction. Netlify serves the public HTTPS build. Challenges The hardest problem was making agent actions useful without collapsing capability into authority. We separated analysis, proposal, human risk decisions, case approval, signature preparation, sending, and signing into independently verifiable states. Accomplishments One shared human-and-agent workflow instead of an agent-only chatbot Exact-source findings with local OCR Six working WebMCP tools over real product state Explicit approval and non-action receipts Live Xano and SerpApi integration Public MIT source and reproducible deployment artifacts What we learned WebMCP is strongest when it exposes a product's real workflow, keeps effects narrow, and makes meaningful transitions independently reviewable. The best agent experience is not maximum autonomy; it is useful capability with trustworthy authority boundaries. What's next Add authenticated private rooms, versioned redlines, provider-backed PDF generation, and a human-controlled e-sign handoff. Those providers will not be claimed until their live calls and terminal receipts are proven. title: Persistent Web Skills Runtime
pitch: A WebMCP-first runtime that learns browser workflows once, reuses them reliably, and repairs them when the web changes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-first runtime that learns browser workflows once, reuses them reliably, and repairs them when the web changes. Like Comment Story Updates Persistent Web Skills Runtime Persistent Web Skills Runtime (PWS) is a WebMCP-first Chrome runtime that lets agents learn a browser workflow once, reuse it as a versioned skill, and repair it when the web changes. The problem Agentic browser tasks are commonly rediscovered through fragile clicks on every run. Small UI changes can break a workflow, while useful structured WebMCP tools may be ignored or forgotten. Repeated exploration is slow, brittle, token-intensive, and hard to trust. The solution PWS routes each task through a clear priority ladder: Native WebMCP → Cached Web Skill → Browser/DOM learning fallback It discovers the page's current WebMCP tools first. If there is no suitable native tool, it learns a successful semantic browser workflow, stores it in IndexedDB with immutable version history, validates the outcome on reuse, and repairs only the failed step when a dependency changes. The live taskboard demo shows an 11-action Learn → Reuse → Repair flow: it learns a create-task workflow, reuses it, survives a Create Task → Add Task UI change with a validated v1 → v2 skill repair, and demonstrates live native tool registration through toolchange . Key features Native-first WebMCP routing via document.modelContext.getTools() , live toolchange synchronization, and current-tool rebinding. Safe capability snapshots that persist metadata, not executable tool handlers. Semantic locators based on role, name, labels, stable attributes, and meaningful text instead of brittle structural selectors. Dependency-only DOM fingerprints, explicit result validation, and targeted step repair. An inspectable Runtime Inspector, execution log, timings, validation status, and skill versions. Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, a Chrome Manifest V3 extension, IndexedDB, Node.js, and an optional OpenAI Responses API service. API keys remain server-side; the interactive demo runs without a key through deterministic local learning and repair adapters. Career value I work as an agent engineer and repeatedly test browser automation over many fresh pages. I wanted a way for agents to achieve stronger results with fewer tokens. Building PWS made the practical value of WebMCP clear: expose structured tools, preserve proven workflows as reusable skills, and give agents a safe answer to reuse instead of forcing them to rediscover the UI. This can make agent browser work faster, more reliable, and easier to trust. title: PantryPilot — Your Kitchen, Co-Piloted
pitch: An agent-native kitchen app: 8 WebMCP tools registered on document.modelContext let your AI agent plan meals around expiry dates and kill food waste — with the human in the loop.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native kitchen app: 8 WebMCP tools registered on document.modelContext let your AI agent plan meals around expiry dates and kill food waste — with the human in the loop.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 The problem 

 Roughly a third of household food is wasted, and meal planning is the chore nobody wants. PantryPilot splits that work the way it should be split: humans keep judgment (what looks fresh, what we feel like eating), agents take bulk iteration (expiry triage, week planning, list consolidation). 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Reducing food waste is a stateful planning problem: the agent must read pantry state, write a coherent plan, and derive a shopping list, repeatedly, as reality changes. Scraping a DOM for that is fragile and slow. PantryPilot instead publishes a typed contract: 8 tools registered on document.modelContext with JSON Schema inputs and structured JSON results, exactly per the WebMCP spec. 

 What humans and agents can do together 

 
 Humans: add groceries by hand, swap a dinner when the mood strikes, check off shopping items in the store. 
 Agents: read the pantry, triage what is about to spoil, plan 7 dinners expiry-first, derive an aisle-consolidated shopping list, log groceries and cooked meals. 
 Together: the ask that used to mean a hundred UI turns - plan my week around what is expiring, then tell me what to buy - becomes one tool call, while the human keeps every final decision. 
 

 How WebMCP is implemented 

 js/webmcp.js defines the tool table and calls document.modelContext.registerTool({name, description, inputSchema, execute}) for each of: get_pantry, add_pantry_items, consume_pantry_items, find_recipes, plan_week, get_plan, get_shopping_list, suggest_use_it_up. The exact same implementations also power the built-in Agent Console, so anyone can exercise the agent surface in any browser and judges can verify the tools without a flag. Planning is a deterministic greedy scorer (expiry-first weighting, repeat penalty) that runs fully client-side. 

 Engineering 

 Zero dependencies, zero backend, no build step: plain HTML/CSS/JS, offline-capable, localStorage state, 36-recipe graph, expiry model, aisle-aware consolidation. MIT licensed.
